I know indeed that the Authors who first introduced these names of Sympathy and Antipathy wished to signify by them certain occult qualities of things; nevertheless, I believe that we are permitted to understand by the same names also qualities that are known or manifest.
PROPOSITION XVI

From the mere fact that we imagine a thing to have something similar to an object which is accustomed to affect the Mind with Joy or Sadness, although that in which the thing is similar to the object is not the efficient cause of these affects, we shall nevertheless love or hold it in hatred.
DEMONSTRATION

That which is similar to the object, in the object itself we have contemplated (by hypothesis) with an affect of Joy or Sadness; and therefore (by Prop. 14 of this part), when the Mind is affected by its image, it will immediately also be affected by this or that affect. Consequently, the thing which we perceive to have this same thing will be (by Prop. 15 of this part) accidentally a cause of Joy or Sadness; and therefore (by the preceding Corollary), although that in which it is similar to the object is not the efficient cause of these affects, we shall nevertheless love or hold it in hatred. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XVII

If we imagine that a thing which is accustomed to affect us with an affect of Sadness has something similar to another thing which is accustomed to affect us with an equally great affect of Joy, we shall hold it in hatred and at the same time love it.
DEMONSTRATION

For this thing is (by hypothesis) in itself a cause of Sadness, and (by the Scholium to Proposition 13 of this Part), insofar as we imagine it with this affect, we hate it; and insofar as we further imagine it to have something similar to another thing, which is accustomed to affect us with an equally great affect of Joy, we shall love it with an equally great striving of Joy (by the preceding Proposition); and thus we shall hate and at the same time love it. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

This constitution of the Mind, which indeed arises from two contrary affects, is called Fluctuation of Mind, which therefore stands in relation to affect as doubt does to imagination (see the Scholium to Proposition 44, Part II); nor do Fluctuation of Mind and doubt differ from one another except according to greater and less. But it should be noted that, in the preceding Proposition, I deduced these fluctuations of mind from causes which are through themselves the cause of one affect, and accidentally of the other; this I did because they could thus be more easily deduced from what preceded; but not because I deny that fluctuations of mind for the most part arise from an object which is the efficient cause of both affects. For the human Body (by Postulate 1, Part II) is composed of very many individuals of diverse nature, and therefore (by Axiom 1 after Lemma 3, which see after Proposition 13, Part

II) can be affected by one and the same body in very many and diverse ways; and conversely, since one and the same thing can be affected in many ways, it will therefore also be able to affect one and the same part of the Body in many and diverse ways. From these things we can easily conceive that one and the same object can be the cause of many and contrary affects.
PROPOSITION XVIII
A man is affected with the same affect of Joy and Sadness by the image of a past or future thing as by the image of a present thing.
DEMONSTRATION

So long as a man is affected by the image of some thing, he will contemplate the thing as present, even though it does not exist (by Proposition 17, Part II, with its Corollary), nor does he imagine it as past or future except insofar as its image is joined to the image of past or future time (see the Scholium to Proposition 44, Part II). Therefore the image of a thing, considered in itself alone, is the same whether it is referred to future or past time, or to the present; that is (by Corollary 2 to Proposition 16, Part II), the constitution or affect of the Body is the same whether the image is of a past or future thing, or of a present thing; and therefore the affect of Joy and Sadness is the same whether the image is of a past or future thing, or of a present thing. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM I

Here I call a thing past or future insofar as we have been or shall be affected by it. For example, insofar as we have seen or shall see it, it has refreshed or will refresh us, it has harmed or will harm us, etc. For insofar as we imagine it in this way, we affirm its existence; that is, the Body is affected by no affect that excludes the existence of the thing, and therefore (by Proposition 17, Part II) the Body is affected by the image of the same thing in the same manner as if the thing itself were present. But since it most often happens that those who have experienced more things fluctuate, so long as they contemplate a thing as future or past, and for the most part doubt the outcome of the thing (see the Scholium to Proposition 44, Part II), it follows that the affects arising from similar images of things are not so constant, but are for the most part disturbed by images of other things, until men become more certain about the outcome of the thing.
SCHOLIUM II

From what has just been said, we understand what Hope, Fear, Security, Despair, Gladness, and remorse of Conscience are. For Hope is nothing other than an inconstant Joy arising from the image of a future or past thing, concerning whose outcome we doubt. Fear, on the other hand, is an inconstant Sadness, likewise arising from the image of a doubtful thing. Further, if doubt is removed from these affects, Hope becomes Security and Fear Despair; namely, Joy or Sadness arising from the image of a thing which we feared or hoped for. Gladness, moreover, is Joy arising from the image of a past thing, concerning whose outcome we had doubted. Finally, remorse of Conscience is Sadness, opposed to Gladness.
PROPOSITION XIX
He who imagines that what he loves is destroyed will be saddened; but if he imagines it preserved, he will rejoice.
DEMONSTRATION

The Mind, as far as it can, strives to imagine those things which increase or assist the Body's power of acting (by Proposition 12 of this Part), that is (by the Scholium to Proposition 13 of this Part), those things which it loves. But imagination is assisted by things which posit the existence of a thing, and, on the contrary, is restrained by things which exclude the existence of a thing (by Proposition 17, Part II); therefore images of things which posit the existence of the thing loved assist the striving of the Mind by which it strives to imagine the thing loved, that is (by the Scholium to Proposition 11 of this Part), they affect the Mind with Joy; and those which, on the contrary, exclude the existence of the thing loved restrain the same striving of the Mind, that is (by the same Scholium), they affect the Mind with Sadness. Therefore he who imagines that what he loves is destroyed will be saddened, etc. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XX
He who imagines that what he hates is destroyed will rejoice.
DEMONSTRATION

The Mind (by Proposition 13 of this Part) strives to imagine those things which exclude the existence of things by which the Body's power of acting is diminished or restrained; that is (by the Scholium to the same Proposition), it strives to imagine those things which exclude the existence of things which it hates; and therefore the image of a thing which excludes the existence of what the Mind hates assists this striving of the Mind, that is (by the Scholium to Proposition 11 of this Part) affects the Mind with Joy. Therefore he who imagines that what he hates is destroyed will rejoice. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XXI

He who imagines that what he loves is affected with Joy or Sadness will also be affected with Joy or Sadness; and each of these affects will be greater or less in the lover, according as each is greater or less in the thing loved.
DEMONSTRATION

Images of things (as we demonstrated in Proposition 19 of this Part) which posit the existence of a thing loved assist the striving of the Mind by which it strives to imagine the thing loved itself. But Joy posits the existence of the joyful thing, and does so the more as the affect of Joy is greater; for it is (by the Scholium to Proposition 11 of this Part) a transition to greater perfection: therefore the image of the Joy of the thing loved assists, in the lover, the striving of his own Mind, that is (by the Scholium to Proposition 11 of this Part), it affects the lover with Joy, and with so much the greater Joy as this affect has been greater in the thing loved. This was the first point. Next, insofar as a thing is affected with Sadness, it is destroyed, and the more so as it is affected with greater Sadness (by the same Scholium to Proposition 11 of this Part); and thus (by Proposition 19 of this Part) he who imagines that what he loves is affected with Sadness will also be affected with Sadness, and with so much the greater Sadness as this affect has been greater in the thing loved. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XXII

If we imagine that someone affects with Joy a thing which we love, we shall also be affected with Love toward him. If, on the contrary, we imagine that the same person affects the same thing with Sadness, we shall also, on the contrary, be affected with Hatred toward him.
DEMONSTRATION

He who affects with Joy or Sadness a thing which we love also affects us with Joy or Sadness, provided, of course, that we imagine the beloved thing to be affected with that Joy or Sadness (by the preceding Prop.). But this Joy or Sadness is supposed to be given in us accompanied by the idea of an external cause; therefore (by the Schol. of Prop. 13 of this part), if we imagine that someone affects with Joy or Sadness a thing which we love, we shall be affected toward him with Love or Hatred. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Proposition 21 explains to us what Compassion is, which we may define as Sadness arising from another's harm. But by what name the Joy which arises from another's good is to be called, I do not know. Further, we shall call Love toward him who has done good to another Favor, and, conversely, Hatred toward him who has done evil to another Indignation. Finally, it must be noted that we not only pity a thing which we have loved (as we showed in Prop. 21), but also one which we have previously pursued with no affect, provided that we judge it to be similar to ourselves (and I shall show this below); and thus we also favor him who has done good to one like ourselves, and conversely are indignant with him who has inflicted harm upon one like ourselves.
PROPOSITION XXIII

He who imagines that that which he hates is affected with Sadness will rejoice; if, on the contrary, he imagines that it is affected with Joy, he will be saddened; and each of these affects will be greater or lesser according as its contrary is greater or lesser in that which he hates.
DEMONSTRATION

Insofar as a hateful thing is affected with Sadness, it is destroyed, and the more so as it is affected with greater Sadness (by the Schol. of Prop. 11 of this part). Therefore he who (by Prop. 20 of this part) imagines that a thing which he hates is affected with Sadness will, on the contrary, be affected with Joy; and with so much the greater Joy as he imagines the hateful thing to be affected with greater Sadness. This was the first point. Next, Joy posits the existence of the joyful thing (by the same Schol. of Prop. 11 of this part), and the more so as greater Joy is conceived. If someone imagines that he whom he hates is affected with Joy, this imagination (by Prop. 13 of this part) will restrain his striving; that is (by the Schol. of Prop. 11 of this part), he who hates will be affected with Sadness, etc. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

This Joy can scarcely be solid and without any conflict of mind. For (as I shall show immediately in Proposition 27 of this part), insofar as he imagines a thing similar to himself to be affected with an affect of Sadness, he must be saddened; and conversely, if he imagines it to be affected with Joy. But here we attend only to Hatred.
PROPOSITION XXIV

If we imagine that someone affects with Joy a thing which we hate, we shall also be affected with Hatred toward him. If, on the contrary, we imagine that the same person affects the same thing with Sadness, we shall therefore be affected with Love toward him.
DEMONSTRATION
This Proposition is demonstrated in the same manner as Proposition 22 of this part; see it.
SCHOLIUM

These and similar affects of Hatred are referred to Envy, which therefore is nothing other than Hatred itself, insofar as it is considered to dispose a man in such a way that he rejoices at another's misfortune and, conversely, is saddened at the same person's good.
PROPOSITION XXV

We strive to affirm of ourselves and of a thing loved everything which we imagine affects us, or the loved thing, with Joy; and, conversely, to deny everything which we imagine affects us, or the loved thing, with Sadness.
DEMONSTRATION

Whatever we imagine to affect a loved thing with Joy or Sadness affects us with Joy or Sadness (by Prop. 21 of this part). But the Mind (by Prop. 12 of this part) strives, as far as it can, to imagine those things which affect us with Joy, that is (by Prop. 17, part II, and its Coroll.) to contemplate them as present; and conversely (by Prop. 13 of this part), to exclude the existence of those things which affect us with Sadness; therefore we strive to affirm of ourselves and of a loved thing everything which we imagine affects us, or the loved thing, with Joy, and conversely. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XXVI
We strive to affirm of a thing which we hate everything which we imagine affects it with Sadness, and, conversely, to deny that which we imagine affects it with Joy.
DEMONSTRATION
This Proposition follows from Proposition 23, as the preceding one from Proposition 21 of this Part.
SCHOLIUM

From these things we see that it easily happens that a man thinks more highly than is just of himself and of a thing loved, and, on the contrary, less highly than is just of a thing which he hates; this imagination, indeed, when it concerns the man himself, who thinks more highly than is just of himself, is called Pride, and is a species of Delirium, because a man dreams with his eyes open that he can do all those things which he attains by imagination alone, and which he therefore contemplates as though real, and exults in them, so long as he cannot imagine those things which exclude the existence of these and determine his own power of acting. Pride, therefore, is Joy arising from the fact that a man thinks more highly than is just of himself. Further, Joy which arises from the fact that a man thinks more highly than is just of another is called Esteem; and finally, that Joy which arises from the fact that he thinks less highly than is just of another is called Contempt.
PROPOSITION XXVII
From the fact that we imagine a thing similar to ourselves, and which we have pursued with no affect, to be affected with some affect, we are thereby affected with a similar affect.
DEMONSTRATION

Images of things are affections of the human Body, the ideas of which represent external bodies as though present to us (by Schol. Prop. 17 p. II); that is (by Prop. 16 p. II), the ideas of which involve the nature of our Body, and at the same time the present nature of the external body. If, therefore, the nature of the external body is similar to the nature of our Body, then the idea of the external body which we imagine will involve an affection of our Body similar to the affection of the external body; and consequently, if we imagine someone similar to ourselves to be affected with some affect, this imagination will express an affection of our Body similar to this affect; and hence, from the fact that we imagine a thing similar to ourselves to be affected with some affect, we are affected with an affect similar to it. But if we hate a thing similar to ourselves, then (by Prop. 23 of this Part) we shall be affected with an affect contrary to it, not with a similar one. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

This imitation of the affects, when it is referred to Sadness, is called Pity (concerning which see Schol. Prop. 22 of this Part); but when referred to Desire, Emulation, which consequently is nothing other than the Desire for some thing that is engendered in us from the fact that we imagine others similar to ourselves to have the same Desire.
COROLLARY I

If we imagine someone whom we have pursued with no affect to affect with Joy a thing similar to ourselves, we shall be affected with Love toward him. If, on the contrary, we imagine him to affect the same thing with Sadness, we shall, on the contrary, be affected with Hatred toward him.
DEMONSTRATION
This is demonstrated in the same way from the preceding Proposition as Proposition 22 of this Part from Proposition 21.
COROLLARY II
We cannot hate a thing which we pity on the ground that its misery affects us with Sadness.
DEMONSTRATION
For if on that ground we could hate the same thing, then (by Prop. 23 of this Part) we should rejoice at its Sadness, which is contrary to the hypothesis.
COROLLARY III
We shall endeavor, as far as we can, to free from misery a thing which we pity.
DEMONSTRATION

That by which the thing which we pity is affected with Sadness also affects us with a similar Sadness (by the preceding Prop.); and hence we shall endeavor to think of everything which takes away the existence of that thing, or which destroys the thing (by Prop. 13 of this Part), that is (by Schol. Prop. 9 of this Part), we shall desire to destroy it, or shall be determined to destroy it; and hence we shall endeavor to free the thing which we pity from its misery. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

This will, or Desire, to do good, which arises from the fact that we pity the thing upon which we wish to confer a benefit, is called Benevolence, which consequently is nothing other than Desire arising from pity. Moreover, concerning Love and Hatred toward one who has done good or evil to a thing which we imagine to be similar to ourselves, see Schol. Prop. 22 of this Part.
PROPOSITION XXVIII

We strive to further the occurrence of everything that we imagine to conduce to Joy; but, on the other hand, we strive to remove or destroy whatever we imagine to be opposed to it, or to conduce to Sadness.
DEMONSTRATION

We strive, as far as we can, to imagine that which we imagine to conduce to Joy (by Prop. 12 of this Part); that is (by Prop. 17, Part II), we shall strive, as far as we can, to contemplate it as present, or as actually existing. But the striving, or power, of the Mind in thinking is equal and simultaneous by nature with the striving, or power, of the Body in acting (as follows clearly from Coroll. Prop. 7 and Coroll. Prop. 11, Part II); therefore we strive absolutely that it should exist, or (which, by Schol. Prop. 9 of this Part, is the same) we desire and intend it; which was the first point. Next, if we imagine that that which we believe to be a cause of Sadness, that is (by Schol. Prop. 13 of this Part), that which we hate, is destroyed, we shall rejoice (by Prop. 20 of this Part); and therefore (by the first part of this demonstration) we shall strive to destroy the same, or (by Prop. 13 of this Part) to remove it from us, lest we contemplate it as present; which was the second point. Therefore, everything that conduces to Joy, etc. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XXIX
We shall also strive to do everything which we imagine men regard with Joy; and, on the other hand, we shall be averse to doing that which we imagine men are averse to.
DEMONSTRATION

From our imagining that men love or hate something, we shall love or hate the same thing (by Prop. 27 of this Part); that is (by Schol. Prop. 13 of this Part), by that very fact we shall rejoice or be saddened at the presence of that thing; and therefore (by the preceding Prop.) we shall strive to do everything which we imagine men regard with Joy, etc. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

This striving to do something, and also to omit something, solely in order that we may please men, is called Ambition, especially when we strive so eagerly to please the multitude that, to our own or another's detriment, we do or omit certain things; otherwise it is usually called Humanity. Further, I call the Joy by which we imagine another's action, by which he has striven to delight us, Praise; but the Sadness by which, on the contrary, we are averse to that same action, I call Blame.
PROPOSITION XXX

If anyone has done something which he imagines affects the rest with Joy, he will be affected with Joy, accompanied by the idea of himself as cause; or he will contemplate himself with Joy. If, on the contrary, he has done something which he imagines affects the rest with Sadness, he will, on the contrary, contemplate himself with Sadness.
DEMONSTRATION

He who imagines that he affects the rest with Joy or Sadness is, by that very fact (by Prop. 27 of this Part), affected with Joy or Sadness. But since man (by Prop. 19 and 23, Part II) is conscious of himself through the affections by which he is determined to act; therefore, he who has done something which he himself imagines affects the rest with Joy will be affected with Joy, together with consciousness of himself as cause; or, he will contemplate himself with Joy, and conversely. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Since Love (by Schol. Prop. 13 of this Part) is Joy accompanied by the idea of an external cause, and Hatred is Sadness likewise accompanied by the idea of an external cause, this Joy and Sadness will therefore be species of Love and Hatred. But because Love and Hatred are referred to external objects, we shall signify these Affects by other names; namely, Joy accompanied by the idea of an internal cause we shall call Glory, and the Sadness contrary to this we shall call Shame. Understand this when Joy or Sadness arises from a man's believing that he is praised or blamed; otherwise, Joy accompanied by the idea of an internal cause I shall call Self-contentment, while the Sadness contrary to it I shall call Repentance. Further, since (by Coroll. 17, Part II) it can happen that the Joy by which someone imagines that he affects the rest is merely imaginary, and (by Prop.

25 of this Part) everyone strives to imagine of himself everything which he imagines affects him with Joy, it can therefore easily happen that one who is glorious is proud, and imagines himself pleasing to all when he is troublesome to all.
PROPOSITION XXXI

If we imagine someone to love, or desire, or hate something which we ourselves love, desire, or hate, we shall, by that very fact, love the thing more steadfastly, etc. But if we imagine him to be averse to that which we love, we shall suffer a fluctuation of mind contrary to this.
DEMONSTRATION

From the mere fact that we imagine someone to love something, we shall, by that very fact, love the same thing (by Prop. 27 of this Part). But without this we are supposed to love the same thing; therefore, a new cause is added to Love, by which it is fostered; and hence we shall, by this very fact, love that which we love more steadfastly. Further, from our imagining someone to be averse to something, we shall be averse to the same thing (by the same Prop.). But if we suppose that at the same time we love that very thing, then at the same time we shall love and be averse to this same thing, or (see Schol. Prop. 17 of this Part) we shall suffer a fluctuation of mind. Q. E. D.
COROLLARY

Hence, and from Prop. 28 of this Part, it follows that everyone strives, as far as he can, that everyone should love what he himself loves, and should also hate what he himself hates; whence that saying of the Poet:
Let us lovers hope alike, let us fear alike;
He is made of iron, if anyone loves what another permits.
SCHOLIUM

This endeavor to bring it about that everyone should approve what he himself loves or hates is in reality Ambition (see the Scholium to Prop. 29 of this Part); and thus we see that everyone, from nature, strives that the rest should live according to his own disposition; and while all alike strive after this, they are alike an obstacle to one another, and while all wish to be praised or loved by all, they are mutually hateful.
PROPOSITION XXXII
If we imagine someone to take pleasure in some thing of which only one can be possessed, we shall strive to bring it about that he does not possess that thing.
DEMONSTRATION

From the sole fact that we imagine someone to take pleasure in some thing (by Prop. 27 of this Part together with its Corollary 1), we shall love that thing and desire to take pleasure in it. But (by the hypothesis) we imagine that his taking pleasure in this same thing stands in the way of this Joy; therefore (by Prop. 28 of this Part), we shall strive that he does not possess the same thing. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

sources.title: Pars tertia - De origine et natura affectuum · passage 3
sources.text:
Videmus itaque, cum hominum natura plerumque ita comparatum esse, ut eorum, quibus male est, misereantur, et quibus bene est, invideant, et (per Prop. præc.) eo majore odio, quo rem, qua alium potiri imaginantur, magis amant. Videmus deinde, ex eadem naturæ humanæ proprietate, ex qua sequitur, homines esse misericordes, sequi etiam, eosdem esse invidos et ambitiosos. Denique, si ipsam experientiam consulere velimus, ipsam hæc omnia docere experiemur ; præsertim si ad priores nostræ ætatis annos attenderimus. Nam pueros, quia eorum corpus continuo veluti in æquilibrio est, ex hoc solo ridere vel flere experimur, quod alios ridere vel flere vident ; et quicquid præterea vident alios facere, id imitari statim cupiunt, et omnia denique sibi cupiunt quibus alios delectari imaginantur ; nimirum quia rerum imagines, ut diximus, sunt ipsæ humani Corporis affectiones, sive modi, quibus Corpus humanum a causis externis afficitur disponiturque ad hoc vel illud agendum.

PROPOSITIO XXXIII

Cum rem nobis similem amamus, conamur, quantum possumus, efficere, ut nos contra amet.

DEMONSTRATIO

Rem, quam amamus præ reliquis, quantum possumus, imaginari conamur (per Prop. 12 hujus). Si igitur res nobis sit similis, ipsam præ reliquis Lætitia afficere conabimur (per Prop. 29 hujus), sive conabimur, quantum possumus, efficere, ut res amata Lætitia afficiatur concomitante idea nostri, hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus), ut nos contra amet. Q. E. D.

PROPOSITIO XXXIV

Quo majori affectu rem amatam erga nos affectam esse imaginamur, eo magis gloriabimur.

DEMONSTRATIO

Nos (per Prop. præced.) conamur, quantum possumus, ut res amata. nos contra amet ; hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus), ut res amata Lætitia afficiatur concomitante idea nostri. Quo itaque rem amatam majori Lætitia nostra de causa affectam esse imaginamur, eo magis hic conatus juvatur ; hoc est (per Prop. 11 hujus cum ejus Schol.), eo majore Lætitia afficimur. At cum ex eo lætemur, quod alium nobis similem Lætitia affecimus, tum nosmet cum Lætitia contemplamur (per Prop. 30 hujus) : ergo quo majori affectu rem amatam erga nos affectam esse imaginamur, eo majori Lætitia nosmet contemplabimur, sive (per Schol. Prop. 30 hujus) eo magis gloriabimur. Q. E. D.

PROPOSITIO XXXV

Si quis imaginatur rem amatam eodem vel arctiore vinculo Amicitiæ, quo ipse eadem solus potiebatur, alium sibi jungere, Odio erga ipsam rem amatam afficietur, et illi alteri invidebit.

DEMONSTRATIO

Quo quis majore amore rem amatam erga se affectam esse imaginatur, eo magis gloriabitur (per præced. Prop.), hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 30 hujus) lætabitur ; adeoque (per Prop. 28 hujus) conabitur, quantum potest, imaginarirem amatam ipsi quum arctissime devinctam ; qui quidem conatus sive appetitus fomentatur, si alium idem sibi cupere imaginatur (per Prop. 31 hujus). At hic conatus sive appetitus ab ipsius rei amatæ imagine concomitante imagine illius, quem res amata sibi jungit coerceri supponitur ; ergo (per Schol. Prop. 11 hujus) eo ipso Tristitia afficietur, concomitante idea rei amatæ tanquam causa, et simul imagine alterius, hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus), odio erga rem amatam afficietur, et simul erga illum alterum (per Coroll. Prop. 15 hujus), cui propterea (per Prop. 23 hujus), quod re amata delectatur, invidebit. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Hoc Odium erga rem amatam Invidiæ junctum Zelotypia vocatur, quæ proinde nihil aliud est, quam animi fluctuatio orta ex Amore et Odio simul, concomitante idea alterius, cui invidetur. Præterea hoc Odium erga rem amatam majus erit pro ratione Lætitiæ, qua Zelotypus ex reciproco rei amatæ Amore solebat affici, et etiam pro ratione affectus, quo erga illum, quem sibi rem amatam jungere imaginatur, affectus erat. Nam si eum oderat, eo ipso rem amatam (per Prop. 24 hujus) odio habebit, quia ipsam id, quod ipse odio habet, Lætitia afficere imaginatur ; et etiam (per Coroll. Prop. 15 hujus) ex eo, quod rei amatæ imaginem imagini ejus, quem odit, jungere cogitur. Quæ ratio plerumque locum habet in Amore erga fæminam ; qui enim imaginatur mulierem, quam amat, alteri sese prostituere, non solum ex eo, quod ipsius appetitus coercetur, contristabitur, sed etiam, quia rei amatæ imaginem pudendis et excrementis alterius jungere cogitur, eandem aversatur ; ad quod denique accedit, quod Zelotypus non eodem vultu, quem res amata ei præbere solebat, ab eadem excipiatur, qua etiam de causa amans contristatur, ut jam ostendam.

PROPOSITIO XXXVI

Qui rei, qua semel delectatusest, recordatur, cupit eamdem cum iisdem potiri circumstantiis, ac cum primo ipsa delectatus est.

DEMONSTRATIO

Quicquid homo simul cum re, quæ ipsum delectavit, vidit, id omne (per Prop. 15 hujus) eri per accidens Lætitiae causa ; adeoque (per Prop. 28 hujus) omni eo simul cum re, quæ ipsum delectavit, potiri cupiet, sive re cum omnibus iisdem circumstantiis potiri cupiet, ac cum primo eadem delectatus est. Q. E. D.

COROLLARIUM

Si itaque unam ex iis circumstantiis deficere compererit, amans contristabitur.

DEMONSTRATIO

Nam quatenus aliquam circumstantiam deficere comperit, eatenus aliquid imaginatur, quod ejus rei existentiam secludit. Cum autem ejus rei sive circumstantiæ (per Prop. præc.) sit præ amore cupidus, ergo (per Prop. 19 hujus), quatenus eandem deficere imaginatur, contristabitur. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Hæc Tristitia, quatenus absentiam ejus, quod amamus, respicit, Desiderium vocatur.

PROPOSITIO XXXVII

Cupiditas, quæ præ Tristitia vel Lætitia præque Odio vel Amore oritur, eo est major, quo affectus major est.

DEMONSTRATIO

Tristitia hominis agendi potentiam (per Schol. Prop. 11 hujus) minuit vel coercet, hoc est (per Prop. 7 hujus), conatum, quo homo in suo esse perseverare conatur, minuit vel coercet ; adeoque (per Prop. 5 hujus) huic conatui est contraria ; et quicquid homo Tristitia affectus conatur est Tristitiam amovere. At (per Tristitiæ Defin.) quo Tristitia major est, eo majori parti hominis agendi potentiæ necesse est opponi ; ergo quo major Tristitia est, eo majore agendi potentia conabitur homo contra Tristitiam amovere ; hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 9 hujus), eo majore cupiditate sive appetitu conabitur Tristitiam amovere. Deinde, quoniam Lætitia (per idem Schol. Prop. 11 hujus) hominis agendi potentiam auget vel juvat, facile eadem via demonstratur, quod homo, Lætitia affectus, nihil aliud cupit quam eandem conservare, idque eo majore Cupiditate, quo Lætitia major erit. Denique, quoniam Odium et Amor sunt ipsi Tristitiæ vel Lætitiæ affectus, sequitur eodem modo, quod conatus, appetitus, sive Cupiditas, quæ præ Odio vel Amore oritur, major erit pro ratione Odii et Amoris. Q. E. D.

PROPOSITIO XXXVIII

Si quis rem amatam odio habere inceperit, ita ut Amor plane aboleatur, eandem majore odio, ex pari causa, prosequetur, quam si ipsam nunquam amavisset, et eo majori, quo Amor antea major fuerat.

DEMONSTRATIO

Nam si quis rem, quam amat, odio habere incipit, plures ejus appetitus coercentur, quam si eandem non amavisset. Amor namque Lætitia est (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus) quam homo, quantum potest (per Prop. 28 hujus), conservare conatur ; idque (per idem Schol.) rem amatam ut præsentem contemplando, eandemque (per Prop. 21 hujus) Lætitia, quantum potest, afficiendo ; qui quidem conatus (per Prop. præc.) eo est major quo amor major est, ut et conatus efficiendi, ut res amata ipsum contra amet (vid. Prop. 33 hujus). At hi conatus odio erga rem amatam coercentur (per Coroll. Prop. 13 et per Prop. 23 hujus) ; ergo amans (per Schol. Prop. 11 hujus) hac etiam de causa Tristitia afficietur, et eo majori, quo Amor major fuerat ; hoc est, præter Tristitiam, quæ Odii fuit causa, alia ex eo oritur, quod rem amavit, et consequenter majore Tristitiæ affectu rem amatam contemplabitur, hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus) majori odio prosequetur, quam si eandem non amavisset, et eo majori, quo amor major fuerat. Q. E. D.

PROPOSITIO XXXIX

Qui aliquem Odio habet, ei malum inferre conabitur, nisi ex eo majus sibi malum oriri timeat : et contra, qui aliquem amat, ei eadem lege benefacere conabitur.

DEMONSTRATIO

Aliquem odio habere est (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus) aliquem ut Tristitiæ causam imaginari ; adeoque (per Prop. 28 hujus) is, qui aliquem odio habet, eundem amovere vel destruere conabitur. Sed si inde aliquid tristius, sive (quod idem est) majus malum sibi timeat, idque se vitare posse credit, non inferendo ei, quem odit, malum, quod meditabatur, a malo inferendo (per eandem Prop. 28 hujus) abstinere cupiet ; idque (per Prop. 37 hujus) majore conatu, quam quo tenebatur inferendi malum, qui propterea prævalebit, ut volebamus. Secundæ partis demonstratio eodem modo procedit. Ergo qui aliquem odio habet etc. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Per bonum hic intelligo omne genus Lætitiæ, et quicquid porro ad eandem conducit, et, præcipue id, quod desiderio, qualecunque illud sit, satisfacit. Per malum autem omne Tristitiæ genus, et præcipue id, quod desiderium frustratur. Supra enim (in Schol. Prop. 9 hujus) ostendimus, nos nihil cupere, quia id bonum esse judicamus, sed contra id bonum vocamus, quod cupimus ; et consequenter id, quod aversamur, malum appellamus ; quare unusquisque ex suo affectu judicat seu æstimat, quid bonum, quid malum, quid melius, quid pejus, et quid denique optimum, quidve pessimum sit. Sic Avarus argenti copiam optimum, ejus autem inopiam pessimum judicat Ambitiosus autem nihil æque ac Gloriam cupit, et contra nihil æque ac Pudorem reformidat. Invido deinde nihil jucundius quam alterius infelicitas, et nihil molestius quam aliena felicitas ; ac sic unusquisque ex suo affectu rem aliquam bonam aut malam, utilem aut inutilem esse judicat. Cæterum hic affectus, quo homo ita disponitur, ut id, quod vult, nolit, vel ut id, quod non vult, velit, Timor vocatur, qui proinde nihil aliud est, quam metus quatenus homo ab eodem disponitur ad malum, quod futurum judicat, minore vitandum (Vid. Prop. 28 hujus). Sed si malum, quod timet, Pudor sit, tum Timor appellatur Verecundia. Denique si Cupiditas malum futurum vitandi coercetur Timore alterius mali, ita ut quid potius velit, nesciat, tum Metus vocatur Consternatio, præcipue si utrumque malum, quod timetur, ex maximis sit.

PROPOSITIO XL

Qui se odio haberi ab aliquo imaginatur, nec se ullam odii causam illi dedisse credit, eundem odio contra habebit.

DEMONSTRATIO

Qui aliquem odio affectum imaginatur, eo ipso etiam odio afficietur (per Prop. 27 hujus), hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus), Tristitia concomitante idea causæ externæ. At ipse (per hypothesin) nullam hujus Tristitiæ causam imaginatur præter illum, ipsum odio habet ; ergo ex hoc, quod se odio haberi ab aliquo imaginatur, Tristitia afficietur concomitante idea ejus, qui ipsum odio habet, sive (per idem Schol.) eundem odio habebit. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Quod si se justam Odii causam præbuisse imaginatur, tum (per Prop. 30 hujus et ejusdem Schol.) Pudore afficietur. Sed hoc (per Prop. 25 hujus) raro contingit. Præterea hæc Odii reciprocatio oriri etiam potest ex eo, quod Odium sequatur conatus malum inferendi ei, qui odio habetur (per Prop. 39 hujus). Qui igitur se odio haberi ab aliquo imaginatur, eundem alicujus mali sive Tristitiæ causam imaginabitur ; atque adeo Tristitia afficietur, seu Metu, concomitante idea ejus, qui ipsum odio habet, tanquam causa, hoc est, odio contra afficietur, ut supra.

COROLLARIUM I

Qui, quem amat, odio erga se affectum imaginatur, Odio et Amore simul conflictabitur. Nam quatenus imaginatur, ab eodem se odio haberi, determinatur (per Prop. præced.) ad eundem contra odio habendum. At (per hypothesin) ipsum nihilominus amat : ergo Odio et Amore simul conflictabitur.

COROLLARIUM II

Si aliquis imaginatur, ab aliquo, quem antea nullo affectu prosecutus est, malum aliquod præ Odio sibi illatum esse, statim idem malum eidem referre conabitur.

DEMONSTRATIO

Qui aliquem Odio erga se affectum esse imaginatur, eum contra (per præced. Prop.) odio habebit, et (per Prop. 26 hujus) id omne comminisci conabitur, quod eundem possit Tristitia afficere, atque id eidem (per Prop. 39 hujus) inferre studebit. At (per hypothesin) primum, quod hujusmodi imaginatur, est malum sibi illatum ; ergo idem statim eidem inferre conabitur. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Conatus malum inferendi ei, quem odimus, Ira vocatur ; conatus autem malum nobis illatum referendi Vindicta appellatur.

PROPOSITIO XLI

Si quis ab aliquo se amari imaginatur, nec se ullam ad id causam dedisse credit (quod per Coroll. Prop. 15 et per Prop. 16 hujus fieri potest), eundem contra amabit.

DEMONSTRATIO

Hæc Propositio eadem via demonstratur ac præcedens. Cujus etiam Scholium vide.

SCHOLIUM

Quod si se justam Amoris causam præbuisse crediderit, gloriabitur (per Prop. 30 hujus cum ejusdem Schol.) ; quod quidem (per Prop. 25 hujus) frequentius contingit, et cujus contrarium evenire diximus, quando aliquis ab aliquo se odio haberi imaginatur (vide Schol. Prop. præced.). Porro hic reciprocus Amor, et consequenter (per Prop. 39 hujus) conatus benefaciendi ei, qui nos amat, quique (per eandem Prop. 39 hujus) nobis benefacere conatur, Gratia seu Gratitudo vocatur ; atque adeo apparet, homines longe paratiores esse ad Vindictam, quam ad referendum beneficium.

COROLLARIUM

Qui ab eo, quem odio habet, se amari imaginatur, Odio et Amore simul conflictabitur. Quod eadem via, qua primum præcedentis Coroll., demonstratur.

SCHOLIUM

Quod si Odium prævaluerit, ei, a quo amatur, malum inferre conabitur ; qui quidem affectus Crudelitas appellatur, præcipue si illum, qui amat, nullam Odii communem causam præbuisse creditur.

PROPOSITIO XLII

Qui in aliquem, Amore aut spe Gloriae motus, beneficium contulit, contristabitur, si viderit, beneficium ingrato animo accipi.

DEMONSTRATIO

Qui rem aliquam sibi similem amat, conatur, quantum potest, efficere, ut ab ipsa contra ametur (per Prop. 33 hujus). Qui igitur præ amore in aliquem beneficium contulit, id fecit desiderio, quo tenetur, ut contra ametur, hoc est (per Prop. 34 hujus) spe Gloriæ sive (per Schol. Prop. 30 hujus) Lætitiæ ; adeoque (per Prop. 12 hujus) hanc Gloriæ causam, quantum potest, imaginari, sive ut actu existentem contemplari conabitur. At (per hypothesin) aliud imaginatur, quod ejusdem causæ existentiam secludit : ergo (per Prop. 19 hujus) eo ipso contristabitur. Q. E. D.

PROPOSITIO XLIII

Odium reciproco odio augetur, et Amore contra deleri potest.

DEMONSTRATIO

Qui eum, quem odit, Odio contra erga se affectum esse imaginatur eo ipso (per Prop. 40 hujus) novum Odium oritur, durante (per hypothesin) adhuc primo. Sed si contra eundem Amore erga se affectum esse imaginatur, quatenus hoc imaginatur, eatenus (per Prop. 30 hujus) se ipsum cum Lætitia contemplatur, et eatenus (per Prop. 29 hujus) eidem placere conabitur ; hoc est (per Prop. 41 hujus), eatenus conatur ipsum odio non habere, nullaque Tristitia afficere ; qui quidem conatus (per Prop. 37 hujus) major vel minor erit pro ratione affectus, ex quo oritur ; atque adeo si major fuerit illo, qui ex Odio oritur et quo rem, quam odit (per Prop. 26 hujus), Tristitia afficere conatur, ei prævalebit, et odium ex animo delebit. Q. E. D.

PROPOSITIO XLIV

Odium, quod Amore plane vincitur, in Amorem transit ; et Amor propterea major est, quam si Odium non præcessisset.

DEMONSTRATIO

Eodem modo procedit ac Propositions 38 hujus. Nam qui rem, quam odit, sive quam cum Tristitia contemplari solebat, amare incipit, eo ipso, quod amat, lætatur, et huic Lætitiæ, quam Amor involvit (vide ejus Defin. in Schol. Prop. 13 hujus), illa etiam accedit quæ ex. eo oritur, quod conatus amovendi Tristitiam, quem Odium involvit (ut in Prop. 37 hujus ostendimus), prorsus juvatur, concomitante idea ejus, quem odio habuit, tanquam causa.

SCHOLIUM

Quamvis res ita se habeat, nemo tamen conabitur rem aliquam odio habere, vel Tristitia affici, ut majori hac Lætitia fruatur ; hoc est, nemo spe damnum recuperandi, damnum sibi inferri cupiet, nec ægrotare desiderabit spe convalescendi. Nam unusquisque suum esse conservare, et Tristitiam, quantum potest, amovere semper conabitur. Quod si contra concipi posset, hominem posse cupere aliquem odio habere, ut eum postea majori amore prosequatur, tum eundem odio habere semper desiderabit. Nam quo Odium majus fuerit, eo Amor erit major, atque adeo desiderabit semper, ut Odium magis magisque augeatur, et eadem de causa homo magis ac magis ægrotare conabitur, ut majori Laetitia ex restauranda valetudine postea fruatur ; atque adeo semper ægrotare conabitur, quod (per Prop. 6 hujus) est absurdum.

PROPOSITIO XLV

Si quis aliquem sibi similem Odio in rem sibi similem, quam amat, affectum esse imaginatur, eum odio habebit.

DEMONSTRATIO

Nam res amata eum, qui ipsam odit, odio contra habet (per Prop. 40 hujus) : adeoque amans, qui aliquem imaginatur rem amatam odio habere, eo ipso rem amatam Odio hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus) Tristitia, affectam esse imaginatur et consequenter (per Prop. 21 hujus) contristatur, idque concomitante idea ejus, qui rem amatam odit, tanquam causa ; hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus) ipsum odio habebit. Q. E. D.

PROPOSITIO XLVI

Si quis ab aliquo cujusdam classis sive nationis a sua diversæ, Lætitia vel Tristitia affectus fuerit, concomitante ejus idea, sub nomine universali classis vel nationis, tanquam causa : is non tantum illum, sed omnes ejusdem classis vel nationis amabit vel odio habebit.

DEMONSTRATIO

Hujus rei demonstratio patet ex Propositione 16 hujus Partis.

PROPOSITIO XLVII

Lætitia quæ ex eo oritur, quod scilicet rem, quam odimus, destrui aut alio malo affici imaginamur, non oritur absque ulla animi Tristitia.

DEMONSTRATIO

Patet ex Prop. 27 hujus. Nam quatenus rem nobis similem Tristitia affici imaginamur, eatenus constristamur.

SCHOLIUM

Potest hæc Propositio etiam demonstrari ex Corollario Propositionis 17 Partis II. Quoties enim rei recordamur, quamvis ipsa actu non existat, eandem tamen ut præsentem contemplamur, Corpusque eodem modo afficitur ; quare quatenus rei memoria viget, eatenus homo determinatur ad eandem cum Tristitia contemplandum, quæ determinatio, manente adhuc rei imagine, coercetur quidem memoria illarum rerum, quæ hujus existentiam secludunt, sed non tollitur : atque adeo homo eatenus tantum lætatur, quatenus hæc determinatio coercetur ; et hinc fit, ut hæc Laetitia, quæ ex rei, quam odimus, malo oritur, toties repetatur, quoties ejusdem rei recordamur. Nam, uti diximus, quando ejusdem rei imago excitatur, quia hæc ipsius rei existentiam involvit, hominem determinat ad rem cum eadem Tristitia contemplandum, qua eandem contemplari solebat, cum ipsa existeret. Sed quia ejusdem rei imagini alias junxit, quæ ejusdem existentiam secludunt, ideo hæc ad Tristitiam determinatio statim coercetur, et homo de novo lætatur, et hoc toties, quoties hæc repetitio fit. Atque hæc eadem est causa, cur homines lætantur, quoties alicujus jam præteriti mali recordantur, et cur pericula, a quibus liberati sunt, narrare gaudeant. Nam ubi aliquod periculum imaginantur, idem veluti adhuc futurum contemplantur, et ad id metuendum determinantur ; quæ determinatio de novo coercetur idea libertatis, quam hujus periculi ideæ junxerunt, cum ab eodem liberati sunt, quæque eos de novo securos reddit ; atque adeo de novo lætantur.

PROPOSITIO XLVIII

Amor et Odium ex. gr. erga Petrum destruitur, si Tristitia, quam hoc, et Lætitia, quam ille involvit, ideæ alterius causæ jungatur ; et eatenus uterque diminuitur, quatenus imaginamur Petrum non solum fuisse alterutrius causam.

DEMONSTRATIO

Patet ex sola Amoris et Odii definitione ; quam vide in Schol. Prop. 13 hujus. Nam propter hoc solum Lætitia vocatur Amor, et Tristitia Odium erga Petrum, quia scilicet Petrus hujus vel illius affectus causa esse consideratur. Hoc itaque prorsus vel ex parte sublato, affectus quoque erga Petrum prorsus vel parte diminuitur. Q. E. D.

PROPOSITIO XLIX

Amor et Odium erga rem, quam liberam esse imaginamur, major ex pari causa uterque debet esse, quam erga necessariam.

DEMONSTRATIO

Res, quam liberam esse imaginamur, debet (per Defin. 7 p. I) per se absque aliis percipi. Si igitur eandem Lætitiæ vel Tristitiæ causam esse imaginemur, eo ipso (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus) eandem amabimus vel odio habebimus, idque (per Prop. præced.) summo Amore vel Odio, qui ex dato affectu oriri potest. Sed si rem, quæ ejusdem affectus est causa ut necessariam imaginemur, tum (per eandem Defin. 7 p. I) ipsam non solam, sed cum aliis ejusdem affectus causam esse imaginabimur, atque adeo (per Prop. præc.) Amor et Odium erga ipsam minor erit. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Hinc sequitur, homines, quia se liberos esse existimant, majore Amore vel odio se invicem prosequi, quam alia ; ad quod accedit affectuum imitatio, de qua vide Prop. 27, 34, 40 et 43 hujus.

PROPOSITIO L

Res quæcunque potest esse per accidens Spei aut Metus causa.

DEMONSTRATIO

Hæc Propositio eadem via demonstratur, qua Propositio 15 hujus quam vide una cum Schol. 2 Propositionis 18 hujus.

SCHOLIUM

Res, quæ per accidens Spei aut Metus sunt causæ, bona aut mala omina vocantur. Deinde quatenus hæc eadem omina sunt Spei aut Metus causa, eatenus (per Defin. Spei et Metus, quam vide in Schol. 2 Prop. 18 hujus) Lætitiæ aut Tristitiæ sunt causa, et consequenter (per Coroll. Prop. 15 hujus) eatenus eadem amamus vel odio habemus, et (per Prop. 28 hujus) tanquam media ad ea, quæ speramus adhibere, vel tanquam obstacula aut Metus causas amovere conamur. Præterea ex Propositione 25 hujus sequitur, nos natura ita esse constitutos, ut ea, quæ speramus, facile, quæ autem timemus, difficile credamus, et ut de iis plus minusve justo sentiamus. Atque ex his ortæ sunt Superstitiones, quibus homines ubique conflictantur. Cæterum non puto operæ esse pretium, animi hic ostendere fluctuationes, quæ ex Spe et Metu oriuntur ; quandoquidem ex sola horum affectuum definitione sequitur, non dari Spem sine Metu, neque Metum sine Spe (ut fusius suo loco explicabimus) ; et præterea quandoquidem, quatenus aliquid speramus aut metuimus, eatenus idem amamus vel odio habemus ; atque adeo quicquid de Amore et Odio diximus, facile unusquisque Spei et Metui applicare poterit.

PROPOSITIO LI

Diversi homines ab uno eodemque objecto diversimode affici possunt, et unus idemque homo ab uno eodemque objecto potest diversis temporibus diversimode affici.

DEMONSTRATIO

Corpus humanum (per Post. 3 p. II) a corporibus externis plurimis modis afficitur. Possunt igitur eodem tempore duo homines diversimode esse affecti ; atque adeo (per Axiom. 1, quod est post Lemma 3, quod vide post Prop. 13 p. II) ab uno eodemque objecto possunt diversimode affici. Deinde (per idem Postul.) Corpus humanum potest jam hoc jam alio modo esse affectum ; et consequenter (per idem Axiom.) ab uno eodemque objecto diversis temporibus diversimode affici. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

paragraphs.text: Videmus itaque, cum hominum natura plerumque ita comparatum esse, ut eorum, quibus male est, misereantur, et quibus bene est, invideant, et (per Prop. præc.) eo majore odio, quo rem, qua alium potiri imaginantur, magis amant. Videmus deinde, ex eadem naturæ humanæ proprietate, ex qua sequitur, homines esse misericordes, sequi etiam, eosdem esse invidos et ambitiosos. Denique, si ipsam experientiam consulere velimus, ipsam hæc omnia docere experiemur ; præsertim si ad priores nostræ ætatis annos attenderimus.

Nam pueros, quia eorum corpus continuo veluti in æquilibrio est, ex hoc solo ridere vel flere experimur, quod alios ridere vel flere vident ; et quicquid præterea vident alios facere, id imitari statim cupiunt, et omnia denique sibi cupiunt quibus alios delectari imaginantur ; nimirum quia rerum imagines, ut diximus, sunt ipsæ humani Corporis affectiones, sive modi, quibus Corpus humanum a causis externis afficitur disponiturque ad hoc vel illud agendum.
PROPOSITIO XXXIII
Cum rem nobis similem amamus, conamur, quantum possumus, efficere, ut nos contra amet.
DEMONSTRATIO

Rem, quam amamus præ reliquis, quantum possumus, imaginari conamur (per Prop. 12 hujus). Si igitur res nobis sit similis, ipsam præ reliquis Lætitia afficere conabimur (per Prop. 29 hujus), sive conabimur, quantum possumus, efficere, ut res amata Lætitia afficiatur concomitante idea nostri, hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus), ut nos contra amet. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITIO XXXIV
Quo majori affectu rem amatam erga nos affectam esse imaginamur, eo magis gloriabimur.
DEMONSTRATIO

Nos (per Prop. præced.) conamur, quantum possumus, ut res amata. nos contra amet ; hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus), ut res amata Lætitia afficiatur concomitante idea nostri. Quo itaque rem amatam majori Lætitia nostra de causa affectam esse imaginamur, eo magis hic conatus juvatur ; hoc est (per Prop. 11 hujus cum ejus Schol.), eo majore Lætitia afficimur. At cum ex eo lætemur, quod alium nobis similem Lætitia affecimus, tum nosmet cum Lætitia contemplamur (per Prop. 30 hujus) : ergo quo majori affectu rem amatam erga nos affectam esse imaginamur, eo majori Lætitia nosmet contemplabimur, sive (per Schol. Prop. 30 hujus) eo magis gloriabimur. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITIO XXXV
Si quis imaginatur rem amatam eodem vel arctiore vinculo Amicitiæ, quo ipse eadem solus potiebatur, alium sibi jungere, Odio erga ipsam rem amatam afficietur, et illi alteri invidebit.
DEMONSTRATIO

Quo quis majore amore rem amatam erga se affectam esse imaginatur, eo magis gloriabitur (per præced. Prop.), hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 30 hujus) lætabitur ; adeoque (per Prop. 28 hujus) conabitur, quantum potest, imaginarirem amatam ipsi quum arctissime devinctam ; qui quidem conatus sive appetitus fomentatur, si alium idem sibi cupere imaginatur (per Prop. 31 hujus). At hic conatus sive appetitus ab ipsius rei amatæ imagine concomitante imagine illius, quem res amata sibi jungit coerceri supponitur ; ergo (per Schol. Prop. 11 hujus) eo ipso Tristitia afficietur, concomitante idea rei amatæ tanquam causa, et simul imagine alterius, hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus), odio erga rem amatam afficietur, et simul erga illum alterum (per Coroll. Prop. 15 hujus), cui propterea (per Prop. 23 hujus), quod re amata delectatur, invidebit. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Hoc Odium erga rem amatam Invidiæ junctum Zelotypia vocatur, quæ proinde nihil aliud est, quam animi fluctuatio orta ex Amore et Odio simul, concomitante idea alterius, cui invidetur. Præterea hoc Odium erga rem amatam majus erit pro ratione Lætitiæ, qua Zelotypus ex reciproco rei amatæ Amore solebat affici, et etiam pro ratione affectus, quo erga illum, quem sibi rem amatam jungere imaginatur, affectus erat. Nam si eum oderat, eo ipso rem amatam (per Prop. 24 hujus) odio habebit, quia ipsam id, quod ipse odio habet, Lætitia afficere imaginatur ; et etiam (per Coroll. Prop. 15 hujus) ex eo, quod rei amatæ imaginem imagini ejus, quem odit, jungere cogitur.

Quæ ratio plerumque locum habet in Amore erga fæminam ; qui enim imaginatur mulierem, quam amat, alteri sese prostituere, non solum ex eo, quod ipsius appetitus coercetur, contristabitur, sed etiam, quia rei amatæ imaginem pudendis et excrementis alterius jungere cogitur, eandem aversatur ; ad quod denique accedit, quod Zelotypus non eodem vultu, quem res amata ei præbere solebat, ab eadem excipiatur, qua etiam de causa amans contristatur, ut jam ostendam.
PROPOSITIO XXXVI
Qui rei, qua semel delectatusest, recordatur, cupit eamdem cum iisdem potiri circumstantiis, ac cum primo ipsa delectatus est.
DEMONSTRATIO

Quicquid homo simul cum re, quæ ipsum delectavit, vidit, id omne (per Prop. 15 hujus) eri per accidens Lætitiae causa ; adeoque (per Prop. 28 hujus) omni eo simul cum re, quæ ipsum delectavit, potiri cupiet, sive re cum omnibus iisdem circumstantiis potiri cupiet, ac cum primo eadem delectatus est. Q. E. D.
COROLLARIUM
Si itaque unam ex iis circumstantiis deficere compererit, amans contristabitur.
DEMONSTRATIO

Nam quatenus aliquam circumstantiam deficere comperit, eatenus aliquid imaginatur, quod ejus rei existentiam secludit. Cum autem ejus rei sive circumstantiæ (per Prop. præc.) sit præ amore cupidus, ergo (per Prop. 19 hujus), quatenus eandem deficere imaginatur, contristabitur. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM
Hæc Tristitia, quatenus absentiam ejus, quod amamus, respicit, Desiderium vocatur.
PROPOSITIO XXXVII
Cupiditas, quæ præ Tristitia vel Lætitia præque Odio vel Amore oritur, eo est major, quo affectus major est.
DEMONSTRATIO

Tristitia hominis agendi potentiam (per Schol. Prop. 11 hujus) minuit vel coercet, hoc est (per Prop. 7 hujus), conatum, quo homo in suo esse perseverare conatur, minuit vel coercet ; adeoque (per Prop. 5 hujus) huic conatui est contraria ; et quicquid homo Tristitia affectus conatur est Tristitiam amovere. At (per Tristitiæ Defin.) quo Tristitia major est, eo majori parti hominis agendi potentiæ necesse est opponi ; ergo quo major Tristitia est, eo majore agendi potentia conabitur homo contra Tristitiam amovere ; hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 9 hujus), eo majore cupiditate sive appetitu conabitur Tristitiam amovere. Deinde, quoniam Lætitia (per idem Schol. Prop. 11 hujus) hominis agendi potentiam auget vel juvat, facile eadem via demonstratur, quod homo, Lætitia affectus, nihil aliud cupit quam eandem conservare, idque eo majore Cupiditate, quo Lætitia major erit.

Denique, quoniam Odium et Amor sunt ipsi Tristitiæ vel Lætitiæ affectus, sequitur eodem modo, quod conatus, appetitus, sive Cupiditas, quæ præ Odio vel Amore oritur, major erit pro ratione Odii et Amoris. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITIO XXXVIII
Si quis rem amatam odio habere inceperit, ita ut Amor plane aboleatur, eandem majore odio, ex pari causa, prosequetur, quam si ipsam nunquam amavisset, et eo majori, quo Amor antea major fuerat.
DEMONSTRATIO

Nam si quis rem, quam amat, odio habere incipit, plures ejus appetitus coercentur, quam si eandem non amavisset. Amor namque Lætitia est (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus) quam homo, quantum potest (per Prop. 28 hujus), conservare conatur ; idque (per idem Schol.) rem amatam ut præsentem contemplando, eandemque (per Prop. 21 hujus) Lætitia, quantum potest, afficiendo ; qui quidem conatus (per Prop. præc.) eo est major quo amor major est, ut et conatus efficiendi, ut res amata ipsum contra amet (vid. Prop. 33 hujus). At hi conatus odio erga rem amatam coercentur (per Coroll. Prop. 13 et per Prop. 23 hujus) ; ergo amans (per Schol. Prop. 11 hujus) hac etiam de causa Tristitia afficietur, et eo majori, quo Amor major fuerat ; hoc est, præter Tristitiam, quæ Odii fuit causa, alia ex eo oritur, quod rem amavit, et consequenter majore Tristitiæ affectu rem amatam contemplabitur, hoc est (per Schol.
Prop. 13 hujus) majori odio prosequetur, quam si eandem non amavisset, et eo majori, quo amor major fuerat. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITIO XXXIX
Qui aliquem Odio habet, ei malum inferre conabitur, nisi ex eo majus sibi malum oriri timeat : et contra, qui aliquem amat, ei eadem lege benefacere conabitur.
DEMONSTRATIO

Aliquem odio habere est (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus) aliquem ut Tristitiæ causam imaginari ; adeoque (per Prop. 28 hujus) is, qui aliquem odio habet, eundem amovere vel destruere conabitur. Sed si inde aliquid tristius, sive (quod idem est) majus malum sibi timeat, idque se vitare posse credit, non inferendo ei, quem odit, malum, quod meditabatur, a malo inferendo (per eandem Prop. 28 hujus) abstinere cupiet ; idque (per Prop. 37 hujus) majore conatu, quam quo tenebatur inferendi malum, qui propterea prævalebit, ut volebamus. Secundæ partis demonstratio eodem modo procedit. Ergo qui aliquem odio habet etc. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Per bonum hic intelligo omne genus Lætitiæ, et quicquid porro ad eandem conducit, et, præcipue id, quod desiderio, qualecunque illud sit, satisfacit. Per malum autem omne Tristitiæ genus, et præcipue id, quod desiderium frustratur. Supra enim (in Schol. Prop. 9 hujus) ostendimus, nos nihil cupere, quia id bonum esse judicamus, sed contra id bonum vocamus, quod cupimus ; et consequenter id, quod aversamur, malum appellamus ; quare unusquisque ex suo affectu judicat seu æstimat, quid bonum, quid malum, quid melius, quid pejus, et quid denique optimum, quidve pessimum sit. Sic Avarus argenti copiam optimum, ejus autem inopiam pessimum judicat Ambitiosus autem nihil æque ac Gloriam cupit, et contra nihil æque ac Pudorem reformidat.

Invido deinde nihil jucundius quam alterius infelicitas, et nihil molestius quam aliena felicitas ; ac sic unusquisque ex suo affectu rem aliquam bonam aut malam, utilem aut inutilem esse judicat. Cæterum hic affectus, quo homo ita disponitur, ut id, quod vult, nolit, vel ut id, quod non vult, velit, Timor vocatur, qui proinde nihil aliud est, quam metus quatenus homo ab eodem disponitur ad malum, quod futurum judicat, minore vitandum (Vid. Prop. 28 hujus). Sed si malum, quod timet, Pudor sit, tum Timor appellatur Verecundia. Denique si Cupiditas malum futurum vitandi coercetur Timore alterius mali, ita ut quid potius velit, nesciat, tum Metus vocatur Consternatio, præcipue si utrumque malum, quod timetur, ex maximis sit.
PROPOSITIO XL
Qui se odio haberi ab aliquo imaginatur, nec se ullam odii causam illi dedisse credit, eundem odio contra habebit.
DEMONSTRATIO

Qui aliquem odio affectum imaginatur, eo ipso etiam odio afficietur (per Prop. 27 hujus), hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus), Tristitia concomitante idea causæ externæ. At ipse (per hypothesin) nullam hujus Tristitiæ causam imaginatur præter illum, ipsum odio habet ; ergo ex hoc, quod se odio haberi ab aliquo imaginatur, Tristitia afficietur concomitante idea ejus, qui ipsum odio habet, sive (per idem Schol.) eundem odio habebit. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Quod si se justam Odii causam præbuisse imaginatur, tum (per Prop. 30 hujus et ejusdem Schol.) Pudore afficietur. Sed hoc (per Prop. 25 hujus) raro contingit. Præterea hæc Odii reciprocatio oriri etiam potest ex eo, quod Odium sequatur conatus malum inferendi ei, qui odio habetur (per Prop. 39 hujus). Qui igitur se odio haberi ab aliquo imaginatur, eundem alicujus mali sive Tristitiæ causam imaginabitur ; atque adeo Tristitia afficietur, seu Metu, concomitante idea ejus, qui ipsum odio habet, tanquam causa, hoc est, odio contra afficietur, ut supra.
COROLLARIUM I

Qui, quem amat, odio erga se affectum imaginatur, Odio et Amore simul conflictabitur. Nam quatenus imaginatur, ab eodem se odio haberi, determinatur (per Prop. præced.) ad eundem contra odio habendum. At (per hypothesin) ipsum nihilominus amat : ergo Odio et Amore simul conflictabitur.
COROLLARIUM II
Si aliquis imaginatur, ab aliquo, quem antea nullo affectu prosecutus est, malum aliquod præ Odio sibi illatum esse, statim idem malum eidem referre conabitur.
DEMONSTRATIO

Qui aliquem Odio erga se affectum esse imaginatur, eum contra (per præced. Prop.) odio habebit, et (per Prop. 26 hujus) id omne comminisci conabitur, quod eundem possit Tristitia afficere, atque id eidem (per Prop. 39 hujus) inferre studebit. At (per hypothesin) primum, quod hujusmodi imaginatur, est malum sibi illatum ; ergo idem statim eidem inferre conabitur. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM
Conatus malum inferendi ei, quem odimus, Ira vocatur ; conatus autem malum nobis illatum referendi Vindicta appellatur.
PROPOSITIO XLI
Si quis ab aliquo se amari imaginatur, nec se ullam ad id causam dedisse credit (quod per Coroll. Prop. 15 et per Prop. 16 hujus fieri potest), eundem contra amabit.
DEMONSTRATIO
Hæc Propositio eadem via demonstratur ac præcedens. Cujus etiam Scholium vide.
SCHOLIUM

Quod si se justam Amoris causam præbuisse crediderit, gloriabitur (per Prop. 30 hujus cum ejusdem Schol.) ; quod quidem (per Prop. 25 hujus) frequentius contingit, et cujus contrarium evenire diximus, quando aliquis ab aliquo se odio haberi imaginatur (vide Schol. Prop. præced.). Porro hic reciprocus Amor, et consequenter (per Prop. 39 hujus) conatus benefaciendi ei, qui nos amat, quique (per eandem Prop. 39 hujus) nobis benefacere conatur, Gratia seu Gratitudo vocatur ; atque adeo apparet, homines longe paratiores esse ad Vindictam, quam ad referendum beneficium.
COROLLARIUM
Qui ab eo, quem odio habet, se amari imaginatur, Odio et Amore simul conflictabitur. Quod eadem via, qua primum præcedentis Coroll., demonstratur.
SCHOLIUM
Quod si Odium prævaluerit, ei, a quo amatur, malum inferre conabitur ; qui quidem affectus Crudelitas appellatur, præcipue si illum, qui amat, nullam Odii communem causam præbuisse creditur.
PROPOSITIO XLII
Qui in aliquem, Amore aut spe Gloriae motus, beneficium contulit, contristabitur, si viderit, beneficium ingrato animo accipi.
DEMONSTRATIO

Qui rem aliquam sibi similem amat, conatur, quantum potest, efficere, ut ab ipsa contra ametur (per Prop. 33 hujus). Qui igitur præ amore in aliquem beneficium contulit, id fecit desiderio, quo tenetur, ut contra ametur, hoc est (per Prop. 34 hujus) spe Gloriæ sive (per Schol. Prop. 30 hujus) Lætitiæ ; adeoque (per Prop. 12 hujus) hanc Gloriæ causam, quantum potest, imaginari, sive ut actu existentem contemplari conabitur. At (per hypothesin) aliud imaginatur, quod ejusdem causæ existentiam secludit : ergo (per Prop. 19 hujus) eo ipso contristabitur. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITIO XLIII
Odium reciproco odio augetur, et Amore contra deleri potest.
DEMONSTRATIO

Qui eum, quem odit, Odio contra erga se affectum esse imaginatur eo ipso (per Prop. 40 hujus) novum Odium oritur, durante (per hypothesin) adhuc primo. Sed si contra eundem Amore erga se affectum esse imaginatur, quatenus hoc imaginatur, eatenus (per Prop. 30 hujus) se ipsum cum Lætitia contemplatur, et eatenus (per Prop. 29 hujus) eidem placere conabitur ; hoc est (per Prop. 41 hujus), eatenus conatur ipsum odio non habere, nullaque Tristitia afficere ; qui quidem conatus (per Prop. 37 hujus) major vel minor erit pro ratione affectus, ex quo oritur ; atque adeo si major fuerit illo, qui ex Odio oritur et quo rem, quam odit (per Prop. 26 hujus), Tristitia afficere conatur, ei prævalebit, et odium ex animo delebit. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITIO XLIV
Odium, quod Amore plane vincitur, in Amorem transit ; et Amor propterea major est, quam si Odium non præcessisset.
DEMONSTRATIO

Eodem modo procedit ac Propositions 38 hujus. Nam qui rem, quam odit, sive quam cum Tristitia contemplari solebat, amare incipit, eo ipso, quod amat, lætatur, et huic Lætitiæ, quam Amor involvit (vide ejus Defin. in Schol. Prop. 13 hujus), illa etiam accedit quæ ex. eo oritur, quod conatus amovendi Tristitiam, quem Odium involvit (ut in Prop. 37 hujus ostendimus), prorsus juvatur, concomitante idea ejus, quem odio habuit, tanquam causa.
SCHOLIUM

Quamvis res ita se habeat, nemo tamen conabitur rem aliquam odio habere, vel Tristitia affici, ut majori hac Lætitia fruatur ; hoc est, nemo spe damnum recuperandi, damnum sibi inferri cupiet, nec ægrotare desiderabit spe convalescendi. Nam unusquisque suum esse conservare, et Tristitiam, quantum potest, amovere semper conabitur. Quod si contra concipi posset, hominem posse cupere aliquem odio habere, ut eum postea majori amore prosequatur, tum eundem odio habere semper desiderabit. Nam quo Odium majus fuerit, eo Amor erit major, atque adeo desiderabit semper, ut Odium magis magisque augeatur, et eadem de causa homo magis ac magis ægrotare conabitur, ut majori Laetitia ex restauranda valetudine postea fruatur ; atque adeo semper ægrotare conabitur, quod (per Prop. 6 hujus) est absurdum.
PROPOSITIO XLV
Si quis aliquem sibi similem Odio in rem sibi similem, quam amat, affectum esse imaginatur, eum odio habebit.
DEMONSTRATIO

Nam res amata eum, qui ipsam odit, odio contra habet (per Prop. 40 hujus) : adeoque amans, qui aliquem imaginatur rem amatam odio habere, eo ipso rem amatam Odio hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus) Tristitia, affectam esse imaginatur et consequenter (per Prop. 21 hujus) contristatur, idque concomitante idea ejus, qui rem amatam odit, tanquam causa ; hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus) ipsum odio habebit. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITIO XLVI

Si quis ab aliquo cujusdam classis sive nationis a sua diversæ, Lætitia vel Tristitia affectus fuerit, concomitante ejus idea, sub nomine universali classis vel nationis, tanquam causa : is non tantum illum, sed omnes ejusdem classis vel nationis amabit vel odio habebit.
DEMONSTRATIO
Hujus rei demonstratio patet ex Propositione 16 hujus Partis.
PROPOSITIO XLVII
Lætitia quæ ex eo oritur, quod scilicet rem, quam odimus, destrui aut alio malo affici imaginamur, non oritur absque ulla animi Tristitia.
DEMONSTRATIO
Patet ex Prop. 27 hujus. Nam quatenus rem nobis similem Tristitia affici imaginamur, eatenus constristamur.
SCHOLIUM

Potest hæc Propositio etiam demonstrari ex Corollario Propositionis 17 Partis II. Quoties enim rei recordamur, quamvis ipsa actu non existat, eandem tamen ut præsentem contemplamur, Corpusque eodem modo afficitur ; quare quatenus rei memoria viget, eatenus homo determinatur ad eandem cum Tristitia contemplandum, quæ determinatio, manente adhuc rei imagine, coercetur quidem memoria illarum rerum, quæ hujus existentiam secludunt, sed non tollitur : atque adeo homo eatenus tantum lætatur, quatenus hæc determinatio coercetur ; et hinc fit, ut hæc Laetitia, quæ ex rei, quam odimus, malo oritur, toties repetatur, quoties ejusdem rei recordamur. Nam, uti diximus, quando ejusdem rei imago excitatur, quia hæc ipsius rei existentiam involvit, hominem determinat ad rem cum eadem Tristitia contemplandum, qua eandem contemplari solebat, cum ipsa existeret.

Sed quia ejusdem rei imagini alias junxit, quæ ejusdem existentiam secludunt, ideo hæc ad Tristitiam determinatio statim coercetur, et homo de novo lætatur, et hoc toties, quoties hæc repetitio fit. Atque hæc eadem est causa, cur homines lætantur, quoties alicujus jam præteriti mali recordantur, et cur pericula, a quibus liberati sunt, narrare gaudeant. Nam ubi aliquod periculum imaginantur, idem veluti adhuc futurum contemplantur, et ad id metuendum determinantur ; quæ determinatio de novo coercetur idea libertatis, quam hujus periculi ideæ junxerunt, cum ab eodem liberati sunt, quæque eos de novo securos reddit ; atque adeo de novo lætantur.
PROPOSITIO XLVIII

Amor et Odium ex. gr. erga Petrum destruitur, si Tristitia, quam hoc, et Lætitia, quam ille involvit, ideæ alterius causæ jungatur ; et eatenus uterque diminuitur, quatenus imaginamur Petrum non solum fuisse alterutrius causam.
DEMONSTRATIO

Patet ex sola Amoris et Odii definitione ; quam vide in Schol. Prop. 13 hujus. Nam propter hoc solum Lætitia vocatur Amor, et Tristitia Odium erga Petrum, quia scilicet Petrus hujus vel illius affectus causa esse consideratur. Hoc itaque prorsus vel ex parte sublato, affectus quoque erga Petrum prorsus vel parte diminuitur. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITIO XLIX
Amor et Odium erga rem, quam liberam esse imaginamur, major ex pari causa uterque debet esse, quam erga necessariam.
DEMONSTRATIO

Res, quam liberam esse imaginamur, debet (per Defin. 7 p. I) per se absque aliis percipi. Si igitur eandem Lætitiæ vel Tristitiæ causam esse imaginemur, eo ipso (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus) eandem amabimus vel odio habebimus, idque (per Prop. præced.) summo Amore vel Odio, qui ex dato affectu oriri potest. Sed si rem, quæ ejusdem affectus est causa ut necessariam imaginemur, tum (per eandem Defin. 7 p. I) ipsam non solam, sed cum aliis ejusdem affectus causam esse imaginabimur, atque adeo (per Prop. præc.) Amor et Odium erga ipsam minor erit. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM
Hinc sequitur, homines, quia se liberos esse existimant, majore Amore vel odio se invicem prosequi, quam alia ; ad quod accedit affectuum imitatio, de qua vide Prop. 27, 34, 40 et 43 hujus.
PROPOSITIO L
Res quæcunque potest esse per accidens Spei aut Metus causa.
DEMONSTRATIO
Hæc Propositio eadem via demonstratur, qua Propositio 15 hujus quam vide una cum Schol. 2 Propositionis 18 hujus.
SCHOLIUM

Res, quæ per accidens Spei aut Metus sunt causæ, bona aut mala omina vocantur. Deinde quatenus hæc eadem omina sunt Spei aut Metus causa, eatenus (per Defin. Spei et Metus, quam vide in Schol. 2 Prop. 18 hujus) Lætitiæ aut Tristitiæ sunt causa, et consequenter (per Coroll. Prop. 15 hujus) eatenus eadem amamus vel odio habemus, et (per Prop. 28 hujus) tanquam media ad ea, quæ speramus adhibere, vel tanquam obstacula aut Metus causas amovere conamur. Præterea ex Propositione 25 hujus sequitur, nos natura ita esse constitutos, ut ea, quæ speramus, facile, quæ autem timemus, difficile credamus, et ut de iis plus minusve justo sentiamus. Atque ex his ortæ sunt Superstitiones, quibus homines ubique conflictantur.

Cæterum non puto operæ esse pretium, animi hic ostendere fluctuationes, quæ ex Spe et Metu oriuntur ; quandoquidem ex sola horum affectuum definitione sequitur, non dari Spem sine Metu, neque Metum sine Spe (ut fusius suo loco explicabimus) ; et præterea quandoquidem, quatenus aliquid speramus aut metuimus, eatenus idem amamus vel odio habemus ; atque adeo quicquid de Amore et Odio diximus, facile unusquisque Spei et Metui applicare poterit.
PROPOSITIO LI
Diversi homines ab uno eodemque objecto diversimode affici possunt, et unus idemque homo ab uno eodemque objecto potest diversis temporibus diversimode affici.
DEMONSTRATIO

Corpus humanum (per Post. 3 p. II) a corporibus externis plurimis modis afficitur. Possunt igitur eodem tempore duo homines diversimode esse affecti ; atque adeo (per Axiom. 1, quod est post Lemma 3, quod vide post Prop. 13 p. II) ab uno eodemque objecto possunt diversimode affici. Deinde (per idem Postul.) Corpus humanum potest jam hoc jam alio modo esse affectum ; et consequenter (per idem Axiom.) ab uno eodemque objecto diversis temporibus diversimode affici. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

translations.title: Pars tertia - De origine et natura affectuum · passage 3

paragraphs.text: We see, therefore, that, since human nature is for the most part so constituted that people pity those who fare badly, and envy those who fare well, and (by the preceding Proposition) do so with greater hatred the more they love the thing which they imagine another to possess. We see next that, from the same property of human nature from which it follows that men are compassionate, it also follows that they are envious and ambitious. Finally, if we should wish to consult experience itself, we shall find that it teaches all these things; especially if we attend to the earlier years of our life.

For we find that children, because their body is continually as it were in a state of equilibrium, laugh or weep from this alone, that they see others laugh or weep; and whatever else they see others do, they immediately desire to imitate, and finally they desire for themselves all things by which they imagine others are delighted; namely because, as we have said, the images of things are themselves affections of the human Body, or modes by which the human Body is affected by external causes and disposed to do this or that.
PROPOSITION XXXIII
When we love a thing similar to ourselves, we strive, as far as we can, to bring it about that it loves us in return.
DEMONSTRATION

We strive, as far as we can, to imagine a thing which we love above all others (by Prop. 12 of this Part). If, therefore, the thing is similar to ourselves, we shall strive to affect it with Joy above all others (by Prop. 29 of this Part), that is, we shall strive, as far as we can, to bring it about that the beloved thing is affected with Joy accompanied by the idea of ourselves; that is (by the Scholium to Prop. 13 of this Part), that it loves us in return. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XXXIV
The greater the affect with which we imagine the beloved thing to be affected toward us, the more we shall glory.
DEMONSTRATION

We strive (by the preceding Proposition), as far as we can, that the beloved thing should love us in return; that is (by the Scholium to Prop. 13 of this Part), that the beloved thing should be affected with Joy accompanied by the idea of ourselves. Therefore, the greater the Joy with which we imagine the beloved thing to be affected on our account, the more this striving is assisted; that is (by Prop. 11 of this Part with its Scholium), the greater the Joy with which we are affected. But when we rejoice because we have affected another similar to ourselves with Joy, then we contemplate ourselves with Joy (by Prop. 30 of this Part); therefore, the greater the affect with which we imagine the beloved thing to be affected toward us, the greater the Joy with which we shall contemplate ourselves, or (by the Scholium to Prop. 30 of this Part) the more we shall glory. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XXXV

If anyone imagines that a beloved thing is joining another to itself by the same or a closer bond of Friendship than that by which he alone possessed the same thing, he will be affected with Hatred toward the beloved thing itself, and will envy that other person.
DEMONSTRATION

The greater the love with which anyone imagines the beloved thing to be affected toward him, the more he will glory (by the preceding Proposition), that is (by the Scholium to Prop. 30 of this Part), he will rejoice; and consequently (by Prop. 28 of this Part) he will strive, as far as he can, to imagine the beloved thing bound to him as closely as possible; which striving, or appetite, is indeed fostered if he imagines that another desires the same thing for himself (by Prop. 31 of this Part). But this striving, or appetite, is supposed to be checked by the image of the beloved thing itself accompanied by the image of the one whom the beloved thing joins to itself; therefore (by the Scholium to Prop. 11 of this Part) he will thereby be affected with Sadness, accompanied by the idea of the beloved thing as a cause, and at the same time by the image of the other person; that is (by the Scholium to Prop. 13 of this Part), he will be affected with hatred toward the beloved thing, and at the same time toward that other person (by the Corollary to Prop. 15 of this Part), whom consequently (by Prop. 23 of this Part), because he delights in the beloved thing, he will envy. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

This Hatred toward the beloved thing, joined with Envy, is called Jealousy, which is therefore nothing but a fluctuation of the mind arising from Love and Hatred together, accompanied by the idea of another whom one envies. Moreover, this Hatred toward the beloved thing will be greater in proportion to the Joy by which the jealous person used to be affected from the reciprocal Love of the beloved thing, and also in proportion to the affect by which he was affected toward the person whom he imagines to be joining the beloved thing to himself. For if he hated him, by that very fact he will hate the beloved thing (by Prop. 24 of this Part), because he imagines that it affects with Joy that which he hates; and also (by the Corollary to Prop. 15 of this Part), because he is compelled to join the image of the beloved thing to the image of him whom he hates.

This account has for the most part a place in Love toward a woman; for he who imagines that the woman whom he loves prostitutes herself to another will be saddened not only because his own appetite is checked, but also because, being compelled to join the image of the beloved thing to the genitals and excrements of another, he is averse to her; to which there finally is added that the jealous person is not received by the beloved thing with the same countenance which it used to present to him, for which reason also the lover is saddened, as I shall now show.
PROPOSITION XXXVI
He who recalls a thing by which he was once delighted desires to possess the same thing with the same circumstances as when he was first delighted by it.
DEMONSTRATION

Whatever a man saw at the same time as the thing which delighted him, all of it will be, by accident, a cause of Joy (by Prop. 15 of this Part); and consequently (by Prop. 28 of this Part) he will desire to possess all of it together with the thing which delighted him, or to possess the thing with all the same circumstances as when he was first delighted by it. Q. E. D.
COROLLARY
If, therefore, he discovers that one of those circumstances is lacking, the lover will be saddened.
DEMONSTRATION

For insofar as he finds that some circumstance is lacking, to that extent he imagines something which excludes the existence of that thing. But since he is desirous of that thing or circumstance out of love (by the preceding Prop.), therefore (by Prop. 19 of this Part), insofar as he imagines it to be lacking, he will be saddened. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM
This Sadness, insofar as it concerns the absence of what we love, is called Desire.
PROPOSITION XXXVII
Desire which arises from Sadness or Joy, and from Hatred or Love, is greater in proportion as the affect is greater.
DEMONSTRATION

Sadness diminishes or restrains a man's power of acting (by the Schol. of Prop. 11 of this Part), that is (by Prop. 7 of this Part), it diminishes or restrains the striving by which a man strives to persevere in his being; and therefore (by Prop. 5 of this Part) it is contrary to this striving; and whatever a man affected with Sadness strives for is to remove Sadness. But (by the Def. of Sadness), the greater the Sadness, the greater the part of the man's power of acting to which it must be opposed; therefore the greater the Sadness, the greater the power of acting with which the man will strive to remove Sadness; that is (by the Schol. of Prop. 9 of this Part), with the greater desire or appetite he will strive to remove Sadness. Further, since Joy (by the same Schol. of Prop. 11 of this Part) increases or assists a man's power of acting, it is easily demonstrated in the same way that a man affected with Joy desires nothing other than to preserve it, and does so with the greater Desire, the greater the Joy may be.

Finally, since Hatred and Love are themselves affects of Sadness or Joy, it follows in the same manner that the striving, appetite, or Desire which arises from Hatred or Love will be greater in proportion to the Hatred and Love. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XXXVIII

If someone begins to hate a thing loved, so that Love is utterly abolished, he will pursue it, from an equal cause, with greater hatred than if he had never loved it, and with so much the greater hatred as the Love had previously been greater.
DEMONSTRATION

For if someone begins to hate a thing which he loves, more of his appetites are restrained than if he had not loved it. For Love is Joy (by the Schol. of Prop. 13 of this Part), which a man strives, as far as he can (by Prop. 28 of this Part), to preserve; and this he does (by the same Schol.) by contemplating the loved thing as present, and by affecting it with Joy, as far as he can (by Prop. 21 of this Part); which striving indeed (by the preceding Prop.) is greater the greater the love is, as is also the striving to bring it about that the loved thing should love him in return (see Prop. 33 of this Part).
