But these strivings are restrained by hatred toward the loved thing (by the Corollary of Prop. 13 and by Prop. 23 of this Part); therefore the lover (by the Schol. of Prop. 11 of this Part) will for this reason also be affected with Sadness, and with so much the greater Sadness as the Love had been greater; that is, besides the Sadness which was the cause of Hatred, another arises from the fact that he loved the thing, and consequently he will contemplate the loved thing with a greater affect of Sadness, that is (by the Schol.
of Prop. 13 of this Part) he will pursue it with greater hatred than if he had not loved it, and with so much the greater hatred as the love had been greater. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XXXIX

He who hates someone will strive to inflict evil upon him, unless he fears that a greater evil will arise for himself from it; and conversely, he who loves someone will strive, by the same law, to do him good.
DEMONSTRATION

To hate someone is (by the Schol. of Prop. 13 of this Part) to imagine someone as a cause of Sadness; and therefore (by Prop. 28 of this Part), he who hates someone will strive to remove or destroy him. But if he fears from this something sadder, or (which is the same) a greater evil, for himself, and believes that he can avoid it by not inflicting upon him whom he hates the evil which he had intended, he will desire to abstain from inflicting the evil (by the same Prop. 28 of this Part); and this (by Prop. 37 of this Part) with a greater striving than that by which he was impelled to inflict evil, which therefore will prevail, as we wished. The demonstration of the second part proceeds in the same manner. Therefore, he who hates someone, etc. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

By good here I understand every kind of Joy, and whatever further contributes to it, and especially that which satisfies desire, whatever that may be. By evil, however, I understand every kind of Sadness, and especially that which frustrates desire. For we have shown above (in the Schol. of Prop. 9 of this Part) that we desire nothing because we judge it to be good; but, on the contrary, we call good that which we desire; and consequently we call evil that which we are averse to; wherefore each judges or esteems, from his own affect, what is good, what evil, what better, what worse, and finally what is best and what worst. Thus the Avaricious man judges an abundance of money to be best, but a lack of it to be worst. The Ambitious man, however, desires nothing so much as Glory, and dreads nothing so much as Shame.

Further, to the Envious nothing is more pleasing than another's misfortune, and nothing more troublesome than another's good fortune; and thus each judges, from his own affect, that some thing is good or bad, useful or useless. Moreover, this affect by which a man is so disposed that he is unwilling to will what he wills, or that he wills what he does not will, is called Fear, which therefore is nothing other than timidity insofar as a man is thereby disposed to avoid, by a lesser evil, an evil which he judges to be future (See Prop. 28 of this Part). But if the evil which he fears is Shame, then Fear is called Modesty. Finally, if the Desire of avoiding a future evil is restrained by Fear of another evil, so that he does not know what he would rather will, then Fear is called Consternation, especially if each of the two evils feared is among the greatest.
PROPOSITION XL
He who imagines that he is hated by someone, and does not believe that he has given him any cause for hatred, will in turn hate him.
DEMONSTRATION

He who imagines someone affected with hatred will thereby also be affected with hatred (by Prop. 27 of this Part), that is (by the Schol. of Prop. 13 of this Part), with Sadness accompanied by the idea of an external cause. But he (by the hypothesis) imagines no cause of this Sadness besides the one who hates him; therefore, from imagining himself to be hated by someone, he will be affected with Sadness accompanied by the idea of him who hates him, or (by the same Schol.) he will hate him in return. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

But if he imagines that he has furnished a just cause for Hatred, then (by Prop. 30 of this Part and its Scholium) he will be affected with Shame. But this (by Prop. 25 of this Part) rarely happens. Moreover, this reciprocation of Hatred can also arise from the fact that Hatred is followed by an endeavor to inflict evil upon him who is hated (by Prop. 39 of this Part). Therefore, he who imagines that he is hated by someone will imagine that same person to be the cause of some evil or Sadness; and thus he will be affected with Sadness, or Fear, accompanied by the idea of him who hates him as cause, that is, he will in return be affected with Hatred, as above.
COROLLARY I

He who imagines that one whom he loves is affected with Hatred toward him will be torn by Hatred and Love at the same time. For insofar as he imagines that he is hated by that person, he is determined (by the preceding Prop.) to hate that person in return. But (by hypothesis) he nevertheless loves him; therefore he will be torn by Hatred and Love at the same time.
COROLLARY II

If anyone imagines that some evil has been inflicted upon him out of Hatred by someone whom he had previously pursued with no affect, he will immediately endeavor to repay that same evil to that person.
DEMONSTRATION

He who imagines that someone is affected with Hatred toward him will hate him in return (by the preceding Prop.), and (by Prop. 26 of this Part) will endeavor to devise everything that can affect him with Sadness, and (by Prop. 39 of this Part) will strive to inflict it upon him. But (by hypothesis) the first thing that he imagines of this kind is an evil inflicted upon himself; therefore he will immediately endeavor to inflict the same upon him. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM
The endeavor to inflict evil upon one whom we hate is called Anger; but the endeavor to repay an evil inflicted upon us is called Vengeance.
PROPOSITION XLI

If anyone imagines that he is loved by someone, and does not believe that he has given any cause for this (which can occur by Coroll. of Prop. 15 and by Prop. 16 of this Part), he will love that person in return.
DEMONSTRATION
This Proposition is demonstrated by the same method as the preceding one. See also its Scholium.
SCHOLIUM

But if he believes that he has furnished a just cause for Love, he will glory (by Prop. 30 of this Part together with its Scholium); and this indeed (by Prop. 25 of this Part) happens more frequently, and we said that its contrary occurs when someone imagines that he is hated by someone else (see Schol. of the preceding Prop.). Furthermore, this reciprocal Love, and consequently (by Prop. 39 of this Part) the endeavor to do good to one who loves us and who (by the same Prop. 39 of this Part) endeavors to do good to us, is called Favor or Gratitude; and thus it appears that men are far more ready for Vengeance than for returning a benefit.
COROLLARY
He who imagines that he is loved by one whom he hates will be torn by Hatred and Love at the same time. This is demonstrated by the same method as the first Corollary of the preceding Proposition.
SCHOLIUM

But if Hatred prevails, he will endeavor to inflict evil upon him by whom he is loved; this affect is called Cruelty, especially if he who loves is believed to have furnished no common cause of Hatred.
PROPOSITION XLII
He who, moved by Love or by hope of Glory, has conferred a benefit upon someone will be saddened if he sees the benefit received with an ungrateful mind.
DEMONSTRATION

He who loves some thing like himself endeavors, as far as he can, to bring it about that he is loved in return by it (by Prop. 33 of this Part). Therefore, he who out of love has conferred a benefit upon someone has done so from the desire by which he is bound to be loved in return, that is (by Prop. 34 of this Part), from hope of Glory, or (by the Schol. of Prop. 30 of this Part) of Joy; and consequently (by Prop. 12 of this Part) he will endeavor, as far as he can, to imagine this cause of Glory, or to contemplate it as actually existing. But (by hypothesis) he imagines something else which excludes the existence of that cause; therefore (by Prop. 19 of this Part) he will thereby be saddened. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XLIII
Hatred is increased by reciprocal hatred, and can, on the other hand, be destroyed by Love.
DEMONSTRATION

He who imagines that he whom he hates is affected toward him with reciprocal Hatred, by that very fact (by Prop. 40 of this Part) a new Hatred arises, while the first (by hypothesis) still endures. But if, on the contrary, he imagines that the same person is affected toward him with Love, insofar as he imagines this, he contemplates himself with Joy (by Prop. 30 of this Part), and insofar (by Prop. 29 of this Part) he will strive to please him; that is (by Prop. 41 of this Part), insofar he strives not to hate him and not to affect him with any Sadness; and this striving (by Prop. 37 of this Part) will be greater or less in proportion to the affect from which it arises. And therefore, if it is greater than that which arises from Hatred, and by which he strives to affect with Sadness the thing which he hates (by Prop. 26 of this Part), it will prevail over it and will erase hatred from the mind. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XLIV
Hatred which is wholly conquered by Love passes into Love; and Love is therefore greater than if Hatred had not preceded it.
DEMONSTRATION

It proceeds in the same way as in Proposition 38 of this Part. For he who begins to love a thing which he hates, or which he was accustomed to contemplate with Sadness, rejoices by that very fact that he loves; and to this Joy, which Love involves (see its Definition in the Scholium to Prop. 13 of this Part), there is added also that which arises from the fact that the striving to remove the Sadness which Hatred involves (as we showed in Prop. 37 of this Part) is wholly aided, accompanied by the idea, as cause, of him whom he hated.
SCHOLIUM

Although things stand thus, nevertheless no one will strive to hate any thing, or to be affected with Sadness, in order that he may enjoy this greater Joy; that is, no one will desire that harm be inflicted upon him in the hope of recovering a loss, nor will he desire to be ill in the hope of recovering. For everyone will always strive to preserve his own being and to remove Sadness, as far as he can. But if, on the contrary, it could be conceived that a man could desire to hate someone, so that he might afterward pursue him with greater love, then he would always desire to hate him. For the greater the Hatred, the greater will be the Love; and consequently he would always desire that the Hatred be increased more and more. And for the same reason a man would strive to be ill more and more, so that he might afterward enjoy greater Joy from restored health; and consequently he would always strive to be ill, which (by Prop. 6 of this Part) is absurd.
PROPOSITION XLV
If someone imagines that one like himself is affected with Hatred toward a thing like himself which he loves, he will hate him.
DEMONSTRATION

For the loved thing has reciprocal hatred toward him who hates it (by Prop. 40 of this Part); and thus the lover who imagines that someone hates the loved thing, by that very fact imagines the loved thing to be affected with Hatred, that is (by the Scholium to Prop. 13 of this Part), with Sadness; and consequently (by Prop. 21 of this Part) he is saddened, accompanied by the idea, as cause, of him who hates the loved thing; that is (by the Scholium to Prop. 13 of this Part), he will hate him. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XLVI

If anyone has been affected with Joy or Sadness by someone of a class or nation different from his own, accompanied by the idea of that person, under the universal name of the class or nation, as cause: he will love or hate not only that person, but all of the same class or nation.
DEMONSTRATION
The demonstration of this is evident from Proposition 16 of this Part.
PROPOSITION XLVII
The Joy which arises from our imagining that a thing which we hate is destroyed or affected by some other evil does not arise without some Sadness of mind.
DEMONSTRATION
This is evident from Prop. 27 of this Part. For insofar as we imagine a thing like ourselves to be affected with Sadness, we are saddened.
SCHOLIUM

This Proposition can also be demonstrated from the Corollary to Proposition 17 of Part II. For whenever we remember a thing, although it does not actually exist, we nevertheless contemplate it as present, and the Body is affected in the same way. Therefore, insofar as the memory of the thing remains vigorous, a man is determined to contemplate it with Sadness; which determination, while the image of the thing still remains, is indeed restrained by the memory of those things which exclude its existence, but is not removed. And therefore a man rejoices only insofar as this determination is restrained; and hence it comes about that this Joy, which arises from the evil of a thing which we hate, is repeated as often as we remember that same thing. For, as we have said, when the image of that same thing is aroused, because it involves the existence of the thing itself, it determines a man to contemplate the thing with the same Sadness with which he was accustomed to contemplate it when it existed.

But because he has joined to the image of the same thing other images which exclude its existence, this determination toward Sadness is immediately restrained, and the man rejoices anew; and this happens as often as this repetition occurs. And this is likewise the cause why men rejoice whenever they recall some evil now past, and why they delight in recounting dangers from which they have been freed. For when they imagine some danger, they contemplate it as if it were still to come, and are determined to fear it; which determination is anew restrained by the idea of freedom, which they joined to the idea of this danger when they were freed from it, and which makes them secure anew; and consequently they rejoice anew.
PROPOSITION XLVIII

Love and Hatred, for example toward Peter, are destroyed if the Sadness which the latter, and the Joy which the former involves, are joined to the idea of another cause; and each is diminished insofar as we imagine that Peter was not the sole cause of either.
DEMONSTRATION

This is evident from the definition of Love and Hatred alone; see it in the Scholium to Proposition 13 of this Part. For it is solely because of this that Joy is called Love, and Sadness Hatred, toward Peter: namely, because Peter is considered to be the cause of this or that affect. Therefore, if this is wholly or in part removed, the affect toward Peter likewise is wholly or in part diminished. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XLIX
Love and Hatred toward a thing which we imagine to be free must, from an equal cause, each be greater than toward a necessary thing.
DEMONSTRATION

A thing which we imagine to be free must (by Def. 7, Part I) be perceived through itself, without other things. If, therefore, we imagine it to be the cause of Joy or Sadness, by that very fact (by the Scholium to Prop. 13 of this Part) we shall love or hate it; and this (by the preceding Prop.) with the greatest Love or Hatred which can arise from the given affect. But if we imagine as necessary the thing which is the cause of the same affect, then (by the same Def. 7, Part I) we shall imagine it to be not the sole cause, but a cause of the same affect together with others; and consequently (by the preceding Prop.) Love and Hatred toward it will be less. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

From this it follows that men, because they believe themselves to be free, pursue one another with greater Love or Hatred than they do other things; to which is added the imitation of the affects, concerning which see Props. 27, 34, 40, and 43 of this Part.
PROPOSITION L
Anything whatsoever can accidentally be a cause of Hope or Fear.
DEMONSTRATION
This Proposition is demonstrated in the same way as Proposition 15 of this Part; see that together with Scholium 2 to Proposition 18 of this Part.
SCHOLIUM

Things which are accidentally causes of Hope or Fear are called good or bad omens. Further, insofar as these same omens are causes of Hope or Fear, they are (by the definition of Hope and Fear, which see in Scholium 2 to Prop. 18 of this Part) causes of Joy or Sadness, and consequently (by the Corollary to Prop. 15 of this Part) insofar as this is so, we love or hate them, and (by Prop. 28 of this Part) endeavor to use them as means for attaining the things we hope for, or to remove them as obstacles or causes of Fear. Moreover, from Proposition 25 of this Part it follows that we are so constituted by nature that we easily believe those things which we hope for, but with difficulty those which we fear, and that we judge of them more or less favorably than is just. And from these have arisen the Superstitions with which men everywhere are afflicted.

Besides, I do not think it worth the trouble here to set forth the fluctuations of mind which arise from Hope and Fear; since from the definition of these affects alone it follows that there can be no Hope without Fear, nor Fear without Hope (as we shall explain more fully in its place); and further, since insofar as we hope or fear something, we love or hate it; and therefore whatever we have said concerning Love and Hatred, anyone will easily be able to apply to Hope and Fear.
PROPOSITION LI
Different men can be affected in different ways by one and the same object, and one and the same man can be affected in different ways by one and the same object at different times.
DEMONSTRATION

The human Body (by Post. 3, Part II) is affected in very many ways by external bodies. Therefore, at the same time two men can be affected in different ways; and consequently (by Axiom 1, which follows Lemma 3, see it after Prop. 13, Part II) they can be affected in different ways by one and the same object. Further (by the same Postulate), the human Body can now be affected in this way, now in another way; and consequently (by the same Axiom) it can be affected in different ways by one and the same object at different times. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

sources.title: Pars tertia - De origine et natura affectuum · passage 4
sources.text:
Videmus itaque fieri posse, ut quod hic amat, alter odio habeat ; et quod hic metuit, alter non metuat ; et ut unus idemque homo jam amet, quod antea oderit, et ut jam audeat, quod antea timuit, etc. Deinde quia unusquisque ex suo affectu judicat, quid bonum, quid malum, quid melius, et quid pejus sit (vide Schol. Prop. 39 hujus), sequitur, homines tam judicio quam affectu variare posse ; et hinc fit, ut cum alios aliis comparamus, ex sola affectuum differentia a nobis distinguantur, et ut alios intrepidos, alios timidos, alios denique alio nomine appellemus. Ex. gr. illum ego intrepidum vocabo, qui malum contemnit, quod ego timere soleo ; et si præterea ad hoc attendam, quod ejus Cupiditas malum inferendi ei, quem odit, et benefaciendi ei, quem amat, non coercetur timore mali, a quo ego contineri soleo, ipsum audacem appellabo. Deinde ille mihi timidus videbitur, qui malum timet, quod ego contemnere soleo ; et si insuper ad hoc attendam, quod ejus Cupiditas coercetur timore mali, quod me continere nequit, ipsum pusillanimem esse dicam ; et sic unusquisque judicabit. Denique ex hac hominis natura et judicii inconstantia, ut et quod homo sæpe ex solo affectu de rebus judicat, et quod res, quas ad Lætitiam vel Tristitiam facere credit, quasque propterea (per Prop. 28 hujus), ut fiant, promovere, vel amovere conatur, sæpe non nisi imaginariæ sint ; ut jam taceam alia, quæ in 2 Parte ostendimus, de rerum incertitudine ; facile concipimus, hominem posse sæpe in causa esse, tam ut contristetur, quam ut lætetur, sive ut tam Tristitia quam Lætitia afficiatur, concomitante idea sui tanquam causa ; atque adeo facile intelligimus, quid Pœnitentia, et quid Acquiescentia in se ipso sit. Nempe Pœnitentia est Tristitia concomitante idea sui, et Acquiescentia in se ipso est Lætitia concomitante idea sui, tanquam causa, et hi affectus vehementissimi sunt, quia homines se liberos esse credunt (vid. Prop. 49 hujus).

PROPOSITIO LII

Objectum, quod simul cum aliis antea vidimus, vel quod nihil habere imaginamur, nisi quod commune est pluribus, non tamdiu contemplabimur, ac illud, quod aliquid singulare habere imaginamur.

DEMONSTRATIO

Simulatque objectum, quod cum aliis vidimus, imaginamur, statim et aliorum recordamur (per Prop. 18 p. II, cujus etiam Schol. vide), et sic ex unius contemplatione statim in contemplationem alterius incidimus. Atque eadem est ratio objecti, quod nihil habere imaginamur, nisi quod commune est pluribus. Nam eo ipso supponimus, nos nihil in eo contemplari, quod antea cum aliis non viderimus. Verum cum supponimus, nos in objecto aliquo aliquid singulare, quod antea nunquam vidimus, imaginari, nihil aliud dicimus, quam quod Mens, dum illud objectum contemplatur, nullum aliud in se habeat, in cujus contemplationem ex contemplatione illius incidere potest ; atque adeo ad illud solum contemplandum determinata est. Ergo objectum, etc. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Hæc Mentis affectio, sive rei singularis imaginatio, quatenus sola in Mente versatur, vocatur Admiratio ; quæ si ab objecto, quod timemus, moveatur, Consternatio dicitur, quia mali Admiratio hominem suspensum in sola sui contemplatione ita tenet, ut de aliis cogitare non valeat, quibus illud malum vitare posset. Sed si id, quod admiramur, sit hominis alicujus prudentia, industria, vel aliquid hujusmodi, quia eo ipso hominem nobis longe antecellere contemplamur, tum Admiratio vocatur Veneratio ; alias Horror, si hominis iram, invidiam, etc., admiramur. Deinde, si hominis, quem amamus, prudentiam, industriam, etc., admiramur, Amor eo ipso (per Prop. 12 hujus) major erit, et hunc Amorem Admirationi sive Venerationi junctum Devotionem vocamus. Et ad hunc modum concipere etiam possumus Odium, Spem, Securitatem, et alios Affectus Admirationi junctos ; atque adeo plures Affectus deducere poterimus, quam qui receptis vocabulis indicari solent. Unde apparet, Affectuum nomina inventa esse magis ex eorum vulgari usu, quam ex eorundem accurata cognitione.

Admirationi opponitur Contemptus, cujus tamen causa hæc plerumque est, quod sc. ex eo, quod aliquem rem aliquam admirari, amare, metuere, etc., videmus, vel ex eo, quod res aliqua primo aspectu apparet, similis rebus, quas admiramur, amamus, metuimus, etc. (per Prop. 15 cum ejus Coroll. et Prop. 27 hujus), determinamur ad eandem rem admirandum, amandum, metuendum, etc. Sed si ex ipsius rei præsentia, vel accuratiore contemplatione, id omne de eadem negare cogamur, quod causa Admirationis, Amoris, Metus, etc. esse potest, tum Mens ex ipsa rei præsentia magis ad ea cogitandum, quæ in objecto non sunt, quam quæ in ipso sunt, determinata manet ; cum tamen contra ex objecti præsentia id præcipue cogitare soleat, quod id objecto est. Porro sicut Devotio ex rei, quam amamus, Admiratione, sic Irrisio ex rei, quam odimus vel metuimus, Contemptu oritur, et Dedignatio ex stultitiæ Contemptu, sicuti Veneratio ex Admiratione prudentiæ. Possumus denique, Amorem, Spem, Gloriam, et alios Affectus junctos Contemptui concipere atque inde alios præterea Affectus deducere, quos etiam nullo singulari vocabulo ab aliis distinguera solemus.

PROPOSITIO LIII

Cum Mens se ipsam, suamque agendi potentiam contemplatur, lætatur ; et eo magis, quo se suamque agendi potentiam distinctius imaginatur.

DEMONSTRATIO

Homo se ipsum non cognoscit, nisi per affectiones sui Corporis earumque ideas (per Prop. 19 et 23 p. II). Cum ergo fit, ut Mens se ipsam possit contemplari, eo ipso ad majorem perfectionem transire, hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 11 hujus), Lætitia affici supponitur et eo majori, quo se suamque agendi potentiam distinctius imaginari potest. Q. E. D.

COROLLARIUM

Hæc Lætitia magis magisque fovetur, quo magis homo se ab aliis laudari imaginatur. Nam quo magis se ab aliis laudari imaginatur, eo majori Lætitia alios ab ipso affici imaginatur, idque concomitante idea sui (per Schol. Prop. 29 hujus) ; atque adeo (per Prop. 27 hujus) ipse majore Lætitia concomitante idea sui afficitur. Q. E. D.

PROPOSITIO LIV

Mens ea tantum imaginari conatur, quæ ipsius agendi potentiam ponunt.

DEMONSTRATIO

Mentis conatus sive potentia est ipsa ipsius Mentis essentia (per Prop. 7 hujus) ; Mentis autem essentia (ut per se notum) id tantum, quod Mens est et potest, affirmat ; at non id, quod non est neque potest ; adeoque id tantum imaginari conatur, quod ipsius agendi potentiam affirmat sive ponit. Q. E. D.

PROPOSITIO LV

Cum Mens suam impotentiam imaginatur, eo ipso contristatur.

DEMONSTRATIO

Mentis essentia id tantum, quod Mens est et potest, affirmat, sive de natura Mentis est, ea tantummodo imaginari, quæ ipsius agendi potentiam ponunt (per Prop. præced.). Cum itaque dicimus, quod Mens, dum se ipsam contemplatur, suam imaginatur impotentiam, nihil aliud dicimus, quam quod, dum Mens aliquid imaginari conatur, quod ipsius agendi potentiam ponit, hic ejus conatus coercetur, sive (per Schol. Prop. 11 hujus) quod ipsa contristatur. Q. E. D.

COROLLARIUM

Hæc Tristitia magis ac magis fovetur, si se ab aliis vituperari imaginatur ; quod eodem demonstratur, ac Coroll. Prop. 53 hujus.

SCHOLIUM

Hæc Tristitia concomitante idea nostræ imbecillitatis Humilitas appellatur ; Lætitia autem, quæ ex contemplatione nostri oritur, Philautia, vel Acquiescentia in se ipso vocatur. Et quoniam hæc toties repetitur, quoties homo suas virtutes sive suam agendi potentiam contemplatur, hinc ergo etiam fit, ut unusquisque facta sua narrare, suique tam corporis quam animi vires ostentare gestiat, et ut homines hac de causa sibi invicem molesti sint. Ex quibus iterum sequitur, homines natura esse invidos (vid. Schol. Prop. 24 et Schol. Prop. 32 hujus), sive ob suorum æqualium imbecillitatem gaudere, et contra propter eorundem virtutem contristari. Nam quoties unusquisque suas actiones imaginatur, toties Lætitia (per Prop. 53 hujus) afficitur, et eo majore, quo actiones plus perfectionis exprimere, et easdem distinctius imaginatur ; hoc est (per illa, quæ in Schol. 1 Prop. 40 p. II dicta sunt), quo magis easdem ab aliis distinguere et ut res singulares contemplari potest. Quare unusquisque ex contemplatione sui tunc maxime gaudebit, quando aliquid in se contemplatur, quod de reliquis negat. Sed si id, quod de se affirmat, ad universalem hominis vel animalis ideam refert, non tantopere gaudebit ; et contra contristabitur, si suas, ad aliorum actiones comparatas, imbecilliores esse imaginetur ; quam quidem Tristitiam (per Prop. 28 hujus) amovere conabitur, idque suorum æqualium actiones perperam interpretando, vel suas quantum potest adornando. Apparet igitur, homines natura proclives esse ad Odium et Invidiam, ad quam accedit ipsa educatio. Nam parentes solo honoris et Invidiæ stimulo liberos ad virtutem concitare solent. Sed scrupulus forsan remanet, quod non raro hominum virtutes admiremur, eosque veneremur. Hunc ergo ut amoveam, sequens addam Corollarium.

COROLLARIUM

Nemo virtutem alicui, nisi æquali, invidet.

DEMONSTRATIO

Invidia est ipsum Odium (vid. Schol. Prop. 24 hujus), sive (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus) Tristitia, hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 11 hujus) affectio, qua hominis agendi potentia seu conatus coercetur. At homo (per Schol. Prop. 9 hujus) nihil agere conatur neque cupit, nisi quod ex data sua natura sequi potest ; ergo homo nullam de se agendi potentiam seu (quod idem est) virtutem prædicari cupiet, quæ naturæ alterius est propria, et suæ aliena ; adeoque ejus Cupiditas coerceri, hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 11 hujus) ipse contristari, nequit ex eo, quod aliquam virtutem in aliquo ipsi dissimili contemplatur, et consequenter neque ei invidere poterit. At quidem suo æquali, qui cum ipso ejusdem naturæ supponitur. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Cum igitur supra in Scholio Propositionis 52 hujus Partis dixerimus, nos hominem venerari ex eo, quod ipsius prudentiam, fortitudinem, etc., admiramur, id fit (ut ex ipsa Prop. patet) quia has virtutes et singulariter inesse, et non ut nostræ naturæ communes imaginamur ; adeoque easdem ipsi non magis invidebimus, quam arboribus altitudinem, et leonibus fortitudinem, etc.

PROPOSITIO LVI

Lætitiæ, Tristitiæ, et Cupiditatis, et consequenter uniuscujusque affectus, qui ex his componitur, ut animi Fluctuationis, vel qui ab his derivatur nempe Amoris, Odii, Spei, Metus, etc., tot species dantur, quot sunt species objectorum, a quibus afficimur.

DEMONSTRATIO

Lætitia et Tristitia, et consequenter affectus, qui ex his componuntur vel ex his derivantur, passiones sunt (per Schol. Prop. 11 hujus) ; nos autem (per Prop. 1 hujus) necessario patimur, quatenus ideas habemus inadæquatas ; et quatenus easdem habemus (per Prop. 3 hujus), eatenus tantum patimur, hoc est (vid. Schol. 1 Prop. 40 p. II), eatenus tantum necessario patimur, quatenus imaginamur, sive (vid. Prop. 17 p. II cum ejus Schol.) quatenus afficimur affectu, qui naturam nostri Corporis et naturam corporis externi involvit. Natura igitur uniuscujusque passionis ita necessario debet explicari, ut objecti, a quo afficimur, natura exprimatur. Nempe Lætitia, quæ ex objecto ex. gr. A oritur, naturam ipsius objecti A, et Lætitia, quæ ex objecto B oritur ; ipsius objecti B naturam involvit ; atque adeo hi duo Lætitiæ affectus natura sunt diversi, quia ex causis diversæ naturæ oriuntur. Sic etiam Tristitiæ affectus, qui ex uno objecto oritur, diversus natura est a Tristitia, quæ ab alia causa oritur ; quod etiam de Amore, Odio, Spe, Metu, animi Fluctuatione, etc., intelligendum est : ac proinde Lætitiæ, Tristitiæ, Amoris, Odii, etc., tot species necessario dantur, quot sunt species objectorum, a quibus afficimur. At Cupiditas est ipsa uniuscujusque essentia, seu natura, quatenus ex data quacunque ejus constitutione determinata concipitur ad aliquid agendum (vid. Schol. Prop. 9 hujus) ; ergo, prout unusquisque a causis externis hac aut illa Lætitiæ, Tristitiæ, Amoris, Odii, etc., specie afficitur, hoc est, prout ejus natura hoc aut alio modo constituitur, ita ejus Cupiditas alia atque alia esse, et natura unius a natura alterius Cupiditatis tantum differre necesse est, quantum affectus, a quibus unaquæque oritur, inter se differunt. Dantur itaque tot species Cupiditatis, quot sunt species Lætitiæ, Tristitiæ, Amoris, etc., et consequenter (per jam ostensa) quot sunt objectorum species, a quibus afficimur. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Inter affectuum species, quæ (per Prop. præc.) perplurimæ esse debent, insignes sunt Luxuria, Ebrietas, Libido, Avaritia et Ambitio, quæ non nisi Amoris vel Cupiditatis sunt notiones, quæ hujus utriusque affectus naturam explicant per objecta, ad quæ referuntur. Nam per Luxuriam, Ebrietatem, Libidinem, Avaritiam, et Ambitionem nihil aliud intelligimus, quam convivandi, potandi, coeundi, divitiarum et gloriæ immoderatum Amorem vel Cupiditatem. Præterea hi affectus, quatenus eos per solum objectum, ad quod referuntur, ab aliis distinguimus, contrarios non habent. Nam Temperantia, quam Luxuriæ, et Sobrietas, quam Ebrietati, et denique Castitas, quam Libidini opponere solemus, affectus seu passiones non sunt, sed animi indicant potentiam, quæ hos affectus moderatur. Cæterum reliquas Affectuum species hic explicare nec possum (quia tot sunt, quot objectorum species), nec, si possem, necesse est. Nam ad id, quod intendimus, nempe ad affectuum vires, et Mentis in eosdem potentiam, determinandum, nobis sufficit, uniuscujusque affectus generalem habere definitionem. Sufficit, inquam, nobis, Affectuum et Mentis communes proprietates intelligere, ut determinare possimus, qualis et quanta sit Mentis potentia in moderandis et coercendis Affectibus. Quamvis itaque magna sit differentia inter hunc et illum Amoris, Odii, vel Cupiditatis affectum, ex. gr. inter Amorem erga liberos et inter amorem erga uxorem, nobis tamen has differentias cognoscere, et affectuum naturam et originem ulterius indagare, non est opus.

PROPOSITIO LVII

Quilibet uniuscujusque individui affectus ab affectu alterius tantum discrepat, quantum essentia unius ab essentia alterius differt.

DEMONSTRATIO

Hæc Propositio patet ex Axiom. 1, quod vide post Lem. 3 Schol. Prop. 13, p. 2. At nihilominus eandem ex trium primitivorum affectuum definitionibus demonstrabimus.

Omnes affectus ad Cupiditatem, Lætitiam, vel Tristitiam referuntur, ut eorum quas dedimus definitiones ostendunt. At Cupiditas est ipsa uniuscujusque natura seu essentia (vide ejus Defin. in Schol. Prop. 9 ujus) ; ergo uniuscujusque individui Cupiditas a Cupiditate alterius tantum discrepat, quantum natura seu essentia unius ab essentia alterius differt. Lætitia deinde et Tristitia passiones sunt, quibus uniuscujusque potentia seu conatus in suo esse perseverandi, augetur vel minuitur, juvatur vel coercetur (per Prop. 11 hujus et ejus Schol.). At per conatum in suo esse perseverandi, quatenus ad Mentem et Corpus simul refertur. Appetitum et Cupiditatem intelligimus (vide Schol. Prop. 9 hujus) ; ergo Lætitia et Tristitia est ipsa Cupiditas sive Appetitus, quatenus a causis externis augetur vel minuitur, juvatur vel coercetur, hoc est (per idem Schol.) est ipsa cujusque natura ; atque adeo uniuscujusque Lætitia vel Tristitia a Lætitia vel Tristitia alterius tantum etiam discrepat, quantum natura seu essentia unius ab essentia alterius differt et consequenter quilibet uniuscujusque individui affectus ab affectu alterius tantum discrepat, etc. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Hinc sequitur, affectus animalium, quæ irrationalia dicuntur (bruta enim sentire nequaquam dubitare possumus, postquam Mentis novimus originem), ab affectibus hominum tantum differre, quantum eorum natura a natura humana differt. Fertur quidem equus et homo Libidine procreandi ; at ille Libidine equina, hic autem humana. Sic etiam Libidines et Appetitus insectorum, piscium, et avium, alii atque alii esse debent. Quamvis itaque unumquodque individuum sua, qua constat natura contentum vivat eaque gaudeat, vita tamen illa, qua unumquodque est contentum, et gaudium nihil aliud est, quam idea seu anima ejusdem individui, atque adeo gaudium unius a gaudio alterius tantum natura discrepat, quantum essentia unius ab essentia alterius differt. Denique ex præcedenti Propositione sequitur, non parum etiam interesse inter gaudium, quo ebrius ex. gr. ducitur, et inter gaudium, quo potitur Philosophus, quod hic in transitu monere volui. Atque hæc de affectibus, qui ad hominem referuntur, quatenus patitur. Superest, ut pauca addam de iis, qui ad eundem referuntur, quatenus agit.

PROPOSITIO LVIII

Præter Lætitiam et Cupiditatem, quæ passiones sunt, alii Lætitiæ et Cupiditatis affectus dantur, qui ad nos, quatenus agimus, referuntur.

DEMONSTRATIO

Cum Mens se ipsam suamque agendi potentiam concipit, lætatur (per Prop. 53 hujus) : Mens autem se ipsam necessario contemplatur, quando veram sive adæquatam ideam concipit (per Prop. 43 p. II). At Mens quasdam ideas adæquatas concipit (per Schol. 2 Prop. 40 p. II). Ergo eatenus etiam lætatur, quatenus ideas adæquatas concipit, hoc est (per Prop. 1 hujus) quatenus agit. Deinde Mens tam quatenus claras et distinctas, quam quatenus confusas habeL ideas, in suo esse persevare conatur (per Prop. 9 hujus). At per conatum Cupiditatem intelligimus (per ejusdem Schol.) ; ergo Cupiditas ad nos refertur, etiam quatenus întelligimus, sive (per Prop. 1 hujus) quatenus agimus. Q. E. D.

PROPOSITIO LIX

Inter omnes affectus, qui ad Mentem, quatenus agit, referuntur, nulli sunt, quam qui ad Lætitiam vel Cupiditatem referuntur.

DEMONSTRATIO

Omnes affectus ad Cupiditatem, Lætitiam, vel Tristitiam referuntur, ut eorum quas dedimus, definitiones ostendunt. Per Tristitiam autem intelligimus, quod Mentis cogitandi potentia minuitur vel coercetur (per Prop. 11 hujus et ejus Schol.) ; adeoque Mens quatenus contristatur, eatenus ejus intelligendi, hoc est ejus agendi potentia (per Prop. 1 hujus) minuitur vel coercetur ; adeoque nulli Tristitiæ affectus ad Mentem referri possunt, quatenus agit ; sed tantum affectus Lætitiæ et Cupiditatis qui (per Prop. præc.) eatenus etiam ad Mentem referuntur. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Omnes actiones, quæ sequuntur ex affectibus, qui ad Mentem referuntur, quatenus intelligit ad Fortitudinem refero, quam in Animositatem et Generositatem distinguo. Nam per Animositatem intelligo Cupiditatem, qua unusquisque conatur suum esse ex solo Rationis dictamine conservare.

Per Generositatem autem Cupiditatem intelligo, qua unusquisque ex solo Rationis dictamine conatur reliquos homines juvare, et sibi amicitia jungere. Eas itaque actiones, quæ solum agentis utile intendunt, ad Animositatem, et quæ alterius etiam utile intendunt, ad Generositatem refero. Temperantia igitur, Sobrietas, et Animi in periculis Præsentia, etc. Animositatis sunt species ; Modestia autem, Clementia, etc., species Generositatis sunt. Atque his puto me præcipuos affectus, animique fluctuationes, quæ ex compositione trium primitivorum affectuum, nempe Cupiditatis, Lætitiæ, et Tristitiæ oriuntur, explicuisse, perque primas suas causas ostendisse. Ex quibus apparet, nos a causis externis multis modis agitari, nosque perinde ut maris undæ, a contrariis ventis agitatæ, fluctuari, nostri eventus atque fati inscios. At dixi, me præcipuos tantum, non omnes, qui dari possunt, animi conflictus ostendisse. Nam eadem via, qua supra, procedendo, facile possumus ostendere, Amorem esse junctum Pœnitentiæ, Dedignationi, Pudori, etc. Imo unicuique ex jam dictis clare constare credo, affectus tot modis alii cum aliis componi, indeque tot variationes oriri, ut nullo numero definiri queant. Sed ad meum institutum præcipuos tantum enumeravisse sufficit : nam reliqui, quos omisi, plus curiositatis quam utilitatis haberent. Attamen de Amore hoc notandum restat, quod scilicet sæpissime contingit, dum re, quam appetebamus, fruimur, ut Corpus ex ea fruitione novam acquirat constitutionem, a qua aliter determinatur, et aliæ rerum imagines in eo excitantur, et simul Mens alia imaginari, aliaque cupere incipit. Ex. gr. cum aliquid, quod nos sapore delectare solet, imaginamur, eodem frui, nempe comedere cupimus. At quamdiu eodem sic fruimur, stomachus adimpletur, Corpusque aliter constituitur. Si igitur, Corpore jam aliter disposito, ejusdem cibi imago, quia ipse præsens adest, fomentetur, et consequenter conatus etiam, sive Cupiditas, eundem comedendi ; huic Cupiditati seu conatui nova illa constitutio repugnabit, et consequenter cibi, quem appetebamus, præsentia odiosa erit, et hoc est quod Fastidium et Tædium vocamus. Cæterum Corporis affectiones externas, quæ in affectibus observantur, ut sunt tremor, livor, singultus, risus, etc., neglexi, quia ad solum Corpus absque ulla ad Mentem relatione referuntur. Denique de affectuum definitionibus quædam notanda sunt, quas propterea hic ordine repetam, et quid in unaquaque observandum est, iisdem interponam.

AFFECTUUM DEFINITIONES

I

Cupiditas est ipsa hominis essentia, quatenus ex data quacunque ejus affectione determinata concipitur ad aliquid agendum.

EXPLICATIO

Diximus supra in Scholio Propositions 9 hujus Partis, Cupiditatem esse appetitum cum ejusdem conscientia ; appetitum autem esse ipsam hominis essentiam, quatenus determinata est ad ea agendum quæ ipsius conservationi inserviunt. Sed in eodem Scholio etiam monui, me revera inter humanum appetitum et Cupiditatem nullam agnoscere differentiam. Nam sive homo sui appetitus sit conscius, sive non sit, manet tamen appetitus unus idemque ; a que adeo, ne tautologiam committere viderer, Cupiditatem per appetitum explicare nolui, sed eandem ita definire studui, ut omnes humanæ naturæ conatus, quos nomine appetitus, voluntatis, cupiditatis, vel impetus significamus, una comprehenderem. Potueram enim dicere, Cupiditatem esse ipsam hominis essentiam, quatenus determinata concipitur ad aliquid agendum ; sed ex hac definitione (per Prop. 23 p. II) non sequeretur, quod Mens possit suæ Cupiditatis sive appetitus esse conscia. Igitur, ut hujus conscientiæ causam involverem, necesse fuit (per eandem Prop.) addere, quatenus ex data quacunque ejus affectione determinata, etc. Nam per affectionem humanæ essentiæ quamcunque ejusdem essentiæ constitutionem intelligimus, sive ea sit innata, sive adventicia, sive quod ipsa per solum Cogitationis, sive per solum Extensionis attributum concipiatur, sive denique quod ad utrumque simul referatur. Hic igitur Cupiditatis nomine intelligo hominis quoscunque conatus, impetus, appetitus, et volitiones, qui pro varia ejusdem hominis constitutione varii, et non raro adeo sibi invicem oppositi sunt, ut homo diversimode trahatur, et, quo se vertat, nesciat.

II

Lætitia est hominis transitio a minore ad majorem perfectionem.

III

Tristitia est hominis transitio a majore ad minorem perfectionem.

EXPLICATIO

Dico transitionem. Nam Laetitia non est ipsa perfectio. Si enim homo cum perfectione, ad quam transit, nasceretur, ejusdem absque Lætitiæ affectu compos esset ; quod clarius apparet ex Tristitiæ affectu, qui huic est contrarius. Nam quod Tristitia in transitione ad minorem perfectionem consistit, non autem in ipsa minore perfectione, nemo negare potest quandoquidem homo eatenus contristari nequit, quatenus alicujus perfectionis est particeps. Nec dicere possumus, quod Tristitia in privatione majoris perfectionis consistat ; nam privatio nihil est, Tristitiæ autem affectus actus est, qui propterea nullus alius esse potest, quam actus transeundi ad minorem perfectionem hoc est, actus quo hominis agendi potentia minuitur vel coercetur (vide Schol. Prop. 11 hujus). Cæterum definitiones Hilaritatis, Titillationis, Melancholiæ, et Doloris omitto, quia ad Corpus potissimum referuntur, et non nisi Lætitiæ aut Tristitiæ sunt species.

IV

Admiratio est rei alicujus imaginatio, in qua Mens defixa propterea manet, quia hæc singularis imaginatio nullam cum reliquis habet connexionem (vide Prop. 52 hujus cum ejusdem Schol.)

EXPLICATIO

paragraphs.text: Videmus itaque fieri posse, ut quod hic amat, alter odio habeat ; et quod hic metuit, alter non metuat ; et ut unus idemque homo jam amet, quod antea oderit, et ut jam audeat, quod antea timuit, etc. Deinde quia unusquisque ex suo affectu judicat, quid bonum, quid malum, quid melius, et quid pejus sit (vide Schol. Prop. 39 hujus), sequitur, homines tam judicio quam affectu variare posse ; et hinc fit, ut cum alios aliis comparamus, ex sola affectuum differentia a nobis distinguantur, et ut alios intrepidos, alios timidos, alios denique alio nomine appellemus. Ex. gr. illum ego intrepidum vocabo, qui malum contemnit, quod ego timere soleo ; et si præterea ad hoc attendam, quod ejus Cupiditas malum inferendi ei, quem odit, et benefaciendi ei, quem amat, non coercetur timore mali, a quo ego contineri soleo, ipsum audacem appellabo.

Deinde ille mihi timidus videbitur, qui malum timet, quod ego contemnere soleo ; et si insuper ad hoc attendam, quod ejus Cupiditas coercetur timore mali, quod me continere nequit, ipsum pusillanimem esse dicam ; et sic unusquisque judicabit. Denique ex hac hominis natura et judicii inconstantia, ut et quod homo sæpe ex solo affectu de rebus judicat, et quod res, quas ad Lætitiam vel Tristitiam facere credit, quasque propterea (per Prop. 28 hujus), ut fiant, promovere, vel amovere conatur, sæpe non nisi imaginariæ sint ; ut jam taceam alia, quæ in 2 Parte ostendimus, de rerum incertitudine ; facile concipimus, hominem posse sæpe in causa esse, tam ut contristetur, quam ut lætetur, sive ut tam Tristitia quam Lætitia afficiatur, concomitante idea sui tanquam causa ; atque adeo facile intelligimus, quid Pœnitentia, et quid Acquiescentia in se ipso sit.

Nempe Pœnitentia est Tristitia concomitante idea sui, et Acquiescentia in se ipso est Lætitia concomitante idea sui, tanquam causa, et hi affectus vehementissimi sunt, quia homines se liberos esse credunt (vid. Prop. 49 hujus).
PROPOSITIO LII
Objectum, quod simul cum aliis antea vidimus, vel quod nihil habere imaginamur, nisi quod commune est pluribus, non tamdiu contemplabimur, ac illud, quod aliquid singulare habere imaginamur.
DEMONSTRATIO

Simulatque objectum, quod cum aliis vidimus, imaginamur, statim et aliorum recordamur (per Prop. 18 p. II, cujus etiam Schol. vide), et sic ex unius contemplatione statim in contemplationem alterius incidimus. Atque eadem est ratio objecti, quod nihil habere imaginamur, nisi quod commune est pluribus. Nam eo ipso supponimus, nos nihil in eo contemplari, quod antea cum aliis non viderimus. Verum cum supponimus, nos in objecto aliquo aliquid singulare, quod antea nunquam vidimus, imaginari, nihil aliud dicimus, quam quod Mens, dum illud objectum contemplatur, nullum aliud in se habeat, in cujus contemplationem ex contemplatione illius incidere potest ; atque adeo ad illud solum contemplandum determinata est. Ergo objectum, etc. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Hæc Mentis affectio, sive rei singularis imaginatio, quatenus sola in Mente versatur, vocatur Admiratio ; quæ si ab objecto, quod timemus, moveatur, Consternatio dicitur, quia mali Admiratio hominem suspensum in sola sui contemplatione ita tenet, ut de aliis cogitare non valeat, quibus illud malum vitare posset. Sed si id, quod admiramur, sit hominis alicujus prudentia, industria, vel aliquid hujusmodi, quia eo ipso hominem nobis longe antecellere contemplamur, tum Admiratio vocatur Veneratio ; alias Horror, si hominis iram, invidiam, etc., admiramur. Deinde, si hominis, quem amamus, prudentiam, industriam, etc., admiramur, Amor eo ipso (per Prop. 12 hujus) major erit, et hunc Amorem Admirationi sive Venerationi junctum Devotionem vocamus.

Et ad hunc modum concipere etiam possumus Odium, Spem, Securitatem, et alios Affectus Admirationi junctos ; atque adeo plures Affectus deducere poterimus, quam qui receptis vocabulis indicari solent. Unde apparet, Affectuum nomina inventa esse magis ex eorum vulgari usu, quam ex eorundem accurata cognitione.

Admirationi opponitur Contemptus, cujus tamen causa hæc plerumque est, quod sc. ex eo, quod aliquem rem aliquam admirari, amare, metuere, etc., videmus, vel ex eo, quod res aliqua primo aspectu apparet, similis rebus, quas admiramur, amamus, metuimus, etc. (per Prop. 15 cum ejus Coroll. et Prop. 27 hujus), determinamur ad eandem rem admirandum, amandum, metuendum, etc. Sed si ex ipsius rei præsentia, vel accuratiore contemplatione, id omne de eadem negare cogamur, quod causa Admirationis, Amoris, Metus, etc. esse potest, tum Mens ex ipsa rei præsentia magis ad ea cogitandum, quæ in objecto non sunt, quam quæ in ipso sunt, determinata manet ; cum tamen contra ex objecti præsentia id præcipue cogitare soleat, quod id objecto est.

Porro sicut Devotio ex rei, quam amamus, Admiratione, sic Irrisio ex rei, quam odimus vel metuimus, Contemptu oritur, et Dedignatio ex stultitiæ Contemptu, sicuti Veneratio ex Admiratione prudentiæ. Possumus denique, Amorem, Spem, Gloriam, et alios Affectus junctos Contemptui concipere atque inde alios præterea Affectus deducere, quos etiam nullo singulari vocabulo ab aliis distinguera solemus.
PROPOSITIO LIII
Cum Mens se ipsam, suamque agendi potentiam contemplatur, lætatur ; et eo magis, quo se suamque agendi potentiam distinctius imaginatur.
DEMONSTRATIO

Homo se ipsum non cognoscit, nisi per affectiones sui Corporis earumque ideas (per Prop. 19 et 23 p. II). Cum ergo fit, ut Mens se ipsam possit contemplari, eo ipso ad majorem perfectionem transire, hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 11 hujus), Lætitia affici supponitur et eo majori, quo se suamque agendi potentiam distinctius imaginari potest. Q. E. D.
COROLLARIUM

Hæc Lætitia magis magisque fovetur, quo magis homo se ab aliis laudari imaginatur. Nam quo magis se ab aliis laudari imaginatur, eo majori Lætitia alios ab ipso affici imaginatur, idque concomitante idea sui (per Schol. Prop. 29 hujus) ; atque adeo (per Prop. 27 hujus) ipse majore Lætitia concomitante idea sui afficitur. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITIO LIV
Mens ea tantum imaginari conatur, quæ ipsius agendi potentiam ponunt.
DEMONSTRATIO

Mentis conatus sive potentia est ipsa ipsius Mentis essentia (per Prop. 7 hujus) ; Mentis autem essentia (ut per se notum) id tantum, quod Mens est et potest, affirmat ; at non id, quod non est neque potest ; adeoque id tantum imaginari conatur, quod ipsius agendi potentiam affirmat sive ponit. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITIO LV
Cum Mens suam impotentiam imaginatur, eo ipso contristatur.
DEMONSTRATIO

Mentis essentia id tantum, quod Mens est et potest, affirmat, sive de natura Mentis est, ea tantummodo imaginari, quæ ipsius agendi potentiam ponunt (per Prop. præced.). Cum itaque dicimus, quod Mens, dum se ipsam contemplatur, suam imaginatur impotentiam, nihil aliud dicimus, quam quod, dum Mens aliquid imaginari conatur, quod ipsius agendi potentiam ponit, hic ejus conatus coercetur, sive (per Schol. Prop. 11 hujus) quod ipsa contristatur. Q. E. D.
COROLLARIUM
Hæc Tristitia magis ac magis fovetur, si se ab aliis vituperari imaginatur ; quod eodem demonstratur, ac Coroll. Prop. 53 hujus.
SCHOLIUM

Hæc Tristitia concomitante idea nostræ imbecillitatis Humilitas appellatur ; Lætitia autem, quæ ex contemplatione nostri oritur, Philautia, vel Acquiescentia in se ipso vocatur. Et quoniam hæc toties repetitur, quoties homo suas virtutes sive suam agendi potentiam contemplatur, hinc ergo etiam fit, ut unusquisque facta sua narrare, suique tam corporis quam animi vires ostentare gestiat, et ut homines hac de causa sibi invicem molesti sint. Ex quibus iterum sequitur, homines natura esse invidos (vid. Schol. Prop. 24 et Schol. Prop. 32 hujus), sive ob suorum æqualium imbecillitatem gaudere, et contra propter eorundem virtutem contristari. Nam quoties unusquisque suas actiones imaginatur, toties Lætitia (per Prop. 53 hujus) afficitur, et eo majore, quo actiones plus perfectionis exprimere, et easdem distinctius imaginatur ; hoc est (per illa, quæ in Schol. 1 Prop. 40 p.

II dicta sunt), quo magis easdem ab aliis distinguere et ut res singulares contemplari potest. Quare unusquisque ex contemplatione sui tunc maxime gaudebit, quando aliquid in se contemplatur, quod de reliquis negat. Sed si id, quod de se affirmat, ad universalem hominis vel animalis ideam refert, non tantopere gaudebit ; et contra contristabitur, si suas, ad aliorum actiones comparatas, imbecilliores esse imaginetur ; quam quidem Tristitiam (per Prop. 28 hujus) amovere conabitur, idque suorum æqualium actiones perperam interpretando, vel suas quantum potest adornando. Apparet igitur, homines natura proclives esse ad Odium et Invidiam, ad quam accedit ipsa educatio. Nam parentes solo honoris et Invidiæ stimulo liberos ad virtutem concitare solent. Sed scrupulus forsan remanet, quod non raro hominum virtutes admiremur, eosque veneremur. Hunc ergo ut amoveam, sequens addam Corollarium.
COROLLARIUM
Nemo virtutem alicui, nisi æquali, invidet.
DEMONSTRATIO

Invidia est ipsum Odium (vid. Schol. Prop. 24 hujus), sive (per Schol. Prop. 13 hujus) Tristitia, hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 11 hujus) affectio, qua hominis agendi potentia seu conatus coercetur. At homo (per Schol. Prop. 9 hujus) nihil agere conatur neque cupit, nisi quod ex data sua natura sequi potest ; ergo homo nullam de se agendi potentiam seu (quod idem est) virtutem prædicari cupiet, quæ naturæ alterius est propria, et suæ aliena ; adeoque ejus Cupiditas coerceri, hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 11 hujus) ipse contristari, nequit ex eo, quod aliquam virtutem in aliquo ipsi dissimili contemplatur, et consequenter neque ei invidere poterit. At quidem suo æquali, qui cum ipso ejusdem naturæ supponitur. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Cum igitur supra in Scholio Propositionis 52 hujus Partis dixerimus, nos hominem venerari ex eo, quod ipsius prudentiam, fortitudinem, etc., admiramur, id fit (ut ex ipsa Prop. patet) quia has virtutes et singulariter inesse, et non ut nostræ naturæ communes imaginamur ; adeoque easdem ipsi non magis invidebimus, quam arboribus altitudinem, et leonibus fortitudinem, etc.
PROPOSITIO LVI

Lætitiæ, Tristitiæ, et Cupiditatis, et consequenter uniuscujusque affectus, qui ex his componitur, ut animi Fluctuationis, vel qui ab his derivatur nempe Amoris, Odii, Spei, Metus, etc., tot species dantur, quot sunt species objectorum, a quibus afficimur.
DEMONSTRATIO

Lætitia et Tristitia, et consequenter affectus, qui ex his componuntur vel ex his derivantur, passiones sunt (per Schol. Prop. 11 hujus) ; nos autem (per Prop. 1 hujus) necessario patimur, quatenus ideas habemus inadæquatas ; et quatenus easdem habemus (per Prop. 3 hujus), eatenus tantum patimur, hoc est (vid. Schol. 1 Prop. 40 p. II), eatenus tantum necessario patimur, quatenus imaginamur, sive (vid. Prop. 17 p. II cum ejus Schol.) quatenus afficimur affectu, qui naturam nostri Corporis et naturam corporis externi involvit. Natura igitur uniuscujusque passionis ita necessario debet explicari, ut objecti, a quo afficimur, natura exprimatur. Nempe Lætitia, quæ ex objecto ex. gr. A oritur, naturam ipsius objecti A, et Lætitia, quæ ex objecto B oritur ; ipsius objecti B naturam involvit ; atque adeo hi duo Lætitiæ affectus natura sunt diversi, quia ex causis diversæ naturæ oriuntur.

Sic etiam Tristitiæ affectus, qui ex uno objecto oritur, diversus natura est a Tristitia, quæ ab alia causa oritur ; quod etiam de Amore, Odio, Spe, Metu, animi Fluctuatione, etc., intelligendum est : ac proinde Lætitiæ, Tristitiæ, Amoris, Odii, etc., tot species necessario dantur, quot sunt species objectorum, a quibus afficimur. At Cupiditas est ipsa uniuscujusque essentia, seu natura, quatenus ex data quacunque ejus constitutione determinata concipitur ad aliquid agendum (vid. Schol. Prop. 9 hujus) ; ergo, prout unusquisque a causis externis hac aut illa Lætitiæ, Tristitiæ, Amoris, Odii, etc., specie afficitur, hoc est, prout ejus natura hoc aut alio modo constituitur, ita ejus Cupiditas alia atque alia esse, et natura unius a natura alterius Cupiditatis tantum differre necesse est, quantum affectus, a quibus unaquæque oritur, inter se differunt.
Dantur itaque tot species Cupiditatis, quot sunt species Lætitiæ, Tristitiæ, Amoris, etc., et consequenter (per jam ostensa) quot sunt objectorum species, a quibus afficimur. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Inter affectuum species, quæ (per Prop. præc.) perplurimæ esse debent, insignes sunt Luxuria, Ebrietas, Libido, Avaritia et Ambitio, quæ non nisi Amoris vel Cupiditatis sunt notiones, quæ hujus utriusque affectus naturam explicant per objecta, ad quæ referuntur. Nam per Luxuriam, Ebrietatem, Libidinem, Avaritiam, et Ambitionem nihil aliud intelligimus, quam convivandi, potandi, coeundi, divitiarum et gloriæ immoderatum Amorem vel Cupiditatem. Præterea hi affectus, quatenus eos per solum objectum, ad quod referuntur, ab aliis distinguimus, contrarios non habent. Nam Temperantia, quam Luxuriæ, et Sobrietas, quam Ebrietati, et denique Castitas, quam Libidini opponere solemus, affectus seu passiones non sunt, sed animi indicant potentiam, quæ hos affectus moderatur.

Cæterum reliquas Affectuum species hic explicare nec possum (quia tot sunt, quot objectorum species), nec, si possem, necesse est. Nam ad id, quod intendimus, nempe ad affectuum vires, et Mentis in eosdem potentiam, determinandum, nobis sufficit, uniuscujusque affectus generalem habere definitionem. Sufficit, inquam, nobis, Affectuum et Mentis communes proprietates intelligere, ut determinare possimus, qualis et quanta sit Mentis potentia in moderandis et coercendis Affectibus. Quamvis itaque magna sit differentia inter hunc et illum Amoris, Odii, vel Cupiditatis affectum, ex. gr. inter Amorem erga liberos et inter amorem erga uxorem, nobis tamen has differentias cognoscere, et affectuum naturam et originem ulterius indagare, non est opus.
PROPOSITIO LVII
Quilibet uniuscujusque individui affectus ab affectu alterius tantum discrepat, quantum essentia unius ab essentia alterius differt.
DEMONSTRATIO
Hæc Propositio patet ex Axiom. 1, quod vide post Lem. 3 Schol. Prop. 13, p. 2. At nihilominus eandem ex trium primitivorum affectuum definitionibus demonstrabimus.

Omnes affectus ad Cupiditatem, Lætitiam, vel Tristitiam referuntur, ut eorum quas dedimus definitiones ostendunt. At Cupiditas est ipsa uniuscujusque natura seu essentia (vide ejus Defin. in Schol. Prop. 9 ujus) ; ergo uniuscujusque individui Cupiditas a Cupiditate alterius tantum discrepat, quantum natura seu essentia unius ab essentia alterius differt. Lætitia deinde et Tristitia passiones sunt, quibus uniuscujusque potentia seu conatus in suo esse perseverandi, augetur vel minuitur, juvatur vel coercetur (per Prop. 11 hujus et ejus Schol.). At per conatum in suo esse perseverandi, quatenus ad Mentem et Corpus simul refertur. Appetitum et Cupiditatem intelligimus (vide Schol. Prop. 9 hujus) ; ergo Lætitia et Tristitia est ipsa Cupiditas sive Appetitus, quatenus a causis externis augetur vel minuitur, juvatur vel coercetur, hoc est (per idem Schol.)

est ipsa cujusque natura ; atque adeo uniuscujusque Lætitia vel Tristitia a Lætitia vel Tristitia alterius tantum etiam discrepat, quantum natura seu essentia unius ab essentia alterius differt et consequenter quilibet uniuscujusque individui affectus ab affectu alterius tantum discrepat, etc. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Hinc sequitur, affectus animalium, quæ irrationalia dicuntur (bruta enim sentire nequaquam dubitare possumus, postquam Mentis novimus originem), ab affectibus hominum tantum differre, quantum eorum natura a natura humana differt. Fertur quidem equus et homo Libidine procreandi ; at ille Libidine equina, hic autem humana. Sic etiam Libidines et Appetitus insectorum, piscium, et avium, alii atque alii esse debent. Quamvis itaque unumquodque individuum sua, qua constat natura contentum vivat eaque gaudeat, vita tamen illa, qua unumquodque est contentum, et gaudium nihil aliud est, quam idea seu anima ejusdem individui, atque adeo gaudium unius a gaudio alterius tantum natura discrepat, quantum essentia unius ab essentia alterius differt. Denique ex præcedenti Propositione sequitur, non parum etiam interesse inter gaudium, quo ebrius ex. gr.

ducitur, et inter gaudium, quo potitur Philosophus, quod hic in transitu monere volui. Atque hæc de affectibus, qui ad hominem referuntur, quatenus patitur. Superest, ut pauca addam de iis, qui ad eundem referuntur, quatenus agit.
PROPOSITIO LVIII
Præter Lætitiam et Cupiditatem, quæ passiones sunt, alii Lætitiæ et Cupiditatis affectus dantur, qui ad nos, quatenus agimus, referuntur.
DEMONSTRATIO

Cum Mens se ipsam suamque agendi potentiam concipit, lætatur (per Prop. 53 hujus) : Mens autem se ipsam necessario contemplatur, quando veram sive adæquatam ideam concipit (per Prop. 43 p. II). At Mens quasdam ideas adæquatas concipit (per Schol. 2 Prop. 40 p. II). Ergo eatenus etiam lætatur, quatenus ideas adæquatas concipit, hoc est (per Prop. 1 hujus) quatenus agit. Deinde Mens tam quatenus claras et distinctas, quam quatenus confusas habeL ideas, in suo esse persevare conatur (per Prop. 9 hujus). At per conatum Cupiditatem intelligimus (per ejusdem Schol.) ; ergo Cupiditas ad nos refertur, etiam quatenus întelligimus, sive (per Prop. 1 hujus) quatenus agimus. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITIO LIX
Inter omnes affectus, qui ad Mentem, quatenus agit, referuntur, nulli sunt, quam qui ad Lætitiam vel Cupiditatem referuntur.
DEMONSTRATIO

Omnes affectus ad Cupiditatem, Lætitiam, vel Tristitiam referuntur, ut eorum quas dedimus, definitiones ostendunt. Per Tristitiam autem intelligimus, quod Mentis cogitandi potentia minuitur vel coercetur (per Prop. 11 hujus et ejus Schol.) ; adeoque Mens quatenus contristatur, eatenus ejus intelligendi, hoc est ejus agendi potentia (per Prop. 1 hujus) minuitur vel coercetur ; adeoque nulli Tristitiæ affectus ad Mentem referri possunt, quatenus agit ; sed tantum affectus Lætitiæ et Cupiditatis qui (per Prop. præc.) eatenus etiam ad Mentem referuntur. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Omnes actiones, quæ sequuntur ex affectibus, qui ad Mentem referuntur, quatenus intelligit ad Fortitudinem refero, quam in Animositatem et Generositatem distinguo. Nam per Animositatem intelligo Cupiditatem, qua unusquisque conatur suum esse ex solo Rationis dictamine conservare.

Per Generositatem autem Cupiditatem intelligo, qua unusquisque ex solo Rationis dictamine conatur reliquos homines juvare, et sibi amicitia jungere. Eas itaque actiones, quæ solum agentis utile intendunt, ad Animositatem, et quæ alterius etiam utile intendunt, ad Generositatem refero. Temperantia igitur, Sobrietas, et Animi in periculis Præsentia, etc. Animositatis sunt species ; Modestia autem, Clementia, etc., species Generositatis sunt. Atque his puto me præcipuos affectus, animique fluctuationes, quæ ex compositione trium primitivorum affectuum, nempe Cupiditatis, Lætitiæ, et Tristitiæ oriuntur, explicuisse, perque primas suas causas ostendisse. Ex quibus apparet, nos a causis externis multis modis agitari, nosque perinde ut maris undæ, a contrariis ventis agitatæ, fluctuari, nostri eventus atque fati inscios.

At dixi, me præcipuos tantum, non omnes, qui dari possunt, animi conflictus ostendisse. Nam eadem via, qua supra, procedendo, facile possumus ostendere, Amorem esse junctum Pœnitentiæ, Dedignationi, Pudori, etc. Imo unicuique ex jam dictis clare constare credo, affectus tot modis alii cum aliis componi, indeque tot variationes oriri, ut nullo numero definiri queant. Sed ad meum institutum præcipuos tantum enumeravisse sufficit : nam reliqui, quos omisi, plus curiositatis quam utilitatis haberent. Attamen de Amore hoc notandum restat, quod scilicet sæpissime contingit, dum re, quam appetebamus, fruimur, ut Corpus ex ea fruitione novam acquirat constitutionem, a qua aliter determinatur, et aliæ rerum imagines in eo excitantur, et simul Mens alia imaginari, aliaque cupere incipit. Ex. gr. cum aliquid, quod nos sapore delectare solet, imaginamur, eodem frui, nempe comedere cupimus.

At quamdiu eodem sic fruimur, stomachus adimpletur, Corpusque aliter constituitur. Si igitur, Corpore jam aliter disposito, ejusdem cibi imago, quia ipse præsens adest, fomentetur, et consequenter conatus etiam, sive Cupiditas, eundem comedendi ; huic Cupiditati seu conatui nova illa constitutio repugnabit, et consequenter cibi, quem appetebamus, præsentia odiosa erit, et hoc est quod Fastidium et Tædium vocamus. Cæterum Corporis affectiones externas, quæ in affectibus observantur, ut sunt tremor, livor, singultus, risus, etc., neglexi, quia ad solum Corpus absque ulla ad Mentem relatione referuntur. Denique de affectuum definitionibus quædam notanda sunt, quas propterea hic ordine repetam, et quid in unaquaque observandum est, iisdem interponam.
AFFECTUUM DEFINITIONES

I

Cupiditas est ipsa hominis essentia, quatenus ex data quacunque ejus affectione determinata concipitur ad aliquid agendum.
EXPLICATIO

Diximus supra in Scholio Propositions 9 hujus Partis, Cupiditatem esse appetitum cum ejusdem conscientia ; appetitum autem esse ipsam hominis essentiam, quatenus determinata est ad ea agendum quæ ipsius conservationi inserviunt. Sed in eodem Scholio etiam monui, me revera inter humanum appetitum et Cupiditatem nullam agnoscere differentiam. Nam sive homo sui appetitus sit conscius, sive non sit, manet tamen appetitus unus idemque ; a que adeo, ne tautologiam committere viderer, Cupiditatem per appetitum explicare nolui, sed eandem ita definire studui, ut omnes humanæ naturæ conatus, quos nomine appetitus, voluntatis, cupiditatis, vel impetus significamus, una comprehenderem. Potueram enim dicere, Cupiditatem esse ipsam hominis essentiam, quatenus determinata concipitur ad aliquid agendum ; sed ex hac definitione (per Prop. 23 p.

II) non sequeretur, quod Mens possit suæ Cupiditatis sive appetitus esse conscia. Igitur, ut hujus conscientiæ causam involverem, necesse fuit (per eandem Prop.) addere, quatenus ex data quacunque ejus affectione determinata, etc. Nam per affectionem humanæ essentiæ quamcunque ejusdem essentiæ constitutionem intelligimus, sive ea sit innata, sive adventicia, sive quod ipsa per solum Cogitationis, sive per solum Extensionis attributum concipiatur, sive denique quod ad utrumque simul referatur. Hic igitur Cupiditatis nomine intelligo hominis quoscunque conatus, impetus, appetitus, et volitiones, qui pro varia ejusdem hominis constitutione varii, et non raro adeo sibi invicem oppositi sunt, ut homo diversimode trahatur, et, quo se vertat, nesciat.
II
Lætitia est hominis transitio a minore ad majorem perfectionem.
III
Tristitia est hominis transitio a majore ad minorem perfectionem.
EXPLICATIO

Dico transitionem. Nam Laetitia non est ipsa perfectio. Si enim homo cum perfectione, ad quam transit, nasceretur, ejusdem absque Lætitiæ affectu compos esset ; quod clarius apparet ex Tristitiæ affectu, qui huic est contrarius. Nam quod Tristitia in transitione ad minorem perfectionem consistit, non autem in ipsa minore perfectione, nemo negare potest quandoquidem homo eatenus contristari nequit, quatenus alicujus perfectionis est particeps. Nec dicere possumus, quod Tristitia in privatione majoris perfectionis consistat ; nam privatio nihil est, Tristitiæ autem affectus actus est, qui propterea nullus alius esse potest, quam actus transeundi ad minorem perfectionem hoc est, actus quo hominis agendi potentia minuitur vel coercetur (vide Schol. Prop. 11 hujus).
Cæterum definitiones Hilaritatis, Titillationis, Melancholiæ, et Doloris omitto, quia ad Corpus potissimum referuntur, et non nisi Lætitiæ aut Tristitiæ sunt species.
IV
Admiratio est rei alicujus imaginatio, in qua Mens defixa propterea manet, quia hæc singularis imaginatio nullam cum reliquis habet connexionem (vide Prop. 52 hujus cum ejusdem Schol.)
EXPLICATIO

translations.title: Pars tertia - De origine et natura affectuum · passage 4

paragraphs.text: We see, therefore, that it can happen that what one person loves, another may hate; and that what one fears, another may not fear; and that one and the same man may now love what he formerly hated, and may now dare what he formerly feared, etc. Further, because everyone judges from his own affect what is good, what evil, what better, and what worse (see the Scholium to Prop. 39 of this Part), it follows that men can vary both in judgment and in affect; and hence it comes about that, when we compare some with others, we distinguish them from one another solely by the difference of their affects, and call some intrepid, others timid, and finally others by some other name. For example, I shall call that man intrepid who despises an evil which I am accustomed to fear; and if, moreover, I attend to this, that his Desire to inflict evil on him whom he hates, and to do good to him whom he loves, is not restrained by the fear of an evil by which I am accustomed to be restrained, I shall call him daring.

Further, he will seem timid to me who fears an evil which I am accustomed to despise; and if I further attend to this, that his Desire is restrained by the fear of an evil which cannot restrain me, I shall say that he is faint-hearted; and thus everyone will judge. Finally, from this nature of man and inconstancy of judgment—namely, both that a man often judges concerning things from affect alone, and that the things which he believes conduce to Joy or Sadness, and which therefore (by Prop. 28 of this Part) he strives to promote or remove in order that they may come about, are often merely imaginary—to say nothing now of the other things which we have shown in Part II concerning the uncertainty of things, we easily conceive that a man can often be the cause both that he be saddened and that he be gladdened, or that he be affected both with Sadness and with Joy, accompanied by the idea of himself as cause; and thus we easily understand what Repentance and what Acquiescence in oneself are.

Namely, Repentance is Sadness accompanied by the idea of oneself, and Acquiescence in oneself is Joy accompanied by the idea of oneself as cause; and these affects are most vehement because men believe themselves to be free (see Prop. 49 of this Part).
PROPOSITION LII

We shall not contemplate an object which we have previously seen together with others, or which we imagine to have nothing except what is common to many, as long as one which we imagine to have something singular.
DEMONSTRATION

As soon as we imagine an object which we have seen with others, we immediately also recollect the others (by Prop. 18, Part II, see also its Scholium), and thus from the contemplation of one we immediately fall into the contemplation of another. The same reasoning applies to an object which we imagine to have nothing except what is common to many. For by that very fact we suppose that we contemplate nothing in it which we have not previously seen with others. But when we suppose that we imagine in some object something singular which we have never before seen, we say nothing other than that the Mind, while it contemplates that object, has in itself no other object into whose contemplation it can fall from the contemplation of that one; and thus it is determined to contemplate that one alone. Therefore the object, etc. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

This affection of the Mind, or imagination of a singular thing, insofar as it occupies the Mind alone, is called Wonder; and if it is aroused by an object which we fear, it is called Consternation, because Wonder at an evil so holds a man suspended in the contemplation of that evil alone that he cannot think of other things by which he could avoid that evil. But if what we wonder at is a certain man's prudence, diligence, or something of this sort, because thereby we contemplate the man as greatly surpassing us, then Wonder is called Veneration; otherwise, Horror, if we wonder at a man's anger, envy, etc. Further, if we wonder at the prudence, diligence, etc. of a man whom we love, Love will thereby (by Prop. 12 of this Part) be greater, and this Love joined with Wonder or Veneration we call Devotion.

And in this way we can also conceive Hatred, Hope, Security, and other Affects joined with Wonder; and thus we shall be able to deduce more Affects than are customarily indicated by received terms. From this it is apparent that the names of the Affects were invented more from their common use than from an accurate knowledge of them.

Contempt is opposed to Wonder, the cause of which, however, is generally this: namely, because, from seeing that someone wonders at, loves, fears, etc. some thing, or because some thing at first sight appears similar to things which we wonder at, love, fear, etc. (by Prop. 15 with its Corollary and Prop. 27 of this Part), we are determined to wonder at, love, fear, etc. the same thing. But if, from the presence of the thing itself, or from a more careful contemplation of it, we are compelled to deny of it everything which can be the cause of Wonder, Love, Fear, etc., then, from the very presence of the thing, the Mind remains more determined to think of those things which are not in the object than of those which are in it; whereas, on the contrary, from the presence of an object it is ordinarily accustomed especially to think of that which is in the object.

Further, just as Devotion arises from Wonder at a thing which we love, so Mockery arises from Contempt for a thing which we hate or fear, and Indignation from Contempt for stupidity, just as Veneration arises from Wonder at prudence. Finally, we can conceive Love, Hope, Glory, and other Affects joined with Contempt, and thence deduce yet other Affects, which we are also not accustomed to distinguish from others by any singular term.
PROPOSITION LIII
When the Mind contemplates itself and its power of acting, it rejoices; and it does so the more as it imagines itself and its power of acting more distinctly.
DEMONSTRATION

A man does not know himself except through the affections of his Body and their ideas (by Props. 19 and 23, Part II). Therefore, when it happens that the Mind can contemplate itself, by that very fact it is supposed to pass to a greater perfection, that is (by the Scholium to Prop. 11 of this Part), to be affected with Joy; and with the greater Joy, the more distinctly it can imagine itself and its power of acting. Q. E. D.
COROLLARY

This Joy is fostered more and more as a man imagines himself to be praised by others. For the more he imagines himself to be praised by others, the greater the Joy with which he imagines others to be affected by him, and this accompanied by the idea of himself (by the Scholium to Prop. 29 of this Part); and hence (by Prop. 27 of this Part) he himself is affected with greater Joy accompanied by the idea of himself. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION LIV
The Mind strives to imagine only those things which posit its power of acting.
DEMONSTRATION

The striving, or power, of the Mind is the very essence of the Mind itself (by Prop. 7 of this Part); but the essence of the Mind (as is self-evident) affirms only that which the Mind is and can do, but not that which it is not and cannot do; and therefore it strives to imagine only that which affirms or posits its power of acting. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION LV
When the Mind imagines its own powerlessness, it is thereby saddened.
DEMONSTRATION

The essence of the Mind affirms only that which the Mind is and can do; or, it belongs to the nature of the Mind to imagine only those things which posit its power of acting (by the preceding Proposition). Therefore, when we say that the Mind, while it contemplates itself, imagines its own impotence, we say nothing other than that, while the Mind endeavors to imagine something which posits its power of acting, this endeavor of it is restrained, or (by the Scholium to Proposition 11 of this Part) that it is saddened. Q. E. D.
COROLLARY
This Sadness is more and more fostered if it imagines that it is blamed by others; this is demonstrated in the same way as the Corollary to Proposition 53 of this Part.
SCHOLIUM

This Sadness, accompanied by the idea of our weakness, is called Humility; but Joy, which arises from the contemplation of ourselves, is called Self-love, or Acquiescence in oneself. And since this is repeated as often as a man contemplates his virtues, or his power of acting, it therefore also comes about that everyone is eager to recount his deeds and to display the powers both of his body and of his mind, and that men are for this reason troublesome to one another. From this it again follows that men are by nature envious (see the Scholium to Proposition 24 and the Scholium to Proposition 32 of this Part), or that they rejoice at the weakness of their equals and, conversely, are saddened by their virtue. For as often as everyone imagines his actions, he is affected with Joy (by Proposition 53 of this Part), and with the greater Joy the more perfection the actions express and the more distinctly he imagines them; that is (by those things which were said in Scholium 1 to Proposition 40, p.

II), the more he can distinguish them from others and contemplate them as singular things. Therefore, everyone will rejoice most from the contemplation of himself when he contemplates in himself something which he denies of the rest. But if he refers what he affirms of himself to the universal idea of man or animal, he will not rejoice so greatly; and conversely he will be saddened if he imagines his own actions, compared with the actions of others, to be weaker; which Sadness indeed he will endeavor to remove (by Proposition 28 of this Part), and this by wrongly interpreting the actions of his equals, or by embellishing his own as much as he can. It is clear, therefore, that men are by nature prone to Hatred and Envy, to which education itself is added. For parents are accustomed to incite their children to virtue by the stimulus of honor and Envy alone. But perhaps there remains a scruple, namely, that we not infrequently admire and venerate men's virtues. Therefore, in order to remove this, I shall add the following Corollary.
COROLLARY
No one envies virtue in another unless in an equal.
DEMONSTRATION

Envy is Hatred itself (see the Scholium to Proposition 24 of this Part), or (by the Scholium to Proposition 13 of this Part) Sadness, that is (by the Scholium to Proposition 11 of this Part), an affection by which a man's power of acting, or endeavor, is restrained. But a man (by the Scholium to Proposition 9 of this Part) endeavors to do and desires nothing except what can follow from his given nature; therefore, a man will desire no power of acting, or (which is the same thing) virtue, to be ascribed to himself that is proper to the nature of another and alien to his own; and consequently his Desire cannot be restrained, that is (by the Scholium to Proposition 11 of this Part), he cannot be saddened, from the fact that he contemplates some virtue in someone unlike himself, and consequently he will not be able to envy him. But he can indeed envy his equal, who is supposed to be of the same nature as himself. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Therefore, since above, in the Scholium to Proposition 52 of this Part, we said that we venerate a man because we admire his prudence, fortitude, etc., this happens (as is clear from the Proposition itself) because we imagine these virtues to be singularly present in him, and not as common to our nature; and consequently we shall no more envy him for them than we envy trees their height, or lions their fortitude, etc.
PROPOSITION LVI

There are as many species of Joy, Sadness, and Desire, and consequently of every affect composed of these, such as Fluctuation of Mind, or derived from them, namely Love, Hatred, Hope, Fear, etc., as there are species of objects by which we are affected.
DEMONSTRATION

Joy and Sadness, and consequently the affects which are composed of or derived from them, are passions (by the Scholium to Proposition 11 of this Part); but we (by Proposition 1 of this Part) necessarily suffer insofar as we have inadequate ideas; and insofar as we have them (by Proposition 3 of this Part), we suffer only insofar, that is (see Scholium 1 to Proposition 40, p. II), we necessarily suffer only insofar as we imagine, or (see Proposition 17, p. II, with its Scholium) insofar as we are affected by an affect which involves the nature of our Body and the nature of an external body. Therefore the nature of each passion must necessarily be so explained that the nature of the object by which we are affected is expressed. Namely, Joy which arises from object A, for example, involves the nature of object A itself; and Joy which arises from object B involves the nature of object B itself; and therefore these two affects of Joy are different in nature, because they arise from causes of different nature.

Thus also the affect of Sadness which arises from one object differs in nature from the Sadness which arises from another cause; and this is likewise to be understood of Love, Hatred, Hope, Fear, Fluctuation of Mind, etc. And therefore there are necessarily as many species of Joy, Sadness, Love, Hatred, etc., as there are species of objects by which we are affected. But Desire is the very essence, or nature, of each individual, insofar as it is conceived as determined from any given constitution of it to doing something (see the Scholium to Proposition 9 of this Part); therefore, according as each individual is affected by external causes with this or that species of Joy, Sadness, Love, Hatred, etc., that is, according as his nature is constituted in this or that manner, so his Desire must be now one, now another, and the nature of one Desire must differ from the nature of another Desire as much as the affects from which each arises differ from one another.
