Therefore there are as many species of Desire as there are species of Joy, Sadness, Love, etc., and consequently (by what has now been shown) as there are species of objects by which we are affected. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Among the species of affects, which (by the preceding Proposition) must be very numerous, notable are Gluttony, Drunkenness, Lust, Avarice, and Ambition; these are nothing but notions of Love or Desire, which explain the nature of each of these two affects through the objects to which they are referred. For by Gluttony, Drunkenness, Lust, Avarice, and Ambition we understand nothing but an immoderate Love or Desire of feasting, drinking, copulating, riches, and glory. Furthermore, these affects, insofar as we distinguish them from others by the object alone to which they are referred, have no contraries. For Temperance, which we are accustomed to oppose to Gluttony, and Sobriety, which to Drunkenness, and finally Chastity, which to Lust, are not affects or passions, but indicate a power of mind which moderates these affects.

Moreover, I can neither explain here the remaining species of Affects (because there are as many as there are species of objects), nor, if I could, is it necessary. For in order to determine what we intend, namely, the powers of the affects and the power of the Mind over them, it suffices for us to have a general definition of each affect. It suffices, I say, for us to understand the common properties of the Affects and of the Mind, so that we may determine what and how great is the power of the Mind in moderating and restraining the Affects. Although, therefore, there is a great difference between this and that affect of Love, Hatred, or Desire—for example, between love toward children and love toward a wife—it is nevertheless not necessary for us to know these differences or to investigate further the nature and origin of the affects.
PROPOSITION LVII
The affect of each individual differs from the affect of another as much as the essence of the one differs from the essence of the other.
DEMONSTRATION
This Proposition is evident from Axiom 1, which see after Lemma 3, Scholium of Proposition 13, Part 2. Nevertheless, we shall demonstrate it from the definitions of the three primitive affects.

All affects are referred to Desire, Joy, or Sadness, as the definitions of them which we have given show. But Desire is the very nature or essence of each individual (see its Definition in the Scholium of Proposition 9 of this Part); therefore the Desire of each individual differs from the Desire of another only insofar as the nature or essence of the one differs from the essence of the other. Joy and Sadness, moreover, are passions by which the power of each individual, or its striving to persevere in its being, is increased or diminished, aided or restrained (by Proposition 11 of this Part and its Scholium). But by striving to persevere in its being, insofar as it is referred to Mind and Body together, we understand Appetite and Desire (see the Scholium of Proposition 9 of this Part); therefore Joy and Sadness are Desire itself, or Appetite, insofar as it is increased or diminished, aided or restrained by external causes, that is (by the same Scholium)

the very nature of each; and thus the Joy or Sadness of each individual likewise differs from the Joy or Sadness of another only insofar as the nature or essence of the one differs from the essence of the other, and consequently each affect of each individual differs from an affect of another only insofar, etc. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Hence it follows that the affects of animals, which are called irrational (for after we have known the origin of the Mind, we can in no way doubt that brutes feel), differ from the affects of human beings only insofar as their nature differs from human nature. A horse indeed is carried by the lust of procreation, and so is a human being; but the former by equine lust, the latter by human lust. Thus too the lusts and appetites of insects, fishes, and birds must be different in each case. Therefore, although each individual lives content with its own nature, of which it consists, and rejoices in it, nevertheless that life with which each is content, and that joy, is nothing other than the idea or soul of the same individual; and thus the joy of one differs by nature from the joy of another only insofar as the essence of the one differs from the essence of the other. Finally, it follows from the preceding Proposition that there is also no small difference between the joy by which a drunkard, for example,

is carried away, and the joy possessed by a Philosopher, which I wished to note here in passing. And these matters concern affects that are referred to a human being insofar as he is acted upon. It remains for me to add a few words concerning those which are referred to him insofar as he acts.
PROPOSITION LVIII
Besides Joy and Desire, which are passions, there are other affects of Joy and Desire which are referred to us insofar as we act.
DEMONSTRATION

When the Mind conceives itself and its power of acting, it rejoices (by Proposition 53 of this Part); but the Mind necessarily contemplates itself when it conceives a true, or adequate, idea (by Proposition 43, Part II). But the Mind conceives some adequate ideas (by Scholium 2 of Proposition 40, Part II). Therefore, it also rejoices insofar as it conceives adequate ideas, that is (by Proposition 1 of this Part), insofar as it acts. Further, the Mind strives to persevere in its being both insofar as it has clear and distinct ideas and insofar as it has confused ideas (by Proposition 9 of this Part). But by striving we understand Desire (by the Scholium to that Proposition); therefore Desire is referred to us even insofar as we understand, or (by Proposition 1 of this Part) insofar as we act. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION LIX
Among all the affects which are referred to the Mind insofar as it acts, there are none except those which are referred to Joy or Desire.
DEMONSTRATION

All affects are referred to Desire, Joy, or Sadness, as the definitions of them which we have given show. But by Sadness we understand that the Mind's power of thinking is diminished or restrained (by Proposition 11 of this Part and its Scholium); and therefore, insofar as the Mind is saddened, its power of understanding, that is, its power of acting (by Proposition 1 of this Part), is diminished or restrained; and therefore no affects of Sadness can be referred to the Mind insofar as it acts, but only affects of Joy and Desire, which (by the preceding Proposition) are also referred to the Mind insofar as it acts. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

I refer all actions which follow from affects that are referred to the Mind insofar as it understands to Fortitude, which I distinguish into Strength of Mind and Generosity. For by Strength of Mind I understand the Desire by which each one strives, from the dictate of Reason alone, to preserve his own being.

But by Generosity I understand the Desire by which each one strives, from the dictate of Reason alone, to aid other human beings and to join them to himself in friendship. Therefore I refer those actions which intend the advantage of the agent alone to Strength of Mind, and those which also intend the advantage of another to Generosity. Thus Temperance, Sobriety, and Presence of Mind amid dangers, etc., are species of Strength of Mind; whereas Modesty, Clemency, etc., are species of Generosity. And by these, I think, I have explained the principal affects and fluctuations of the mind which arise from the composition of the three primitive affects, namely Desire, Joy, and Sadness, and have shown them through their first causes. From these it appears that we are agitated in many ways by external causes, and that, like waves of the sea stirred by contrary winds, we fluctuate, unaware of our outcome and fate.

But I said that I had shown only the principal conflicts of the mind, not all that can be given. For, proceeding by the same method as above, we can easily show that Love is joined with Repentance, Indignation, Shame, etc. Indeed, I believe it is clear to everyone from what has already been said that affects are combined with one another in so many ways, and that hence so many variations arise that they cannot be determined by any number. But for my purpose it suffices to have enumerated only the principal ones; for the rest, which I have omitted, would have more curiosity than utility. Yet concerning Love this point remains to be noted: namely, that it very often happens, while we enjoy a thing which we had desired, that from this enjoyment the Body acquires a new constitution, by which it is otherwise determined, and other images of things are aroused in it, and at the same time the Mind begins to imagine other things and to desire other things. For example, when we imagine something that is wont to delight us by its taste, we desire to enjoy it, namely, to eat it.

But while we thus enjoy it, the stomach is filled and the Body is otherwise constituted. If, therefore, once the Body has been otherwise disposed, the image of the same food is fostered because it is itself present, and consequently the striving also, or Desire, to eat the same food, this new constitution will resist that Desire or striving; and consequently the presence of the food which we had desired will be hateful, and this is what we call Disgust and Weariness. Besides, I have passed over the external affections of the Body which are observed in affects, such as trembling, pallor, sobbing, laughter, etc., because they are referred to the Body alone, without any relation to the Mind. Finally, there are certain points to be noted concerning the definitions of the affects; for that reason I shall repeat them here in order, and shall insert along with them what is to be observed in each.
DEFINITIONS OF THE AFFECTS

I

Desire is the very essence of a human being, insofar as it is conceived as determined, from any given affection of it, to do something.
EXPLANATION

We said above, in the Scholium of Proposition 9 of this Part, that Desire is appetite together with consciousness thereof; but appetite is the very essence of a human being, insofar as it is determined to do those things which serve his preservation. But in the same Scholium I also noted that I recognize in reality no difference between human appetite and Desire. For whether a human being is conscious of his appetite or is not conscious of it, the appetite nevertheless remains one and the same; and therefore, lest I should seem to commit a tautology, I did not wish to explain Desire through appetite, but endeavored to define it in such a way as to comprehend in one all the strivings of human nature which we signify by the name of appetite, will, desire, or impulse. For I could have said that Desire is the very essence of a human being, insofar as it is conceived as determined to do something; but from this definition (by Proposition 23, Part

II) it would not follow that the Mind can be conscious of its Desire, or appetite. Therefore, in order to involve the cause of this consciousness, it was necessary (by the same Proposition) to add, insofar as from any given affection of it determined, etc. For by any affection of the human essence we understand any constitution of that same essence, whether it be innate or adventitious, whether it be conceived through the attribute of Thought alone, or through that of Extension alone, or finally whether it be referred to both together. Here, therefore, by the name Desire I understand any strivings, impulses, appetites, and volitions of a man, which vary according to the varying constitution of the same man, and are not infrequently so opposed to one another that the man is drawn in different directions and does not know where to turn.
II
Joy is man's transition from a lesser to a greater perfection.
III
Sadness is man's transition from a greater to a lesser perfection.
EXPLANATION

I say transition. For Joy is not perfection itself. For if a man were born with the perfection to which he passes, he would possess it without an affect of Joy; this appears more clearly from the affect of Sadness, which is contrary to it. For that Sadness consists in the transition to a lesser perfection, and not in lesser perfection itself, no one can deny, since a man cannot be saddened insofar as he partakes of some perfection. Nor can we say that Sadness consists in the privation of a greater perfection; for privation is nothing, whereas the affect of Sadness is an act, which consequently can be no other than the act of passing to a lesser perfection, that is, an act by which man's power of acting is diminished or restrained (see the Scholium to Proposition 11 of this Part).
Moreover, I omit the definitions of Cheerfulness, Titillation, Melancholy, and Pain, because they are referred chiefly to the Body, and are only species of Joy or Sadness.
IV

Wonder is the imagination of some thing, in which the Mind remains fixed because this singular imagination has no connection with the rest (see Proposition 52 of this Part together with its Scholium).
EXPLANATION

sources.title: Pars tertia - De origine et natura affectuum · passage 5
sources.text:
In Scholio Propositionis 18 Partis II ostendimus, quænam sit causa cur Mens ex contemplatione unius rei statim in alterius rei cogitationem incidat, videlicet quia earum rerum imagines invicem concatenatæ et ita ordinatæ sunt, ut alia aliam sequatur ; quod quidem concipi nequit quando rei imago nova est, sed Mens in ejusdem rei contemplatione detinebitur, donec ab aliis causis ad alia cogitandum determinetur. Rei itaque novæ imaginatio in se considerata ejusdem naturæ est ac reliquæ ; et hac de causa ego Admirationem inter affectus non numero, nec causam video, cur id facerem, quandoquidem hæc Mentis distractio ex nulla causa positiva, quæ Mentem ab aliis distrahat, oritur, sed tantum ex eo, quod causa, cur Mens ex unius rei contemplatione ad alia cogitandum determinatur, deficit. Tres igitur (ut in Schol. Prop. 11 hujus monui) tantum affectus primitivos seu primarios agnosco, nempe Lætitiæ, Tristitiæ, et Cupiditatis ; nec alia de causa verba de Admiratione feci, quam quia usu factum est, ut quidam affectus, qui ex tribus primitivis derivantur, aliis nominibus indicari soleant, quando ad objecta, quæ admiramur, referuntur ; quæ quidem ratio me ex æquo movet, ut etiam Contemptus definitionem his adjungam.

V

Contemptus est rei alicujus imaginatio, quæ Mentem adeo parum tangit, ut ipsa Mens ex rei præsentia magis moveatur ad ea imaginandum, quæ in ipsa re non sunt, quam quæ in ipsa sunt (vide Schol. Prop. 52 hujus).

Definitiones Venerationis et Dedignationis missas hic facio, quia nulli, quod sciam, affectus ex his nomen trahunt.

VI

Amor est Lætitia concomitante idea causæ externæ.

EXPLICATIO

Hæc Definitio satis clare Amoris essentiam explicat ; illa vero Auctorum, qui definiunt Amorem esse voluntatem amantis se jungendi rei amatæ, non Amoris essentiam, sed ejus proprietatem exprimit, et, quia Amoris essentia non satis ab Auctoribus perspecta fuit, ideo neque ejus proprietatis ullum clarum conceptum habere potuerunt ; et hinc factum, ut eorum definitionem admodum obscuram esse omnes judicaverint. Verum notandum, cum dico, proprietatem esse in amante, se voluntate jungere rei amatæ, me per voluntatem non intelligere consensum, vel animi deliberationem seu liberum decretum (nam hoc fictitium esse demonstraviinus Propositione 48 partis II), nec etiam Cupiditatem sese jungendi rei amatæ, quando abest, vel perseverandi in ipsius præsentia, quando adest ; potest namque amor absque hac aut illa Cupiditate concipi ; sed per voluntatem me Acquiescentiam intelligere, quæ est in Amante ob rei amatæ præsentiam, a qua Lætitia amantis corroboratur, aut saltem fovetur.

VII

Odium est Tristitia concomitante idea causæ externæ.

EXPLICATIO

Quæ hic notanda sunt, ex dictis in præcedentis Definitionis Explicatione facile percipiuntur (vide præterea Schol. Prop. 13 hujus).

VIII

Propensio est Lætitia concomitante idea alicujus rei, quæ per accidens causa est Lætitiæ.

IX

Aversio est Tristitia concomitante idea alicujus rei, quæ per accidens causa est Tristitiæ (de his vide Prop. 15 Schol. hujus).

X

Devotio est Amor erga eum, quem admiramur.

EXPLICATIO

Admirationem oriri ex rei novitate, ostendimus Propositione 52 hujus. Si igitur contingat, ut id, quod admiramur, sæpe imaginemur, idem admirari desinemus ; atque adeo videmus, Devotionis affectum facile in simplicem Amorem degenerare.

XI

Irrisio est Lætitia orta ex eo, quod aliquid, quod contemnimus, in re quam odimus, inessse imaginamur.

EXPLICATIO

Quatenus rem, quam odimus, contemnimus, eatenus de eadem existentiam negamus (vide Schol. Prop. 52 hujus), et eatenus (per Prop. 20 hujus) lætamur. Sed quoniam supponimus, hominem id, quod irridet, odio tamen habere, sequitur, hanc Lætitiam solidam non esse (vid. Schol. Prop. 47 hujus).

XII

Spes est inconstans Lætitia, orta ex idea rei futuræ vel præteritæ, de cujus eventu aliquatenus dubitamus.

XIII

Metus est inconstans Tristitia, orta ex irea rei futuræ vel præteritæ, de cujus eventu aliquatenus dubitamus (vide de his Schol. 2 Prop. 18 hujus).

EXPLICATIO

Ex his definitionibus sequitur, non dari Spem sine Metu, neque Metum sine Spe. Qui enim Spe pendet et de rei eventu dubitat, is aliquid imaginari supponitur, quod rei futuræ existentiam secludit; atque adeo eatenus contristari (per Prop. 19 hujus), et consequenter, dum Spe pendet, metuere, ut res eveniat. Qui autem contra in Metu est, hoc est, de rei, quam odit, eventu dubitat, aliquid etiam imaginatur, quod ejusdem rei existentiam secludit ; atque adeo (per Prop. 20 hujus) lætatur, et consequenter eatenus Spem habet, ne eveniat.

XIV

Securitas est Lætitia orta ex idea rei futuræ vel præteritæ, de qua dubitandi causa sublata est.

XV

Desperatio est Tristitia orta ex idea rei futuræ vel præteritæ de qua dubitandi causa sublata est.

EXPLICATIO

Oritur itaque ex Spe Securitas, et ex Metu Desperatio, quando de rei eventu dubitandi causa tollitur ; quod fit, quia homo rem præteritam vel futuram adesse imaginatur et ut præsentem contemplatur, vel quia alia imaginatur, quæ existentiam earum rerum secludunt, quæ ipsi dubium injiciebant. Nam tametsi de rerum singularium eventu (per Coroll. Prop. 31 p. II) nunquam possumus esse certi, fieri tamen potest, ut de earum eventu non dubitemus. Aliud enim esse ostendimus (vide Schol. Prop. 49 p. II) de re non dubitare, aliud rei certitudinem habere ; atque adeo fieri potest, ut ex imagine rei præteritæ aut futuræ eodem Lætitiæ vel Tristitiæ affectu afficiamur, ac ex rei præsentis imagine, ut in Propositione 18 hujus demonstravimus, quam cum ejusdem Scholio vide.

XVI

Gaudium est Lætitia concomitante idea rei præteritæ, quæ præter Spem evenit.

XVII

Conscientiæ morsus est Tristitia concomitante idea rei præteritæ, quæ præter Spem evenit.

XVIII

Commiseratio est Tristitia concomitante idea mali, quod alteri, quem nobis similem esse imaginamur, evenit (vid. Schol. Prop. 22 et Schol. 27 hujus).

EXPLICATIO

Inter Commiserationem et Misericordiam nulla videtur esse differentia, nisi forte, quod Commiseratio singularem affectum respiciat, Misericordia autem ejus habitum.

XIX

Favor est Amor erga aliquem, qui alteri benefecit.

XX

Indignatio est Odium erga aliquem, qui alteri malefecit.

EXPLICATIO

Hæc nomina ex communi usu aliud significare scio. Sed meum institutum non est, verborum significationem, sed rerum naturam explicare, easque iis vocabulis indicare, quorum significatio, quam ex usu habent, a significatione, qua eadem usurpare volo, non omnino abhorret, quod semel monuisse sufficiat. Caeterum horum affectuum causam vide in Corollario 1 Propositionis 27 et Scholio Propositionis 22 hujus Partis.

XXI

Existimatio est de aliquo præ Amore plus justo sentire.

XXII

Despectus est de aliquo præ Odio minus justo sentire.

EXPLICATIO

Est itaque Existimatio Amoris, et Despectus Odii effectus sive proprietas ; atque adeo potest Existimatio etiam definiri, quod sit Amor, quatenus hominem ita afficit, ut de re amata plus justo sentiat, et contra Despectus, quod sit. Odium, quatenus hominem ita afficit, ut de eo, quem odio habet, minus justo sentiat (vide de his Schol. Prop. 26 hujus).

XXIII

Invidia est Odium, quatenus hominem ita afficit, ut ex alterius felicitate contristetur, et contra, ut ex alterius malo gaudeat.

EXPLICATIO

Invidiæ opponitur communiter Misericordia, quæ proinde, invita vocabuli significatione, sic definiri potest :

XXIV

Misericordia est Amor, quatenus hominem ita afficit, ut ex bono alterius gaudeat, et contra ut ex alterius malo contristetur.

EXPLICATIO

Caeterum de Invidia vide Schol. Prop. 24 et Schol. Prop. 32 hujus. Atque hi affectus Lætitiæ et Tristitiæ sunt, quos idea rei externæ comitatur tanquam causa per se vel per accidens. Hinc ad alios transeo, quos idea rei internæ comitatur tanquam causa.

XXV

Acquiescentia in se ipso est Lætitia orta ex eo, quod homo se ipsum suamque agendi potentiam contemplatur.

XXVI

Humilitas est Tristitia orta ex eo, quod homo suam impotentiam sive imbecillitatem contemplatur.

EXPLICATIO

Acquiescentia in se ipso Humilitati opponitur, quatenus per eandem intelligimus Lætitiam, quæ ex eo oritur, quod nostram agendi potentiam contemplamur ; sed quatenus per ipsam etiam intelligimus Lætitiam concomitante idea alicujus facti, quod nos ex Mentis libero decreto fecisse credimus, tum Pœnitentiae opponitur, quæ a nobis sic definitur :

XXVII

Pœnitentia est Tristitia concomitante idea alicujus facti, quod nos ex libero Mentis decreto fecisse credimus.

EXPLICATIO

Horum affectuum causas ostendimus in Schol. Prop. 51 hujus, et Prop. 53, 54 et 55 hujus, ejusque Schol. De libero autem Mentis decreto vide Schol. Prop. 35 p. II. Sed hic præterea notandum venit, mirum non esse, quod omnes omnino actus, qui ex consuetudine pravi vocantur, sequatur Tristitia, et illos, qui recti dicuntur, Lætitia. Nam hoc ab educatione potissimum pendere, facile ex supra dictis intelligimus. Parentes nimirum, illos exprobrando, liberosque propter eosdem sæpe objurgando, hos contra suadendo et laudando, effecerunt, ut Tristitiæ commotiones illis, Lætitiæ vero his jungerentur. Quod ipsa etiam experientia comprobatur. Nam consuetudo et Religio non est omnibus eadem, sed contra, quæ apud alios sacra, apud alios profana, et quæ apud alios honesta, apud alios turpia sunt. Prout igitur unusquisque educatus est, ita facti alicujus pœnitet, vel eodem gloriatur.

XXVIII

Superbia est de se præ Amore sui plus justo sentire.

EXPLICATIO

Differt igitur Superbia ab Existimatione, quod hæc ad objectum externum, Superbia autem ad ipsum hominem, de se plus justo sentientem, referatur. Cæterum, ut Existimatio Amoris, sic Superbia Philautiæ effectus vel proprietas est, quæ propterea etiam definiri potest, quod sit Amor sui, sive Acquiescentia in se ipso, quatenus hominem ita afficit, ut de se plus justo sentiat (vid. Schol. Prop. 26 hujus). Huic affectui non datur contrarius. Nam nemo de se, præ Odio sui, minus justo sentit ; imo nemo de se minus justo sentit, quatenus imaginatur, se hoc vel illud non posse. Nam quicquid homo imaginatur se non posse, id necessario imaginatur, et hac imaginatione ita disponitur, ut id agere revera non possit, quod se non posse imaginatur. Quamdiu enim imaginatur se hoc vel illud non posse, tamdiu ad agendum non est determinatus, et consequenter tamdiu impossibile ei est, ut id agat. Verumenimvero si ad illa attendamus, quæ a sola opinione pendent, concipere poterimus fieri posse, ut homo de se minus justo sentiat ; fieri enim potest, ut aliquis, dum tristis imbecillitatem contemplatur suam, imaginetur, se ab omnibus contemni, idque dum reliqui nihil minus cogitant, quam ipsum contemnere. Potest præterea homo de se minus justo sentire, si aliquid de se in præsenti neget cum relatione ad futurum tempus, cujus est incertus ; ut quod neget, se nihil certi posse concipere, nihilque nisi prava vel turpia posse cupere vel agere, etc. Possumus deinde dicere, aliquem de se minus justo sentire, cum videmus, ipsum ex nimio pudoris metu ea non audere, quæ alii ipsi æquales audent. Hunc igitur affectum possumus Superbiæ opponere, quem Abjectionem vocabo ; nam ut ex Acquiescentia in se ipso Superbia, sic ex Humilitate Abjectio oritur, quæ proinde a nobis sic definitur.

XXIX

Abjectio est de se præ Tristitia minus justo sentire.

EXPLICATIO

Solemus tamen sæpe Superbiæ Humililatem opponere, sed tum magis ad utriusque effectus quam naturam attendimus. Solemus namque illum superbum vocare, qui nimis gloriatur (vid. Schol. Prop. 30 hujus), qui non nisi virtutes suas, et aliorum non nisi vitia narrat, qui omnibus præferri vult, et qui denique ea gravitate et ornatu incedit, quo solent alii, qui longe supra ipsum sunt positi. Contra illum humilem vocamus, qui sæpius erubescit, qui sua vitia fatetur, et aliorum virtutes narrat, qui omnibus cedit, et qui denique submisso capite ambulat, et se ornare negligit. Cæterum hi affectus, nempe Humilitas et Abjectio, rarissimi sunt. Nam natura humana, in se considerata, contra eosdem quantum potest, nititur (vide Prop. 13 et 54 hujus) ; et ideo, qui maxime creduntur abjecti et humiles esse, maxime plerumque ambitiosi et invidi sunt.

XXX

Gloria est Lætitia concomitante idea alicujus nostræ actionis, quam alios laudare imaginamur.

XXXI

Pudor est Tristitia concomitante idea alicujus actionis, quam alios vituperare imaginamur.

EXPLICATIO

De his vide Scholium Propositionis 30 hujus Partis. Sed hic notanda est differentia, quæ est inter Pudorem et Verecundiam. Est enim Pudor Tristitia, quæ sequitur factum, cujus pudet. Verecundia autem est Metus seu Timor Pudoris, quo homo continetur, ne aliquid turpe committat. Verecundiæ opponi solet Impudentia, quæ revera affectus non est, ut suo loco ostendam ; sed affectuum nomina (ut jam monui) magis eorum usum quam naturam respiciunt. Atque his Lætitiæ et Tristitiæ affectus, quos explicare proposueram, absolvi. Pergo itaque ad illos, quos ad Cupiditatem refero.

XXXII

Desiderium est Cupiditas sive Appetitus re aliqua potiundi, quæ ejusdem rei memoria fovetur, et simul aliarum rerum memoria, quæ ejusdem rei appetendæ existentiam secludunt, coercetur.

EXPLICATIO

Cum alicujus rei recordamur, ut jam sæpe diximus, eo ipso disponimur ad eandem eodem affectu contemplandum, ac si res præsens adesset ; sed hæc dispositio, seu conatus, dum vigilamus, plerumque cohibetur ab imaginibus rerum, quæ existentiam ejus, cujus recordamur, secludunt. Quando itaque rei meminimus, quæ nos aliquo Lætitiæ genere afficit, eo ipso conamur eandem, cum eodem Lætitiæ affectu ut præsentem contemplari, qui quidem conatus statim cohibetur memoria rerum, quæ illius existentiam secludunt. Quare desiderium revera Tristitia est, quæ Lætitiæ opponitur illi, quæ ex absentia rei, quam odimus, oritur, de qua vide Scholium Propositionis 47 hujus partis. Sed quia nomen Desiderium Cupiditatem respicere videtur, ideo hunc affectum ad Cupiditatis affectus refero.

XXXIII

Æmulatio est alicujus rei Cupiditas, quæ nobis ingeneratur ex eo, quod alios eandem Cupiditatem habere imaginamur.

EXPLICATIO

Qui fugit, quia alios fugere, vel qui timet, quia alios timere videt ; vel etiam ille, qui ex eo, quod aliquem manum suam combussisse videt, manum ad se contrahit, corpusque movet, quasi ipsius manus combureretur ; eum imitari quidem alterius affectum, sed non eundem æmulari dicemus ; non quia aliam æmulationis, aliam imitationis novimus causam, sed quia usu factum est, ut illum tantum vocemus æmulum, qui id, quod honestum utile, vel jucundum esse judicamus, imitatur. Cæterum de Æmulalionis causa vide Propositionem 27 hujus Partis cum ejus Scholio. Cur autem huic affectui plerumque juncta sit Invidia, de eovide Propositionem 32 hujus cum ejusdem Scholio.

XXXIV

Gratia seu Gratitudo est Cupiditas, seu Amoris studium, quo ei benefacere conamur, qui in nos pari amoris affectu beneficium contulit. Vide Prop. 39 cum Schol. Prop. 41 hujus.

XXXV

Benevolentia est Cupiditas benefaciendi ei, cujus nos miseret. Vide Schol. Prop. 27 hujus.

XXXVI

Ira est Cupiditas, qua ex Odio incitamur ad illi, quem odimus, malum inferendum. Vide Prop. 39 hujus.

XXXVII

Vindicta est Cupiditas, qua ex reciproco Odio concitamur ad malum inferendum ei, qui nobis pari affectu damnum intulit Vide 2 Coroll. Prop. 40 hujus cum ejusdem Schol.

XXXVIII

Crudelitas seu Sævitia est Cupiditas, qua aliquis concitatur ad malum inferendum ei, quem amamus, vel cujus non miseret.

EXPLICATIO

Crudelitati opponitur Clementia, quæ passio non est, sed animi potentia, quo homo iram et vindictam moderatur.

XXXIX

Timor est Cupiditas majus, quod metuimus, malum minore vitandi. Vide Schol. Prop. 39 hujus.

XL

Audacia est Cupiditas, qua aliquis incitatur ad aliquid agendum cum periculo, quod ejus æquales subire metuunt.

XLI

Pusillanimitas dicitur de eo, cujus Cupiditas coercetur timore periculi, quod ejus æquales subire audent.

EXPLICATIO

Est igitur Pusillanimitas nihil aliud, quam Metus alicujus mali, quod plerique non solent metuere ; quare ipsam ad Cupiditatis affectus non refero. Eandem tamen hic explicare volui, quia, quatenus ad Cupiditatem attendimus, affectui Audaciæ revera opponitur.

XLII

Consternatio dicitur de eo, cujus Cupiditas malum vitandi coercetur admiratione mali, quod timet.

EXPLICATIO

Est itaque Consternatio Pusillanimitatis species. Sed quia Consternatio ex duplici Timore oritur, ideo commodius definiri potest, quod sit Metus, qui hominem stupefactum aut fluctuantem ita continet, ut is malum amovere non possit. Dico stupefactum, quatenus ejus Cupiditatem malum amovendi admiratione coerceri intelligimus. Fluctuantem autem dico, quatenus concipimus eandem Cupiditatem coerceri Timore alterius mali, quod ipsum æque cruciat : unde fit, ut, quodnam ex duobus avertat, nesciat. De his vide Schol. Prop. 39 et Schol. Prop. 52 hujus. Cæterum de Pusillanimitate et Audacia vide Schol. Prop. 51 hujus.

XLIII

Humanitas seu Modestia est Cupiditas ea faciendi, quæ hominibus placent, et omittendi, quæ displicent.

XLIV

Ambitio est immodica gloriæ Cupiditas.

EXPLICATIO

Ambitio est Cupiditas, qua omnes affectus (per Prop. 27 et 31 hujus) foventur et corroborantur ; et ideo hic affectus vix superari potest. Nam quamdiu homo aliqua Cupiditate tenetur, hac simul necessario tenetur. Optimus quisque, inquit Cicero, maxime gloria ducitur. Philosophi etiam libris, quos de contemnenda gloria scribunt, nomen suum inscribunt, etc.

XLV

Luxuria est immoderata convivandi Cupiditas, vel etiam Amor.

XLVI

Ebrietas est immoderata potandi Cupiditas et Amor.

XLVII

Avaritia est immoderata divitiarum Cupiditas et Armor.

XLVIII

Libido est etiam Cupiditas et Amor in commiscendis corporibus.

EXPLICATIO

Sive hæc coeundi Cupiditas moderata sit, sive non sit, Libido appellari solet. Porro hi quinque affectus (ut in Schol. Prop. 56 hujus monui) contrarios non habent. Nam Modestia species est Ambitionis, de qua vide Schol. Prop. 29 hujus. Temperantiam deinde, Sobrietatem, et Castitatem Mentis potentiam, non autem passionem indicare, jam etiam monui. Et tametsi fieri potest, ut homo avarus, ambitiosus, vel timidus a nimio cibo, potu, et coitu, abstineat ; Avaritia tamen, Ambitio et Timor luxuriæ, ebrietati, vel libidini non sunt contrarii. Nam avarus in cibum et potum alienum se ingurgitare plerumque desiderat. Ambitiosus autem, modo speret fore clam, in nulla re sibi temperabit, et si inter ebrios vivat et libidinosos, ideo quia ambitiosus est, proclivior erit ad eadem vitia. Timidus denique id, quod non vult, facit. Nam quamvis mortis vitandæ causa divitias in mare projiciat, manet tamen avarus et si libidinosus tristis est, quod sibi morem gerere nequeat, non desinit propterea libidinosus esse. Et absolute hi affectus non tam ipsos actus convivandi, potandi, etc., respiciunt, quam ipsum Appetitum et Amorem. Nihil igitur his affectibus opponi potest, præter Generositatem et Animositatem, de quibus in seqq.

Definitiones Zelotypiæ et reliquarum animi fluctuationum silentio prætermitto, tam quia ex compositione affectuum, quos jam definivimus oriuntur, quam quia pleræque nomina non habent ; quod ostendit ad usum vitæ sufficere, easdem in genere tantummodo noscere. Cæterum ex Definitionibus affectuum, quos explicuimus, liquet eos omnes a Cupiditate, Lætitia, vel Tristitia oriri, seu potius nihil præter hos tres esse, quorum unusquisque variis nominibus appellari solet propter varias eorum relationes et denominationes extrinsecas. Si jam ad hos primitivos, et ad ea, quæ de natura Mentis supra diximus, attendere velimus, affectus, quatenus ad solam Mentem referuntur, sic definere poterimus.

AFFECTUUM GENERALIS DEFINITIO

Affectus, qui animi Pathema dicitur, est confusa idea qua Mens majorem vel minorem sui Corporis, vel alicujus ejus partis, existendi vim, quam antea, affirmat, et qua data ipsa Mens ad hoc potius quam ad illud cogitandum determinatur.

EXPLICATIO

Dico primo. Affectum seu passionem animi esse confusam ideam. Nam Mentem eatenus tantum pati ostendimus (vide Prop. 3 hujus), quatenus ideas inadæquatas sive confusas habet. Dico deinde, qua Mens majorem vel minorem sui Corporis, vel alicujus ejus partis, existendi vim, quam antea, affirmat. Omnes enim corporum ideæ, quas habemus, magis nostri Corporis actualem constitutionem (per Coroll. 2 Prop. 16 p. II), quam corporis externi naturam indicant ; at hæc, quæ affectus formam constituit, Corporis, vel alicujus ejus partis, constitutionem indicare vel exprimere debet, quam ipsum Corpus vel aliqua ejus pars habet, ex eo, quod ipsius agendi potentia sive existendi vis augetur vel minuitur, juvatur vel coercetur. Sed notandum, cum dico, majorem vel minorem existendi vim, quam antea, me non intelligere, quod Mens præsentem, Corporis constitutionem cum præterita comparat, sed quod idea, quæ affectus formam constituit, aliquid de Corpore affirmat, quod plus minusve realitatis revera involvit, quam antea. Et quia essentia Mentis in hoc consistit (per Prop. 11 et 13 p. II), quod sui Corporis actualem existentiam affirmat, et nos per perfectionem ipsam rei essentiam intelligimus ; sequitur ergo, quod Mens ad majorem minoremve perfectionem transit, quando ei aliquid de suo Corpore, vel aliqua ejus parte, affirmare contingit, quod plus minusve realitatis involvit, quam antea. Cum igitur supra dixerim, Mentis cogitandi potentiam augeri vel minui, nihil aliud intelligere volui, quam quod Mens ideam sui Corporis, vel alicujus ejus partis, formaverit, quæ plus minusve realitatis exprimit, quam de suo Corpore affirmaverat. Nam idearum præstantia, et actualis cogitandi potentia, ex objecti præstantia, æstimatur. Addidi denique, et qua data idea Mens ad hoc potius quam ad aliud cogitandum determinatur, ut præter Laetitiæ et Tristitiæ naturam, quam prima definitionis pars explicat, Cupiditatis etiam naturam exprimerem.

Finis Tertiæ Partis

paragraphs.text: In Scholio Propositionis 18 Partis II ostendimus, quænam sit causa cur Mens ex contemplatione unius rei statim in alterius rei cogitationem incidat, videlicet quia earum rerum imagines invicem concatenatæ et ita ordinatæ sunt, ut alia aliam sequatur ; quod quidem concipi nequit quando rei imago nova est, sed Mens in ejusdem rei contemplatione detinebitur, donec ab aliis causis ad alia cogitandum determinetur. Rei itaque novæ imaginatio in se considerata ejusdem naturæ est ac reliquæ ; et hac de causa ego Admirationem inter affectus non numero, nec causam video, cur id facerem, quandoquidem hæc Mentis distractio ex nulla causa positiva, quæ Mentem ab aliis distrahat, oritur, sed tantum ex eo, quod causa, cur Mens ex unius rei contemplatione ad alia cogitandum determinatur, deficit. Tres igitur (ut in Schol. Prop.

11 hujus monui) tantum affectus primitivos seu primarios agnosco, nempe Lætitiæ, Tristitiæ, et Cupiditatis ; nec alia de causa verba de Admiratione feci, quam quia usu factum est, ut quidam affectus, qui ex tribus primitivis derivantur, aliis nominibus indicari soleant, quando ad objecta, quæ admiramur, referuntur ; quæ quidem ratio me ex æquo movet, ut etiam Contemptus definitionem his adjungam.

V

Contemptus est rei alicujus imaginatio, quæ Mentem adeo parum tangit, ut ipsa Mens ex rei præsentia magis moveatur ad ea imaginandum, quæ in ipsa re non sunt, quam quæ in ipsa sunt (vide Schol. Prop. 52 hujus).
Definitiones Venerationis et Dedignationis missas hic facio, quia nulli, quod sciam, affectus ex his nomen trahunt.
VI
Amor est Lætitia concomitante idea causæ externæ.
EXPLICATIO

Hæc Definitio satis clare Amoris essentiam explicat ; illa vero Auctorum, qui definiunt Amorem esse voluntatem amantis se jungendi rei amatæ, non Amoris essentiam, sed ejus proprietatem exprimit, et, quia Amoris essentia non satis ab Auctoribus perspecta fuit, ideo neque ejus proprietatis ullum clarum conceptum habere potuerunt ; et hinc factum, ut eorum definitionem admodum obscuram esse omnes judicaverint.

Verum notandum, cum dico, proprietatem esse in amante, se voluntate jungere rei amatæ, me per voluntatem non intelligere consensum, vel animi deliberationem seu liberum decretum (nam hoc fictitium esse demonstraviinus Propositione 48 partis II), nec etiam Cupiditatem sese jungendi rei amatæ, quando abest, vel perseverandi in ipsius præsentia, quando adest ; potest namque amor absque hac aut illa Cupiditate concipi ; sed per voluntatem me Acquiescentiam intelligere, quæ est in Amante ob rei amatæ præsentiam, a qua Lætitia amantis corroboratur, aut saltem fovetur.
VII
Odium est Tristitia concomitante idea causæ externæ.
EXPLICATIO
Quæ hic notanda sunt, ex dictis in præcedentis Definitionis Explicatione facile percipiuntur (vide præterea Schol. Prop. 13 hujus).
VIII
Propensio est Lætitia concomitante idea alicujus rei, quæ per accidens causa est Lætitiæ.
IX
Aversio est Tristitia concomitante idea alicujus rei, quæ per accidens causa est Tristitiæ (de his vide Prop. 15 Schol. hujus).

X

Devotio est Amor erga eum, quem admiramur.
EXPLICATIO

Admirationem oriri ex rei novitate, ostendimus Propositione 52 hujus. Si igitur contingat, ut id, quod admiramur, sæpe imaginemur, idem admirari desinemus ; atque adeo videmus, Devotionis affectum facile in simplicem Amorem degenerare.
XI
Irrisio est Lætitia orta ex eo, quod aliquid, quod contemnimus, in re quam odimus, inessse imaginamur.
EXPLICATIO

Quatenus rem, quam odimus, contemnimus, eatenus de eadem existentiam negamus (vide Schol. Prop. 52 hujus), et eatenus (per Prop. 20 hujus) lætamur. Sed quoniam supponimus, hominem id, quod irridet, odio tamen habere, sequitur, hanc Lætitiam solidam non esse (vid. Schol. Prop. 47 hujus).
XII
Spes est inconstans Lætitia, orta ex idea rei futuræ vel præteritæ, de cujus eventu aliquatenus dubitamus.
XIII
Metus est inconstans Tristitia, orta ex irea rei futuræ vel præteritæ, de cujus eventu aliquatenus dubitamus (vide de his Schol. 2 Prop. 18 hujus).
EXPLICATIO

Ex his definitionibus sequitur, non dari Spem sine Metu, neque Metum sine Spe. Qui enim Spe pendet et de rei eventu dubitat, is aliquid imaginari supponitur, quod rei futuræ existentiam secludit; atque adeo eatenus contristari (per Prop. 19 hujus), et consequenter, dum Spe pendet, metuere, ut res eveniat. Qui autem contra in Metu est, hoc est, de rei, quam odit, eventu dubitat, aliquid etiam imaginatur, quod ejusdem rei existentiam secludit ; atque adeo (per Prop. 20 hujus) lætatur, et consequenter eatenus Spem habet, ne eveniat.
XIV
Securitas est Lætitia orta ex idea rei futuræ vel præteritæ, de qua dubitandi causa sublata est.
XV
Desperatio est Tristitia orta ex idea rei futuræ vel præteritæ de qua dubitandi causa sublata est.
EXPLICATIO

Oritur itaque ex Spe Securitas, et ex Metu Desperatio, quando de rei eventu dubitandi causa tollitur ; quod fit, quia homo rem præteritam vel futuram adesse imaginatur et ut præsentem contemplatur, vel quia alia imaginatur, quæ existentiam earum rerum secludunt, quæ ipsi dubium injiciebant. Nam tametsi de rerum singularium eventu (per Coroll. Prop. 31 p. II) nunquam possumus esse certi, fieri tamen potest, ut de earum eventu non dubitemus. Aliud enim esse ostendimus (vide Schol. Prop. 49 p. II) de re non dubitare, aliud rei certitudinem habere ; atque adeo fieri potest, ut ex imagine rei præteritæ aut futuræ eodem Lætitiæ vel Tristitiæ affectu afficiamur, ac ex rei præsentis imagine, ut in Propositione 18 hujus demonstravimus, quam cum ejusdem Scholio vide.
XVI
Gaudium est Lætitia concomitante idea rei præteritæ, quæ præter Spem evenit.
XVII
Conscientiæ morsus est Tristitia concomitante idea rei præteritæ, quæ præter Spem evenit.
XVIII
Commiseratio est Tristitia concomitante idea mali, quod alteri, quem nobis similem esse imaginamur, evenit (vid. Schol. Prop. 22 et Schol. 27 hujus).
EXPLICATIO
Inter Commiserationem et Misericordiam nulla videtur esse differentia, nisi forte, quod Commiseratio singularem affectum respiciat, Misericordia autem ejus habitum.
XIX
Favor est Amor erga aliquem, qui alteri benefecit.
XX
Indignatio est Odium erga aliquem, qui alteri malefecit.
EXPLICATIO

Hæc nomina ex communi usu aliud significare scio. Sed meum institutum non est, verborum significationem, sed rerum naturam explicare, easque iis vocabulis indicare, quorum significatio, quam ex usu habent, a significatione, qua eadem usurpare volo, non omnino abhorret, quod semel monuisse sufficiat. Caeterum horum affectuum causam vide in Corollario 1 Propositionis 27 et Scholio Propositionis 22 hujus Partis.
XXI
Existimatio est de aliquo præ Amore plus justo sentire.
XXII
Despectus est de aliquo præ Odio minus justo sentire.
EXPLICATIO

Est itaque Existimatio Amoris, et Despectus Odii effectus sive proprietas ; atque adeo potest Existimatio etiam definiri, quod sit Amor, quatenus hominem ita afficit, ut de re amata plus justo sentiat, et contra Despectus, quod sit. Odium, quatenus hominem ita afficit, ut de eo, quem odio habet, minus justo sentiat (vide de his Schol. Prop. 26 hujus).
XXIII
Invidia est Odium, quatenus hominem ita afficit, ut ex alterius felicitate contristetur, et contra, ut ex alterius malo gaudeat.
EXPLICATIO
Invidiæ opponitur communiter Misericordia, quæ proinde, invita vocabuli significatione, sic definiri potest :
XXIV
Misericordia est Amor, quatenus hominem ita afficit, ut ex bono alterius gaudeat, et contra ut ex alterius malo contristetur.
EXPLICATIO

Caeterum de Invidia vide Schol. Prop. 24 et Schol. Prop. 32 hujus. Atque hi affectus Lætitiæ et Tristitiæ sunt, quos idea rei externæ comitatur tanquam causa per se vel per accidens. Hinc ad alios transeo, quos idea rei internæ comitatur tanquam causa.
XXV
Acquiescentia in se ipso est Lætitia orta ex eo, quod homo se ipsum suamque agendi potentiam contemplatur.
XXVI
Humilitas est Tristitia orta ex eo, quod homo suam impotentiam sive imbecillitatem contemplatur.
EXPLICATIO

Acquiescentia in se ipso Humilitati opponitur, quatenus per eandem intelligimus Lætitiam, quæ ex eo oritur, quod nostram agendi potentiam contemplamur ; sed quatenus per ipsam etiam intelligimus Lætitiam concomitante idea alicujus facti, quod nos ex Mentis libero decreto fecisse credimus, tum Pœnitentiae opponitur, quæ a nobis sic definitur :
XXVII
Pœnitentia est Tristitia concomitante idea alicujus facti, quod nos ex libero Mentis decreto fecisse credimus.
EXPLICATIO

Horum affectuum causas ostendimus in Schol. Prop. 51 hujus, et Prop. 53, 54 et 55 hujus, ejusque Schol. De libero autem Mentis decreto vide Schol. Prop. 35 p. II. Sed hic præterea notandum venit, mirum non esse, quod omnes omnino actus, qui ex consuetudine pravi vocantur, sequatur Tristitia, et illos, qui recti dicuntur, Lætitia. Nam hoc ab educatione potissimum pendere, facile ex supra dictis intelligimus. Parentes nimirum, illos exprobrando, liberosque propter eosdem sæpe objurgando, hos contra suadendo et laudando, effecerunt, ut Tristitiæ commotiones illis, Lætitiæ vero his jungerentur. Quod ipsa etiam experientia comprobatur. Nam consuetudo et Religio non est omnibus eadem, sed contra, quæ apud alios sacra, apud alios profana, et quæ apud alios honesta, apud alios turpia sunt. Prout igitur unusquisque educatus est, ita facti alicujus pœnitet, vel eodem gloriatur.
XXVIII
Superbia est de se præ Amore sui plus justo sentire.
EXPLICATIO

Differt igitur Superbia ab Existimatione, quod hæc ad objectum externum, Superbia autem ad ipsum hominem, de se plus justo sentientem, referatur. Cæterum, ut Existimatio Amoris, sic Superbia Philautiæ effectus vel proprietas est, quæ propterea etiam definiri potest, quod sit Amor sui, sive Acquiescentia in se ipso, quatenus hominem ita afficit, ut de se plus justo sentiat (vid. Schol. Prop. 26 hujus). Huic affectui non datur contrarius. Nam nemo de se, præ Odio sui, minus justo sentit ; imo nemo de se minus justo sentit, quatenus imaginatur, se hoc vel illud non posse. Nam quicquid homo imaginatur se non posse, id necessario imaginatur, et hac imaginatione ita disponitur, ut id agere revera non possit, quod se non posse imaginatur. Quamdiu enim imaginatur se hoc vel illud non posse, tamdiu ad agendum non est determinatus, et consequenter tamdiu impossibile ei est, ut id agat.

Verumenimvero si ad illa attendamus, quæ a sola opinione pendent, concipere poterimus fieri posse, ut homo de se minus justo sentiat ; fieri enim potest, ut aliquis, dum tristis imbecillitatem contemplatur suam, imaginetur, se ab omnibus contemni, idque dum reliqui nihil minus cogitant, quam ipsum contemnere. Potest præterea homo de se minus justo sentire, si aliquid de se in præsenti neget cum relatione ad futurum tempus, cujus est incertus ; ut quod neget, se nihil certi posse concipere, nihilque nisi prava vel turpia posse cupere vel agere, etc. Possumus deinde dicere, aliquem de se minus justo sentire, cum videmus, ipsum ex nimio pudoris metu ea non audere, quæ alii ipsi æquales audent. Hunc igitur affectum possumus Superbiæ opponere, quem Abjectionem vocabo ; nam ut ex Acquiescentia in se ipso Superbia, sic ex Humilitate Abjectio oritur, quæ proinde a nobis sic definitur.
XXIX
Abjectio est de se præ Tristitia minus justo sentire.
EXPLICATIO

Solemus tamen sæpe Superbiæ Humililatem opponere, sed tum magis ad utriusque effectus quam naturam attendimus. Solemus namque illum superbum vocare, qui nimis gloriatur (vid. Schol. Prop. 30 hujus), qui non nisi virtutes suas, et aliorum non nisi vitia narrat, qui omnibus præferri vult, et qui denique ea gravitate et ornatu incedit, quo solent alii, qui longe supra ipsum sunt positi. Contra illum humilem vocamus, qui sæpius erubescit, qui sua vitia fatetur, et aliorum virtutes narrat, qui omnibus cedit, et qui denique submisso capite ambulat, et se ornare negligit. Cæterum hi affectus, nempe Humilitas et Abjectio, rarissimi sunt. Nam natura humana, in se considerata, contra eosdem quantum potest, nititur (vide Prop. 13 et 54 hujus) ; et ideo, qui maxime creduntur abjecti et humiles esse, maxime plerumque ambitiosi et invidi sunt.
XXX
Gloria est Lætitia concomitante idea alicujus nostræ actionis, quam alios laudare imaginamur.
XXXI
Pudor est Tristitia concomitante idea alicujus actionis, quam alios vituperare imaginamur.
EXPLICATIO

De his vide Scholium Propositionis 30 hujus Partis. Sed hic notanda est differentia, quæ est inter Pudorem et Verecundiam. Est enim Pudor Tristitia, quæ sequitur factum, cujus pudet. Verecundia autem est Metus seu Timor Pudoris, quo homo continetur, ne aliquid turpe committat. Verecundiæ opponi solet Impudentia, quæ revera affectus non est, ut suo loco ostendam ; sed affectuum nomina (ut jam monui) magis eorum usum quam naturam respiciunt. Atque his Lætitiæ et Tristitiæ affectus, quos explicare proposueram, absolvi. Pergo itaque ad illos, quos ad Cupiditatem refero.
XXXII
Desiderium est Cupiditas sive Appetitus re aliqua potiundi, quæ ejusdem rei memoria fovetur, et simul aliarum rerum memoria, quæ ejusdem rei appetendæ existentiam secludunt, coercetur.
EXPLICATIO

Cum alicujus rei recordamur, ut jam sæpe diximus, eo ipso disponimur ad eandem eodem affectu contemplandum, ac si res præsens adesset ; sed hæc dispositio, seu conatus, dum vigilamus, plerumque cohibetur ab imaginibus rerum, quæ existentiam ejus, cujus recordamur, secludunt. Quando itaque rei meminimus, quæ nos aliquo Lætitiæ genere afficit, eo ipso conamur eandem, cum eodem Lætitiæ affectu ut præsentem contemplari, qui quidem conatus statim cohibetur memoria rerum, quæ illius existentiam secludunt. Quare desiderium revera Tristitia est, quæ Lætitiæ opponitur illi, quæ ex absentia rei, quam odimus, oritur, de qua vide Scholium Propositionis 47 hujus partis. Sed quia nomen Desiderium Cupiditatem respicere videtur, ideo hunc affectum ad Cupiditatis affectus refero.
XXXIII
Æmulatio est alicujus rei Cupiditas, quæ nobis ingeneratur ex eo, quod alios eandem Cupiditatem habere imaginamur.
EXPLICATIO

Qui fugit, quia alios fugere, vel qui timet, quia alios timere videt ; vel etiam ille, qui ex eo, quod aliquem manum suam combussisse videt, manum ad se contrahit, corpusque movet, quasi ipsius manus combureretur ; eum imitari quidem alterius affectum, sed non eundem æmulari dicemus ; non quia aliam æmulationis, aliam imitationis novimus causam, sed quia usu factum est, ut illum tantum vocemus æmulum, qui id, quod honestum utile, vel jucundum esse judicamus, imitatur. Cæterum de Æmulalionis causa vide Propositionem 27 hujus Partis cum ejus Scholio. Cur autem huic affectui plerumque juncta sit Invidia, de eovide Propositionem 32 hujus cum ejusdem Scholio.
XXXIV
Gratia seu Gratitudo est Cupiditas, seu Amoris studium, quo ei benefacere conamur, qui in nos pari amoris affectu beneficium contulit. Vide Prop. 39 cum Schol. Prop. 41 hujus.
XXXV
Benevolentia est Cupiditas benefaciendi ei, cujus nos miseret. Vide Schol. Prop. 27 hujus.
XXXVI
Ira est Cupiditas, qua ex Odio incitamur ad illi, quem odimus, malum inferendum. Vide Prop. 39 hujus.
XXXVII
Vindicta est Cupiditas, qua ex reciproco Odio concitamur ad malum inferendum ei, qui nobis pari affectu damnum intulit Vide 2 Coroll. Prop. 40 hujus cum ejusdem Schol.
XXXVIII
Crudelitas seu Sævitia est Cupiditas, qua aliquis concitatur ad malum inferendum ei, quem amamus, vel cujus non miseret.
EXPLICATIO
Crudelitati opponitur Clementia, quæ passio non est, sed animi potentia, quo homo iram et vindictam moderatur.
XXXIX
Timor est Cupiditas majus, quod metuimus, malum minore vitandi. Vide Schol. Prop. 39 hujus.
XL
Audacia est Cupiditas, qua aliquis incitatur ad aliquid agendum cum periculo, quod ejus æquales subire metuunt.
XLI
Pusillanimitas dicitur de eo, cujus Cupiditas coercetur timore periculi, quod ejus æquales subire audent.
EXPLICATIO

Est igitur Pusillanimitas nihil aliud, quam Metus alicujus mali, quod plerique non solent metuere ; quare ipsam ad Cupiditatis affectus non refero. Eandem tamen hic explicare volui, quia, quatenus ad Cupiditatem attendimus, affectui Audaciæ revera opponitur.
XLII
Consternatio dicitur de eo, cujus Cupiditas malum vitandi coercetur admiratione mali, quod timet.
EXPLICATIO

Est itaque Consternatio Pusillanimitatis species. Sed quia Consternatio ex duplici Timore oritur, ideo commodius definiri potest, quod sit Metus, qui hominem stupefactum aut fluctuantem ita continet, ut is malum amovere non possit. Dico stupefactum, quatenus ejus Cupiditatem malum amovendi admiratione coerceri intelligimus. Fluctuantem autem dico, quatenus concipimus eandem Cupiditatem coerceri Timore alterius mali, quod ipsum æque cruciat : unde fit, ut, quodnam ex duobus avertat, nesciat. De his vide Schol. Prop. 39 et Schol. Prop. 52 hujus. Cæterum de Pusillanimitate et Audacia vide Schol. Prop. 51 hujus.
XLIII
Humanitas seu Modestia est Cupiditas ea faciendi, quæ hominibus placent, et omittendi, quæ displicent.
XLIV
Ambitio est immodica gloriæ Cupiditas.
EXPLICATIO

Ambitio est Cupiditas, qua omnes affectus (per Prop. 27 et 31 hujus) foventur et corroborantur ; et ideo hic affectus vix superari potest. Nam quamdiu homo aliqua Cupiditate tenetur, hac simul necessario tenetur. Optimus quisque, inquit Cicero, maxime gloria ducitur. Philosophi etiam libris, quos de contemnenda gloria scribunt, nomen suum inscribunt, etc.
XLV
Luxuria est immoderata convivandi Cupiditas, vel etiam Amor.
XLVI
Ebrietas est immoderata potandi Cupiditas et Amor.
XLVII
Avaritia est immoderata divitiarum Cupiditas et Armor.
XLVIII
Libido est etiam Cupiditas et Amor in commiscendis corporibus.
EXPLICATIO

Sive hæc coeundi Cupiditas moderata sit, sive non sit, Libido appellari solet. Porro hi quinque affectus (ut in Schol. Prop. 56 hujus monui) contrarios non habent. Nam Modestia species est Ambitionis, de qua vide Schol. Prop. 29 hujus. Temperantiam deinde, Sobrietatem, et Castitatem Mentis potentiam, non autem passionem indicare, jam etiam monui. Et tametsi fieri potest, ut homo avarus, ambitiosus, vel timidus a nimio cibo, potu, et coitu, abstineat ; Avaritia tamen, Ambitio et Timor luxuriæ, ebrietati, vel libidini non sunt contrarii. Nam avarus in cibum et potum alienum se ingurgitare plerumque desiderat. Ambitiosus autem, modo speret fore clam, in nulla re sibi temperabit, et si inter ebrios vivat et libidinosos, ideo quia ambitiosus est, proclivior erit ad eadem vitia. Timidus denique id, quod non vult, facit.

Nam quamvis mortis vitandæ causa divitias in mare projiciat, manet tamen avarus et si libidinosus tristis est, quod sibi morem gerere nequeat, non desinit propterea libidinosus esse. Et absolute hi affectus non tam ipsos actus convivandi, potandi, etc., respiciunt, quam ipsum Appetitum et Amorem. Nihil igitur his affectibus opponi potest, præter Generositatem et Animositatem, de quibus in seqq.

Definitiones Zelotypiæ et reliquarum animi fluctuationum silentio prætermitto, tam quia ex compositione affectuum, quos jam definivimus oriuntur, quam quia pleræque nomina non habent ; quod ostendit ad usum vitæ sufficere, easdem in genere tantummodo noscere. Cæterum ex Definitionibus affectuum, quos explicuimus, liquet eos omnes a Cupiditate, Lætitia, vel Tristitia oriri, seu potius nihil præter hos tres esse, quorum unusquisque variis nominibus appellari solet propter varias eorum relationes et denominationes extrinsecas. Si jam ad hos primitivos, et ad ea, quæ de natura Mentis supra diximus, attendere velimus, affectus, quatenus ad solam Mentem referuntur, sic definere poterimus.
AFFECTUUM GENERALIS DEFINITIO

Affectus, qui animi Pathema dicitur, est confusa idea qua Mens majorem vel minorem sui Corporis, vel alicujus ejus partis, existendi vim, quam antea, affirmat, et qua data ipsa Mens ad hoc potius quam ad illud cogitandum determinatur.
EXPLICATIO

Dico primo. Affectum seu passionem animi esse confusam ideam. Nam Mentem eatenus tantum pati ostendimus (vide Prop. 3 hujus), quatenus ideas inadæquatas sive confusas habet. Dico deinde, qua Mens majorem vel minorem sui Corporis, vel alicujus ejus partis, existendi vim, quam antea, affirmat. Omnes enim corporum ideæ, quas habemus, magis nostri Corporis actualem constitutionem (per Coroll. 2 Prop. 16 p. II), quam corporis externi naturam indicant ; at hæc, quæ affectus formam constituit, Corporis, vel alicujus ejus partis, constitutionem indicare vel exprimere debet, quam ipsum Corpus vel aliqua ejus pars habet, ex eo, quod ipsius agendi potentia sive existendi vis augetur vel minuitur, juvatur vel coercetur.

Sed notandum, cum dico, majorem vel minorem existendi vim, quam antea, me non intelligere, quod Mens præsentem, Corporis constitutionem cum præterita comparat, sed quod idea, quæ affectus formam constituit, aliquid de Corpore affirmat, quod plus minusve realitatis revera involvit, quam antea. Et quia essentia Mentis in hoc consistit (per Prop. 11 et 13 p. II), quod sui Corporis actualem existentiam affirmat, et nos per perfectionem ipsam rei essentiam intelligimus ; sequitur ergo, quod Mens ad majorem minoremve perfectionem transit, quando ei aliquid de suo Corpore, vel aliqua ejus parte, affirmare contingit, quod plus minusve realitatis involvit, quam antea.

Cum igitur supra dixerim, Mentis cogitandi potentiam augeri vel minui, nihil aliud intelligere volui, quam quod Mens ideam sui Corporis, vel alicujus ejus partis, formaverit, quæ plus minusve realitatis exprimit, quam de suo Corpore affirmaverat. Nam idearum præstantia, et actualis cogitandi potentia, ex objecti præstantia, æstimatur. Addidi denique, et qua data idea Mens ad hoc potius quam ad aliud cogitandum determinatur, ut præter Laetitiæ et Tristitiæ naturam, quam prima definitionis pars explicat, Cupiditatis etiam naturam exprimerem.
Finis Tertiæ Partis

translations.title: Pars tertia - De origine et natura affectuum · passage 5

paragraphs.text: In the Scholium to Proposition 18 of Part II we showed what is the cause why the Mind, from the contemplation of one thing, immediately falls upon the thought of another thing: namely, because the images of those things are mutually concatenated and so ordered that one follows another; which indeed cannot be conceived when the image of a thing is new, but the Mind will be held in the contemplation of the same thing until it is determined by other causes to think of other things. Therefore, the imagination of a new thing, considered in itself, is of the same nature as the rest; and for this reason I do not number Admiration among the affects, nor do I see any reason why I should do so, since this distraction of the Mind arises from no positive cause that distracts the Mind from other things, but only from the fact that the cause is lacking why the Mind is determined, from the contemplation of one thing, to think of other things. Therefore I acknowledge only three (as I noted in the Schol. to Prop.

11 of this Part) primitive or primary affects, namely Joy, Sadness, and Desire; nor did I speak of Admiration for any other reason than that it has become customary for certain affects that are derived from the three primitive ones to be designated by other names when they are referred to objects which we admire; and this same reason equally moves me to add here also the definition of Contempt.

V

Contempt is the imagination of some thing which affects the Mind so little that the Mind itself, from the presence of the thing, is moved more to imagine those things which are not in the thing than those which are in it (see the Schol. to Prop. 52 of this Part).
I pass over here the definitions of Veneration and Indignation, because, so far as I know, no affects take their name from these.
VI
Love is Joy accompanied by the idea of an external cause.
EXPLANATION

This Definition explains the essence of Love sufficiently clearly; but that of the Authors who define Love as the will of the lover to unite himself with the thing loved expresses not the essence of Love but a property of it; and because the essence of Love was not sufficiently perceived by the Authors, they could therefore have no clear conception of its property either; and hence it came about that everyone judged their definition to be exceedingly obscure.

But it should be noted that, when I say that it is a property in the lover to unite himself by will with the thing loved, by will I do not understand consent, or deliberation of the mind, or a free decree (for I have demonstrated that this is fictitious in Proposition 48 of Part II), nor even the Desire to unite oneself with the thing loved when it is absent, or to persevere in its presence when it is present; for love can be conceived without this or that Desire; but by will I understand the Acquiescence that is in the Lover on account of the presence of the thing loved, by which the Joy of the lover is strengthened, or at least cherished.
VII
Hate is Sadness accompanied by the idea of an external cause.
EXPLANATION
What should here be noted is easily understood from what was said in the Explanation of the preceding Definition (see moreover the Schol. to Prop. 13 of this Part).
VIII
Inclination is Joy accompanied by the idea of some thing which is accidentally a cause of Joy.
IX
Aversion is Sadness accompanied by the idea of some thing which is accidentally a cause of Sadness (concerning these, see the Schol. to Prop. 15 of this Part).

X

Devotion is Love toward one whom we admire.
EXPLANATION

We showed in Proposition 52 of this Part that Admiration arises from the novelty of a thing. If therefore it happens that we frequently imagine what we admire, we shall cease to admire the same thing; and thus we see that the affect of Devotion easily degenerates into simple Love.
XI
Derision is Joy arising from the fact that we imagine that something which we contemn is present in a thing which we hate.
EXPLANATION

Insofar as we contemn a thing which we hate, we deny existence to it (see the Schol. to Prop. 52 of this Part), and insofar (by Prop. 20 of this Part) we rejoice. But since we suppose that a man nevertheless hates that which he derides, it follows that this Joy is not solid (see the Schol. to Prop. 47 of this Part).
XII
Hope is an inconstant Joy, arising from the idea of a future or past thing, about whose outcome we to some extent doubt.
XIII
Fear is an inconstant Sadness, arising from the idea of a future or past thing, about whose outcome we to some extent doubt (see Scholium 2 of Proposition 18 of this Part).
EXPLANATION

From these definitions it follows that there is no Hope without Fear, nor Fear without Hope. For one who depends on Hope and doubts the outcome of a thing is supposed to imagine something that excludes the existence of the future thing; and accordingly, to that extent, to be saddened (by Proposition 19 of this Part), and consequently, while he depends on Hope, to fear that the thing may come to pass. But one who, on the contrary, is in Fear—that is, who doubts the outcome of a thing which he hates—also imagines something that excludes the existence of that same thing; and accordingly (by Proposition 20 of this Part) he rejoices, and consequently to that extent has Hope that it may not come to pass.
XIV
Security is Joy arising from the idea of a future or past thing, concerning which the cause for doubting has been removed.
XV
Despair is Sadness arising from the idea of a future or past thing, concerning which the cause for doubting has been removed.
EXPLANATION

Thus Security arises from Hope, and Despair from Fear, when the cause for doubting about the outcome of a thing is removed; which happens because a man imagines the past or future thing to be at hand and contemplates it as present, or because he imagines other things that exclude the existence of those things which cast doubt upon him. For although we can never be certain of the outcome of singular things (by the Corollary of Proposition 31, Part II), it can nevertheless happen that we do not doubt their outcome. For we have shown (see the Scholium of Proposition 49, Part II) that not to doubt a thing is one thing, and to have certainty of the thing another; and accordingly, it can happen that we are affected by the image of a past or future thing with the same affect of Joy or Sadness as by the image of a present thing, as we demonstrated in Proposition 18 of this Part; see that Proposition together with its Scholium.
XVI
Gladness is Joy accompanied by the idea of a past thing which has come to pass beyond Hope.
XVII
Remorse of conscience is Sadness accompanied by the idea of a past thing which has come to pass beyond Hope.
XVIII

Compassion is Sadness accompanied by the idea of an evil which has befallen another whom we imagine to be like ourselves (see the Scholium of Proposition 22 and the Scholium of Proposition 27 of this Part).
EXPLANATION
There seems to be no difference between Compassion and Mercy, unless perhaps that Compassion concerns a singular affect, while Mercy concerns its habitual disposition.
XIX
Favor is Love toward someone who has done good to another.
XX
Indignation is Hatred toward someone who has done harm to another.
EXPLANATION

I know that these names signify something else in common usage. But my purpose is not to explain the meaning of words, but the nature of things, and to indicate them by those terms whose meaning, as they have it from usage, does not altogether differ from the meaning in which I wish to employ them; it will suffice to have given this warning once. For the rest, see the cause of these affects in Corollary 1 of Proposition 27 and the Scholium of Proposition 22 of this Part.
XXI
Esteem is thinking of someone, on account of Love, more highly than is just.
XXII
Contempt is thinking of someone, on account of Hatred, less highly than is just.
EXPLANATION

Esteem, therefore, is an effect or property of Love, and Contempt of Hatred; and accordingly Esteem may also be defined as Love insofar as it affects a man so that he thinks of the thing loved more highly than is just; and, conversely, Contempt as Hatred insofar as it affects a man so that he thinks less highly than is just of him whom he hates (see concerning these the Scholium of Proposition 26 of this Part).
XXIII
Envy is Hatred insofar as it affects a man so that he is saddened by another's good fortune and, conversely, rejoices in another's misfortune.
EXPLANATION
Mercy is commonly opposed to Envy, and therefore, contrary to the meaning of the word, may be defined as follows:
XXIV
Mercy is Love insofar as it affects a man so that he rejoices in another's good and, conversely, is saddened by another's evil.
EXPLANATION

For the rest, concerning Envy see the Scholium of Proposition 24 and the Scholium of Proposition 32 of this Part. And these are affects of Joy and Sadness which are accompanied by the idea of an external thing as cause, either through itself or accidentally. Hence I pass on to others, which are accompanied by the idea of an internal thing as cause.
XXV
Self-contentment is Joy arising from the fact that a man contemplates himself and his power of acting.
XXVI
Humility is Sadness arising from the fact that a man contemplates his own powerlessness or weakness.
EXPLANATION

Self-contentment is opposed to Humility, insofar as by the latter we understand the Joy which arises from the fact that we contemplate our power of acting; but insofar as by it we also understand Joy accompanied by the idea of some deed which we believe that we have done from the free decree of the Mind, it is then opposed to Repentance, which we define as follows:
XXVII
Repentance is Sadness accompanied by the idea of some deed which we believe that we have done from a free decree of the Mind.
EXPLANATION

We have shown the causes of these affects in the Scholium to Proposition 51 of this [Part], and in Propositions 53, 54, and 55 of this [Part], and its Scholium. But concerning the free decree of the Mind, see the Scholium to Proposition 35, Part II. Yet here it should further be noted that it is not surprising that Sadness should follow absolutely all acts that are customarily called wrong, and Joy those that are called right. For that this depends chiefly on education is easily understood from what has been said above. For parents, by reproaching the former, and often scolding their children on account of them, but by approving and praising the latter, have brought it about that the agitations of Sadness are joined to the former, and those of Joy to the latter. Experience itself also confirms this. For custom and Religion are not the same for everyone; but, on the contrary, what is sacred among some is profane among others, and what is honorable among some is shameful among others. Therefore, according as each person has been educated, so he repents of some deed, or glories in it.
XXVIII
Pride is thinking of oneself more highly than is just, from Self-love.
EXPLANATION

Pride therefore differs from Esteem in that the latter is referred to an external object, whereas Pride is referred to the very man himself, who thinks of himself more highly than is just. Moreover, just as Esteem is an effect or property of Love, so Pride is an effect or property of Self-love; and therefore it can also be defined as Love of oneself, or Acquiescence in oneself, insofar as it affects a man so that he thinks of himself more highly than is just (see Schol. Prop. 26 of this [Part]). No contrary is given to this affect. For no one thinks of himself less highly than is just from Hatred of himself; indeed, no one thinks of himself less highly than is just insofar as he imagines that he cannot do this or that. For whatever a man imagines that he cannot do, he necessarily imagines, and by this imagination he is so disposed that he is in fact unable to do that which he imagines he cannot do. For as long as he imagines that he cannot do this or that, so long is he not determined to act, and consequently, so long is it impossible for him to do it.

But indeed, if we attend to those things which depend on opinion alone, we shall be able to conceive that it can come about that a man thinks of himself less highly than is just. For it can happen that someone, while sadly contemplating his own weakness, imagines himself to be despised by everyone, while the rest think of nothing less than despising him. Moreover, a man can think of himself less highly than is just if, with relation to a future time of which he is uncertain, he denies something of himself in the present; for example, if he denies that he can conceive anything certain, and that he can desire or do nothing except what is wrong or shameful, etc. We can further say that someone thinks of himself less highly than is just when we see that, from an excessive fear of shame, he does not dare to do those things which others equal to himself dare to do. Therefore we can oppose this affect to Pride, and I shall call it Abjectness; for as Pride arises from Acquiescence in oneself, so Abjectness arises from Humility, and hence is defined by us as follows.
XXIX
Abjectness is thinking of oneself less highly than is just, from Sadness.
EXPLANATION

Yet we often oppose Humility to Pride, but then we attend more to the effects of each than to their nature. For we are accustomed to call proud one who boasts too much (see Schol. Prop. 30 of this [Part]), who recounts only his own virtues and only others' vices, who wishes to be preferred to everyone, and who finally proceeds with that gravity and adornment with which others who are placed far above him are accustomed [to proceed]. On the other hand, we call humble one who blushes more often, who confesses his own vices and recounts the virtues of others, who yields to everyone, and who finally walks with bowed head and neglects to adorn himself. Moreover, these affects—namely, Humility and Abjectness—are exceedingly rare. For human nature, considered in itself, strives against them as much as it can (see Props. 13 and 54 of this [Part]); and therefore those who are believed to be most abject and humble are for the most part most ambitious and envious.
XXX
Glory is Joy accompanied by the idea of some action of ours which we imagine others to praise.
XXXI
Shame is Sadness accompanied by the idea of some action which we imagine others to blame.
EXPLANATION

On these, see the Scholium to Proposition 30 of this Part. But here the difference between Shame and Modesty is to be noted. For Shame is the Sadness which follows a deed of which one is ashamed. Modesty, however, is the Fear or Dread of Shame, by which a man is restrained from committing something shameful. Impudence is customarily opposed to Modesty; but in truth it is not an affect, as I shall show in its place. But the names of affects (as I have already warned) regard their use more than their nature. And with these I have completed the affects of Joy and Sadness which I had proposed to explain. I proceed therefore to those which I refer to Desire.
XXXII

Longing is Desire or Appetite for obtaining some thing, which is fostered by the memory of that same thing and is at the same time restrained by the memory of other things that exclude the existence of the thing to be desired.
EXPLANATION

When we remember some thing, as we have often already said, by that very fact we are disposed to contemplate it with the same affect as if the thing were present; but this disposition, or striving, while we are awake, is for the most part checked by images of things that exclude the existence of that which we remember. Therefore, when we remember a thing that affects us with some kind of Joy, by that very fact we strive to contemplate it as present with the same affect of Joy; and this striving is immediately checked by the memory of things that exclude its existence. Wherefore Longing is in truth a Sadness, which is opposed to that Joy which arises from the absence of a thing that we hate, concerning which see the Scholium to Proposition 47 of this Part. But because the name Longing seems to have regard to Desire, I therefore refer this affect to the affects of Desire.
XXXIII
Emulation is Desire for some thing which is generated in us from the fact that we imagine others to have the same Desire.
EXPLANATION

He who flees because he sees others flee, or who fears because he sees others fear; or likewise he who, because he sees that someone has burned his hand, draws his own hand back toward himself and moves his body as though his own hand were being burned—we shall indeed say that he imitates another's affect, but not that he emulates the same one; not because we know one cause of emulation and another of imitation, but because usage has made it the case that we call only that man an emulator who imitates what we judge to be honorable, useful, or pleasant. For the rest, concerning the cause of Emulation, see Proposition 27 of this Part with its Scholium. But why Envy is for the most part joined to this affect, see Proposition 32 of this Part with its Scholium.
XXXIV

Favor, or Gratitude, is Desire, or the striving of Love, by which we endeavor to do good to one who has conferred a benefit upon us with an equal affect of love. See Prop. 39 with the Scholium of Prop. 41 of this Part.
XXXV
Benevolence is the Desire to do good to one whom we pity. See the Scholium of Prop. 27 of this Part.
XXXVI
Anger is the Desire by which, from Hate, we are incited to inflict evil upon one whom we hate. See Prop. 39 of this Part.
XXXVII

Vengeance is the Desire by which, from reciprocal Hate, we are stirred to inflict evil upon one who has inflicted harm upon us with an equal affect. See Corollary 2 of Prop. 40 of this Part with its Scholium.
XXXVIII
Cruelty, or Savagery, is the Desire by which someone is stirred to inflict evil upon one whom we love, or upon one whom we do not pity.
EXPLANATION
Clemency is opposed to Cruelty; it is not a passion, but a power of mind by which a man moderates anger and vengeance.
XXXIX
Fear is the Desire to avoid a lesser evil which we fear by means of a greater one. See the Scholium of Prop. 39 of this Part.
XL
Boldness is the Desire by which someone is incited to undertake something with a danger which his equals fear to undergo.
XLI
Faintheartedness is said of one whose Desire is checked by the fear of a danger which his equals dare to undergo.
EXPLANATION

Faintheartedness, therefore, is nothing but the Fear of some evil which most people are not accustomed to fear; and for this reason I do not refer it to the affects of Desire. Yet I have wished to explain it here, because, insofar as we attend to Desire, it is truly opposed to the affect of Boldness.
XLII
Consternation is said of one whose Desire to avoid an evil is checked by astonishment at the evil which he fears.
EXPLANATION

Consternation, therefore, is a species of Faint-heartedness. But because Consternation arises from a twofold Fear, it can more conveniently be defined as a Dread that so holds a man stupefied or wavering that he cannot remove the evil. I say stupefied, insofar as we understand that his Desire to remove the evil is restrained by astonishment. But I say wavering insofar as we conceive that the same Desire is restrained by the Fear of another evil, which torments him equally; whence it comes about that he does not know which of the two to avert. On these matters see the Schol. to Prop. 39 and the Schol. to Prop. 52 of this Part. Moreover, concerning Faint-heartedness and Boldness, see the Schol. to Prop. 51 of this Part.
XLIII
Humanity, or Modesty, is the Desire to do those things that please men, and to omit those that displease them.
XLIV
Ambition is an immoderate Desire for glory.
EXPLANATION

Ambition is the Desire by which all the affects are fostered and strengthened (by Props. 27 and 31 of this Part); and therefore this affect can scarcely be overcome. For so long as a man is held by any Desire, he is at the same time necessarily held by this one. “The best of men,” says Cicero, “are most especially led by glory.” Even philosophers inscribe their names on the books that they write concerning the contempt of glory, etc.
XLV
Luxury is an immoderate Desire, or also Love, of feasting.
XLVI
Drunkenness is an immoderate Desire and Love of drinking.
XLVII
Avarice is an immoderate Desire and Love of riches.
XLVIII
Lust is likewise Desire and Love in the mingling of bodies.
EXPLANATION

Whether this Desire for coition be moderate or not, it is usually called Lust. Moreover, these five affects (as I have noted in the Schol. to Prop. 56 of this Part) have no contraries. For Modesty is a species of Ambition; concerning which see the Schol. to Prop. 29 of this Part. Further, I have already noted that Temperance, Sobriety, and Chastity indicate a power of the Mind, not a passion. And although it can happen that an avaricious, ambitious, or timid man abstains from excessive food, drink, and coition, Avarice, nevertheless, Ambition, and Fear are not contrary to luxury, drunkenness, or lust. For the avaricious man generally desires to gorge himself on another’s food and drink. But the ambitious man, provided he hopes that it will be done secretly, will restrain himself in nothing; and if he lives among drunkards and lustful men, precisely because he is ambitious, he will be more prone to the same vices. Finally, the timid man does what he does not will.

For although, in order to avoid death, he casts his riches into the sea, he nevertheless remains avaricious; and if the lustful man is sad because he cannot indulge himself, he does not for that reason cease to be lustful. And absolutely, these affects have regard not so much to the very acts of feasting, drinking, etc., as to Appetite and Love themselves. Therefore nothing can be opposed to these affects except Generosity and Strength of Mind, concerning which in what follows.

I pass over in silence the definitions of Jealousy and the remaining fluctuations of the mind, both because they arise from a composition of the affects that we have already defined, and because most of them have no names; which shows that, for the use of life, it suffices to know them only in general. Moreover, from the definitions of the affects that we have explained, it is clear that they all arise from Desire, Joy, or Sadness; or rather, that they are nothing other than these three, each of which is usually called by various names on account of their various relations and extrinsic denominations. If we now wish to attend to these primitive affects, and to what we have said above concerning the nature of the Mind, we shall be able to define the affects, insofar as they are referred to the Mind alone, as follows.
GENERAL DEFINITION OF THE AFFECTS
