Agens qui propter finem agit id appetit quo caret.
Deus nullo bono, obiecto vel perfectione extra se indiget.
Ignorantia causarum efficientium non constituit probationem causae finalis.
Homines res bonas vel malas iudicant prout res eorum valetudini, usui vel affectionibus conducunt aut repugnant.
Imaginatio rerum dispositiones secundum facilitatem repraesentandi et recordandi ordinat.
Dispositiones imaginativae diversorum corporum et cerebrorum inter homines discrepant.
Perfectio rei ex sola eius natura et potentia aestimanda est.
Leges Naturae ad omnia producenda quae ab intellectu infinito concipi possunt sufficiunt.
Natura non est agens deliberans quod media ad finem externum disponit.
Deus non agit ad obtinendum quod nondum possidet.
Causa finalis non est principium explicativum aequale causae efficienti.
Concursus circumstantiarum ignotus non est casus qui voluntatem divinam postulat.
Admiratio corporis humani non demonstrat structuram eius esse supernaturalem vel non-mechanicam.
Ordo non est attributum Naturae extra relationem ad facilitatem humanae imaginationis.
Bonum, malum, pulchritudo et deformitas non indicant naturas intrinsecas rerum.
Imperfectio rerum non sequitur ex eo quod res sensum humanum offendunt aut utilitati humanae repugnant.
Vocabula imaginationis non sunt entia realia quae argumentis contra necessitatem Naturae adhiberi possunt.
Doctrina finium invertit relationem causae et effectus, cum effectum postulatum tamquam rationem causae antecedentis tractet.
Si res immediate productae media ad finem divinum essent, effectus ultimi praeponerentur causis prioribus contra gradum perfectionis causaliter constitutum.
Teleologia perfectionem divinam tollit, quia Deum desiderio carentis subicit.
Regressus a causa ignota ad voluntatem Dei explicandi munus non perficit, sed ignorantiam nomine causae occultat.
Notiones aestimativae et sensibiles indicant constitutionem imaginationis iudicantis, non naturam obiecti iudicati.
Dissensio iudiciorum humanorum sequitur ex varietate dispositionum imaginativarum, non necessario ex varietate naturarum rerum.
Quaestio de malis et imperfectionibus Naturae solvenda est per naturam et potentiam rerum, non per comparationem cum commodo humano.
Systema teleologicum simul producit theologicam imminutam perfectionem Dei et epistemologiam imminutam cognitionem causarum efficientium.
Humanus anthropocentrismus transformat affectiones locales corporis in iudicia universalia de constitutione Naturae.
Sublata causalitate finali, Natura apparet ut campus productionis necessariae cuius varietas perfectionum non requirit normam externam.
Stupor conservat auctoritatem interpretum tantum dum causae verae occultae manent; cognitio causarum medium illius auctoritatis evacuat.
Falsum esse debet quod utilitas humana sit mensura ontologica perfectionis rerum.
Falsum esse debet quod ignorantia causalitatis licentiam praebeat ad causam transcendentem affirmandam.
Falsum esse debet quod cognitio Naturae ex admiratione vel horrore sensibiliter constituto oriatur.
Falsum esse debet quod Deus sit artifex qui finem praeconceptum per instrumenta ordinat.
Falsum esse debet quod vocabula valoris et ordinis, quia nomina habent, res sive proprietates rerum significent.
Systema excludit omnem normam extrinsecam ex qua Natura deficiens, prava vel incompleta iudicari possit.
Systema excludit mundum factum propter hominem, quia haec possibilitas necessitatem productionis naturalis in privilegium imaginarium convertit.
Systema excludit transitum legitimam ab experientia subiectiva ad structuram metaphysicam rerum sine cognitione causarum.
Necessitas naturae divinae → productio rerum sine fine praestituto.
Productio sine fine → exclusio Dei indigentis et exclusio inversionis causae-effectus.
Ignorantia causarum efficientium + inquisitio finis → voluntas divina ut asylum ignorantiae.
Utilitas humana + imaginatio affecta → vocabula aestimativa, ordinativa et moralia tamquam modi imaginandi.
Reductio vocabulorum ad imaginationem + mensura perfectionis ex natura et potentia → dissolutio objectionis ex malo, deformitate et corruptione.
Leges Naturae amplissimae → varietas graduum perfectionis sine defectu materiae, finis vel ordinis transcendentis.
Praeiudicium finis naturalis → detectio originis humanae et utilitariae.
Finis suppositus → inversio causalitatis + imminutio perfectionis divinae.
Circumstantiae ignotae → regressus interrogationum → voluntas Dei ut nomen ignorantiae.
Utilitas et affectio corporis → bonum/malum, ordo/confusio, pulchritudo/deformitas.
Varietas imaginandi → controversia et scepticismus → distinctio imaginationis ab intellectu.
Distinctio imaginationis ab intellectu → perfectio ex natura et potentia → defensio necessitatis Naturae.
Causa finalis reclassificatur ab elemento Naturae ad figmentum humanum ex ignorantia et utilitate ortum.
Deus reclassificatur ab artifice finem quaerente ad naturam infinitam cuius productio ex necessitate sequitur.
Malum, deformitas, confusio et corruptio reclassificantur ab imperfectionibus ontologicis ad relationes imaginativas vel utilitarias.
Ordo reclassificatur ab architectura obiectiva rerum ad modum quo res imaginationi facile repraesentantur et memoriae traduntur.
Scepticismus reclassificatur ab effectu necessario cognitionis ad effectum iudiciorum fundatorum in dispositionibus imaginativis discrepantibus.
Surface — Textus negat Naturam propter finem agere et negat imperfectiones vulgo nominatas contra perfectionem Naturae valere.
Structural — Praeiudicium teleologicum generatur per concatenationem ignorantiae causarum, quaestus utilitatis et imaginationis corpore affectae.
Metastrategic — Argumentatio adversaria a quaestione “cur hoc factum est?” ad quaestionem de causis efficientibus et de conditionibus iudicii transfertur.
Ontological/Temporal — Natura constituitur ut ordo necessarius in quo prioritas causalis et gradus perfectionis non a finibus futuris, sed a potentia producente dependent.
Axiomata de necessitate Naturae, exclusionis finis et prioritate causae efficientis sufficiunt ad nucleum critique teleologiae restituendum.
Axiomata de utilitate, imaginatione et varietate corporum sufficiunt ad generationem notionum aestimativarum et controversiarum explicandam.

Nexus inter doctrinam metaphysicam necessitatis et doctrinam psychologicam imaginationis manet validus, sed transitum a dispositione corporali ad formas historicas auctoritatis tantum breviter determinat.
Firmissimum systematis punctum est reductio causae finalis ad contradictionem causalitatis inversae, indigentiae divinae et ignorantiae explicativae.

Commissura fragilis manet in reductione ordinis, pulchritudinis et valoris ad imaginationem, quia textus distinctionem inter relationem imaginativam et structuram obiectivam singulorum casuum non plene formalizat.
Restitutio motum textus servat, si necessitas Naturae, critica teleologiae, genealogia notionum vulgarium et mensura perfectionis ex natura rei in eadem catena tenentur.
The text asks on what foundation the doctrine of natural ends and the common terms by which Nature is called imperfect can be sustained.
The text establishes that Nature acts for no end, but that all things follow from the eternal necessity and perfection of the divine nature.
The polemical-diagnostic argument transforms end from an explaining cause into an effect of the human imagination seeking its own advantage.
Final causality is dissolved because it inverts the causal order, makes God needy, and concludes a regress of questions in ignorance.
The notions of good, evil, order, confusion, beauty, and deformity are reduced to imaginative affections of human bodies.
The assessment of perfection is restored from its effect upon human senses to the nature and power of singular things.
All things in nature follow from the eternal necessity of the divine nature.
Nature sets before itself no end.
An efficient cause is by nature prior to the effect that it produces.
An effect immediately produced by God is more perfect than an effect that requires several intermediate causes.
An agent that acts for an end desires that which it lacks.
God needs no good, object, or perfection outside himself.
Ignorance of efficient causes does not constitute proof of a final cause.
Human beings judge things good or evil insofar as things conduce or are opposed to their health, use, or affections.
Imagination orders the dispositions of things according to ease of representing and remembering them.
The imaginative dispositions of different bodies and brains differ among human beings.
The perfection of a thing is to be assessed from its nature and power alone.
The laws of Nature suffice to produce all things that can be conceived by an infinite intellect.
Nature is not a deliberating agent that disposes means toward an external end.
God does not act in order to obtain what he does not yet possess.
A final cause is not an explanatory principle equal to an efficient cause.
An unknown concurrence of circumstances is not chance that requires a divine will.
Wonder at the human body does not demonstrate that its structure is supernatural or non-mechanical.
Order is not an attribute of Nature apart from its relation to the ease of human imagination.
Good, evil, beauty, and deformity do not indicate intrinsic natures of things.
The imperfection of things does not follow from the fact that things offend human sense or conflict with human utility.
The terms of imagination are not real entities that can be employed as arguments against the necessity of Nature.
The doctrine of ends inverts the relation of cause and effect, insofar as it treats the postulated effect as the reason for the antecedent cause.
If immediately produced things were means to a divine end, the final effects would be preferred to prior causes, contrary to the causally established degree of perfection.
Teleology removes divine perfection because it subjects God to the desire of one who lacks.
The regress from an unknown cause to the will of God does not fulfill the explanatory function, but conceals ignorance under the name of cause.
Evaluative and sensible notions indicate the constitution of the judging imagination, not the nature of the judged object.
The disagreement of human judgments follows from the variety of imaginative dispositions, not necessarily from the variety of the natures of things.
The question of the evils and imperfections of Nature must be resolved through the nature and power of things, not through comparison with human convenience.
The teleological system simultaneously produces a theological diminution of God's perfection and an epistemological diminution of knowledge of efficient causes.
Human anthropocentrism transforms local affections of the body into universal judgments about the constitution of Nature.
With final causality removed, Nature appears as a field of necessary production whose variety of perfections requires no external norm.
Wonder preserves the authority of interpreters only so long as true causes remain hidden; knowledge of causes voids the means of that authority.
It must be false that human utility is the ontological measure of the perfection of things.
It must be false that ignorance of causality grants license to affirm a transcendent cause.
It must be false that knowledge of Nature arises from sensibly constituted admiration or horror.
It must be false that God is an artisan who orders a preconceived end through instruments.
It must be false that terms of value and order, because they have names, signify things or properties of things.
The system excludes every extrinsic norm by which Nature could be judged deficient, depraved, or incomplete.
The system excludes a world made for humankind, because this possibility converts the necessity of natural production into an imaginary privilege.
The system excludes a legitimate transition from subjective experience to the metaphysical structure of things without knowledge of causes.
Necessity of the divine nature → production of things without a pre-established end.
Production without an end → exclusion of a needy God and exclusion of the inversion of cause and effect.
Ignorance of efficient causes + inquiry into end → divine will as an asylum of ignorance.
Human utility + affected imagination → evaluative, ordering, and moral terms as modes of imagining.
Reduction of terms to imagination + measure of perfection from nature and power → dissolution of the objection from evil, deformity, and corruption.
Most extensive laws of Nature → variety of degrees of perfection without defect of matter, end, or transcendent order.
Prejudice of natural end → detection of its human and utilitarian origin.
Supposed end → inversion of causality + diminution of divine perfection.
Unknown circumstances → regress of questions → will of God as the name of ignorance.
Utility and affection of the body → good/evil, order/confusion, beauty/deformity.
Variety of imagining → controversy and skepticism → distinction of imagination from intellect.
Distinction of imagination from intellect → perfection from nature and power → defense of the necessity of Nature.
Final cause is reclassified from an element of Nature to a human fiction arising from ignorance and utility.
God is reclassified from an artisan seeking an end to infinite nature whose production follows from necessity.
Evil, deformity, confusion, and corruption are reclassified from ontological imperfections to imaginative or utilitarian relations.
Order is reclassified from an objective architecture of things to the mode in which things are easily represented to imagination and committed to memory.
Skepticism is reclassified from a necessary effect of knowledge to an effect of judgments founded on discrepant imaginative dispositions.
Surface — The text denies that Nature acts for an end and denies that commonly named imperfections count against Nature's perfection.
Structural — Teleological prejudice is generated through the concatenation of ignorance of causes, pursuit of utility, and bodily affected imagination.
Metastrategic — The adversarial argument is shifted from the question “why was this made?” to the question of efficient causes and of the conditions of judgment.
Ontological/Temporal — Nature is constituted as a necessary order in which causal priority and degrees of perfection depend not on future ends, but on productive power.
The axioms concerning the necessity of Nature, the exclusion of end, and the priority of the efficient cause suffice to reconstruct the core of the critique of teleology.
The axioms concerning utility, imagination, and the variety of bodies suffice to explain the generation of evaluative notions and controversies.

The connection between the metaphysical doctrine of necessity and the psychological doctrine of imagination remains valid, but determines only briefly the transition from bodily disposition to historical forms of authority.
The strongest point of the system is the reduction of final cause to the contradiction of inverted causality, divine need, and explanatory ignorance.

A fragile joint remains in the reduction of order, beauty, and value to imagination, because the text does not fully formalize the distinction between imaginative relation and the objective structure of individual cases.

The reconstruction preserves the movement of the text if the necessity of Nature, the critique of teleology, the genealogy of common notions, and the measure of perfection from the nature of the thing are held in the same chain.

units.title: Pars secunda - De natura et origine mentis · passage 1

items.text: Textus quaerit quo ordine Mens humana ex necessitate divinae naturae intelligenda sit, ut via ad cognitionem mentis et beatitudinis aperiatur.
Thesis constitutiva est Mentem humanam non substantiam esse, sed ideam rei singularis actu existentis, cuius obiectum Corpus humanum est.
Argumentatio est metaphysico-deductiva et reconstructiva: a necessitate Dei et attributorum ad seriem modorum, inde ad structuram Mentis humanae procedit.
Causalitas intra attributum et identitas ordinis idearum cum ordine rerum impediunt ne Mens et Corpus ut res separatae aut causaliter transversae concipiantur.
Demonstratio Mentis in cognitionem Corporis transfertur, quia unionis Mentis et Corporis ratio atque graduum mentis differentia ex natura Corporis dependere ponuntur.
Essentiam rei constituit id quo dato res necessario ponitur, quo sublato necessario tollitur, atque quod sine re nec esse nec concipi potest et vice versa.
Res singularis est res finita existentiam determinatam habens.
Nihil sine Deo esse neque concipi potest.
Deus est unica causa tam essentiae quam existentiae rerum.
Potentia Dei est eius essentia actuosa, ex qua Deus eadem necessitate agit qua se intelligit.
Cogitatio est attributum Dei quod eius essentiam aeternam et infinitam exprimit.
Extensio est attributum Dei quod eius essentiam aeternam et infinitam exprimit.
Substantia cogitans et substantia extensa una eademque substantia sunt, sub diversis attributis concepta.
Modus cuiusque attributi Deum causam habet quatenus sub illo solo attributo consideratur.
Esse formale idearum Deum causam habet quatenus res cogitans est.
Ordo et connexio idearum idem est ac ordo et connexio rerum.
Idea rei singularis non existentis non est nisi quatenus in infinita Dei idea comprehenditur.
Essentia hominis necessariam existentiam non involvit, nec substantia formam hominis constituit.
Homo cogitat.
Idea in eodem individuo natura prior est reliquis modis cogitandi.
Homo Corpus multis modis affici sentit.
Homo nullas res singulares praeter corpora et cogitandi modos sentit aut percipit.
Corpora ratione motus et quietis distinguuntur, et determinatio cuiusque corporis ad motum vel quietem ab aliis corporibus in infinitum pendet.
Potentia Dei non est libera voluntas regia neque ius contingenter destruendi aut conservandi res.
Idea non ab ideato, neque a modo alterius attributi, causam efficientem recipit.
Cogitatio et Extensio non sunt duae substantiae realiter separatae.
Homo non est substantia nec ex sua essentia necessario existit.
Deus, quamvis sine ipso res singulares nec sint nec concipiantur, ad essentiam earum secundum definitionem reciprocitatis non pertinet.
Primum esse actuale Mentis humanae non est idea rei non existentis neque rei infinitae.
Obiectum Mentis humanae non est aliquid praeter Corpus actu existens.
Adaequatio ideae non per convenientiam externam cum ideato definitur, sed per proprietates intrinsecas ideae verae.
Deus necessario ideam suae essentiae format et omnium quae ex ea necessario sequuntur.
Idea Dei ex qua infinita infinitis modis sequuntur unica est.
Ideae formaliter intra attributum Cogitationis producuntur, sicut modi cuiusque alterius attributi intra proprium attributum producuntur.
Modus Extensionis et idea eius non sunt res duae, sed una res per Extensionalem et Cogitativam expressionem intellecta.
Essentia hominis est certa modificatio attributorum Dei, non ens per se subsistens.
Primum quod actuale Mentis humanae esse constituit est idea rei singularis actu existentis.
Mens humana pars est infiniti intellectus Dei et rem inadæquate percipit, cum idea eius simul ad seriem idearum aliarum rerum pertinet.
Obiectum ideae Mentem humanam constituentis est Corpus actu existens et nihil aliud.
Quicquid in Corpore, quod Mentis humanae obiectum est, contingit, a Mente humana necessario percipitur.
Homo constat Mente et Corpore, atque Corpus humanum existit prout sentitur.

Aptitudo Mentis ad plura simul percipiendum proportionatur aptitudini Corporis ad plura simul agendum vel patiendum; distinctior intellectio crescit quo actiones Corporis magis ex ipso solo dependent.
Problema commercii causalis inter Mentem et Corpus dissolvitur: causalitas transversalis inter attributa excluditur, dum identitas rei sub duplici expressione retinetur.
Cognitio humana non est accessus ad res in se separatas, sed ordo idearum localiter constitutus per Corpus cuius Mens idea est.
Differentia mentium non ex diversitate substantiarum animarum, sed ex gradu compositionis, passionis et actionis Corporum derivatur.
Necessitas divina, series modorum intra attributa et determinatio corporum constituunt naturam sine contingentia principiali et sine causa finali externa.
Exemplar Dei transcendentis, qui extra naturam decretis voluntariis mundum gubernat, falsum esse debet ut causalitas immanens necessaria valeat.
Exemplar animae incorporeae quae Corpus extrinsece movet vel a Corpore causaliter afficitur falsum esse debet ut attributorum causalitas propria servetur.
Exemplar individui humani ut fundamenti sui ipsius falsum esse debet, quia homo est modificatio finita et necessario causata.
Exemplar cognitionis humanae ut comprehensio totalitatis falsum esse debet, quia Mens humana pars intellectus infiniti et idea corporis singularis est.
Exemplar essentiae ut mera dependentia unilateralis a Deo falsum esse debet, quia essentia reciprocitatem inter rem et id quod eam constituit postulat.
Systema nullum locum ontologicum extra Deum relinquit, ex quo Deus, res finitae, ideae et corpora ut entia independenter comparanda conspici possint.
Systema nullam mediationem primitivam inter Cogitationem et Extensionem admittit: quod mediatio videretur est eadem res sub diversis attributis expressa.
Systema nullum criterium veritatis mere externum admittit, quia ratio ideae adaequatae in ipsa idea, non in sola relatione comparativa ad obiectum, collocatur.
Essentia divina actuosa necessaria → attributa infinita → modi necessario consequentes.
Attributum determinatum → causalitas intra idem attributum → exclusio causalitatis inter attributa.
Unica substantia + pluralitas attributorum → idem ens dupliciter expressum → parallelismus ordinis idearum et rerum.
Homo non-substantialis + homo cogitans + prioritas ideae → essentia humana ut modificatio cogitativa ordinata circa ideam.
Idea actualis rei singularis + sensus affectionum Corporis + exclusio aliorum obiectorum perceptorum → Mens humana ut idea Corporis actu existentis.
Corpus ut obiectum Mentis → omnis eius affectio perceptibilis → gradus cognitionis ex gradu compositionis et autonomiae corporis → transitus ad physicam corporum.

Necessitas essentiae divinae → Cogitatio et Extensio ut attributa → causalitas attributiva → parallelismus idearum et rerum → homo ut modus finitus → Mens ut idea actualis → Corpus ut obiectum unicum → perceptio affectionum Corporis → analysis motus et quietis.
Promissio cognitionis summae beatitudinis → constitutio metaphysica Mentis → definitio unionis Mentis et Corporis → praeparatio physica nondum absolutae beatitudinis demonstratio.
Deus reclassificatur ex voluntate externa et regia in causam immanentem, necessariam et actuosam omnium essentiarum atque existentiarum.
Unio Mentis et Corporis reclassificatur ex relatione inter duas res in relationem ideae ad idem Corpus sub alio attributo expressum.
Idea reclassificatur ex imagine a re recepta in modum Cogitationis formaliter intra Cogitationem causatum.
Individualitas corporis reclassificatur ex differentia substantiae in rationem motus, quietis, celeritatis et tarditatis.
Praestantia mentis reclassificatur ex dignitate animae separatae in potentiam corporis plura simul agendi, patiendi et ex se ordinandi.
Surface — Mens humana idea est Corporis actu existentis, et ea quae in hoc Corpore contingunt necessario percipit.
Structural — Modi cogitandi et modi extensi secundum causalitates attributivas distinctas ordinantur, quarum ordines tamen unum eundemque nexum rerum exprimunt.
Metastrategic — Ordo philosophandi a rebus sensuum ad Deum ascendens reicitur; natura divina, cognitione et natura prior, fundamentum explicativum ante res naturales collocatur.
Ontological/Temporal — Deus aeternus necessario agit, res singulares finite et determinate existunt, earum duratio indefinita est, et corporum determinatio in seriem infinitam causarum extenditur.
Systema extractum sufficit ad conclusionem immediatam restituendam quod Mens humana sit idea Corporis actu existentis.
Demonstratio pendet a principiis Partis primae de unica substantia, causalitate Dei et distinctione attributorum, quae hic assumuntur potius quam iterum fundantur.
Commissura principalis manet inter identitatem Mentis et Corporis ut unius rei et necessitatem eos per causalitates attributivas omnino separatas explicandi.

Distinctio inter Deum ut condicionem sine qua res finita nec est nec concipitur et Deum ut non pertinentem ad essentiam rei finitae solum per strictam reciprocitatis definitionem essentiae continetur.
Correlatio inter potentiam Corporis et perfectionem Mentis affirmatur, sed mechanismus compositionis corporalis qui gradus illos explicet ad doctrinam physicam subsequentem differtur.
Motus argumenti ad cognitionem beatitudinis dirigi dicitur, sed haec pars tantum condicionem ontologicam et epistemicam itineris ponit, non beatitudinem ipsam deducit.

translations.title: Part Two - On the Nature and Origin of the Mind · passage 1

items.text: The text asks in what order the human Mind is to be understood from the necessity of the divine nature, so that the way to knowledge of the mind and blessedness may be opened.
The constitutive thesis is that the human Mind is not a substance, but the idea of an actually existing singular thing, whose object is the human Body.
The argumentation is metaphysical-deductive and reconstructive: it proceeds from the necessity of God and the attributes to the series of modes, thence to the structure of the human Mind.
Causality within an attribute and the identity of the order of ideas with the order of things prevent Mind and Body from being conceived as separate things or as causally transverse.

The demonstration of the Mind is transferred into knowledge of the Body, because the account of the union of Mind and Body and the difference in degrees of minds are held to depend on the nature of the Body.

The essence of a thing is constituted by that which, if given, necessarily posits the thing, and which, if removed, necessarily removes it, and which can neither be nor be conceived without the thing, and vice versa.
A singular thing is a finite thing having determinate existence.
Nothing can be or be conceived without God.
God is the sole cause both of the essence and of the existence of things.
The power of God is his active essence, from which God acts with the same necessity by which he understands himself.
Thought is an attribute of God that expresses his eternal and infinite essence.
Extension is an attribute of God that expresses his eternal and infinite essence.
Thinking substance and extended substance are one and the same substance, conceived under different attributes.
A mode of each attribute has God as its cause insofar as he is considered under that attribute alone.
The formal being of ideas has God as its cause insofar as he is a thinking thing.
The order and connection of ideas is the same as the order and connection of things.
The idea of a singular thing that does not exist is only insofar as it is comprehended in the infinite idea of God.
The essence of man does not involve necessary existence, nor does substance constitute the form of man.
Man thinks.
In the same individual, an idea is by nature prior to the remaining modes of thinking.
Man senses that the Body is affected in many ways.
Man senses or perceives no singular things except bodies and modes of thinking.
Bodies are distinguished by the relation of motion and rest, and the determination of each body to motion or rest depends on other bodies to infinity.
The power of God is not free royal will, nor a right contingently to destroy or preserve things.
An idea does not receive its efficient cause from the ideate, nor from a mode of another attribute.
Thought and Extension are not two really separate substances.
Man is not a substance, nor does he necessarily exist from his essence.
God, although singular things can neither be nor be conceived without him, does not pertain to their essence according to the definition of reciprocity.
The first actual being of the human Mind is not the idea of a non-existing thing nor of an infinite thing.
The object of the human Mind is not anything other than an actually existing Body.
The adequacy of an idea is not defined by external correspondence with the ideate, but by the intrinsic properties of a true idea.
God necessarily forms an idea of his essence and of all things that necessarily follow from it.
The idea of God from which infinitely many things follow in infinitely many ways is unique.
Ideas are formally produced within the attribute of Thought, just as the modes of each other attribute are produced within their own attribute.
A mode of Extension and its idea are not two things, but one thing understood through extensive and cogitative expression.
The essence of man is a certain modification of the attributes of God, not a being subsisting through itself.
The first thing that constitutes the actual being of the human Mind is the idea of an actually existing singular thing.
The human Mind is a part of the infinite intellect of God and perceives a thing inadequately when its idea simultaneously pertains to the series of ideas of other things.
The object of the idea constituting the human Mind is an actually existing Body and nothing else.
Whatever happens in the Body that is the object of the human Mind is necessarily perceived by the human Mind.
Man consists of Mind and Body, and the human Body exists insofar as it is sensed.

The aptitude of the Mind to perceive many things at once is proportionate to the aptitude of the Body to act or be acted upon in many ways at once; more distinct understanding increases insofar as the actions of the Body depend more upon it alone.
The problem of causal commerce between Mind and Body is dissolved: transverse causality between attributes is excluded, while the identity of the thing under a double expression is retained.
Human knowledge is not access to things separately in themselves, but an order of ideas locally constituted through the Body of which the Mind is the idea.
The difference of minds derives not from the diversity of substances of souls, but from the degree of composition, passion, and action of Bodies.
Divine necessity, the series of modes within attributes, and the determination of bodies constitute a nature without principled contingency and without external final cause.
The model of a transcendent God who governs the world outside nature by voluntary decrees must be false if necessary immanent causality is to hold.
The model of an incorporeal soul that moves the Body extrinsically or is causally affected by the Body must be false if the proper causality of the attributes is to be preserved.
The model of the human individual as the foundation of itself must be false, because man is a finite and necessarily caused modification.
The model of human knowledge as comprehension of the totality must be false, because the human Mind is a part of the infinite intellect and the idea of a singular body.
The model of essence as mere unilateral dependence on God must be false, because essence requires reciprocity between a thing and that which constitutes it.
The system leaves no ontological place outside God from which God, finite things, ideas, and bodies could be viewed as independently comparable beings.
The system admits no primitive mediation between Thought and Extension: what would appear to be mediation is the same thing expressed under different attributes.
The system admits no merely external criterion of truth, because the ground of the adequate idea is located in the idea itself, not in a merely comparative relation to the object.
Necessary active divine essence → infinite attributes → necessarily consequent modes.
Determinate attribute → causality within the same attribute → exclusion of causality between attributes.
One substance + plurality of attributes → the same being doubly expressed → parallelism of the order of ideas and things.
Non-substantial man + thinking man + priority of the idea → human essence as a cogitative modification ordered around an idea.
Actual idea of a singular thing + sensing of affections of the Body + exclusion of other perceived objects → human Mind as the idea of an actually existing Body.
Body as object of the Mind → every affection of it perceptible → degrees of knowledge from the degree of composition and autonomy of the body → transition to the physics of bodies.

Necessity of the divine essence → Thought and Extension as attributes → attributive causality → parallelism of ideas and things → man as finite mode → Mind as actual idea → Body as sole object → perception of affections of the Body → analysis of motion and rest.
Promise of knowledge of supreme blessedness → metaphysical constitution of the Mind → definition of the union of Mind and Body → physical preparation, not yet a demonstration of absolute blessedness.
God is reclassified from external and royal will into the immanent, necessary, and active cause of all essences and existences.
The union of Mind and Body is reclassified from a relation between two things into the relation of an idea to the same Body expressed under another attribute.
The idea is reclassified from an image received from a thing into a mode of Thought formally caused within Thought.
The individuality of a body is reclassified from a difference of substance into a relation of motion, rest, speed, and slowness.
The excellence of the mind is reclassified from the dignity of a separate soul into the power of the body to act, be acted upon, and order itself in many ways at once.
Surface — The human Mind is the idea of an actually existing Body, and it necessarily perceives those things that happen in this Body.
Structural — Modes of thinking and extended modes are ordered according to distinct attributive causalities, whose orders nevertheless express one and the same connection of things.

Metastrategic — The order of philosophizing that ascends from sensible things to God is rejected; divine nature, prior in knowledge and nature, is placed as the explanatory foundation before natural things.

Ontological/Temporal — Eternal God necessarily acts, singular things exist finitely and determinately, their duration is indefinite, and the determination of bodies extends into an infinite series of causes.
The extracted system suffices to restore the immediate conclusion that the human Mind is the idea of an actually existing Body.
The demonstration depends on the principles of Part One concerning the one substance, the causality of God, and the distinction of attributes, which are assumed here rather than grounded again.
The principal juncture remains between the identity of Mind and Body as one thing and the necessity of explaining them through wholly separate attributive causalities.

The distinction between God as the condition without which a finite thing neither is nor is conceived and God as not pertaining to the essence of a finite thing is maintained only through the strict definition of reciprocity of essence.

The correlation between the power of the Body and the perfection of the Mind is affirmed, but the mechanism of bodily composition that would explain those degrees is deferred to the subsequent physical doctrine.

The movement of the argument is said to be directed toward knowledge of blessedness, but this part only establishes the ontological and epistemic condition of the path; it does not deduce blessedness itself.

identity.title: Pars secunda - De natura et origine mentis · passage 1

units.title: Pars secunda - De natura et origine mentis · passage 2

items.text: Textus quaerit quomodo ex constitutione motuum corporis compositi percipere, imaginari, meminisse atque se cognoscere Mens humana possit.
Cognitio Mentis non ex accessu immediato ad res, Corpus aut se ipsam oritur, sed ex ideis affectionum quibus Corpus humanum cum corporibus externis determinatur.
Argumentatio physico-genetica est: a perseverantia motus et quietis, per individuationem relationalem corporis, ad condiciones cognitionis et confusionis ascendit.
Identitas corporis componitur ex certa ratione motus et quietis inter partes, non ex identitate materiali partium, figurae, magnitudinis aut motus localis totius.
Affectio corporis simul naturam corporis affecti et corporis afficientis involvit; ideo perceptio externi est praesentatio externa per dispositionem proprii corporis.

Progressio concludit imaginationem et memoriam esse effectus vestigiorum ac concatenationum corporearum, cognitionem autem corporis, externorum et sui esse partialem atque, quatenus sola talibus affectionibus nititur, confusam.
Corpus motum moveri et corpus quiescens quiescere perseverat, nisi causa externa ad contrarium statum determinet.
Omnis modus quo corpus ab alio corpore afficitur ex natura corporis affecti simul et corporis afficientis sequitur.
Individuum corporeum est unio corporum quae motus suos certa ratione invicem communicant.
Natura Individui manet, dum ratio communicationis motus et quietis inter partes manet, etiamsi partes substituantur, magnitudine mutentur, directionem flectant aut Individuum totum moveatur.
Vestigia corporum externorum in partibus fluidis Corporis humani dispositiones relinquere possunt quae posteriores motus reflexos eiusdem generis efficiunt.
Corpus humanum est Individuum valde compositum, a plurimis corporibus externis afficitur, plurimis corporibus ad conservationem indiget, atque ipsa externa corpora disponere potest.
Mens humana est idea Corporis humani, atque Corpus et Mens unum idemque Individuum sub attributis Extensionis et Cogitationis concipiuntur.
Quidquid in Corpore humano contingit, Mens humana percipere debet.
Idea affectionis Corporis humani naturam Corporis humani simul et naturam corporis externi involvit, sed constitutionem Corporis humani magis indicat quam naturam externi corporis per se.
Ordo et connexio idearum idem est ac ordo et connexio causarum; idea cuiusque rei secundum contextum causarum a quo pendet determinatur.
Mutatio motus in quietem aut quietis in motum non ex solo statu praesenti corporis sequitur, sed causam externam requirit.
Identitas Individui non est identitas numerica partium componentium nec immobilitas figurae, magnitudinis aut situs.
Corpus externum non ut res immediate data percipitur, sed tantum quatenus Corpus humanum ab eo afficitur.
Imaginatio in se spectata error non est; error est privatio ideae quae existentiam rei imaginatae secludat.
Memoria non est concatenatio idearum secundum ordinem intellectus et primas causas, sed secundum ordinem affectionum Corporis humani.
Mens nec Corpus suum, nec partes eius, nec corpora externa, nec se ipsam cognitione immediata et adaequata cognoscit.
Mens eo plura percipere potest quo Corpus humanum pluribus modis disponi et affici potest.
Idea quae esse formale Mentis constituit composita est, quia Corpus cuius idea est ex plurimis Individuis compositis constat.
Perceptio cuiuslibet affectionis Corporis humani simul externum corpus et constitutionem proprii corporis exprimit, sed externum non secundum naturam suam independentem.
Mens corpus externum ut praesens contemplatur quamdiu affectio Corporis humani existentiam vel praesentiam illius corporis non secludit.
Vestigium corporale repetitum efficit ut Mens corpus externum iam absens ut praesens imaginari possit.
Affectus olim simul dati concatenationem imaginativam efficiunt, ita ut imaginatio unius rei memoriam alterius excitet secundum consuetudinem corporis.
Mens Corpus suum et corpora externa existentia cognoscit tantum per ideas affectionum sui Corporis.
Mens affectiones Corporis et ideas earum percipit; ideo se ipsam cognoscit tantum quatenus ideas affectionum percipit.
Idea affectionis, quatenus ad Mentem humanam tantum refertur, cognitionem adaequatam nec Corporis humani, nec partium eius, nec corporis externi involvit; ideo est confusa.
Identitas rerum corporalium est stabilitas relationis communicativae per mutationem, non persistentia materiae; individuum est forma dynamica quae substitutionem et variationem tolerat.

Eadem apertio corporis ad plures affectiones simul potentiam perceptivam auget et cognitionem ad constitutionem corporis recipientis alligat; extensio experientiae non transit ipso facto in adaequationem.
Imaginatio et memoria sunt temporalis perseverantia historiae affectionum corporis, qua praeteritum in praesentia mentis recurrit sine praesentia rei externae.
Reflexio mentis in se ipsam non instituit subiectum a corpore separatum, sed cognitionem secundi ordinis quae ex ideis affectionum corporalium procedit.
Systema negat Mentem finitam posse esse centrum cognitionis corpore et affectionibus independens.
Systema negat corpus esse rem cuius essentia in particulis permanentibus aut in figura invariabili consistat.
Systema negat imaginem esse similitudinem figurativam rei externae; imago est idea affectionis quae externum velut praesens repraesentat.
Systema negat concatenationes memoriae ex similitudine rerum aut ex ordine universali intellectus necessario nasci.
Mentis finitae perspectivam extra historiam affectionum proprii corporis positam systema non admittit.
Imaginatio per se absentiam causarum quae rem externam excludant supplere non potest; praesentia imaginata non constituit existentiam rei.
Cognitio corporis externi ex sola affectione non potest naturam externi corporis ut per se et in suo ordine causali constitutam exhaurire.
Perseverantia motus et quietis → necessitas determinationis externae ad omnem mutationem status.
Communicatio motuum certa ratione → constitutio Individui → conservatio identitatis per substitutionem et variationem partium.
Compositio multiplicis Corporis humani et dependentia eius ab externis → pluralitas affectionum, dispositionum atque vestigiorum.
Mens ut idea Corporis → perceptio necessariа affectionum Corporis → capacitas perceptiva proportionalis dispositionibus corporis.
Affectio corporis ab externo → idea quae naturam utriusque corporis involvit → praesentatio externi per constitutionem proprii corporis.
Vestigium corporale perseverans → repetitio affectionis → imaginatio rei absentis ut praesentis.
Simultaneitas affectionum et consuetudo corporis → concatenatio imaginativa → memoria singulariter ordinata.
Mediatio cognitionis per affectiones → absentia cognitionis causalis partium et externorum → confusio idearum; ideae affectionum perceptae → cognitio sui mediata.
Perseverantia motus et quietis → causa externa mutationis → relatio motuum → Individuum compositum → identitas per rationem communicationis.
Corpus humanum multiplex et externis expositum → affectiones plurimae → Mens ut idea Corporis → perceptio plurium proportionalis dispositioni corporis.
Affectio a corpore externo → idea utriusque naturae → praesentia externa condicionata → vestigium repetitum → imaginatio et memoria.
Cognitio per affectiones → cognitio mediata Corporis, externorum et Mentis → defectus contextus causarum → inadaequatio et confusio.
Corpus reclassificatur ex aggregato materiae in individuam relationem motus et quietis, quae mutationes partium sine identitatis dissolutione sustinet.
Externum corpus fit obiectum quod in idea affectionis simul apparet et tamen per constitutionem Corporis humani indicatur.
Imaginatio reclassificatur ex cognitione falsa in praesentiam idealem ex vestigiis corporalibus ortam; falsitas non est forma imaginationis, sed defectus ideae secludentis.
Memoria reclassificatur ex thesauro imaginum in concatenationem idearum corporeis consuetudinibus ordinatam.
Cognitio sui reclassificatur ex intuitu interiori in perceptionem reflexivam idearum affectionum Corporis.
Oppositio inter experientiam multiplicem et cognitionem adaequatam dissolvitur: perceptio plurium potest crescere, dum cognitio causarum partium et externorum manet inadaequata.
Gradus superficiei: Mens plurima percipit, corpora externa imaginatur, absentia memorat, Corpus suum sentit, et se ipsam percipit.
Gradus structuralis: effectus mentales generantur ex compositione corporis, ex reciproca affectione corporum, ex vestigiis fluidorum et ex ordine affectionum.
Gradus metastrategicus: quaestio de veritate perceptionis transfertur ab apparenti similitudine rei ad conditiones corporales et causales sub quibus idea producitur.
Gradus ontologicus et temporalis: Individua sunt rationes motus per variationem perseverantes, et Mens finita historiam corporis sui in imaginando et memorando repetit.
Axiomata extracta sufficiunt ad reconstruendum transitum a physica mutationis et individuationis ad doctrinam affectionis, imaginationis, memoriae et cognitionis mediatae.
Commissura firmissima est nexus inter naturam relationalem Individui, compositam constitutionem Corporis humani, et ideam affectionis quae utrumque corpus involvit.
Systema localiter pendet a principiis antea positis, praesertim a unitate Mentis et Corporis, a perceptione omnium affectionum, et ab identitate ordinis idearum cum ordine causarum.
Transitus a natura singulorum compositorum ad Naturam totam ut unum Individuum proponitur ut facile concipiendus, sed ipse textus demonstrationem ampliorem consulto suspendit.
Explicatio imaginationis per vestigia corporalia unam causam sufficientem exhibet, sed Scholium concedit rem etiam ex aliis causis contingere posse; exclusivitas causalis non demonstratur.
Tensionem apparentem inter maiorem facultatem percipiendi et persistentem inadaequationem systema resolvit distinguendo pluralitatem affectionum a cognitione causarum earum.
Doctrina cognitionis sui immediate sustinet tantum perceptionem reflexivam idearum affectionum; ulterior progressio ideae ideae in infinitum a textu ad tractationem posteriorem differtur.

translations.title: Part Two - On the Nature and Origin of the Mind · passage 2

items.text: The text asks how, from the constitution of the motions of the composite body, the human Mind can perceive, imagine, remember, and know itself.
Knowledge of the Mind arises not from immediate access to things, the Body, or itself, but from ideas of affections by which the human Body is determined together with external bodies.
The argument is physico-genetic: it ascends from the persistence of motion and rest, through the relational individuation of the body, to the conditions of knowledge and confusion.
The identity of the body consists in a determinate ratio of motion and rest among its parts, not in the material identity of the parts, figure, magnitude, or local motion of the whole.

An affection of the body involves at once the nature of the affected body and of the affecting body; therefore perception of the external is a presentation of the external through the disposition of one's own body.

The progression concludes that imagination and memory are effects of bodily traces and concatenations, while knowledge of the body, of external things, and of oneself is partial and, insofar as it rests solely on such affections, confused.
A moving body persists in moving, and a resting body in resting, unless an external cause determines it to the contrary state.
Every mode by which a body is affected by another body follows at once from the nature of the affected body and of the affecting body.
A corporeal individual is a union of bodies which communicate their motions to one another according to a determinate ratio.

The nature of an Individual remains so long as the ratio of communication of motion and rest among its parts remains, even if the parts are replaced, change in magnitude, alter direction, or the whole Individual is moved.
Traces of external bodies can leave in the fluid parts of the human Body dispositions that produce subsequent reflex motions of the same kind.
The human Body is a highly composite Individual, is affected by very many external bodies, requires very many bodies for its preservation, and can itself dispose external bodies.
The human Mind is the idea of the human Body, and Body and Mind are conceived as one and the same Individual under the attributes of Extension and Thought.
Whatever occurs in the human Body, the human Mind must perceive.

The idea of an affection of the human Body involves at once the nature of the human Body and the nature of the external body, but indicates the constitution of the human Body more than the nature of the external body in itself.
The order and connection of ideas is the same as the order and connection of causes; the idea of each thing is determined according to the context of causes on which it depends.
A change from motion to rest or from rest to motion does not follow from the body's present state alone, but requires an external cause.
The identity of an Individual is not the numerical identity of its component parts, nor the immobility of its figure, magnitude, or position.
An external body is not perceived as an immediately given thing, but only insofar as the human Body is affected by it.
Imagination considered in itself is not error; error is the privation of an idea that would exclude the existence of the imagined thing.
Memory is not a concatenation of ideas according to the order of the intellect and first causes, but according to the order of the affections of the human Body.
The Mind knows neither its own Body, nor its parts, nor external bodies, nor itself by immediate and adequate knowledge.
The Mind can perceive more things insofar as the human Body can be disposed and affected in more ways.
The idea that constitutes the formal being of the Mind is composite, because the Body of which it is the idea consists of very many composite Individuals.
The perception of any affection of the human Body expresses at once the external body and the constitution of one's own body, but not the external body according to its independent nature.
The Mind contemplates an external body as present so long as an affection of the human Body does not exclude the existence or presence of that body.
A repeated bodily trace causes the Mind to be able to imagine an external body, now absent, as present.
Affections once given simultaneously produce an imaginative concatenation, such that the imagination of one thing evokes the memory of another according to the custom of the body.
The Mind knows its own Body and external bodies as existing only through ideas of the affections of its Body.
The Mind perceives the affections of the Body and their ideas; therefore it knows itself only insofar as it perceives ideas of affections.

The idea of an affection, insofar as it is referred only to the human Mind, involves adequate knowledge neither of the human Body, nor of its parts, nor of the external body; therefore it is confused.
The identity of corporeal things is the stability of a communicative relation through change, not the persistence of matter; an individual is a dynamic form that tolerates substitution and variation.

The same openness of the body to more affections both increases perceptive power and binds knowledge to the constitution of the receiving body; extension of experience does not ipso facto pass into adequacy.
Imagination and memory are the temporal persistence of the history of the body's affections, by which the past recurs in the presence of the mind without the presence of the external thing.
The Mind's reflection upon itself does not establish a subject separate from the body, but a second-order knowledge proceeding from ideas of bodily affections.
The system denies that the finite Mind can be a center of knowledge independent of body and affections.
The system denies that the body is a thing whose essence consists in permanent particles or an invariant figure.
The system denies that an image is a figurative likeness of an external thing; an image is an idea of an affection that represents the external as if present.
The system denies that concatenations of memory necessarily arise from the similarity of things or from the universal order of the intellect.
The system does not admit a perspective of the finite Mind situated outside the history of the affections of its own body.
Imagination by itself cannot supply the absence of causes that exclude the external thing; imagined presence does not constitute the existence of the thing.
Knowledge of an external body from affection alone cannot exhaust the nature of the external body as constituted in itself and in its own causal order.
Persistence of motion and rest → necessity of external determination for every change of state.
Communication of motions according to a determinate ratio → constitution of an Individual → preservation of identity through substitution and variation of parts.
Composition of the multiple human Body and its dependence on external things → plurality of affections, dispositions, and traces.
Mind as idea of Body → necessary perception of affections of the Body → perceptive capacity proportional to bodily dispositions.
Affection of the body by an external thing → idea involving the nature of both bodies → presentation of the external through the constitution of one's own body.
Persistent bodily trace → repetition of affection → imagination of an absent thing as present.
Simultaneity of affections and custom of the body → imaginative concatenation → singularly ordered memory.
Mediation of knowledge through affections → absence of causal knowledge of parts and external things → confusion of ideas; perceived ideas of affections → mediated self-knowledge.
Persistence of motion and rest → external cause of change → relation of motions → composite Individual → identity through the ratio of communication.
Multiple human Body exposed to external things → very many affections → Mind as idea of Body → perception of more things proportional to bodily disposition.
Affection by an external body → idea of both natures → conditioned external presence → repeated trace → imagination and memory.
Knowledge through affections → mediated knowledge of Body, external things, and Mind → lack of context of causes → inadequacy and confusion.
The body is reclassified from an aggregate of matter into an individual relation of motion and rest that sustains changes of parts without dissolution of identity.
The external body becomes an object that appears at once in the idea of affection and yet is indicated through the constitution of the human Body.
Imagination is reclassified from false knowledge into an ideal presence arising from bodily traces; falsity is not a form of imagination, but the lack of an excluding idea.
Memory is reclassified from a storehouse of images into a concatenation of ideas ordered by bodily customs.
Self-knowledge is reclassified from inner intuition into reflexive perception of ideas of affections of the Body.
The opposition between multiple experience and adequate knowledge is dissolved: perception of more things can increase while knowledge of the causes of parts and external things remains inadequate.
Surface level: the Mind perceives very many things, imagines external bodies, remembers absent things, feels its own Body, and perceives itself.
Structural level: mental effects are generated from the composition of the body, from the reciprocal affection of bodies, from traces in fluids, and from the order of affections.
Metastrategic level: the question of the truth of perception is transferred from the apparent likeness of the thing to the bodily and causal conditions under which the idea is produced.
Ontological and temporal level: Individuals are ratios of motion persisting through variation, and the finite Mind repeats the history of its body in imagining and remembering.
The extracted axioms suffice to reconstruct the transition from the physics of change and individuation to the doctrine of affection, imagination, memory, and mediated knowledge.
The firmest joint is the nexus between the relational nature of the Individual, the composite constitution of the human Body, and the idea of affection that involves both bodies.

The system locally depends on previously established principles, especially on the unity of Mind and Body, the perception of all affections, and the identity of the order of ideas with the order of causes.
The transition from the nature of individual composites to Nature as a whole as one Individual is proposed as easy to conceive, but the text itself deliberately suspends a fuller demonstration.
The explanation of imagination through bodily traces exhibits one sufficient cause, but the Scholium grants that the thing can also occur from other causes; causal exclusivity is not demonstrated.
The system resolves the apparent tension between a greater faculty of perceiving and persistent inadequacy by distinguishing the plurality of affections from knowledge of their causes.

The doctrine of self-knowledge immediately supports only reflexive perception of ideas of affections; the further development of the idea of an idea to infinity is deferred by the text to later treatment.

items.text: Textus quaerit quibus condicionibus Mens humana se, Corpus suum et corpora externa adæquate cognoscere possit, et unde imminutio, error atque certitudo oriantur.

Thesis principalis statuit cognitionem ex affectionibus Corporis necessario mediatam, externam et fortuitam esse mutilatam, cognitionem vero ex communibus proprietatibus et ideis adæquatis ortam esse veram.
Argumentatio est simul diagnostica et reconstructiva: primo originem cognitionis confusæ exponit, deinde condiciones cognitionis rationalis et certæ constituit.
Motus primus procedit ab inadequatione idearum affectionum ad inadequatam cognitionem Mentis, Corporis, corporum externorum atque durationis rerum singularium.
Motus secundus transfert veritatem idearum ad earum relationem ad Deum, falsitatem autem ad privationem cognitionis in mente finita.
Motus tertius ex communibus corporum proprietatibus rationem, ex ideis adæquatis certitudinem, et ex ratione necessitatem rerum sub specie æternitatis deducit.
Terminus textus affirmat ideam cuiuscunque rei singularis actu existentis essentiam Dei æternam et infinitam necessario involvere.
Mens se ipsam, Corpus suum et corpora externa non percipit nisi per ideas affectionum Corporis sui.
Idea affectionis Corporis naturam Corporis non adæquate exprimit, nec idea illius ideæ naturam Mentis humanæ adæquate involvit.

Perceptio ex fortuito rerum occursu externe determinata cognitionem confusam producit; dispositio interna, quae convenientias, differentias et oppugnantias rerum intelligit, cognitionem claram et distinctam producit.
Duratio Corporis et rerum singularium ex infinita serie causarum singularium pendet, non ex essentia rei singularis neque ex absoluta Dei natura.
Omnes ideæ, quatenus ad Deum referuntur, cum suis ideatis conveniunt et veræ sunt.
Ideæ inadæquatæ et confusæ non sunt defectus in Deo, sed proveniunt ex eo quod ideæ ad Mentem singularem referuntur; tamen eadem necessitate consequuntur ac ideæ adæquatæ.
Falsitas nullam formam positivam habet, sed consistit in privatione cognitionis quam ideæ mutilatæ, confusæ et inadæquatæ involvunt.
Id quod omnibus commune est et æque in parte ac in toto adest nullius rei singularis essentiam constituit.
Id quod omnibus commune est atque æque in parte ac in toto adest non potest nisi adæquate concipi.
Proprietas Corpori humano et corporibus externis, a quibus affici solet, communis et propria ideam adæquatam in Mente humana constituit.
Idea quae in Mente ex ideis adæquatis sequitur est ipsa adæquata.
Capacitas imaginativa Corporis finita, cum imaginum multitudo superatur, imagines confundit et terminos transcendentales vel universales ex confusione producit.

Cognitio primi generis ex singularibus confuse per sensus exhibitibus aut ex signis oritur; cognitio secundi generis ex notionibus communibus; scientia intuitiva ex idea adæquata attributorum Dei ad cognitionem essentiarum rerum procedit.
Idea adæquata simul ideam sui continet; qui vere cognoscit simul certus est se vere cognoscere.
Ratio res ut necessarias, non ut contingentes, sub quadam æternitatis specie percipit.
Idea cuiuscunque corporis vel rei singularis actu existentis essentiam Dei æternam et infinitam necessario involvit.
Conscientia actionum cum ignorantia causarum, a quibus actiones determinantor, opinionem libertatis producit; voluntas sine idea causalis explicata nihil explanat.
Mens non habet cognitionem sui, Corporis sui aut corporum externorum immediate datam et a mediatione affectionum corporis independentem.
Ordo communis Naturæ, quatenus fortuitis occursibus Mentem externe determinat, non est via cognitionis claræ et distinctæ.
Duratio Corporis proprii et rerum singularium externarum non potest a Mente humana adæquate cognosci.
Falsitas neque positivum modum cogitandi neque absolutam ignorantiam constituit.
Proprietas communis non est essentia rei singularis.
Termini transcendentales et universalia imaginaria non sunt eo ipso notiones communes vel cognitiones rationales.
Cognitio primi generis non docet verum a falso distinguere.
Ratio res non contemplatur ut contingentes neque ex relationibus temporalibus imaginariis suum iudicium constituit.
Libertas voluntatis non probatur ex conscientia actionum, cum conscientia causarum determinantium abesse possit.
Mens, quoties ex communi Naturæ ordine res percipit, cognitionem sui, Corporis sui et corporum externorum mutilatam atque confusam habet.
Cognitio humana durationis Corporis proprii et rerum singularium externarum est admodum inadæquata, quia causae durationis in infinitum procedunt.
Contingentia et corruptibilitas rerum particularium non designant indeterminationem causalitatis, sed conditionem sub qua earum duratio adæquate cognosci non potest.
Error non requirit ideam positivam falsam, sed oritur ubi idea positiva habetur sine cognitione sufficiente rei et causarum eius.
Ideæ inadæquatæ non sunt effectus contingentes aut extra ordinem Naturæ positi, sed necessario sequuntur cum ad Mentem finitam referuntur.
Notiones communes sunt fundamenta ratiocinii, quia proprietates communes neque essentias singulares constituunt neque in parte a toto variant.
Mens eo aptior est ad plura adæquate percipienda quo Corpus eius plura cum aliis corporibus communia habet.
Universalia imaginaria variant secundum dispositionem Corporis, frequentiam affectionum et id quod Mens facilius imaginatur vel recordatur.
Cognitio primi generis est unica falsitatis causa, dum cognitio secundi et tertii generis necessario vera est.
Verum a falso distingui potest tantum cognitione secundi aut tertii generis, quia talis distinctio ideam adæquatam veri et falsi postulat.
Certitudo non additur ideæ veræ ex probatione externa, sed in reflexiva adæquatione ipsius ideæ consistit.
Imaginatio, ex fluctuante coniunctione imaginum cum ordinibus temporalibus, res futuras vel præteritas ut contingentes exhibet; ratio eas ut necessarias percipit.
Intelligibilitas rei singularis actu existentis finitam eius existentiam cum essentia Dei æterna et infinita coniungit.
Opinatio libertatis est forma erroris qua homo actiones suas sentit, causas autem quibus ad agendum determinatur ignorat.
Veritas et inadequatio non dividunt duas classes idearum per contentum positivum, sed eandem ideationalem realitatem secundum relationem ad intellectum Dei vel ad Mentem finitam ordinant.
Finitudo cognitiva non est imminutio causalitatis Naturæ, sed imminutio expressionis totius nexus causalis in idea ad Mentem singularem relata.
Rationalitas non ex abstractione generica a singularibus oritur, sed ex perceptione proprietatum corporalium realiter communium, quae in parte et in toto invariant.

Hierarchia cognitionis describit transitum ab affectione et signo, per communitatem structuralem, ad intuitivam deductionem essentiarum; incrementum cognitionis est imminutio dependentiae a casu imaginativo.
Contingentia temporalis est effectus imaginationis finitae, dum necessitas æterna est forma sub qua ratio ordinem rerum vere intelligit.
Certitudo vera est proprietas immanens cognitionis adæquatæ et non relatio posterior inter Mentem et tribunal externum verificationis.
Falsum esse debet exemplar Mentis tamquam subiecti sibi, Corpori et rebus externis immediate praesentis.
Falsum esse debet exemplar erroris tamquam entitatis positivæ, facultatis autonomæ aut ordinis causalis a veritate separati.
Falsum esse debet exemplar universalis cognitionis quod universalia ex sola confusione vel depletione differentiarum singularium deducit.
Falsum esse debet exemplar rationis a corpore seiunctæ, cum aptitudo Mentis ad cognitionem adæquatam a communitatibus Corporis cum aliis corporibus pendeat.
Falsum esse debet exemplar contingentiae ut proprietatis rerum ipsarum, cum ratio res ut necessarias percipiat et contingentia ex imaginatione temporali oriatur.
Falsum esse debet exemplar veritatis quod ideam veram solum per comparationem extrinsecam cum ideato cognosci posse supponit.
Falsum esse debet exemplar libertatis quod conscientiam actionis pro origine causali actionis accipit.
Systema nullum locum relinquit Mentis finitae extra ordinem causalem infinitum, unde durationem rerum singularium vel causas actionum suarum totaliter complecti possit.
Systema nullum mundum falsitatis positivæ opponit mundo veritatis, quia ideæ omnes, quatenus in Deo sunt, veræ manent.
Systema tempus imaginatum non admittit ut ultimum horizontem rationalis intelligibilitatis, quia ratio res sub specie æternitatis percipit.
Systema nullam normam veritatis extra ipsam ideam adæquatam requirit, quia veritas se ipsam et falsitatem manifestat.
Affectio Corporis → idea affectionis → cognitio Mentis, Corporis et corporis externi necessario mediata.
Mediatio per fortuitum occursum externum → idea mutilata et confusa → cognitio primi generis → possibilitas falsitatis.
Duratio rei singularis → regressus causarum in infinitum → impossibilitas cognitionis humanæ adæquatæ durationis → contingentia et corruptibilitas quoad cognitionem.
Relatio ideæ ad Deum → convenientia cum ideato → veritas; relatio eiusdem ideæ ad Mentem finitam → inadequatio → privatio cognitionis.
Proprietas communis, æqualiter in parte et toto → non-essentialitas singularis → conceptio necessario adæquata → notio communis.
Notio communis et idea adæquata → consecutio idearum adæquatarum → ratio → cognitio secundi generis.
Idea adæquata → idea ideæ adæquata → certitudo immanens → distinctio veri et falsi.
Ratio → necessitas rerum → species æternitatis → connexio rei singularis actu existentis cum essentia Dei æterna et infinita.
Idea affectionis inadæquata → perceptio externa ex ordine communi Naturæ → cognitio mutilata Mentis, Corporis et corporum externorum → inadequata cognitio durationis.
Infinita concatenatio causarum → contingentia et corruptibilitas quoad cognitionem → relatio omnium idearum ad Deum → veritas idearum et falsitas ut privatio.
Proprietates corporum communes → notiones communes adæquatæ → ratio et consecutio idearum adæquatarum → distinctio inter imaginationem, rationem et scientiam intuitivam.
Idea vera reflexiva → certitudo → ratio rerum necessitas → species æternitatis → idea rei singularis actu existentis Dei essentiam involvens.
Cognitio sui, Corporis et mundi externi reclassificatur ut processus per affectiones Corporis mediatus, non ut praesentia immediata obiecti ad Mentem.
Falsitas reclassificatur ex proprietate positivæ ideæ in privationem cognitionis intra ideam necessario productam.
Oppositio inter universale et singulare dividitur in universalia imaginaria confusa et notiones communes structuraliter adæquatas.
Corpus fit conditio positiva cognitionis rationalis, quia communitates eius cum corporibus externis augent aptitudinem Mentis ad ideas adæquatas.
Contingentia transfertur ab ordine rerum ad modum imaginativum quo res in relationibus temporalibus concipiuntur.
Certitudo transfertur ab externis signis confirmationis ad reflexivam structuram ideæ veræ.
Gradus superficiei — Textus distinguit cognitionem confusam, cognitionem adæquatam, falsitatem, veritatem, certitudinem, imaginationem, rationem et scientiam intuitivam.
Gradus structuralis — Cognitio humana ex relatione inter affectiones Corporis, ordinem causarum infinitum, capacitatem imaginativam finitam et proprietates corporibus communes constituitur.
Gradus metastrategicus — Textus normam cognitionis transfert ab accumulatione imaginum, signorum et experientiarum vagarum ad productionem idearum ex notionibus communibus et ideis adæquatis.
Gradus ontologicus vel temporalis — Veritas idearum fundatur in ordine divino necessario; contingentia pertinet ad imaginationem temporalem; ratio res sub specie æternitatis percipit.
Axiomata data sufficiunt ad restituendum motum principalem ab inadequatione affectionum corporalium ad cognitionem rationalem, certitudinem et necessitatem æternam.
Enuntiatio de idea rei singularis actu existentis et essentia Dei terminalis manet in fonte dato sine demonstratione explicita; eius nexus inferentialis plenus hic restitui non potest.
Systema maxime cohaeret ubi veritatem divinam et inadequationem finitam distinguit per diversam relationem eiusdem ideæ, non per duas ordines idearum positive separatos.

Commissura fragilis manet transitus ab interna rerum contemplatione ad cognitionem clare et distincte formatam, quia conditio interna indicatur sed mechanismus completus eius productionis non plene explicatur.
Distinctio inter notionem communem et universale imaginarium formaliter nititur proprietate æqualiter in parte et toto existente, sed applicatio eius ad conceptus singulares in textu limitata manet.
Falsitas ut privatio et necessitas idearum inadæquatarum inter se cohaerent tantum si servatur distinctio inter positivam ideæ productionem et defectum cognitionis quam idea in Mente finita involvit.
Certitudo ex idea ideæ deducta structuram scepticam excludit, sed vim suam ex principio reflexivitatis ideæ adæquatæ accipit, non ex probatione extrinseca independenter constituta.

translations.title: Part Two - On the Nature and Origin of the Mind · passage 3

items.text: The text asks under what conditions the human Mind can adequately know itself, its Body, and external bodies, and whence inadequacy, error, and certainty arise.

The principal thesis holds that knowledge necessarily mediated through affections of the Body, external and fortuitous, is mutilated, whereas knowledge arising from common properties and adequate ideas is true.
The argumentation is at once diagnostic and reconstructive: first it sets forth the origin of confused knowledge, then it establishes the conditions of rational and certain knowledge.
The first movement proceeds from the inadequacy of ideas of affections to inadequate knowledge of the Mind, the Body, external bodies, and the duration of singular things.
The second movement transfers the truth of ideas to their relation to God, but falsity to a privation of knowledge in the finite mind.
The third movement derives reason from common properties of bodies, certainty from adequate ideas, and the necessity of things under a certain species of eternity from reason.
The terminus of the text affirms that the idea of any singular thing actually existing necessarily involves the eternal and infinite essence of God.
The Mind perceives neither itself, nor its Body, nor external bodies except through ideas of affections of its Body.
The idea of an affection of the Body does not adequately express the nature of the Body, nor does the idea of that idea adequately involve the nature of the human Mind.

Perception externally determined by the fortuitous encounter of things produces confused knowledge; an internal disposition that understands the agreements, differences, and oppositions of things produces clear and distinct knowledge.
The duration of the Body and of singular things depends upon an infinite series of singular causes, not upon the essence of a singular thing nor upon the absolute nature of God.
All ideas, insofar as they are referred to God, agree with their ideata and are true.
Inadequate and confused ideas are not defects in God, but arise from the fact that ideas are referred to a singular Mind; nevertheless, they follow by the same necessity as adequate ideas.
Falsity has no positive form, but consists in the privation of knowledge that mutilated, confused, and inadequate ideas involve.
That which is common to all and is equally present in the part as in the whole constitutes the essence of no singular thing.
That which is common to all and is equally present in the part as in the whole can be conceived only adequately.
A property common and proper to the human Body and to the external bodies by which it is usually affected constitutes an adequate idea in the human Mind.
An idea which follows in the Mind from adequate ideas is itself adequate.
The finite imaginative capacity of the Body, when the multitude of images is exceeded, confuses images and produces transcendental or universal terms from confusion.

Knowledge of the first kind arises from singular things confusedly presented through the senses or from signs; knowledge of the second kind arises from common notions; intuitive knowledge proceeds from an adequate idea of the attributes of God to knowledge of the essences of things.
An adequate idea simultaneously contains the idea of itself; whoever truly knows is at the same time certain that he truly knows.
Reason perceives things as necessary, not as contingent, under a certain species of eternity.
The idea of any body or singular thing actually existing necessarily involves the eternal and infinite essence of God.
Consciousness of actions together with ignorance of the causes by which actions are determined produces the opinion of freedom; will without an explained causal idea explains nothing.
The Mind does not have knowledge of itself, its Body, or external bodies immediately given and independent of the mediation of affections of the body.
The common order of Nature, insofar as it externally determines the Mind through fortuitous encounters, is not a path to clear and distinct knowledge.
The duration of one's own Body and of external singular things cannot be adequately known by the human Mind.
Falsity constitutes neither a positive mode of thinking nor absolute ignorance.
A common property is not the essence of a singular thing.
Transcendental terms and imaginary universals are not thereby common notions or rational cognitions.
Knowledge of the first kind does not teach one to distinguish the true from the false.
Reason does not contemplate things as contingent, nor does it form its judgment from imaginary temporal relations.
Freedom of the will is not proved from consciousness of actions, since consciousness of determining causes may be absent.
Whenever the Mind perceives things from the common order of Nature, it has mutilated and confused knowledge of itself, its Body, and external bodies.
Human knowledge of the duration of its own Body and of external singular things is exceedingly inadequate, because the causes of duration proceed to infinity.
The contingency and corruptibility of particular things do not designate an indeterminacy of causality, but the condition under which their duration cannot be adequately known.
Error does not require a positive false idea, but arises where a positive idea is held without sufficient knowledge of the thing and its causes.
Inadequate ideas are not contingent effects or things posited outside the order of Nature, but necessarily follow when they are referred to a finite Mind.
Common notions are the foundations of reasoning, because common properties neither constitute singular essences nor vary in the part from the whole.
The Mind is the more apt to perceive more things adequately insofar as its Body has more things in common with other bodies.
Imaginary universals vary according to the disposition of the Body, the frequency of affections, and that which the Mind more easily imagines or recollects.
Knowledge of the first kind is the sole cause of falsity, whereas knowledge of the second and third kinds is necessarily true.
The true can be distinguished from the false only by knowledge of the second or third kind, because such a distinction requires an adequate idea of the true and the false.
Certainty is not added to a true idea from external proof, but consists in the reflexive adequacy of the idea itself.
Imagination, from the fluctuating conjunction of images with temporal orders, presents future or past things as contingent; reason perceives them as necessary.
The intelligibility of a singular thing actually existing joins its finite existence with the eternal and infinite essence of God.
The opinion of freedom is a form of error by which a human being feels his actions, but is ignorant of the causes by which he is determined to act.
Truth and inadequacy do not divide two classes of ideas by positive content, but order the same ideational reality according to its relation to the intellect of God or to the finite Mind.
Cognitive finitude is not a diminution of the causality of Nature, but a diminution of the expression of the whole causal nexus in an idea referred to a singular Mind.
Rationality arises not from generic abstraction from singulars, but from the perception of really common bodily properties, which are invariant in the part and in the whole.

The hierarchy of knowledge describes a transition from affection and sign, through structural commonality, to the intuitive deduction of essences; an increase in knowledge is a diminution of dependence on imaginative chance.
Temporal contingency is an effect of finite imagination, whereas eternal necessity is the form under which reason truly understands the order of things.
True certainty is an immanent property of adequate knowledge and not a subsequent relation between the Mind and an external tribunal of verification.
The model of the Mind as a subject immediately present to itself, its Body, and external things must be false.
The model of error as a positive entity, an autonomous faculty, or a causal order separated from truth must be false.
The model of universal knowledge that derives universals from confusion alone or from the depletion of singular differences must be false.
The model of reason separated from the body must be false, since the Mind's aptitude for adequate knowledge depends on the commonalities of the Body with other bodies.
The model of contingency as a property of things themselves must be false, since reason perceives things as necessary and contingency arises from temporal imagination.
The model of truth which supposes that a true idea can be known only through an extrinsic comparison with its ideatum must be false.
The model of freedom that takes consciousness of action for the causal origin of action must be false.
The system leaves no place for a finite Mind outside the infinite causal order, from which it could totally comprehend the duration of singular things or the causes of its own actions.
The system opposes no world of positive falsity to the world of truth, because all ideas, insofar as they are in God, remain true.
The system does not admit imagined time as the ultimate horizon of rational intelligibility, because reason perceives things under a species of eternity.
The system requires no norm of truth outside the adequate idea itself, because truth manifests both itself and falsity.
Affection of the Body → idea of affection → necessarily mediated knowledge of the Mind, the Body, and the external body.
Mediation through fortuitous external encounter → mutilated and confused idea → knowledge of the first kind → possibility of falsity.
