Duration of a singular thing → regress of causes to infinity → impossibility of adequate human knowledge of duration → contingency and corruptibility with respect to knowledge.
Relation of idea to God → agreement with ideatum → truth; relation of the same idea to finite Mind → inadequacy → privation of knowledge.
Common property, equally in part and whole → non-essentiality of the singular → necessarily adequate conception → common notion.
Common notion and adequate idea → succession of adequate ideas → reason → knowledge of the second kind.
Adequate idea → adequate idea of the idea → immanent certainty → distinction of true and false.
Reason → necessity of things → species of eternity → connection of a singular thing actually existing with the eternal and infinite essence of God.
Inadequate idea of affection → external perception from the common order of Nature → mutilated knowledge of Mind, Body, and external bodies → inadequate knowledge of duration.
Infinite concatenation of causes → contingency and corruptibility with respect to knowledge → relation of all ideas to God → truth of ideas and falsity as privation.
Common properties of bodies → adequate common notions → reason and succession of adequate ideas → distinction among imagination, reason, and intuitive knowledge.
Reflexive true idea → certainty → necessity of things through reason → species of eternity → idea of a singular thing actually existing involving the essence of God.
Knowledge of self, Body, and external world is reclassified as a process mediated through affections of the Body, not as the immediate presence of an object to the Mind.
Falsity is reclassified from a property of a positive idea into a privation of knowledge within a necessarily produced idea.
The opposition between universal and singular is divided into confused imaginary universals and structurally adequate common notions.
The Body becomes a positive condition of rational knowledge, because its commonalities with external bodies increase the Mind's aptitude for adequate ideas.
Contingency is transferred from the order of things to the imaginative mode in which things are conceived in temporal relations.
Certainty is transferred from external signs of confirmation to the reflexive structure of the true idea.
Surface level — The text distinguishes confused knowledge, adequate knowledge, falsity, truth, certainty, imagination, reason, and intuitive knowledge.
Structural level — Human knowledge is constituted from the relation among affections of the Body, the infinite order of causes, finite imaginative capacity, and properties common to bodies.
Metastrategic level — The text transfers the norm of knowledge from the accumulation of images, signs, and vague experiences to the production of ideas from common notions and adequate ideas.
Ontological or temporal level — The truth of ideas is founded in the necessary divine order; contingency pertains to temporal imagination; reason perceives things under a species of eternity.
The given axioms suffice to restore the principal movement from the inadequacy of bodily affections to rational knowledge, certainty, and eternal necessity.

The statement concerning the idea of a singular thing actually existing and the essence of God remains terminal in the given source without explicit demonstration; its full inferential nexus cannot be restored here.
The system is most coherent where it distinguishes divine truth and finite inadequacy through the differing relation of the same idea, not through two positively separate orders of ideas.

A fragile joint remains in the transition from the internal contemplation of things to clearly and distinctly formed knowledge, because the internal condition is indicated but the complete mechanism of its production is not fully explained.

The distinction between a common notion and an imaginary universal is formally grounded in a property equally existing in part and whole, but its application to singular concepts remains limited in the text.

Falsity as privation and the necessity of inadequate ideas cohere with one another only if the distinction is preserved between the positive production of an idea and the defect of knowledge which the idea involves in the finite Mind.

Certainty deduced from the idea of the idea excludes a skeptical structure, but derives its force from the principle of the reflexivity of the adequate idea, not from independently established extrinsic proof.

identity.title: Pars secunda - De natura et origine mentis · passage 3

units.title: Pars secunda - De natura et origine mentis · passage 4

items.text: Textus quaerit utrum ideae rerum singularium cognitionem Dei necessariam praebeant, et utrum voluntas sit facultas libera ab intellectu distincta.
Idea rei singularis actualis ad essentiam aeternam et infinitam Dei reducitur, quia res singularis nec concipi nec causari sine Deo potest.
Quod in omni idea rei singularis, tam partis quam totius, commune est, cognitionem Dei adaequatam constituit; Mens humana hanc cognitionem necessario possidet.
Mens, ut modus cogitandi determinatus, voluntatem liberam non habet; volitiones singulares sunt ipsae affirmationes quas ideae involvunt.
Error, dissentio et falsa libertatis experientia ex confusione idearum cum imaginibus, verbis, universalibus et privatione cognitionis oriuntur.
Necessitas divinae naturae cognitionem Dei, disciplinam affectuum, vitam socialem rationalem et libertatem practicam eodem systemate connectit.
Idea rei singularis actu existentis essentiam et existentiam rei necessario involvit.
Res singulares sine Deo concipi non possunt, quia sunt modi attributorum Dei et ab ipso causantur.
Idea cuiusque rei singularis conceptum attributi divini atque essentiam Dei aeternam et infinitam involvit.
Id quod omnibus commune est et aeque in parte ac in toto continetur adaequate cognosci potest.
Mens humana ideas sui Corporis, sui ipsius et corporum externorum actu existentium habet.
Mens est modus cogitandi certus et determinatus, cuius omnis volitio ab alia causa determinatur in infinitum.
Facultates universales, ut intellectus et voluntas, nihil sunt praeter entia rationis ex actibus singularibus abstracta.
Omnis idea, quatenus idea est, affirmationem vel negationem sibi propriam involvit.
Volitio singularis extra ideam cuius est affirmatio nec esse nec concipi potest.
Falsitas non est ens positivum, sed privatio cognitionis quam idea mutilata et confusa involvit.
Imagines et verba ex motibus corporis constituuntur, cum idea sit conceptus Cogitationis.
Iudicii suspensio perceptionem cognitionis inadequatae exprimit, non liberum assensum aut dissensum.
Mens non est causa libera suarum volitionum neque facultatem absolutam volendi et nolendi possidet.
Voluntas non est potentia infinita intellectu latior, sed universale nomen affirmationibus singularibus commune.
Intellectus non est facultas separata a voluntate, quia idea singularis et affirmatio eius unum idemque sunt.
Idea non est imago corporis, pictura muta, neque vox qua res significatur.
Existentia rei singularis non est duratio abstracte concepta vel species quantitatis.
Falsitas non est certitudo positiva nec error est mera perceptio imaginationis secundum se spectata.
Iudicium suspendere non est voluntarie assensum continere, sed ideam insufficientem percipere.
Deus non clare cognoscitur per imagines corporum, quibus nomen Dei vulgo adiungitur.
Quaelibet idea rei singularis actualis cognitionem essentiae Dei aeternae et infinitae continet.
Cognitio Dei quam ideae rerum singularium continent est adaequata, quia id quod eam dat omnibus rebus commune est.
Mens humana cognitionem essentiae Dei aeternae et infinitae adaequatam habet.
Voluntas et intellectus unum idemque sunt, quia utrumque in ideis et volitionibus singularibus exhauritur.
Qui equum alatum imaginatur eiusque existentiam nulla idea contraria tollit, existentiam illius necessario affirmat aut de ea dubitare nequit.
Multi errores et controversiae non ex positiva falsitate sed ex discrepantia inter res, nomina, imagines et intellectus interpretantium procedunt.
Cognitio Dei fundamentum praebet deductionibus ulterioribus et constitutioni tertii generis cognitionis.
Necessitas causarum tollit meriti formam quae virtutem tamquam servitutem praemiis externis compensandam concipit.
Immanentia Dei non cognitionem singularium impedit, sed ipsum principium constituit quo cognitio communis, adaequata et demonstrativa fieri potest.
Libertatis locus a potestate contrarie eligendi ad intellectum necessitatis et actionem ex cognitione Dei procedentem transfertur.
Ethica affectuum et politica civium gubernatio eandem regulam sequuntur: homines non ut servi determinandi sunt, sed ita dirigendi ut ex ratione ea agant quae optima sunt.
Certitudo non est imminutio dubitationis, sed positivitatis cognitio; ideo stabilitas opinionis falsae certitudinem non constituit.
Systema excludit subiectum mentale quod ante ideas suas stat et postea libere assentitur vel dissentit.
Systema excludit cognitionem quae Deum velut obiectum externum et imaginabile apprehendit.
Systema excludit falsitatem ut rem positivam quae ideis veris aequaliter opponatur.
Systema excludit facultates psychologicas universales tamquam causas reales actuum singularium.
Systema excludit oppositionem simplicem inter necessitatem causalitatemque, ex una parte, et vitam rationalem ac socialem, ex altera.
Nulla origo absoluta cogitationis, iudicii vel actionis admissibilis est intra Mentem humanam.
Nulla positio cognoscitiva extra ordinem divinum dari potest, quia res, ideae et earum causae in Deo sunt et per Deum concipiuntur.
Nulla beatitudo legitime fundari potest in praemio extrinseco, cum virtus et Dei cognitio ipsam felicitatem constituant.
Nulla libertas consistit in indifferentia inter contraria, quia indifferentia nihil aliud esset defectus determinationis cognitae.
Res singularis actu existens → idea essentiam et existentiam involvens → attributum divinum → essentia Dei aeterna et infinita → commune omnibus → cognitio adaequata Dei.
Idea Mentis de Corpore, se ipsa et corporibus externis → participatio cognitionis communis Dei → facultas deductionis adaequatae → tertium genus cognitionis.
Mens ut modus determinatus → recusatio voluntatis liberae → resolutio facultatum in actus singulares → identitas ideae et affirmationis → identitas intellectus et voluntatis.
Confusio idearum cum imaginibus et verbis → universalia pro rebus singularibus habita → falsa libertatis et erroris descriptio → distinctio conceptus, imaginis, verbi et privationis.
Necessitas divina intellecta → imminutio spei praemii et timoris fortunae → aequanimitas, ratio socialis et regimen civium ad libertatem ordinatum.
Idea rei singularis actualis → Deus ut causa immanens → essentia divina in idea implicata → communitas cognitionis → cognitio Dei adaequata in Mente humana.
Cognitio adaequata Dei → examen voluntatis → determinatio infinita volitionum → affirmatio ideae intrinseca → voluntas et intellectus idem.
Identitas ideae et affirmationis → recusatio facultatis liberae → reinterpretatio dubitationis, falsitatis et erroris → dissolutio objectionum → usus ethicus et politicus necessitatis.
Deus reclassificatur ex obiecto imaginabili vel nomine vulgari in essentiam aeternam et infinitam ab omni idea rei singularis involutam.
Voluntas reclassificatur ex causa interiori libera in nomen universale affirmationum singularium causaliter determinatarum.
Error reclassificatur ex actu positivo falsum eligente in privationem cognitionis et in incongruentiam inter ideas, imagines et verba.
Iudicii suspensio reclassificatur ex imperio voluntatis in cognitionem propriae perceptionis inadequatae.
Libert as reclassificatur ex indifferentia electionis in actionem rationalem ex cognitione necessitatis et Dei procedentem.
Politica reclassificatur ex disciplina servili in artem qua cives diriguntur ut libere optima agant.
Surface — Textus demonstrat Mentem humanam cognitionem Dei adaequatam habere atque voluntatem liberam nullam habere.
Structural — Ordo idearum, causarum et rerum singularium sub necessitate divina explicat tam cognitionem quam actus volitivos.
Metastrategic — Obiectiones experientiae communis solvuntur non negando experientiam, sed vocabula eius — voluntatem, assensum, dubitationem, errorem — causaliter redefiniendo.
Ontological/Temporal — Existentia singularium est effectus necessitatis aeternae Dei, non duratio abstracta nec eventus contingens extra ordinem divinum.
Axiomata de immanentia Dei, idea rei singularis, communitate cognitionis, determinatione Mentis et affirmatione intrinseca ideae sufficiunt ad nucleum demonstrativum restituendum.
Firmissimus nexus est transitus ab idea rei singularis ad essentiam Dei et inde ad cognitionem Dei adaequatam.
Identitas voluntatis et intellectus cohaeret tantum si voluntas stricte ad affirmationes singulares reducitur; sensus voluntatis ut cupiditatis expresse excludendus manet.

Tensio manet inter cognitionem Dei omnibus datam et inaequalem claritatem qua homines eam actu explicant; textus hanc differentiam imaginibus corporum attribuit, non privationi ipsius cognitionis communis.

Tensio altera manet inter necessitatem universalem et usum normativum doctrinae: ratio socialis et actio libera postulantur, sed transitus a cognitione necessitatis ad efficaciam practicam breviter tantum determinatur.
Restitutio motum textus servat, si demonstratio epistemica, dissolutio voluntatis liberae, correctio erroris et exitus ethico-politicus tamquam una machina continua retinentur.

translations.title: Part Two - On the Nature and Origin of the Mind · passage 4

items.text: The text asks whether ideas of singular things furnish necessary knowledge of God, and whether the will is a free faculty distinct from the intellect.
The idea of an actual singular thing is reduced to the eternal and infinite essence of God, because a singular thing can neither be conceived nor caused without God.
What is common in every idea of a singular thing, both of the part and of the whole, constitutes adequate knowledge of God; the human Mind necessarily possesses this knowledge.
The Mind, as a determinate mode of thinking, has no free will; singular volitions are the very affirmations that ideas involve.
Error, disagreement, and the false experience of freedom arise from the confusion of ideas with images, words, universals, and privation of knowledge.
The necessity of the divine nature connects, within one and the same system, knowledge of God, the discipline of the affects, rational social life, and practical freedom.
The idea of an actually existing singular thing necessarily involves the essence and existence of the thing.
Singular things cannot be conceived without God, because they are modes of God's attributes and are caused by him.
The idea of each singular thing involves the concept of a divine attribute and the eternal and infinite essence of God.
That which is common to all and is equally contained in the part as in the whole can be adequately known.
The human Mind has ideas of its Body, of itself, and of actually existing external bodies.
The Mind is a certain and determinate mode of thinking, each of whose volitions is determined by another cause to infinity.
Universal faculties, such as intellect and will, are nothing but beings of reason abstracted from singular acts.
Every idea, insofar as it is an idea, involves an affirmation or negation proper to itself.
A singular volition can neither be nor be conceived apart from the idea of which it is the affirmation.
Falsity is not a positive being, but a privation of knowledge that a mutilated and confused idea involves.
Images and words are constituted from motions of the body, whereas an idea is a concept of Thought.
Suspension of judgment expresses the perception of inadequate knowledge, not free assent or dissent.
The Mind is not the free cause of its volitions, nor does it possess an absolute faculty of willing and unwilling.
The will is not an infinite power broader than the intellect, but a universal name common to singular affirmations.
The intellect is not a faculty separate from the will, because a singular idea and its affirmation are one and the same.
An idea is not an image of a body, a mute painting, nor the voice by which a thing is signified.
The existence of a singular thing is not duration abstractly conceived or a species of quantity.
Falsity is not positive certainty, nor is error the mere perception of imagination considered in itself.
To suspend judgment is not voluntarily to withhold assent, but to perceive an insufficient idea.
God is not clearly known through images of bodies, to which the name of God is commonly attached.
Every idea of an actual singular thing contains knowledge of the eternal and infinite essence of God.
The knowledge of God that ideas of singular things contain is adequate, because that which gives it is common to all things.
The human Mind has adequate knowledge of the eternal and infinite essence of God.
Will and intellect are one and the same, because each is exhausted in singular ideas and volitions.
Whoever imagines a winged horse, and whose idea of its existence is not removed by any contrary idea, necessarily affirms its existence or cannot doubt it.
Many errors and controversies proceed not from positive falsity but from discrepancy between things, names, images, and the intellects of interpreters.
Knowledge of God provides the foundation for further deductions and for the constitution of the third kind of knowledge.
The necessity of causes removes the form of merit that conceives virtue as servitude to be compensated by external rewards.
The immanence of God does not impede knowledge of singular things, but constitutes the very principle by which common, adequate, and demonstrative knowledge can arise.
The locus of freedom is transferred from the power of choosing contraries to the understanding of necessity and action proceeding from knowledge of God.

The ethics of the affects and the political governance of citizens follow the same rule: human beings are not to be determined as slaves, but directed so that they act from reason in those things which are best.
Certainty is not the diminution of doubt, but knowledge of positivity; therefore, the stability of a false opinion does not constitute certainty.
The system excludes a mental subject that stands before its ideas and subsequently freely assents or dissents.
The system excludes knowledge that apprehends God as an external and imaginable object.
The system excludes falsity as a positive thing equally opposed to true ideas.
The system excludes universal psychological faculties as real causes of singular acts.
The system excludes a simple opposition between necessity and causality, on the one hand, and rational and social life, on the other.
No absolute origin of thought, judgment, or action is admissible within the human Mind.
No cognitive position outside the divine order can be given, because things, ideas, and their causes are in God and are conceived through God.
No blessedness can legitimately be founded on an extrinsic reward, since virtue and knowledge of God constitute happiness itself.
No freedom consists in indifference between contraries, because indifference would be nothing other than a defect of known determination.
Actually existing singular thing → idea involving essence and existence → divine attribute → eternal and infinite essence of God → common to all → adequate knowledge of God.
Idea of the Mind concerning the Body, itself, and external bodies → participation in the common knowledge of God → capacity for adequate deduction → third kind of knowledge.
Mind as determinate mode → rejection of free will → resolution of faculties into singular acts → identity of idea and affirmation → identity of intellect and will.
Confusion of ideas with images and words → universals taken for singular things → false account of freedom and error → distinction among concept, image, word, and privation.
Divine necessity understood → diminution of hope for reward and fear of fortune → equanimity, social reason, and governance of citizens ordered toward freedom.
Idea of an actual singular thing → God as immanent cause → divine essence implicated in the idea → communality of knowledge → adequate knowledge of God in the human Mind.
Adequate knowledge of God → examination of the will → infinite determination of volitions → intrinsic affirmation of the idea → will and intellect the same.
Identity of idea and affirmation → rejection of free faculty → reinterpretation of doubt, falsity, and error → dissolution of objections → ethical and political use of necessity.
God is reclassified from an imaginable object or common name into the eternal and infinite essence involved by every idea of a singular thing.
The will is reclassified from a free inner cause into a universal name for causally determined singular affirmations.
Error is reclassified from a positive act choosing what is false into a privation of knowledge and an incongruity among ideas, images, and words.
Suspension of judgment is reclassified from a command of the will into knowledge of one's own inadequate perception.
Freedom is reclassified from indifference of choice into rational action proceeding from knowledge of necessity and of God.
Politics is reclassified from servile discipline into the art by which citizens are directed to do what is best freely.
Surface — The text demonstrates that the human Mind has adequate knowledge of God and has no free will.
Structural — The order of ideas, causes, and singular things under divine necessity explains both knowledge and volitional acts.
Metastrategic — Objections from common experience are resolved not by denying experience, but by causally redefining its terms — will, assent, doubt, error.
Ontological/Temporal — The existence of singular things is an effect of God's eternal necessity, not abstract duration nor a contingent event outside the divine order.

The axioms concerning the immanence of God, the idea of a singular thing, the communality of knowledge, the determination of the Mind, and the intrinsic affirmation of the idea suffice to restore the demonstrative core.
The strongest connection is the transition from the idea of a singular thing to the essence of God and thence to adequate knowledge of God.
The identity of will and intellect coheres only if the will is strictly reduced to singular affirmations; the sense of will as desire remains expressly to be excluded.

A tension remains between knowledge of God given to all and the unequal clarity with which human beings actually explicate it; the text attributes this difference to images of bodies, not to a privation of common knowledge itself.

A second tension remains between universal necessity and the normative use of the doctrine: social reason and free action are required, but the transition from knowledge of necessity to practical efficacy is determined only briefly.

The reconstruction preserves the movement of the text if epistemic demonstration, the dissolution of free will, the correction of error, and the ethical-political outcome are retained as one continuous machine.

identity.title: Pars secunda - De natura et origine mentis · passage 4

units.title: Pars tertia - De origine et natura affectuum · passage 1

items.text: Textus quaerit quomodo natura, vires et moderandi ratio affectuum determinandae sint, si homo Naturae exceptio non est.
Affectus ex vitiis moralibus vel perturbationibus ordinis Naturae in modos naturales necessario causatos reconstituit.
Argumentatio polemica et metaphysico-geometrica iudicium, derisionem et detestationem affectuum causali intellectione substituit.
Distinctio causae adaequatae et partialis fundamentum ponit quo agere a pati separatur.
Negata corporis in Mentem et Mentis in Corpus causalitate directa, actio et passio mentales ac corporales ut ordines simultanei unius rei describuntur.
Ex impossibilitate destructionis internae deducitur conatus perseverandi ut essentia actualis cuiusque rei, tempore indefinito tendens.
Conatus Mentis, cum corporis potentiae variationibus et imaginibus coniungitur, Cupiditatem, Laetitiam, Tristitiam et directionem imaginativam generat.
Natura ubique eadem legibus et potentia agit, atque affectus eadem necessitate ac cetera singularia consequuntur.
Causa adaequata est illa ex qua effectus per ipsam solam clare et distincte intelligitur; causa partialis ad talem intellectionem non sufficit.
Agere est effectum habere cuius homo causa adaequata est; pati est effectum habere cuius homo causa non nisi partialis est.
Affectus est affectio Corporis quae ipsius agendi potentiam auget, minuit, iuvat vel coercet, simulque idea eius affectionis.
Corpus humanum multis modis affici potest, quibus eius agendi potentia variatur vel immutata manet.
Corpus humanum per mutationes vestigia objectorum et rerum imagines retinere potest.
Mentis actiones ex ideis adaequatis oriuntur, passiones vero ex ideis inad aequatis pendent.
Corpus Mentem ad cogitandum non determinat, neque Mens Corpus ad motum, quietem aut aliam corporalem determinationem determinat.
Mens et Corpus una eademque res sub attributis Cogitationis et Extensionis concipiuntur, ideoque ordines earum actionum et passionum simul natura sunt.
Nulla res ex sola sua natura destrui potest; destructio causam externam requirit.
Contrarietas rerum consistit in incompatibilitate qua una alteram destruere potest.
Unaquaeque res, quantum in se est, in suo esse perseverare conatur.
Conatus perseverandi nihil est praeter essentiam actualem rei.
Conatus rei nullum tempus finitum involvit, sed durationem indefinitam.
Mens sui conatus necessario conscia est.
Voluntas est conatus Mentis, Appetitus conatus Mentis et Corporis, Cupiditas autem appetitus conscius.
Variatio potentiae agendi Corporis simul variationem potentiae cogitandi Mentis inducit.
Mens existentiam actualem Corporis affirmat, et idea quae illam existentiam secludit Mentis essentiae contraria est.
Homo non est imperium in imperio neque res extra Naturae ordinem posita.
Affectus non sunt vitia Naturae, absurda moraliter exsecranda, neque materia derisionis loco causalitatis.
Mens non est princeps incorporeus qui Corpus iubendo movet, nec Corpus est causa efficiens cogitationis.
Decretum Mentis liberum non est principium actionis a memoria, imaginatione, appetitu et causis determinantibus separabile.
Passio totalem causalitatem sui subiecti excludit, quia causam partialem et ideam inad aequatam implicat.
Essentia rei negationem vel destructionem sui non continet, neque contraria in eodem subiecto consistere possunt quatenus se destruunt.
Bonum non est causa primigenia appetitus; iudicium boni appetitum sequitur.
Mens eo pluribus passionibus obnoxia est quo plures ideas inad aequatas habet, atque eo plura agit quo plures adaequatas habet.
Decreta Mentis, appetitus et determinationes Corporis non sunt causae transversae, sed expressiones simultaneae unius ordinis sub attributis diversis.
Homines se liberos credunt quia actionum suarum conscii sunt, causarum autem quibus determinant ur ignorant.
Passio Mentis non est proprietas positiva Mentis ut integrae, sed eius partialitatis et negationis indicium.
Iudicium quo res bona appellatur effectus est Cupiditatis, non causa eius.
Cupiditas, Laetitia et Tristitia affectus primarii constituuntur; Laetitia transitum ad maiorem perfectionem, Tristitia transitum ad minorem perfectionem designat.
Mens, quatenus potest, ea imaginatur quae Corporis potentiam augent, et contra res memorat quae existentiam eorum secludunt quae potentiam minuunt.
Mens praesentem Corporis existentiam affirmare desinit non ex se aut ex mera Corporis cessatione, sed ex alia idea quae illam praesentiam secludit.
Agere et pati gradus causalitatis sunt, non status morales binarii; libertas igitur ut maior adaequatio, non ut exemptio a necessitate, reconfiguratur.
Affectus non in sola Mente aut in solo Corpore collocari potest, quia affectio corporalis et idea eius unum processum sub duplici attributorum expressione constituunt.
Ordo valorum ex conatu emergit: bonum nomen est rei quam conatus iam appetit, non lex externa quae conatum antecedit.
Individuum nullum finem internum destructionis habet; eius duratio indefinita est, dum causae externae compositionem non destruunt.
Potestas Mentis in affectus, si datur, non potest esse imperium voluntatis supra Naturam, sed sola actio quae ex ideis adaequatis intra ordinem Naturae sequitur.
Subiectum humanum causaliter clausum falsum esse debet, quia Mens, quatenus patitur, pars Naturae est quae per se sine aliis clare intelligi non potest.
Passio essentiam positivam Mentis integrae non exprimit, sed defectum causalitatis plenae et negationem in eius intellectione implicat.
Conscientia actionis scientia causarum non est; conscientia proinde libertatem originariam non probat.
Ordo normativus appetitum antecedens falsus esse debet, si iudicia boni a Cupiditate oriuntur.
Voluntas separata ab appetitu, memoria, imaginatione et dispositione Corporis in systemate locum non habet.
Nullum tribunal extra Naturam manet ex quo affectus tamquam culpa, monstruositas aut defectus absolutus iudicari possit.
Initium actionis omnino inconditum et a necessitate naturali liberum admitti non potest.
Principium intrinsecum quo res se ipsam ad non-esse dirigeret excluditur.
Affectus pure mentalis, corporeis potentiae variationibus carens, indisponibilis est.
Natura una et necessaria → affectus ut singularia naturalia → cognitio per leges universales.
Causa adaequata vel partialis → agere vel pati → affectus ut actio vel passio.
Distinctio causalitatis attributorum + identitas Mentis et Corporis → imminutio imperii voluntatis → simultaneitas ordinum mentalium et corporalium.
Absentia destructionis internae + contrarietas destructiva → conatus perseverandi → essentia actualis → duratio indefinita.
Conatus Mentis conscius + variatio potentiae Corporis et Mentis → Appetitus et Cupiditas → Laetitia et Tristitia → iudicium boni posterius.
Vestigia Corporis + affirmatio corporis praesentis + conatus → imaginatio augmenti potentiae et memoria exclusionis imminutivae.
Homo ut exceptio Naturae → affectus ut vitia iudicata → naturalizatio geometrica affectuum.
Naturalizatio → causa adaequata et partialis → actio et passio → ideae adaequatae et inad aequatae.
Dualismus imperativus Mentis et Corporis → causalitas intra attributa → una res sub duplici attributo → critica liberi decreti.
Destructio externa → conatus-essentialitas → Appetitus conscius → potentiae transitus → affectus primarii → imaginatio conservativa.
Affectus ex obiectis moraliter damnandis in effectus naturales certis causis et proprietatibus intelligibiles transferuntur.
Ager agentiae ex oppositione liberae voluntatis et coactionis ad distinctionem causae adaequatae et partialis transfertur.
Oppositio Mentis imperantis et Corporis oboedientis dissolvitur in duplicem expressionem unius ordinis.
Bonum ex causa praevia eligendi in effectum Cupiditatis reclassificatur.
Imaginatio et memoria ex facultatibus voluntarie administratis in operationes conatus, vestigiorum corporalium et variationum potentiae reordinantur.
Surface — Affectus definiuntur ut affectiones Corporis cum ideis earum, et Laetitia, Tristitia, Cupiditas ut formae primariae ponuntur.
Structural — Adequatio causalis, partialitas, parallelismus attributorum, vestigia corporalia et conatus mechanismum actionis, passionis et imaginationis constituunt.
Metastrategic — Textus intellectionem geometricam contra moralizationem affectuum et contra regimen voluntatis in Corpus instituit.
Ontological/Temporal — Essentia rei est conatus affirmativus sine termino temporali interno; destructio et imminutio ex relationibus externis intelliguntur.

Systema extractum sufficit ad restituendam seriem fundamentalem: naturalizatio affectuum, distinctio causalis actionis et passionis, parallelismus Mentis et Corporis, conatus, atque affectuum primariorum formatio.
Argumentatio non est autonoma intra hunc locum, quia demonstratio pendet a doctrinis prioribus de Deo, attributis, idea Corporis et ordine idearum.
Distinctio ideae adaequatae et inad aequatae structuram actionis explicat, sed criterium practicum quo Mens adaequationem augeat hic nondum determinatur.
Firmissimus nexus est concatenatio destructionis externae, conatus, essentiae actualis et durationis indefinitae.
Vocabulum Mentis quae imaginari conatur non est decretum liberum esse debet; cohaerentia servatur tantum si conatus ut necessitas naturae, non ut imperium voluntatis, legitur.
Commissura fragilis manet inter ideam quae Corporis existentiam simpliciter secludit et ideam quae praesentem Corporis existentiam secludit; textus distinctionem adhibet, sed formaliter non explicat.
Taxonomia reliquorum affectuum tantum promittitur; haec unitas machinam trium affectuum primariorum et imaginativae conservationis constituit, non totum systema affectuum complet.

translations.title: Part Three - On the Origin and Nature of the Affects · passage 1

items.text: The text asks how the nature, powers, and manner of regulating the affects are to be determined, if the human being is not an exception to Nature.
It reconstitutes the affects from moral vices or disturbances of Nature's order into naturally and necessarily caused modes.
Polemical and metaphysico-geometrical argumentation replaces judgment, derision, and detestation of the affects with causal understanding.
The distinction between adequate and partial cause lays the foundation by which acting is separated from being acted upon.
With direct causality of Body upon Mind and of Mind upon Body denied, mental and bodily action and passion are described as simultaneous orders of one thing.
From the impossibility of internal destruction is deduced the striving to persevere as the actual essence of each thing, tending toward indefinite time.
The striving of the Mind, when conjoined with variations in the body's power and with images, generates Desire, Joy, Sadness, and imaginative direction.
Nature acts everywhere by the same laws and power, and the affects follow with the same necessity as other singular things.
An adequate cause is that from which the effect is clearly and distinctly understood through it alone; a partial cause does not suffice for such understanding.
To act is to have an effect of which the human being is an adequate cause; to be acted upon is to have an effect of which the human being is only a partial cause.
An affect is an affection of the Body that increases, diminishes, assists, or restrains its power of acting, together with the idea of that affection.
The human Body can be affected in many ways, by which its power of acting is varied or remains unchanged.
Through modifications, the human Body can retain traces of objects and images of things.
The Mind's actions arise from adequate ideas, whereas its passions depend upon inadequate ideas.
The Body does not determine the Mind to think, nor does the Mind determine the Body to motion, rest, or any other bodily determination.
Mind and Body are conceived as one and the same thing under the attributes of Thought and Extension, and therefore the orders of their actions and passions are simultaneous by nature.
No thing can be destroyed by its nature alone; destruction requires an external cause.
The contrariety of things consists in the incompatibility by which one can destroy another.
Each thing, insofar as it is in itself, strives to persevere in its being.
The striving to persevere is nothing but the actual essence of a thing.
The striving of a thing involves no finite time, but an indefinite duration.
The Mind is necessarily conscious of its striving.
Will is the striving of the Mind, Appetite the striving of Mind and Body, while Desire is conscious appetite.
A variation in the Body's power of acting simultaneously brings about a variation in the Mind's power of thinking.
The Mind affirms the actual existence of the Body, and an idea that excludes that existence is contrary to the essence of the Mind.
The human being is not a dominion within a dominion, nor a thing placed outside Nature's order.
The affects are not vices of Nature, moral absurdities to be execrated, nor matter for derision in place of causality.
The Mind is not an incorporeal ruler that moves the Body by commanding, nor is the Body the efficient cause of thought.
A free decree of the Mind is not a principle of action separable from memory, imagination, appetite, and determining causes.
Passion excludes the total causality of its subject, because it entails a partial cause and an inadequate idea.
The essence of a thing does not contain the negation or destruction of itself, nor can contraries subsist in the same subject insofar as they destroy one another.
The good is not the original cause of appetite; judgment of the good follows appetite.
The Mind is subject to more passions insofar as it has more inadequate ideas, and acts more insofar as it has more adequate ideas.
The decrees of the Mind, appetites, and determinations of the Body are not transverse causes, but simultaneous expressions of one order under diverse attributes.
Human beings believe themselves free because they are conscious of their actions but ignorant of the causes by which they are determined.
A passion of the Mind is not a positive property of the Mind as whole, but an indication of its partiality and negation.
The judgment by which a thing is called good is an effect of Desire, not its cause.
Desire, Joy, and Sadness are constituted as primary affects; Joy signifies a transition to greater perfection, Sadness a transition to lesser perfection.
The Mind, insofar as it can, imagines those things that increase the Body's power, and conversely recollects things that exclude the existence of those which diminish power.
The Mind ceases to affirm the present existence of the Body not through itself or through the mere cessation of the Body, but through another idea that excludes that presence.
Acting and being acted upon are degrees of causality, not binary moral states; freedom is therefore reconfigured as greater adequacy, not as exemption from necessity.
An affect cannot be located in Mind alone or in Body alone, because bodily affection and its idea constitute one process under a twofold expression of attributes.
The order of values emerges from striving: good is the name of a thing that striving already desires, not an external law that precedes striving.
The individual has no internal end of destruction; its duration is indefinite, so long as external causes do not destroy its composition.
The power of the Mind over the affects, if it is given, cannot be a dominion of will over Nature, but only an action that follows from adequate ideas within Nature's order.
The causally closed human subject must be false, because the Mind, insofar as it suffers, is a part of Nature that cannot be clearly understood through itself without other things.
Passion does not express the positive essence of the whole Mind, but entails a deficiency of complete causality and a negation in its understanding.
Consciousness of action is not knowledge of causes; consciousness therefore does not prove original freedom.
A normative order preceding appetite must be false if judgments of good arise from Desire.
Will separated from appetite, memory, imagination, and the disposition of the Body has no place in the system.
No tribunal outside Nature remains from which the affects can be judged as guilt, monstrosity, or absolute defect.
An absolutely unconditioned beginning of action, free from natural necessity, cannot be admitted.
An intrinsic principle by which a thing would direct itself toward non-being is excluded.
A purely mental affect, lacking bodily variations of power, is unavailable.
One necessary Nature → affects as natural singular things → knowledge through universal laws.
Adequate or partial cause → acting or being acted upon → affect as action or passion.
Distinction of causality of attributes + identity of Mind and Body → diminution of the dominion of will → simultaneity of mental and bodily orders.
Absence of internal destruction + destructive contrariety → striving to persevere → actual essence → indefinite duration.
Conscious striving of the Mind + variation of the power of Body and Mind → Appetite and Desire → Joy and Sadness → subsequent judgment of good.
Traces of the Body + affirmation of the present body + striving → imagination of increase of power and memory of diminishing exclusion.
Human being as exception to Nature → affects judged as vices → geometrical naturalization of affects.
Naturalization → adequate and partial cause → action and passion → adequate and inadequate ideas.
Imperative dualism of Mind and Body → causality within attributes → one thing under a twofold attribute → critique of free decree.
External destruction → striving-essence → conscious Appetite → transitions of power → primary affects → preservative imagination.
The affects are transferred from morally condemnable objects into natural effects intelligible through determinate causes and properties.
The field of agency is transferred from the opposition of free will and compulsion to the distinction of adequate and partial cause.
The opposition of commanding Mind and obedient Body is dissolved into the twofold expression of one order.
The good is reclassified from a prior cause of choosing into an effect of Desire.
Imagination and memory are reordered from voluntarily administered faculties into operations of striving, bodily traces, and variations of power.
Surface — Affects are defined as affections of the Body together with their ideas, and Joy, Sadness, and Desire are posited as primary forms.
Structural — Causal adequacy, partiality, parallelism of attributes, bodily traces, and striving constitute the mechanism of action, passion, and imagination.
Metastrategic — The text establishes geometrical understanding against the moralization of the affects and against the rule of will over the Body.
Ontological/Temporal — The essence of a thing is affirmative striving without an internal temporal limit; destruction and diminution are understood from external relations.

The extracted system suffices to reconstruct the fundamental sequence: naturalization of the affects, the causal distinction of action and passion, the parallelism of Mind and Body, striving, and the formation of the primary affects.
The argumentation is not autonomous within this passage, because the demonstration depends upon prior doctrines concerning God, attributes, the idea of the Body, and the order of ideas.
The distinction between adequate and inadequate idea explains the structure of action, but the practical criterion by which the Mind may increase adequacy is not yet determined here.
The strongest link is the concatenation of external destruction, striving, actual essence, and indefinite duration.
The expression that the Mind strives to imagine must not be a free decree; coherence is preserved only if striving is read as a necessity of Nature, not as a dominion of will.

A fragile joint remains between the idea that simply excludes the existence of the Body and the idea that excludes the present existence of the Body; the text employs the distinction but does not formally explain it.

The taxonomy of the remaining affects is only promised; this unit constitutes the mechanism of the three primary affects and of imaginative preservation, and does not complete the entire system of affects.

identity.title: Pars tertia - De origine et natura affectuum · passage 1

units.title: Pars tertia - De origine et natura affectuum · passage 2

items.text: Textus quaerit qua lege imago rei, etiam causaliter neutrae, absenti aut incertae, in Lætitiam, Tristitiam, Amorem, Odium, Cupiditatem et actionem transire possit.
Thesis est affectus ex conatibus potentiae, conjunctionibus imaginativis et similitudine corporum generari, ita ut causae affectivae non cum causis efficientibus rei coincidere debeant.
Argumentatio est demonstrativo-genetica: affectiones compositae ex legibus imaginationis, memoriae, conatus et imitationis deducuntur.
Motus principalis progreditur a coaffectione simultanea ad causalitatem per accidens, inde ad Amorem et Odium, fluctuationem animi, temporalitatem imaginatam et affectuum communicationem.
Affectuum imitatio rem private amatam vel odiosam in ordinem socialem transfert, ubi approbatio, gloria, ambitio, imminutio alterius et certamen nascuntur.
Terminus praebitus constituit condicionem conflictus: si res ab uno tantum possideri potest, imaginata alterius fruitio conatum impeditivae privationis producit.
Mens ea praesentia statuere conatur quae ipsius et Corporis agendi potentiam augent vel juvant, atque ea excludere quae eandem minuunt vel coercent.
Lætitia est transitus ad majorem perfectionem seu potentiam; Tristitia est transitus ad minorem perfectionem seu potentiam.
Affectus simul experti ita in memoria conjunguntur ut imminutio vel reimaginatio unius etiam alterum excitet.
Res cuius propria natura Mentis potentiam nec auget nec minuit potest, per conjunctionem affectivam, causa per accidens Lætitiæ, Tristitiæ vel Cupiditatis fieri.
Amor est Lætitia concomitante idea causæ externæ, et Odium est Tristitia concomitante idea causæ externæ.
Qui amat rem praesentem habere et conservare conatur; qui odit rem amovere vel destruere conatur.
Imago rei præteritæ, futuræ vel præsentis eundem affectum producit, quatenus rei existentiam affirmat; dubitatio eventus constantiam affectus minuit.
Unum idemque objectum, propter pluralitatem et diversam affectionum Corporis compositionem, plurium contrariorumque affectuum causa esse potest.
Mentis conatus in cogitando et Corporis conatus in agendo ejusdem naturæ sunt; ideo imaginatio Lætitiæ vel Tristitiæ in appetitum et actionem transire potest.
Imago rei nobis similis affectu affectæ affectum similem producit, nisi res illa odio habeatur, quo casu affectus contrarius oritur.
Homo per affectiones quibus ad agendum determinatur sui conscius est, atque Lætitia vel Tristitia idea causæ internæ coniuncta relationem ad se ipsum constituit.
Si res ab uno tantum possideri potest, imaginata alterius ejusdem rei fruitio impedimentum proprii cupiditatis efficit.
Causa affectiva non restringitur ad causam efficientem rei; res causaliter neutra per accidens amari vel odio haberi potest.
Sympathia et Antipathia non indigent qualitatibus occultis; similitudines manifestæ et conjunctiones imaginativæ ad earum explicationem sufficiunt.
Efficacia affectiva non exigit rem actu præsentem; imago præteriti vel futuri, si existentiam rei affirmat, ut præsens operatur.
Objectum non unicum nec stabilem valorem affectivum possidet; idem objectum simultanee amari et odio haberi potest.
Imitatio affectuum non est transmissio invariabilis; Odium relationem similitudinis in contrarium affectum vertere potest.
Gloria non probat veram aliorum approbationem; homo sibi omnibus gratum esse imaginari potest, cum omnibus sit molestus.
Benevolentia non ponitur voluntas prima aut pura; est Cupiditas ex Commiseratione orta.
Objectum affectui concomitans potest, quamvis non sit causa efficiens, objectum Amoris vel Odii fieri.
Similitudo rei cum objecto prius læto vel tristi sufficit ut res similis per accidens ametur vel odio habeatur.
Fluctuatio animi oritur cum idem objectum simul sub relatione Lætitiæ et sub relatione Tristitiæ imaginatur.
Spes et Metus sunt Lætitia et Tristitia inconstantes ex imagine rei dubiæ; sublata dubitatione in Securitatem et Desperationem transeunt.
Imago conservationis rei amatæ Lætitiam, imago destructionis ejus Tristitiam producit; in re odiosa eadem ratio affectuum invertitur.
Affectus imaginatus in re amata ad amantem eodem signo transit, atque affectus imaginatus in re odiosa ad odientem signo contrario transit.
Qui rem amatam Lætitia vel Tristitia afficere imaginatur Favorem vel Indignationem excitat; qui rem odiosam Lætitia vel Tristitia afficere imaginatur Odium vel Amorem excitat.
Imitatio affectus in re simili Commiserationem, Æmulationem et, ex Commiseratione, Benevolentiam producit; miseratio conatum liberandi rem miseram parit.
Amor et Odium judicium inclinant: homo de se et re amata Lætitiam affirmans plus justo sentit, de re odiosa Lætitiam negans minus justo sentit.
Imaginata aliorum approbatio actionem conformem et Lætitiam sui tanquam causæ producit; imaginata improbatio actionem aversandam et Tristitiam sui producit.
Conatus faciendi ut alii eadem ament et oderint Amorem roborat, sed oppositione affectuum fluctuationem animi et, sub condicione exclusivæ possessionis, conatum impediendi alterum producit.
Ordo affectivus constituitur potius ex reticulo associationum, similitudinum et idearum causalium quam ex proprietatibus intrinsecis objectorum.
Affectus fit mechanismus selectivus cognitionis: quod Lætitiam sustentat affirmari, quod Tristitiam sustinet negari conatur, unde imminutio vel exaggeratio rei sequitur.
Differentia inter præteritum, futurum et præsens non est primaria differentia affectiva; differentiam efficacem constituit dubitatio de eventu.
Socialitas affectiva duplicem structuram habet: similitudo et communio affectuum connexionem pariunt, sed eadem communicatio cupiditatum contentionem et impedimentum reciproca producere potest.
Subjectum sibi ipsi non immediate apparet, sed per imaginatos affectus aliorum et per ideam sui tanquam causæ actionum aestimatur.
Falsum esse debet affectum ex sola natura objecti et ex causis efficientibus cognitis determinari.
Falsum esse debet cupiditates singulorum a relationibus imaginatis ad alios independenter constitui.
Falsum esse debet præsentiam actualem rei condicionem necessariam omnis affectionis esse.
Falsum esse debet unum objectum unam tantum dispositionem affectivam producere.
Falsum esse debet judicium de se, de re amata et de re odiosa affective indifferens aut spontanee proportionatum esse.
Falsum esse debet consensum affectivum inter homines per se stabilem pacem socialem efficere.
Systema excludit cognitionem affectibus vacuam tamquam fundamentum primarium affirmationis, negationis et actionis.
Systema excludit concordiam socialem spontaneam ex eo solo quod homines eadem amare et odio habere conantur.
Systema excludit identitatem inter imaginem sui laudatam et veram aliorum de agente aestimationem.
Systema excludit bonum desideratum tamquam objectum universaliter compatibile, cum exclusivitas possessionis cupiditatem in obstructionem convertat.
Potentia augenda vel minuenda → Lætitia vel Tristitia → imaginatio præsentificans vel excludens → Amor vel Odium → conatus conservandi vel removendi.
Coaffectio simultanea → memoria conjunctiva → revocatio affectus → causalitas per accidens → Amor, Odium aut Cupiditas sine causa efficiente cognita.
Imago temporalis existentiam affirmans → affectus instar præsentis → dubitatio eventus → Spes aut Metus → sublata dubitatione Securitas aut Desperatio.
Similitudo corporis → imitatio affectus → Commiseratio aut Æmulatio → conatus benefaciendi, imitandi, approbandi aut improbando reagendi.
Affectus alterius circa rem amatam vel odiosam → relatio ad agentem → Favor, Indignatio, Invidia, Amor aut Odium.
Imaginata approbatio socialis → actio ad placendum → Gloria vel Acquiescentia in se ipso; imaginata improbatio → aversatio actionis → Pudor vel Pœnitentia.
Cupiditas consensus affectivi → conatus conformandi alios → imminutio reciproca inter plures → conflictus; res unica → conatus ne alter ea potiatur.
Conatus potentiae → Lætitia et Tristitia → Amor et Odium → conservatio rei amatæ vel remotio rei odiosæ.
Affectus simul conjuncti → memoria affectiva → causa per accidens → Amor vel Odium sine causa efficiente cognita.
Similitudo objectorum → translatio affectus → fluctuationes animi ex contrariis relationibus.
Imago præteriti vel futuri → affectus instar præsentis → dubitatio → Spes, Metus, Securitas, Desperatio, Gaudium et Conscientiæ morsus.
Affectus rei amatæ vel odiosæ → affectus observantis → relatio affectiva ad causam externam.
Similitudo inter homines → imitatio affectuum → Commiseratio, Æmulatio et Benevolentia → actio socialiter directa.
Approbatio imaginata → Ambitio et Gloria → conatus universalis conformandi alios → impedimentum mutuum → certamen de re exclusiva.
Affectus reclassificantur a responsionibus ad proprietates objectorum in effectus relationum inter conatum, imaginem, memoriam et ideam causæ.
Sympathia et Antipathia reclassificantur a nominibus qualitatum occultarum in effectus associationis et similitudinis manifestæ.
Præteritum, futurum et præsens reordinantur secundum modum affirmationis imaginativæ et gradum dubitationis, non secundum distantiam temporalem.
Approbatio, vituperium, gloria et pudor reclassificantur ut affectiones reflexivæ ex imaginata aliorum receptione oriundæ.
Beneficentia, misericordia et ambitio reclassificantur ut cupiditates causaliter derivatæ, non ut principia moralia primaria.
Consensus affectivus reclassificatur ut mechanismus simul corroborationis et conflictus, praesertim ubi res exclusive possidenda est.
Surface — Textus definit Amorem, Odium, Spem, Metum, Securitatem, Desperationem, Commiserationem, Æmulationem, Benevolentiam, Ambitionem, Gloriam et Pudorem.
Structural — Affectus ex affectionibus Corporis, conjunctionibus memorialibus, similitudine imaginata et conatu augendæ potentiae producuntur.
Metastrategic — Actio socialis describitur ut conatus affectiones aliorum conformandi, approbationem adipiscendi et impedimenta cupiditatis removendi.

Ontological/Temporal — Realitas affective operans non requirit rei præsentiam actualem, sed imaginationem existentiam rei affirmantem; tempus affectum per dubitationem, non per solam temporalem positionem, modificat.
Series axiomatum sufficit ad restituendum transitum a conatu et affectu primario ad causalitatem per accidens, Amorem, Odium et actionem appetitivam.
Structura interne cohaeret, quia memoria conjunctiva, valorem potentiae et ideam causæ eundem ordinem generativum complent.
Pars firmissima est deductio qua similitudine, imitatione et imaginata aliorum approbatione affectus privatus in relationem socialem transit.
Systema praesupponit propositiones antecedentes de conatu, parallelismo Mentis et Corporis, natura imaginationis et conscientia sui; hae in loco dato non iterum demonstrantur.
Commissura fragilis manet inter causalitatem per accidens et ideam causæ externæ: objectum affective causale fieri potest quamvis causa efficiens affectus non sit.
Fluctuatio animi admittitur, sed regula non datur qua affectus contrarii in actione finali componantur aut alter alterum superet.
Antagonismus socialis non universaliter ex imitatione sola sequitur; indiget vel diversitate affectuum, vel cupiditate approbationis, vel conditione rei ab uno tantum possidendæ.
Restitutio motum textus servat usque ad conatum impediendi alterius possessionem; scholium Propositionis XXXII in materia praebita non continetur.

translations.title: Part Three — On the Origin and Nature of the Affects · passage 2

items.text: The text asks by what law the image of a thing, even one causally neutral, absent, or uncertain, can pass into Joy, Sadness, Love, Hate, Desire, and action.

The thesis is that affects are generated from conatuses of power, imaginative conjunctions, and the similarity of bodies, such that affective causes need not coincide with the efficient causes of a thing.
The argument is demonstrative-genetic: composite affections are deduced from the laws of imagination, memory, conatus, and imitation.
The principal movement proceeds from simultaneous co-affection to accidental causality, thence to Love and Hate, fluctuation of mind, imagined temporality, and the communication of affects.
The imitation of affects transfers a privately loved or hated thing into the social order, where approval, glory, ambition, the diminution of another, and rivalry arise.
The provided limit establishes the condition of conflict: if a thing can be possessed by only one, the imagined enjoyment of another produces a conatus of obstructive deprivation.
The Mind strives to posit as present those things that increase or aid its own and the Body's power of acting, and to exclude those that diminish or restrain the same.
Joy is a transition to greater perfection or power; Sadness is a transition to lesser perfection or power.
Affects experienced simultaneously are so conjoined in memory that the diminution or reimagination of one also arouses the other.
A thing whose own nature neither increases nor diminishes the Mind's power can, through affective conjunction, become an accidental cause of Joy, Sadness, or Desire.
Love is Joy accompanied by the idea of an external cause, and Hate is Sadness accompanied by the idea of an external cause.
One who loves strives to have and preserve the present thing; one who hates strives to remove or destroy the thing.
The image of a past, future, or present thing produces the same affect insofar as it affirms the existence of the thing; uncertainty of the outcome diminishes the constancy of the affect.
One and the same object, owing to the plurality and diverse composition of the affections of the Body, can be the cause of multiple and contrary affects.
The Mind's conatus in thinking and the Body's conatus in acting are of the same nature; therefore the imagination of Joy or Sadness can pass into appetite and action.
The image of a thing similar to us and affected by an affect produces a similar affect, unless that thing is hated, in which case the contrary affect arises.
A human being is conscious of himself through the affections by which he is determined to act, and Joy or Sadness conjoined with the idea of an internal cause establishes a relation to himself.
If a thing can be possessed by only one, the imagined enjoyment by another of that same thing constitutes an impediment to one's own desire.
An affective cause is not restricted to the efficient cause of a thing; a causally neutral thing can be loved or hated accidentally.
Sympathy and Antipathy do not require occult qualities; manifest similarities and imaginative conjunctions suffice for their explanation.
Affective efficacy does not require a thing actually to be present; the image of the past or future, if it affirms the thing's existence, operates as a present thing.
An object does not possess a single or stable affective value; the same object can simultaneously be loved and hated.
The imitation of affects is not invariant transmission; Hate can turn the relation of similarity into a contrary affect.
Glory does not prove the true approval of others; a person can imagine himself pleasing to all while being troublesome to all.
Benevolence is not posited as a primary or pure will; it is Desire arising from Compassion.
An object accompanying an affect can become the object of Love or Hate, although it is not an efficient cause.
The similarity of a thing to an object previously joyful or sad suffices for the similar thing to be loved or hated accidentally.
Fluctuation of mind arises when the same object is imagined simultaneously under the relation of Joy and under the relation of Sadness.
Hope and Fear are inconstant Joy and Sadness arising from the image of a doubtful thing; when doubt is removed, they pass into Security and Despair.
The image of the preservation of a loved thing produces Joy, and the image of its destruction produces Sadness; in the case of a hated thing, the same relation of affects is inverted.
An affect imagined in a loved thing passes to the lover with the same sign, and an affect imagined in a hated thing passes to the hater with the contrary sign.
One who imagines a loved thing to be affected with Joy or Sadness arouses Favor or Indignation; one who imagines a hated thing to be affected with Joy or Sadness arouses Hate or Love.
The imitation of affect in a similar thing produces Compassion, Emulation, and, from Compassion, Benevolence; pity gives rise to a conatus to free the pitiable thing.
Love and Hate incline judgment: a person who affirms Joy of himself and of a loved thing feels more than is just, and one who denies Joy of a hated thing feels less than is just.
The imagined approval of others produces conforming action and Joy in oneself as cause; imagined disapproval produces the avoidance of action and Sadness in oneself.

The conatus to make others love and hate the same things strengthens Love, but through the opposition of affects produces fluctuation of mind and, under the condition of exclusive possession, a conatus to impede another.
The affective order is constituted rather by a network of associations, similarities, and causal ideas than by the intrinsic properties of objects.
Affect becomes a selective mechanism of cognition: what sustains Joy strives to be affirmed, what sustains Sadness strives to be denied, whence the diminution or exaggeration of a thing follows.
The difference between past, future, and present is not a primary affective difference; uncertainty concerning the outcome constitutes the efficacious difference.
Affective sociality has a double structure: similarity and the sharing of affects generate connection, but the same communication of desires can produce contention and reciprocal impediment.
The subject does not appear immediately to itself, but is assessed through the imagined affects of others and through the idea of itself as the cause of actions.
It must be false that an affect is determined by the nature of the object alone and by known efficient causes.
It must be false that the desires of individuals are constituted independently of imagined relations to others.
It must be false that the actual presence of a thing is a necessary condition of every affection.
It must be false that one object produces only one affective disposition.
It must be false that judgment concerning oneself, a loved thing, and a hated thing is affectively indifferent or spontaneously proportionate.
It must be false that affective agreement among human beings by itself produces stable social peace.
The system excludes cognition devoid of affects as the primary foundation of affirmation, negation, and action.
The system excludes spontaneous social concord arising merely from the fact that human beings strive to love and hate the same things.
The system excludes identity between the praised image of oneself and the true assessment of the agent by others.
The system excludes the desired good as a universally compatible object, since exclusivity of possession converts desire into obstruction.
Power to be increased or diminished → Joy or Sadness → imagination making present or excluding → Love or Hate → conatus of preserving or removing.
Simultaneous co-affection → conjunctive memory → recall of affect → accidental causality → Love, Hate, or Desire without a known efficient cause.
Temporal image affirming existence → affect as if present → uncertainty of outcome → Hope or Fear → when doubt is removed, Security or Despair.
Similarity of body → imitation of affect → Compassion or Emulation → conatus of benefiting, imitating, approving, or reacting with disapproval.
Another's affect concerning a loved or hated thing → relation to the agent → Favor, Indignation, Envy, Love, or Hate.
Imagined social approval → action to please → Glory or Acquiescence in oneself; imagined disapproval → avoidance of action → Shame or Repentance.
Desire for affective agreement → conatus to make others conform → reciprocal diminution among many → conflict; a single thing → conatus that another not obtain it.
Conatus of power → Joy and Sadness → Love and Hate → preservation of the loved thing or removal of the hated thing.
Simultaneously conjoined affects → affective memory → accidental cause → Love or Hate without a known efficient cause.
Similarity of objects → transfer of affect → fluctuations of mind from contrary relations.
Image of the past or future → affect as if present → uncertainty → Hope, Fear, Security, Despair, Joy, and pangs of Conscience.
Affect of the loved or hated thing → affect of the observer → affective relation to the external cause.
Similarity among human beings → imitation of affects → Compassion, Emulation, and Benevolence → socially directed action.
Imagined approval → Ambition and Glory → universal conatus to make others conform → mutual impediment → rivalry over an exclusive thing.
Affects are reclassified from responses to the properties of objects into effects of relations among conatus, image, memory, and the idea of cause.
Sympathy and Antipathy are reclassified from names of occult qualities into effects of association and manifest similarity.
Past, future, and present are reordered according to the mode of imaginative affirmation and the degree of uncertainty, not according to temporal distance.
Approval, blame, glory, and shame are reclassified as reflexive affections arising from the imagined reception of others.
Beneficence, mercy, and ambition are reclassified as causally derived desires, not as primary moral principles.
Affective agreement is reclassified as a mechanism both of reinforcement and of conflict, especially where a thing is to be possessed exclusively.
Surface — The text defines Love, Hate, Hope, Fear, Security, Despair, Compassion, Emulation, Benevolence, Ambition, Glory, and Shame.
Structural — Affects are produced from the affections of the Body, memorial conjunctions, imagined similarity, and the conatus to increase power.
Metastrategic — Social action is described as a conatus to make the affections of others conform, to obtain approval, and to remove impediments to desire.

Ontological/Temporal — Affectively operative reality does not require the actual presence of a thing, but an imagination affirming the existence of the thing; time modifies affect through uncertainty, not through temporal position alone.
The series of axioms suffices to reconstruct the passage from conatus and primary affect to accidental causality, Love, Hate, and appetitive action.
The structure coheres internally, because conjunctive memory, the value of power, and the idea of cause complete the same generative order.
The strongest part is the deduction by which, through similarity, imitation, and the imagined approval of others, private affect passes into social relation.

The system presupposes antecedent propositions concerning conatus, the parallelism of Mind and Body, the nature of imagination, and self-consciousness; these are not demonstrated again in the given place.
A fragile juncture remains between accidental causality and the idea of an external cause: an object can become affectively causal although it is not the efficient cause of the affect.
Fluctuation of mind is admitted, but no rule is given by which contrary affects are composed in final action or one overcomes the other.
Social antagonism does not universally follow from imitation alone; it requires either diversity of affects, or desire for approval, or the condition of a thing to be possessed by only one.
The reconstruction preserves the movement of the text up to the conatus to impede another's possession; the scholium of Proposition XXXII is not contained in the provided material.

identity.title: Pars tertia - De origine et natura affectuum · passage 2

units.title: Pars tertia - De origine et natura affectuum · passage 3

items.text: Textus investigat quomodo imagines affectuum aliorum, causae affectivae attributae et conatus conservationis ex paucis mechanismis seriem passionum socialium producant.

Argumentatio est reconstructiva et quasi mechanica: affectiones Corporis, imagines rerum et imminutio vel augmentum potentiae agendi ponuntur ut causae sufficientes amoris, odii, cupiditatis et fluctuationum animi.
Motus primus procedit ab imitatione affectuum et amore rei similis ad conatum amoris reciproci obtinendi atque ad gloriam ex amore imaginato ortam.
Motus secundus ostendit quomodo exclusio, rivalitas, absentia condicionum desideratarum et coercitio appetitus amorem in zelotypiam, tristitiam, invidiam vel odium convertant.
Motus tertius affectus reciprocos constituit: odium imaginatum odium vicissim, malum acceptum vindictam, amor imaginatus amorem et gratiam, atque amor reciprocus dissolutionem odii generat.

Motus ultimus directionem affectuum ex causalitate imaginata explicat: causa redistributa affectum minuit, causa libera imaginata eum intendit, causa sub nomine classis vel nationis universalis affectum extendit, et varietas corporum uniformitatem affectivam impedit.
Imago rei est affectio Corporis humani qua Corpus ab externis causis disponitur ad agendum.
Qui affectum in re sibi simili imaginatur, ad affectum correspondentem imitandum determinatur.
Amor est Laetitia concomitante idea causae externae, et Odium est Tristitia concomitante idea causae externae.
Laetitia potentiam agendi atque conatum iuvat, Tristitia autem eandem minuit vel coercet.
Homo, quatenus Laetitia vel Tristitia afficitur, conatur Laetitiam conservare et Tristitiam amovere.
Amor rei similis conatum producit quo res amata Laetitia afficiatur concomitante idea amantis.
Res vel circumstantia simul imaginata cum re laetificante vel tristicante per accidens causa eiusdem affectus fieri potest.
Qui se causam Laetitiae rei sibi similis imaginatur, se ipsum cum Laetitia contemplatur et gloriam experitur.
Imago rei quae appetitum impedit, vel condicionis desideratae absentiam involvit, Tristitiam cum idea impedientis causae producit.
Amor et Odium in rem durant tantum quatenus res causa Laetitiae vel Tristitiae imaginatur.
Causalitas affectiva inter plures causas distributa amorem vel odium erga unam minuit; causa libera imaginata tamquam causa solitaria affectum auget.
Conatus malum inferendi ei quem quis odit ab intentione maioris mali sibi vitandi superari potest.
Bonum et malum ex cupiditate et aversione affectiva aestimantur, non cupiditas ex iudicio boni vel mali antecedente nascitur.
Spes et Metus affectus connexi sunt, quibus homo rem speratam amat et rem timentem odit, eamque vel obtinere vel amovere conatur.
Homo ea quae sperat facile credit, ea quae timet difficilius credit, atque de utrisque plus minusve iusto iudicat.
Diversa Corporum constitutio efficit ut idem obiectum diversos homines et eundem hominem diversis temporibus diversimode afficiat.
Zelotypia non est affectus simplex, sed fluctuatio animi ex Amore et Odio simul orta, idea rivalis concomitante.
Desiderium non est absentia nuda rei amatae, sed Tristitia quatenus absentiam rei amatae respicit.
Timor non est mera cognitio mali futuri, sed dispositio qua homo malum maius per malum minus vitare conatur.
Verecundia non est genus Timoris separatum, sed Timor cuius malum futurum est Pudor.
Consternatio non est dubitatio theoretica, sed coercitio Cupiditatis per metum duorum malorum, qua homo quid potius velit ignorat.
Bonum et malum non sunt proprietates obiectivae quae Cupiditatem praecedunt, sed nomina affective imposita rebus desideratis vel aversatis.
Laetitia ex malo rei odiosae orta non est Laetitia pura, quia imaginatio Tristitiae rei similis necessario manet.
Amor post Odium auctus non efficit ut homo Odium vel Tristitiam tamquam medium ad maiorem Laetitiam appetat.
Omen non est signum intrinsece bonum aut malum, sed res per accidens Spem vel Metum excitans.
Misericordia, Invidia et Ambitio ex eadem aptitudine ad affectus aliorum imaginandos et imitandos procedunt.
Amor rei similis conatum amoris reciproci parit, et amor reciprocus imaginatus gloriam auget.
Imaginatio rei amatae alteri arctius coniunctae appetitum amoris exclusivi coercet et Zelotypiam, hoc est Amorem et Odium cum Invidia, producit.
Recordatio rei olim laetificantis cupiditatem eandem rem cum iisdem circumstantiis possidendi producit, et defectus unius circumstantiae Tristitiam generat.
Cupiditas Laetitiam conservandi vel Tristitiam removendi eo maior fit quo affectus ex quo oritur maior est.
Amor qui omnino in Odium transit maius Odium producit quam si res amata numquam amata fuisset, quia Odium etiam conatus ab amore relictos coercet.
Qui odit malum inferre, qui amat benefacere conatur, nisi conatus prior metu maioris mali sibi imminentis superetur.
Odium ab alio imaginatum, cum nulla causa proprii odii agnoscitur, Odium reciprocum producit; causa iusta sui odii imaginata Pudorem producit.
Malum ex Odio acceptum Vindictam excitat, dum Amor ab alio imaginatus Amorem reciprocum et Gratitudinem producit; textus tamen homines ad Vindictam promptiores ponit quam ad beneficium referendum.
Beneficium ex Amore vel spe Gloriae datum ingrata receptione Tristitiam producit, quia causa gloriae speratae imaginatur excludi.
Odium odio reciproco augetur, Amor autem imaginatus conatum odii tollendi producit; si hic conatus praevalet, Odium deletur et in Amorem ampliorem transire potest.
Qui aliquem rem amatam odio habere imaginatur, eum odit, quia eum causam Tristitiae rei amatae et consequenter propriae Tristitiae imaginatur.
Laetitia vel Tristitia ab uno membro classis vel nationis diversae accepta ad omnes eiusdem classis vel nationis sub imagine universali extenditur.
Laetitia ex malo rei odiosae repetitur, quia memoria rei Tristitiam pristinam renovat, quam idea mali vel liberationis simul coercet.
Causa affectus ad aliam rem translata Amorem vel Odium erga causam priorem minuit aut destruit; causa libera imaginata eundem affectum intendit.

Res per accidens Spem vel Metum excitantes amantur vel odio habentur, ut media rerum speratarum aut impedimenta rerum metuendarum; ex hac structura et ex credulitatis asymmetria Superstitiones nascuntur.
Nulla affectio obiecti universaliter fixa est, quia idem obiectum pro diversa Corporum dispositione et pro diverso tempore diversos affectus generat.
Affectus interpersonales formam circuitus feedback habent: Amor imaginatus Amorem et Gloriam, Odium imaginatum Odium, et malum imaginatum Vindictam reproducit.
Zelotypia structuram triadicam instituit, in qua amans, res amata et rivalis non tres affectiones independentes, sed una machina coercitionis appetitus et redistributionis odii sunt.
Causalitas imaginata est operator directionis affectivae: individuatio causae affectum intendit, multiplicatio causarum eum diluit, et universalizatio causae sub classe vel natione eum collectivizat.
Memoria et absentia non sunt affective inertes: imago rei praeteritae praesentiam eius simulat, dum defectus circumstantiae vel memoria mali mechanismum Tristitiae et Laetitiae repetitae efficit.
Iudicia boni, mali, utilis, inutilis, ominosi et noxii describunt cartographiam affectivam desiderii, non ordinem valorum a desiderio independentem.
Systema simul admittit propagationem socialem affectuum per imagines universales et negat uniformitatem affectivam per diversitatem constitutivam Corporum.
Systema tacite excludit affectum ut motum pure internum et sine causa externa imaginata, quia Amor et Odium per ideam causae externae constituuntur.
Systema tacite excludit valorem obiectivum boni et mali, quia omnis valor ad structuram cupiditatis, aversionis et affectus reducitur.
Systema tacite excludit relationem affectivam simpliciter dyadicam, quia amor, odium et gloria a tertiis imaginatis, rivalibus, classibus, nationibus et aliis causis mediantur.
Systema tacite excludit identitatem stabilem affectus erga obiectum, quia memoria, circumstantia, causa adiuncta et status Corporis eius directionem mutare possunt.
Systema tacite excludit usum rationaliter voluntarium Tristitiae ut medii ad Laetitiam maiorem, quia conatus necessario Tristitiam amovere et esse suum conservare tendit.
Systema tacite excludit omen tamquam nuntium obiectivum futuri, quia vis ominis ex associatione accidentali cum Spe vel Metu procedit.
Textus ordinatur circa negationem subiecti affective sui iuris: homo affectus suos non ex libera origine interna producit, sed ex imaginibus causarum, imitatione, conatu et constitutione corporis.
Textus ordinatur circa absentiam tribunalium moralium transcendentium: bonum, malum, gratia, vindicta, crudelitas et superstitio ut effectus machinae affectivae ordinantur.
Textus ordinatur circa impossibilitatem Laetitiae prorsus sine residuo Tristitiae, ubi Laetitia ex malo rei odiosae vel ex abolitione odii nascitur.
Textus ordinatur circa impossibilitatem unius obiecti affective identici omnibus, quia obiectum nullam valorem affectivum invariantem praebet extra relationem ad Corpus afficiendum.
Affectio externa → imago Corporis → Laetitia vel Tristitia → idea causae externae → Amor vel Odium.
Imago affectus in re simili → imitatio affectiva → Misericordia, Invidia vel Ambitio → expansio socialis affectus.
Amor rei similis → conatus eam Laetitia afficiendi cum idea sui → Amor reciprocus imaginatus → Gloria.
Rivalis, absentia vel impedimentum → coercitio appetitus → Tristitia → Odium, Invidia, Zelotypia, Vindicta vel Desiderium.
Affectus reciprocus imaginatus → conatus respondendi → circulus augmentationis Odii vel dissolutio eius per Amorem.
Redistributio causae / causa libera imaginata / causa universalis imaginata → imminutio / intensio / collectivizatio affectus.
Memoria, Spes, Metus et associatio accidentalis → repetitio Laetitiae vel Tristitiae → Omina et Superstitio; varietas Corporum → exitus affectivi non uniformes.
Affectio Corporis → imago rei et affectus alterius → imitatio affectiva → Misericordia, Invidia et Ambitio.
Amor rei similis → conatus amoris reciproci → Gloria ex amore imaginato → exclusivitas obstructa → Zelotypia.
Laetitia vel Tristitia intensior → Cupiditas intensior conservandi vel removendi → beneficium, maleficium, Vindicta aut Gratitudo.
Odium vel Amor reciprocus imaginatus → feedback affectivus → augmentum Odii aut eius deletio per Amorem.
Causa affectus reassignata → imminutio amoris vel odii; causa libera imaginata → intensio; causa classis vel nationis → extensio ad collectum.
Memoria et associatio accidentalis → Spes aut Metus → iudicium affectivum boni, mali et ominis → Superstitio; constitutio corporis variabilis → pluralitas exitum.
Amor et Odium reclassificantur ut relationes causales imaginatae, non ut proprietates intrinsecae personarum vel rerum.
Zelotypia, Desiderium, Timor, Verecundia, Consternatio, Ira, Vindicta et Gratitudo describuntur ut figurae compositae ex paucis affectionibus primariis generatae.
Relatio affectiva inter duos agentes fit relatio circulatoria, in qua affectus alterius imaginatus causam novi affectus et actionis propriae constituit.
Individuum, rivalis, classis, natio et omen in eodem campo causali ponuntur, quia omnes imagines capaces sunt Laetitiam, Tristitiam, Spem vel Metum dirigendi.
Distinctio inter causam solitariam, causam multiplicem et causam universalizatam fit principium mensurandi directionem atque intensionem affectus.
Bonum et malum transferuntur ex ordine rerum in ordinem aestimationum affectivarum, ita ut diversitas corporum diversitatem valorum efficiat.
Surface — Textus nomina et nexus passionum determinatarum explicat: Amorem, Odium, Zelotypiam, Desiderium, Timorem, Vindictam, Gratitudinem, Spem et Metum.
Structural — Affectiones Corporis, imagines, associatio causarum, imminutio vel augmentum potentiae agendi et conatus sunt mechanismi qui passiones generant.
Metastrategic — Certamen inter amantes, inimicos, rivales et collecta describitur ut certamen pro directione imaginum causalium, pro conservatione Laetitiae et pro remotione Tristitiae.

Ontological/Temporal — Affectus dependet a relatione corporis ad causas externas et ab imaginibus temporis, quibus memoria praeteritum praesentificat, absentia causam Tristitiae agit, et idem obiectum pro diversa dispositione diversiter operatur.
