Axiomata de imagine corporali, imitatione, conatu, Laetitia, Tristitia et causalitate imaginata sufficiunt ad seriem principalem ab Amore reciproco ad Zelotypiam, Vindictam, Gratitudinem et Superstitionem restituendam.

Restitutio adhuc pendet a definitionibus et propositionibus anterioribus de Corporis affectionibus, similitudo, imaginatione et conatu, quas locus saepe per citationes internas supponit potius quam iterum demonstrat.
Systema firmissimum est ubi una eademque regula, scilicet Laetitia vel Tristitia cum idea causae, ad affectiones diversas reducitur.

Commissura fragilis manet inter causalitatem imaginatam et causalitatem veram, quia locus explicat quomodo imago affectum producat, sed non criterium dat quo imago causae a cognitione causae distinguatur.
Tensio interna oritur inter propagationem affectus ad classes vel nationes et varietatem Corporum, quia prima generalizationem socialem permittit, altera uniformem responsionem affectivam negat.

Tensio altera manet inter causam liberam imaginatam, quae affectum auget, et ordinem affectuum ex necessariis affectionibus Corporis deductum; locus vim imaginationis libertatis explicat, non statum metaphysicum libertatis resolvit.
Transitio a spe et metu individualibus ad Superstitionem est compendiosa, quia mechanismus credulitatis affectivae datur, sed formae sociales stabilitatis superstitionis hic non explicantur.
Structura extracta motum textus servat, quia ab affectione corporali et imagine causae ad circuitus interpersonales, collectivizationem affectuum et variationem corporalem progreditur.

translations.title: Part Three - On the Origin and Nature of the Affects · passage 3

items.text: The text investigates how images of others' affects, attributed affective causes, and the striving for self-preservation produce a series of social passions from a few mechanisms.

The argument is reconstructive and quasi-mechanical: affections of the Body, images of things, and the diminution or increase of the power of acting are posited as sufficient causes of love, hate, desire, and fluctuations of mind.
The first movement proceeds from the imitation of affects and love for a similar thing to the striving to obtain reciprocal love, and to glory arising from imagined love.
The second movement shows how exclusion, rivalry, the absence of desired conditions, and the restraint of appetite transform love into jealousy, sadness, envy, or hate.

The third movement establishes reciprocal affects: imagined hate produces hate in return, evil received produces vengeance, imagined love produces love and gratitude, and reciprocal love produces the dissolution of hate.

The final movement explains the direction of affects through imagined causality: a redistributed cause diminishes an affect, an imagined free cause intensifies it, a cause under the name of a class or universal nation extends the affect, and the variety of bodies prevents affective uniformity.
An image of a thing is an affection of the human Body by which the Body is disposed to act by external causes.
One who imagines an affect in a thing similar to oneself is determined to imitate the corresponding affect.
Love is Joy accompanied by the idea of an external cause, and Hate is Sadness accompanied by the idea of an external cause.
Joy assists the power of acting and striving, whereas Sadness diminishes or restrains it.
A human being, insofar as affected by Joy or Sadness, strives to preserve Joy and remove Sadness.
Love for a similar thing produces a striving by which the loved thing may be affected with Joy accompanied by the idea of the lover.
A thing or circumstance imagined together with a thing that gives joy or sadness can accidentally become a cause of the same affect.
One who imagines oneself to be the cause of the Joy of a thing similar to oneself contemplates oneself with Joy and experiences glory.
The image of a thing that impedes appetite, or involves the absence of a desired condition, produces Sadness with the idea of an impeding cause.
Love and Hate endure toward a thing only insofar as the thing is imagined as a cause of Joy or Sadness.
Affective causality distributed among several causes diminishes love or hate toward one cause; an imagined free cause, as though a solitary cause, increases the affect.
The striving to inflict evil upon one whom one hates can be overcome by the intention of avoiding a greater evil to oneself.
Good and evil are assessed from desire and affective aversion; desire does not arise from a prior judgment of good or evil.
Hope and Fear are connected affects, through which a human being loves the hoped-for thing and hates the feared thing, and strives either to obtain it or to remove it.
A human being readily believes what is hoped for, believes what is feared with greater difficulty, and judges both more or less than is just.
The different constitution of Bodies causes the same object to affect different human beings, and the same human being at different times, in different ways.
Jealousy is not a simple affect, but a fluctuation of mind arising simultaneously from Love and Hate, accompanied by the idea of a rival.
Desire is not the bare absence of the loved thing, but Sadness insofar as it regards the absence of the loved thing.
Fear is not mere cognition of a future evil, but a disposition by which a human being strives to avoid a greater evil through a lesser evil.
Shame is not a separate species of Fear, but Fear whose future evil is Shame.
Consternation is not theoretical doubt, but the restraint of Desire by fear of two evils, whereby a human being does not know what one prefers.
Good and evil are not objective properties that precede Desire, but affectively imposed names for things desired or averted.
Joy arising from the evil of a hated thing is not pure Joy, because the imagination of the Sadness of a similar thing necessarily remains.
Love increased after Hate does not make a human being desire Hate or Sadness as a means to greater Joy.
An omen is not an intrinsically good or evil sign, but a thing that accidentally arouses Hope or Fear.
Pity, Envy, and Ambition proceed from the same aptitude for imagining and imitating the affects of others.
Love for a similar thing gives rise to a striving for reciprocal love, and imagined reciprocal love increases glory.
The imagination of a loved thing more closely joined to another restrains the appetite for exclusive love and produces Jealousy, that is, Love and Hate with Envy.
The recollection of a thing that once gave joy produces a desire to possess the same thing with the same circumstances, and the lack of one circumstance generates Sadness.
The Desire to preserve Joy or remove Sadness becomes greater in proportion as the affect from which it arises is greater.
Love that wholly passes into Hate produces greater Hate than if the loved thing had never been loved, because Hate also restrains the strivings left behind by love.
One who hates strives to inflict evil; one who loves strives to do good, unless the former striving is overcome by fear of a greater evil imminent to oneself.
Hate imagined from another, when no cause of one's own hate is recognized, produces reciprocal Hate; an imagined just cause of one's own hate produces Shame.

Evil received from Hate arouses Vengeance, whereas Love imagined from another produces reciprocal Love and Gratitude; the text nevertheless holds human beings to be more ready for Vengeance than for returning a benefit.
A benefit given from Love or the hope of Glory produces Sadness when received ungratefully, because the cause of hoped-for glory is imagined to be excluded.
Hate is increased by reciprocal hate, whereas imagined Love produces a striving to remove hate; if this striving prevails, Hate is destroyed and can pass into a greater Love.
One who imagines someone to hate a loved thing hates that person, because one imagines that person to be the cause of the Sadness of the loved thing and consequently of one's own Sadness.
Joy or Sadness received from one member of a different class or nation is extended to all of the same class or nation under a universal image.
Joy arising from the evil of a hated thing is repeated, because the memory of the thing renews former Sadness, which the idea of evil or liberation simultaneously restrains.
A cause of affect transferred to another thing diminishes or destroys Love or Hate toward the prior cause; an imagined free cause intensifies the same affect.

Things that accidentally arouse Hope or Fear are loved or hated as means to hoped-for things or as impediments to feared things; Superstitions arise from this structure and from the asymmetry of credulity.
No affection of an object is universally fixed, because the same object generates diverse affects according to the different disposition of Bodies and according to different times.
Interpersonal affects have the form of a feedback circuit: imagined Love reproduces Love and Glory, imagined Hate reproduces Hate, and imagined evil reproduces Vengeance.

Jealousy establishes a triadic structure in which the lover, the loved thing, and the rival are not three independent affections, but a single machine of restraint of appetite and redistribution of hate.

Imagined causality is an operator of affective direction: individuation of the cause intensifies the affect, multiplication of causes dilutes it, and universalization of the cause under a class or nation collectivizes it.
Memory and absence are not affectively inert: the image of a past thing simulates its presence, while the lack of a circumstance or the memory of evil effects a mechanism of Sadness and repeated Joy.
Judgments of good, evil, useful, useless, ominous, and harmful describe an affective cartography of desire, not an order of values independent of desire.
The system simultaneously admits the social propagation of affects through universal images and denies affective uniformity through the constitutive diversity of Bodies.
The system tacitly excludes affect as a purely internal motion without an imagined external cause, because Love and Hate are constituted through the idea of an external cause.
The system tacitly excludes the objective value of good and evil, because every value is reduced to the structure of desire, aversion, and affect.
The system tacitly excludes a simply dyadic affective relation, because love, hate, and glory are mediated by imagined third parties, rivals, classes, nations, and other causes.
The system tacitly excludes a stable identity of affect toward an object, because memory, circumstance, an associated cause, and the state of the Body can alter its direction.
The system tacitly excludes the rationally voluntary use of Sadness as a means to greater Joy, because striving necessarily tends to remove Sadness and preserve its own being.
The system tacitly excludes the omen as an objective message of the future, because the force of the omen proceeds from accidental association with Hope or Fear.

The text is ordered around the negation of an affectively autonomous subject: a human being does not produce one's affects from a free internal origin, but from images of causes, imitation, striving, and bodily constitution.
The text is ordered around the absence of transcendent moral tribunals: good, evil, gratitude, vengeance, cruelty, and superstition are ordered as effects of the affective machine.
The text is ordered around the impossibility of Joy wholly without a residue of Sadness, where Joy arises from the evil of a hated thing or from the abolition of hate.
The text is ordered around the impossibility of one object affectively identical for all, because an object provides no invariant affective value outside its relation to a Body to be affected.
External affection → image of the Body → Joy or Sadness → idea of an external cause → Love or Hate.
Image of an affect in a similar thing → affective imitation → Pity, Envy, or Ambition → social expansion of affect.
Love for a similar thing → striving to affect it with Joy accompanied by the idea of oneself → imagined reciprocal Love → Glory.
Rival, absence, or impediment → restraint of appetite → Sadness → Hate, Envy, Jealousy, Vengeance, or Desire.
Imagined reciprocal affect → striving to respond → cycle of the increase of Hate or its dissolution through Love.
Redistribution of cause / imagined free cause / imagined universal cause → diminution / intensification / collectivization of affect.
Memory, Hope, Fear, and accidental association → repetition of Joy or Sadness → Omens and Superstition; variety of Bodies → non-uniform affective outcomes.
Affection of the Body → image of a thing and of another's affect → affective imitation → Pity, Envy, and Ambition.
Love for a similar thing → striving for reciprocal love → Glory from imagined love → obstructed exclusivity → Jealousy.
More intense Joy or Sadness → more intense Desire to preserve or remove → benefit, maleficence, Vengeance, or Gratitude.
Imagined reciprocal Hate or Love → affective feedback → increase of Hate or its destruction through Love.
Reassigned cause of affect → diminution of love or hate; imagined free cause → intensification; cause of class or nation → extension to the collective.
Memory and accidental association → Hope or Fear → affective judgment of good, evil, and omen → Superstition; variable bodily constitution → plurality of outcomes.
Love and Hate are reclassified as imagined causal relations, not as intrinsic properties of persons or things.
Jealousy, Desire, Fear, Shame, Consternation, Anger, Vengeance, and Gratitude are described as composite figures generated from a few primary affections.
The affective relation between two agents becomes a circulatory relation, in which the imagined affect of the other constitutes the cause of a new affect and action of one's own.
The individual, the rival, the class, the nation, and the omen are placed in the same causal field, because all are images capable of directing Joy, Sadness, Hope, or Fear.
The distinction between a solitary cause, a multiple cause, and a universalized cause becomes a principle for measuring the direction and intensity of affect.
Good and evil are transferred from the order of things to the order of affective evaluations, so that the diversity of bodies produces a diversity of values.
Surface — The text explains the names and connections of determinate passions: Love, Hate, Jealousy, Desire, Fear, Vengeance, Gratitude, Hope, and Fear.
Structural — Affections of the Body, images, association of causes, diminution or increase of the power of acting, and striving are the mechanisms that generate passions.
Metastrategic — The contest among lovers, enemies, rivals, and collectives is described as a contest for the direction of causal images, for the preservation of Joy, and for the removal of Sadness.

Ontological/Temporal — Affect depends on the relation of the body to external causes and on images of time, by which memory makes the past present, absence acts as a cause of Sadness, and the same object operates differently according to different dispositions.

Axioms concerning the bodily image, imitation, striving, Joy, Sadness, and imagined causality suffice to reconstruct the principal series from reciprocal Love to Jealousy, Vengeance, Gratitude, and Superstition.

The reconstruction still depends on earlier definitions and propositions concerning affections of the Body, similarity, imagination, and striving, which the passage often presupposes through internal citations rather than demonstrates again.
The system is strongest where one and the same rule, namely Joy or Sadness with the idea of a cause, is reduced to diverse affections.

A fragile joint remains between imagined causality and true causality, because the passage explains how an image produces an affect, but does not provide a criterion by which the image of a cause is distinguished from cognition of a cause.

An internal tension arises between the propagation of affect to classes or nations and the variety of Bodies, because the former permits social generalization while the latter denies a uniform affective response.

A further tension remains between an imagined free cause, which increases affect, and an order of affects deduced from the necessary affections of the Body; the passage explains the force of the imagination of freedom, but does not resolve the metaphysical status of freedom.

The transition from individual hope and fear to Superstition is abbreviated, because the mechanism of affective credulity is given, but the social forms of the stability of superstition are not explained here.

The extracted structure preserves the movement of the text, because it proceeds from bodily affection and the image of a cause to interpersonal circuits, the collectivization of affects, and bodily variation.

units.title: Pars tertia - De origine et natura affectuum · passage 4

items.text: Textus quaerit qua lege affectus, iudicia de bono et malo, aestimationes sui atque aliorum, et actiones rationales ex essentia individui, obiectis externis, imaginatione et cognitione oriantur.
Thesis est affectus non esse proprietates fixas rerum neque nomina moralia per se clara, sed mutationes potentiae agendi causaliter determinatas.
Argumentatio est diagnostica et reconstructiva: vocabula vulgaria dissolvit, mechanismos imaginativos et causales substituit, deinde ex tribus affectibus primitivis varietates deducit.
Variatio affectuum inter homines et intra eundem hominem dissolvit iudicia affectiva ut mensuras universales et comparationes sociales exponit.
Mechanismus associationis et singularitatis imaginatae explicat Admirationem, Contemptum et affectus compositos.
Distinctio inter imaginationem inadequatam et ideam adaequatam transitum constituit a passionibus ad affectus activos, Fortitudinem, Animositatem et Generositatem.
Cupiditas est ipsa hominis essentia, quatenus ex quacumque affectione determinatur ad agendum, sive homo illius appetitus conscius sit sive non sit.
Conatus Mentis est ipsa eius essentia, quae affirmat id tantum quod Mens est et potest, atque imaginatur quae suam agendi potentiam ponunt.
Laetitia est transitus ad maiorem perfectionem sive augmentum potentiae agendi; Tristitia est transitus ad minorem perfectionem sive imminutio aut coercitio eiusdem potentiae.
Mens se ipsam non cognoscit nisi per affectiones Corporis earumque ideas; contemplatio suae agendi potentiae Laetitiam efficit, tanto maiorem quanto distinctior est.
Mens patitur quatenus ideas inadequatas habet atque imaginatur affectionem quae naturam sui Corporis et corporis externi involvit.
Natura cuiusque passionis naturam obiecti a quo excitatur necessario exprimit.
Affectus cuiusque individui ab affectu alterius tantum differt quantum essentia unius ab essentia alterius differt.
Imaginatio obiecti cum aliis antea visi in contemplationem aliorum transit; imaginatio rei singularis nullo nexu cum reliquis coniunctae Mentem ad unum obiectum figit.
Affectus aliorum, quatenus cum idea sui imaginantur, reflexe proprium affectum de se augent vel minuunt.
Imaginatio proprietatis singularis in se et negatae de reliquis auget Laetitiam sui; comparatio cum aequali potentiori Tristitiam parit.
Mens, cum ideam veram sive adaequatam concipit, se ipsam suamque agendi potentiam contemplatur et eatenus agit.
Nullus affectus Tristitiae ad Mentem quatenus agit referri potest, quia Tristitia ipsam intelligendi et agendi potentiam minuit aut coercet.
Fruitione obiecti Corpus novam constitutionem acquirere potest, qua eadem imago et eadem Cupiditas impeditae in Fastidium aut Taedium convertuntur.
Actiones ex affectibus Mentis intelligentis ortae ad Fortitudinem pertinent, quae in Animositatem et Generositatem dividitur.
Bonum, malum, melius et peius non iudicantur ex proprietate invariabili rerum, sed ex affectu iudicantis.
Intrepidus, audax, timidus et pusillanimis non sunt praedicata absoluta, sed nomina comparativa ex diverso metu et diversa Cupiditate nata.
Admiratio non est cognitio obiecti per se excellentis, sed imaginatio singularis quae Mentem ab aliis contemplationibus excludit.
Contemptus non est mera absentia Admirationis, sed fixatio Mentis in iis quae obiecto desunt postquam causae prioris Admirationis, Amoris aut Metus negantur.
Nomina affectuum non constituunt taxonomiam accuratam naturae affectivae, sed ex usu vulgari plerumque proveniunt.
Cupiditas non distinguitur re ab appetitu inconsciō, voluntate aut impetu, sed eos omnes sub una essentia determinata comprehendit.
Laetitia et Tristitia non sunt status perfectionis aut privationis, sed actus transitus inter gradus potentiae.
Temperantia, Sobrietas et Castitas non sunt passiones neque contraria objectiva Luxuriae, Ebrietatis et Libidinis, sed indicia potentiae quae affectus moderatur.
Tristitia activa non datur; ubi Tristitia adest, imminutio potentiae Mentis actionem excludit.
Affectus humanos non separat ab affectibus animalium aliqua forma affectiva absoluta, sed sola differentia naturarum individualium.
Iudicia de bono et malo atque vocabula characteris variant secundum constitutionem affectivam iudicantis, non secundum normam intrinsecam obiecti.
Paenitentia est Tristitia cum idea sui ut causae, et Acquiescentia in se ipso est Laetitia cum eadem idea sui ut causae.
Singularitas imaginata parit Admirationem; Admiratio mali metuti Consternationem, Admiratio prudentiae Venerationem, et Amor cum Admiratione coniunctus Devotionem producit.
Contemptus expectationem affectivam frustratam in contemplationem defectuum rei convertit, unde Irrisio et Dedignatio oriri possunt.
Imaginatio laudis alienae Acquiescentiam in se ipso fovet, et imaginatio vituperii Humilitatem sive Tristitiam ex idea propriae imbecillitatis auget.
Contemplatio actionum propriarum ut singularium Philautiam, iactationem et studium se ornandi parit; comparatio cum aequalibus fortioribus Invidiam promovet.
Nemo virtutem alicui nisi aequali invidet, quia sola virtus quae cum propria natura comparabilis est propriam Cupiditatem coercere potest.
Species Laetitiae, Tristitiae, Amoris, Odii et Cupiditatis multiplicantur secundum species obiectorum et secundum diversas constitutiones individuorum.
Affectus equi, hominis, insectorum, piscium et avium eandem legem essentialem sequuntur, sed natura variant quia essentiae eorum diversae sunt.
Affectus activos solum Laetitia et Cupiditas constituunt; Animositas utilitatem agentis, Generositas utilitatem aliorum et amicitiam ex ratione intendit.
Eadem res, prius appetita, ex mutatione constitutionis Corporis odiosa fieri potest, quia nova dispositio Cupiditati iam excitatae repugnat.
Definitio generalis affectuum sufficit ad potentiam Mentis moderandi et coercendi affectus intelligendam, quamvis singularum specierum numerus indefinitus sit.
Trias Cupiditatis, Laetitiae et Tristitiae, cum differentiis obiecti, essentiae et imaginationis, machinam generatricem innumerabilium affectuum praebet sine inventario completo specierum.
Valor rerum non antecedit affectum, sed ex motibus potentiae, comparationibus et imaginibus constituitur; iudicium morale fit effectus dynamicae affectivae.
Honor, vituperium, educatio, iactatio et Invidia formant circuitum socialem quo homines potentiam suam per affectus imaginatos aliorum metiuntur et vicissim alterant.
Distinctio actionis et passionis non in exteriori specie facti consistit, sed in modo causali et cognitivo quo Mens ideas adaequatas vel inadequatas habet.
Affectus temporaliter instabiles sunt, quia non res staticae sed transitus potentiae atque mutationes constitutionis corporis sunt.
Falsum esse debet subjectum humanum se ipsum ut causam liberam, immediatam et transparentem sufficienter cognoscere; cognitio sui per affectiones Corporis mediatur.
Falsa esse debet mensura universalis qua res per se bonae, malae, terribiles aut venerandae pronuntiantur independenter ab affectu et constitutione individui.
Falsa esse debet opinio quod nomina recepta affectuum species naturales perfecte dividant; compositio affectuum vocabularium vulgare excedit.
Falsa esse debet opinio quod virtus sit contraria passio vel simplex imminutio Cupiditatis; virtus activa est ordinatio potentiae per rationem.
Falsa esse debet separatio absoluta hominis ab animalibus in ordine affectivo; differentia affectuum proportionem differentiae essentiarum sequitur.
Systema nullum affectum purum admittit, qui a constitutione individui, relatione ad obiectum, idea Corporis et ordine imaginationis omnino solutus sit.
Systema nullam stabilitatem affectivam finalem supponit: potentia transit, corpora reconfigurantur, obiecta variant, et Cupiditates in contraria flecti possunt.
Systema nullam clausuram lexicalem aut enumerationem ultimam affectuum concedit; sola reductio ad causas primitivas infinitam varietatem tractabilem reddit.
Essentia individualis sive conatus + affectio data → Cupiditas determinata ad agendum.
Corpus affectum + obiectum externum + idea inadequata → passio cuius species naturam obiecti exprimit.
Augmentum potentiae → Laetitia; imminutio aut coercitio potentiae → Tristitia; utrumque → novas Cupiditates et affectus compositos.
Associatio imaginativa → transitus ad alia obiecta; singularitas sine nexu → fixatio Mentis → Admiratio vel affectus ex Admiratione compositi.
Contemplatio sui + imago laudis, vituperii aut comparationis → Acquiescentia, Humilitas, Philautia, Invidia et certamen comparativum.
Idea adaequata → actio Mentis → Laetitia et Cupiditas activa → Animositas vel Generositas.
Nova constitutio Corporis ex fruitione → repugnantia ad Cupiditatem priorem → Fastidium aut Taedium → nova series affectuum.
Variatio affectuum inter homines et intra eundem hominem → relativizatio boni, mali et nominum characteris.
Associatio imaginum et singularitas imaginata → Admiratio, Consternatio, Veneratio, Devotio et Contemptus.
Contemplatio potentiae propriae → Laetitia sui → laus, vituperium et comparatio socialis → Humilitas, Philautia et Invidia.
Differentia obiectorum et essentiarum → multiplicatio specierum affectuum → imminutio valoris taxonomiae vulgaris.
Inadequatio et causae externae → passiones et fluctuationes; adaequatio → actio, Laetitia activa et Cupiditas activa.
Distinctio affectuum activorum → Fortitudo → Animositas et Generositas → definitio retroactiva Cupiditatis, Laetitiae, Tristitiae et Admirationis.
Bonum et malum reclassificantur ut iudicia affectiva, non ut qualitates immediatae rerum.
Admiratio et Contemptus reclassificantur ut dispositiones attentionis imaginativae, non ut responsa simplicia ad dignitatem obiectivam obiecti.
Amor sui, Humilitas, laus, vituperium et Invidia collocantur in eodem campo comparationis socialis et reflexionis potentiae.
Affectus innumerabiles intelliguntur per grammaticam causalium primitivorum potius quam per catalogum nominum receptarum.
Virtus reclassificatur ut potentia activa Mentis ratione ordinata, non ut oppositio passionis determinatae.
Differentia hominis et animalis transfertur ab oppositione essentiali ad differentiam graduum et modorum naturae individualis.
Gradus superficiei — Textus definit affectus singulares, inter quos Admirationem, Contemptum, Paenitentiam, Humilitatem, Invidiam, Fastidium, Animositatem et Generositatem.
Gradus structuralis — Affectus producuntur ex conatu, transitu potentiae, affectionibus Corporis, obiectis externis, imaginatione associativa et comparatione sociali.
Gradus metastrategicus — Vocabula moralia et psychologica vulgaria subordinantur methodo quae ex paucis definitionibus communes proprietates affectuum et potentiam Mentis deducit.
Gradus ontologicus vel temporalis — Individuum est essentia perseverans quae sub affectionibus mutabilibus determinatur; affectus sunt transitus et reconfigurationes, non formae immobiles.
Axiomata de Cupiditate, potentia, transitu Laetitiae et Tristitiae, imaginatione, obiectis externis et cognitione adaequata sufficiunt ad praecipuos motus argumentationis restituendos.
Systema maxime cohaeret ubi affectus singulares ex una machina conatus, mutationis potentiae et causae externae deducuntur.
Firmissimum nodum constituit distinctio inter passionem ex inadequatione ortam et actionem ex idea adaequata ortam.
Tensio manet inter infinitam varietatem affectuum ex differentiis obiectorum ortam et sufficientiam practicam definitionum generalium quae has differentias non explicant.
Transitus ab idea adaequata ad actionem Mentis innititur principiis Partis II, quae hic assumuntur potius quam intra hunc locum iterum fundantur.
Distinctio inter aequalem, cuius virtus Invidiam parit, et non-aequalem, cuius virtus Venerationem parit, comparabilitatem naturarum praesupponit quam textus localiter non determinat.
Vehementia Paenitentiae et Acquiescentiae ex credulitate libertatis explicatur, sed ipsa conditio illius credulitatis hic indicatur potius quam plene resolvitur.
Restitutio motum verum servat: a variatione iudiciorum ad mechanismos imaginationis, ab illis ad structuram socialem, a passionibus ad actionem, et denique ad definitiones primitivas revertitur.

translations.title: Part Three - On the Origin and Nature of the Affects · passage 4

items.text: The text asks by what law affects, judgments concerning good and evil, estimations of oneself and others, and rational actions arise from the essence of the individual, external objects, imagination, and cognition.
The thesis is that affects are not fixed properties of things nor moral names clear in themselves, but causally determined changes in the power of acting.
The argumentation is diagnostic and reconstructive: it dissolves common terms, substitutes imaginative and causal mechanisms, then derives varieties from three primitive affects.
The variation of affects among human beings and within the same human being dissolves affective judgments as universal measures and exposes social comparisons.
The mechanism of association and imagined singularity explains Wonder, Contempt, and composite affects.
The distinction between inadequate imagination and adequate idea constitutes the transition from passions to active affects, Fortitude, Strength of Mind, and Generosity.
Desire is the very essence of the human being, insofar as it is determined by any affection to act, whether the human being is conscious of that appetite or not.
The striving of the Mind is its very essence, which affirms only what the Mind is and can do, and imagines those things that posit its power of acting.
Joy is a transition to greater perfection, or an increase in the power of acting; Sadness is a transition to lesser perfection, or a diminution or restraint of that same power.
The Mind does not know itself except through affections of the Body and their ideas; contemplation of its own power of acting produces Joy, greater insofar as it is more distinct.
The Mind is acted upon insofar as it has inadequate ideas and imagines an affection that involves the nature of its own Body and of an external body.
The nature of every passion necessarily expresses the nature of the object by which it is aroused.
The affect of each individual differs from the affect of another only insofar as the essence of one differs from the essence of the other.
Imagination of an object previously seen with others passes into contemplation of the others; imagination of a singular thing joined to the rest by no connection fixes the Mind upon one object.
The affects of others, insofar as they are imagined together with an idea of oneself, reflexively increase or diminish one's own affect concerning oneself.
Imagination of a singular property in oneself and denied of others increases Joy in oneself; comparison with a more powerful equal produces Sadness.
When the Mind conceives a true or adequate idea, it contemplates itself and its own power of acting and, to that extent, acts.
No affect of Sadness can be referred to the Mind insofar as it acts, because Sadness diminishes or restrains the very power of understanding and acting.
Through enjoyment of an object, the Body can acquire a new constitution, by which the same image and the same Desire are impeded and converted into Disgust or Weariness.
Actions arising from the affects of an understanding Mind belong to Fortitude, which is divided into Strength of Mind and Generosity.
Good, evil, better, and worse are not judged from an invariable property of things, but from the affect of the one judging.
The fearless, bold, timid, and faint-hearted are not absolute predicates, but comparative names born from differing fear and differing Desire.
Wonder is not cognition of an object excellent in itself, but a singular imagination that excludes the Mind from other contemplations.
Contempt is not the mere absence of Wonder, but fixation of the Mind on what the object lacks after the causes of prior Wonder, Love, or Fear are denied.
Names of affects do not constitute an accurate taxonomy of affective nature, but for the most part arise from common usage.
Desire is not distinguished in reality from unconscious appetite, will, or impulse, but comprehends them all under one determined essence.
Joy and Sadness are not states of perfection or privation, but acts of transition between degrees of power.
Temperance, Sobriety, and Chastity are neither passions nor objective contraries of Luxury, Drunkenness, and Lust, but signs of a power that moderates affects.
There is no active Sadness; where Sadness is present, the diminution of the Mind's power excludes action.
Human affects are not separated from animal affects by any absolute affective form, but only by the difference of individual natures.
Judgments concerning good and evil and terms of character vary according to the affective constitution of the one judging, not according to an intrinsic norm of the object.
Repentance is Sadness with the idea of oneself as cause, and Self-satisfaction is Joy with the same idea of oneself as cause.
Imagined singularity produces Wonder; Wonder at a feared evil produces Consternation, Wonder at prudence produces Veneration, and Love joined with Wonder produces Devotion.
Contempt converts frustrated affective expectation into contemplation of the defects of a thing, from which Derision and Scorn can arise.
Imagination of another's praise fosters Self-satisfaction, and imagination of blame increases Humility, or Sadness from the idea of one's own weakness.
Contemplation of one's own actions as singular produces Self-love, boasting, and the striving to adorn oneself; comparison with stronger equals promotes Envy.
No one envies virtue in anyone except an equal, because only virtue comparable with one's own nature can restrain one's own Desire.
The species of Joy, Sadness, Love, Hate, and Desire are multiplied according to the species of objects and according to the diverse constitutions of individuals.
The affects of the horse, human being, insects, fish, and birds follow the same essential law, but vary in nature because their essences are different.
Only Joy and Desire constitute active affects; Strength of Mind aims at the agent's advantage, Generosity at the advantage of others and friendship from reason.
The same thing, previously desired, can become hateful through a change in the constitution of the Body, because the new disposition conflicts with Desire already aroused.
The general definition of affects suffices for understanding the Mind's power to moderate and restrain affects, although the number of individual species is indefinite.
The triad of Desire, Joy, and Sadness, together with differences of object, essence, and imagination, provides the generative machine of innumerable affects without a complete inventory of species.
The value of things does not precede affect, but is constituted from movements of power, comparisons, and images; moral judgment becomes an effect of affective dynamics.
Honor, blame, education, boasting, and Envy form a social circuit by which human beings measure and reciprocally alter their power through the imagined affects of others.
The distinction of action and passion does not consist in the external appearance of the deed, but in the causal and cognitive mode by which the Mind has adequate or inadequate ideas.
Affects are temporally unstable because they are not static things but transitions of power and changes in bodily constitution.
It must be false that the human subject sufficiently knows itself as a free, immediate, and transparent cause; self-knowledge is mediated through affections of the Body.
There must be a false universal measure by which things are declared good, evil, terrible, or venerable in themselves independently of the affect and constitution of the individual.
It must be false that received names of affects perfectly divide natural species; the composition of affects exceeds common vocabulary.
It must be false that virtue is a contrary passion or a simple diminution of Desire; active virtue is the ordering of power through reason.
The absolute separation of the human being from animals in the affective order must be false; the difference of affects follows the proportion of the difference of essences.
The system admits no pure affect wholly detached from the constitution of the individual, relation to the object, idea of the Body, and order of imagination.
The system supposes no final affective stability: power passes, bodies are reconfigured, objects vary, and Desires can be bent into their contraries.
The system grants no lexical closure or final enumeration of affects; only reduction to primitive causes renders infinite variety manageable.
Individual essence or striving + given affection → Desire determined to act.
Affected Body + external object + inadequate idea → passion whose species expresses the nature of the object.
Increase of power → Joy; diminution or restraint of power → Sadness; either → new Desires and composite affects.
Imaginative association → transition to other objects; singularity without connection → fixation of the Mind → Wonder or affects composed from Wonder.
Contemplation of oneself + image of praise, blame, or comparison → Self-satisfaction, Humility, Self-love, Envy, and comparative contest.
Adequate idea → action of the Mind → active Joy and Desire → Strength of Mind or Generosity.
New constitution of the Body through enjoyment → opposition to prior Desire → Disgust or Weariness → new series of affects.
Variation of affects among human beings and within the same human being → relativization of good, evil, and names of character.
Association of images and imagined singularity → Wonder, Consternation, Veneration, Devotion, and Contempt.
Contemplation of one's own power → Joy in oneself → praise, blame, and social comparison → Humility, Self-love, and Envy.
Difference of objects and essences → multiplication of species of affects → diminution of the value of common taxonomy.
Inadequacy and external causes → passions and fluctuations; adequacy → action, active Joy, and active Desire.
Distinction of active affects → Fortitude → Strength of Mind and Generosity → retroactive definition of Desire, Joy, Sadness, and Wonder.
Good and evil are reclassified as affective judgments, not as immediate qualities of things.
Wonder and Contempt are reclassified as dispositions of imaginative attention, not as simple responses to the objective worth of the object.
Self-love, Humility, praise, blame, and Envy are placed in the same field of social comparison and reflection on power.
Innumerable affects are understood through a grammar of primitive causes rather than through a catalogue of received names.
Virtue is reclassified as the active power of the Mind ordered by reason, not as the opposition of a determinate passion.
The difference between human being and animal is transferred from essential opposition to difference in degrees and modes of individual nature.
Surface level — The text defines singular affects, among them Wonder, Contempt, Repentance, Humility, Envy, Disgust, Strength of Mind, and Generosity.
Structural level — Affects are produced from striving, transition of power, affections of the Body, external objects, associative imagination, and social comparison.
Metastrategic level — Common moral and psychological terms are subordinated to a method that derives from a few definitions the common properties of affects and the power of the Mind.
Ontological or temporal level — The individual is a persevering essence determined under mutable affections; affects are transitions and reconfigurations, not immobile forms.
Axioms concerning Desire, power, the transition of Joy and Sadness, imagination, external objects, and adequate cognition suffice to reconstruct the principal movements of the argumentation.
The system is most coherent where singular affects are derived from one mechanism of striving, change of power, and external cause.
The strongest node is constituted by the distinction between passion arising from inadequacy and action arising from an adequate idea.
A tension remains between the infinite variety of affects arising from differences of objects and the practical sufficiency of general definitions that do not explain these differences.
The transition from adequate idea to action of the Mind rests upon principles of Part II, which are assumed here rather than grounded again within this passage.
The distinction between the equal, whose virtue produces Envy, and the non-equal, whose virtue produces Veneration, presupposes a comparability of natures that the text does not determine locally.
The vehemence of Repentance and Self-satisfaction is explained from belief in freedom, but the very condition of that belief is indicated here rather than fully resolved.

The reconstruction preserves the true movement: from variation of judgments to mechanisms of imagination, from these to social structure, from passions to action, and finally returns to primitive definitions.

identity.title: Pars tertia - De origine et natura affectuum · passage 4

units.title: Pars tertia - De origine et natura affectuum · passage 5

items.text: Textus quaerit utrum multitudo nominum affectuum multitudinem naturarum primariarum significet, an varias denominationes paucorum motuum fundamentalium.
Textus statuit tres tantum affectus primitivos dari, Lætitiam, Tristitiam et Cupiditatem, ex quibus reliqui per relationes, causas imaginatas et compositiones oriuntur.
Argumentatio est reconstructiva et diagnostica: falsas species affectuum, voluntatem liberam et opposita nominalia removet, ut ordinem causaliter generativum constituat.
Definitio singularis affectus per genus primarium, ideam causae, modum temporalem, relationem socialem vel aestimationem imaginatam componitur.
Clausura generalis affectum passivum ad ideam confusam reducit, qua Mens mutationem potentiae corporis affirmat et ad certum cogitandum determinatur.
Mens eatenus patitur, quatenus ideas inadæquatas sive confusas habet.
Affectus animi, quatenus passio est, idea confusa est qua Mens majorem vel minorem existendi vim sui Corporis affirmat.
Essentia Mentis consistit in affirmatione actualis existentiae sui Corporis, cuius maior vel minor realitas transitum ad majorem vel minorem perfectionem constituit.
Lætitia et Tristitia sunt transitus Mentis ad majorem vel minorem perfectionem seu potentiam agendi.
Cupiditas est determinatio Mentis qua, data idea, ad hoc potius quam ad aliud cogitandum vel agendum fertur.
Lætitia, Tristitia et Cupiditas sunt solae formae affectuum primitivae.
Idea causae externae, internae vel per accidens adjunctae affectum primarium in affectum denominatum determinat.
Imago rei præteritae vel futuræ Mentem eodem affectu afficere potest quo imago rei præsentis, atque dubitatio eventus modum affectus mutat.
Imaginatio similitudinis, cupiditatis, judicii aut actionis aliorum affectus sociales generat.
Educatio, consuetudo et religio Lætitiam aut Tristitiam cum actibus conjungunt et inde judiciorum moralium affectivam vim constituunt.
Liberum Mentis decretum sive deliberatio voluntaria non est causa realis primaria affectuum.
Naturae rerum explicatio praevalet usui vulgari vocabulorum, quamvis vocabula recepta retineri possint ad res indicandas.
Admiratio non numeratur inter affectus, quia distractio Mentis ex novitate non ex causa positiva, sed ex defectu causae ad aliud cogitandum determinantis oritur.
Amor non est voluntas libera amantis sese rei amatæ jungendi, nec Cupiditas absentem rem assequendi aut praesentem retinendi.
Spes sine Metu, nec Metus sine Spe, dari potest, quia dubitatio utriusque rei imaginem et exclusionem implicat.
Sublata dubitandi causa non sequitur certitudo rei singularis, sed tantum status de re non dubitandi.
Pœnitentia non probat decretum Mentis liberum esse, sed ideam facti, quod homo se ex libero decreto fecisse credit, affective efficacem esse.
Impudentia affectus non est, quamvis usu vulgari Verecundiæ opponatur.
Clementia, Temperantia, Sobrietas et Castitas passiones non sunt, sed potentiae animi quibus passiones moderari possunt.
Contrarietas affectuum non ex actibus externis vel abstinentia determinatur, sed ex natura Appetitus et Amoris qui actus movent.
Fluctuationes compositae neque nomen proprium neque definitionem singularem necessario postulant.
Amor et Odium non sunt affectiones simplices sui generis, sed Lætitia et Tristitia idea causae externae concomitatae.
Spes et Metus sunt affectus inconstantes quorum una pars rei eventum affirmat, altera eiusdem rei existentiam imaginando secludit.
Securitas et Desperatio ex Spe et Metu proveniunt, cum dubitationis causa tollitur, non cum cognitio certa eventus acquiritur.
Desiderium, memoria rei jucundæ fultum et imaginibus rei absentiam affirmantibus coercitum, revera Tristitia est, sed ex usu ad Cupiditatem refertur.
Favor, Indignatio, Invidia et Misericordia sunt variationes Amoris vel Odii, quas bonum aut malum alterius et imaginata similitudo ordinant.
Gloria, Pudor et Pœnitentia non ex qualitate morali intrinseca actus oriuntur, sed ex imaginato judicio aliorum, autojudicio et affectiva institutione.
Distinctio inter passionem et animi potentiam impedit ne moderatio Irae aut Vindictae pro affectu contrario habeatur.
Multiplicatio nominum affectuum non multiplicat principia realia, quia denominationes ex relationibus causalibus et extrinsecis oriuntur.
Systema omnem pluralitatem affectivam ad triadem dynamicam reducit, cui adduntur variatio potentiae, idea causae, imaginatio temporalis et relatio socialis.
Affectus non primario naturam rei externae indicant, sed constitutionem actualem corporis et modum quo Mens illam per ideas confusas ordinat.
Tempus affectivum non dividitur stricte in praesens, praeteritum et futurum, quia memoria et exspectatio praesentem vim imaginis assumere possunt.
Iudicia recti, pravi, sacri, profani, honesti et turpis in campo affectuum apparent ut effectus institutionis et consuetudinis, non ut proprietates naturales actuum.
Subiectum affectivum non est auctor liber passionum suarum, sed locus in quo corporalis potentia, imaginatio et causae sociales in formas denominatas componuntur.
Falsum esse oportet affectus nominatos esse naturas simplices et irreductibiles, alioquin reductio ad tres primitivos corrueret.
Falsum esse oportet affectum cognitionem perspicuam causae externae praebere, cum eius idea primario constitutionem corporis indicet.
Falsum esse oportet voluntatem liberam affectus ex nihilo instituere, cum ipsa deliberatio libera ad fictionem referatur.
Falsum esse oportet actus per se laetos, tristes, honestos aut turpes esse, cum earum conjunctionum affectivarum causa in educatione et consuetudine ponatur.
Falsum esse oportet taxonomiam affectuum exhauriri posse per vocabula recepta, cum plurima composita nomine careant et tantum in genere cognosci sufficiat.
Carentia dubitationis affectivae non admittitur ut forma certitudinis de eventu rei singularis.
Vocabularium morale et vulgare non admittitur ut tribunal ultimum naturae affectuum, quia rerum explicatio prior est usu sermonis.
Affectus pure mentalis et a corporeae existentiae affirmatione separatus non admittitur, quia Mens in affectu de suo Corpore aliquid affirmat.
Constitutio Corporis mutata → idea confusa eius constitutionis → passio Mentis.
Augmentum potentiae affirmatum → Lætitia; imminutio potentiae affirmata → Tristitia.
Idea data quae Mentem ad hoc potius quam ad aliud fert → Cupiditas.
Affectus primarius + idea causae externae, internae vel accidentariae → Amor, Odium, Acquiescentia, Humilitas, Propensio vel Aversio.
Affectus primarius + imago rei praeteritae vel futurae + dubitatio aut exclusio imaginata → Spes, Metus, Securitas, Desperatio, Gaudium, Conscientiæ morsus vel Desiderium.
Affectus primarius + imago alterius, similitudinis, laudis, vituperii, beneficii aut damni → affectus sociales, imitativi et comparativi.
Affectus compositus + relatio extrinseca + nomen receptum → pluralitas affectuum denominata sine multiplicatione principiorum.
Exclusio causae positivae, libertatis fictae, oppositionis mere nominalis et virtutis activae e classe passionum → fines systematis.
Novitas rei → defectus transitus associativi → exclusio Admirationis e numero affectuum.
Exclusio falsi primitivi → positio Lætitiæ, Tristitiæ et Cupiditatis ut triadis fundamentalis.
Trias primitiva → idea causae externae, internae aut accidentariae → affectus causales denominati.
Affectus causales → imaginatio temporalis et dubitatio → affectus inconstantes, securi aut desperati.
Imaginatio aliorum et institutio moralis → affectus sociales, comparativi et reflexivi.
Correctio vocabulorum et exclusionum → imminutio specierum apparentium.
Taxonomia derivata → definitio generalis passionis ut idea confusa mutationis potentiae corporis.
Affectus nominati reclassificantur ut modi relationales trium motuum, non ut inventarium naturarum psychologicarum independentium.
Distinctio fit inter causam affectus, ideam causae concomitantem et constitutionem corporis quam idea affectiva immediate exprimit.
Oppositio inter praesens et non-praesens dissolvitur in campo affectivo, quia praeteritum et futurum per imaginationem vim praesentiae obtinere possunt.
Iudicia moralia reponuntur ex ordine proprietatum actuum in ordine affectuum per educationem, consuetudinem et religionem compositorum.
Virtutes moderatrices distinguuntur ab affectibus passivis, ita ut contrarietas moralis non confundatur cum contrarietate affectiva.
Surface — Textus definit seriem nominum affectivorum et eorum relationes immediatas ad Lætitiam, Tristitiam, Cupiditatem, causas et objecta.
Structural — Affectus passivus explicatur per ideam confusam constitutionis corporis in qua potentia existendi et agendi augetur, minuitur, juvatur aut coercetur.
Metastrategic — Argumentatio vocabula vulgariter recepta servat, sed eorum auctoritatem explicativam submittit reductioni rerum ad causas et relationes generativas.
Ontological/Temporal — Mens actualem corporis existentiam affirmat, dum tempora affectiva per imaginationem ordinantur nec dubitationis absentia in certitudinem rei singularis transit.
Nucleus trium affectuum, ideae confusae et mutationis potentiae corporis sufficit ad legem generalem reductionis restituendam.
Distinctiones causae, temporis, imaginationis socialis et institutionis sufficiunt ad familias principales definitionum derivatarum regenerandas.
Derivatio singularum definitionum localium non est omnino autonoma, quia plures gradus ad propositiones et scholia anteriora remittuntur nec hic iterum demonstrantur.
Commissura fragilis manet inter definitionem generalem corpoream et species sociales vel morales, quarum reductio ad variationem potentiae in hoc loco potius praesupponitur quam explicite perficitur.
Tensio semantica manet inter principium naturae rerum et retentionem vocabulorum usu vulgari formatorum, quam textus pragmatico usu, non regula semantica exhaustiva, componit.
Fictio decreti liberi et affectus Pœnitentiæ cohaerent tantum si credulitas libertatis ut causa imaginata efficax accipitur; nexus iste hic affirmatur, sed non plene re-deducitur.
Restitutio motum verum servat, quia ab exclusione apparentium primitivorum procedit ad triadem, ab ea ad denominationes, et denique ad formam generalem passionis.

translations.title: Part Three - On the Origin and Nature of the Affects · passage 5

items.text: The text asks whether the multiplicity of names of affects signifies a multiplicity of primary natures, or various denominations of a few fundamental motions.
The text establishes that there are only three primitive affects, Joy, Sadness, and Desire, from which the rest arise through relations, imagined causes, and compositions.
The argumentation is reconstructive and diagnostic: it removes false species of affects, free will, and nominal opposites, in order to establish a causally generative order.
The definition of a particular affect is composed through a primary genus, the idea of a cause, a temporal mode, a social relation, or an imagined estimation.
The general conclusion reduces a passive affect to a confused idea by which the Mind affirms a change in the body's power and is determined to think in a certain way.
The Mind suffers insofar as it has inadequate or confused ideas.
An affect of the mind, insofar as it is a passion, is a confused idea by which the Mind affirms a greater or lesser force of existence of its Body.
The essence of the Mind consists in the affirmation of the actual existence of its Body, whose greater or lesser reality constitutes a transition to greater or lesser perfection.
Joy and Sadness are transitions of the Mind to greater or lesser perfection, or power of acting.
Desire is a determination of the Mind by which, given an idea, it is borne to think or act upon this rather than that.
Joy, Sadness, and Desire are the sole primitive forms of affects.
The idea of an external, internal, or accidentally conjoined cause determines a primary affect into a denominated affect.
The image of a past or future thing can affect the Mind with the same affect as the image of a present thing, and doubt about the outcome alters the mode of the affect.
The imagination of another's likeness, desire, judgment, or action generates social affects.
Education, custom, and religion join Joy or Sadness with acts and thereby constitute the affective force of moral judgments.
A free decree of the Mind, or voluntary deliberation, is not a primary real cause of affects.
The explanation of the nature of things prevails over the common use of words, although received terms may be retained to indicate things.

Wonder is not counted among the affects, because the distraction of the Mind arising from novelty originates not from a positive cause but from the absence of a cause determining it to think of something else.
Love is not the free will of the lover to join himself to the beloved thing, nor is Desire the striving to attain an absent thing or retain a present one.
Hope cannot be given without Fear, nor Fear without Hope, because doubt implies both the image of each thing and its exclusion.
When the cause of doubting is removed, certainty of a particular thing does not follow, but only a state of not doubting concerning the thing.
Repentance does not prove that the decree of the Mind is free, but that the idea of a deed which a person believes himself to have done by free decree is affectively efficacious.
Shamelessness is not an affect, although in common usage it is opposed to Modesty.
Clemency, Temperance, Sobriety, and Chastity are not passions, but powers of the mind by which passions can be moderated.
The contrariety of affects is determined not by external acts or abstinence, but by the nature of the Appetite and Love that move the acts.
Composite fluctuations do not necessarily require either a proper name or a particular definition.
Love and Hate are not simple affections of their own kind, but Joy and Sadness accompanied by the idea of an external cause.
Hope and Fear are inconstant affects, one part of which affirms the outcome of a thing, while another, by imagining the existence of that same thing, excludes it.
Security and Despair arise from Hope and Fear when the cause of doubt is removed, not when certain knowledge of the outcome is acquired.
Longing, sustained by the memory of a pleasant thing and restrained by images affirming the thing's absence, is in truth Sadness, but by usage is referred to Desire.
Favor, Indignation, Envy, and Pity are variations of Love or Hate, ordered by another's good or evil and imagined likeness.
Glory, Shame, and Repentance arise not from the intrinsic moral quality of an act, but from the imagined judgment of others, self-judgment, and affective institution.
The distinction between passion and power of mind prevents the moderation of Anger or Vengeance from being regarded as a contrary affect.
The multiplication of names of affects does not multiply real principles, because denominations arise from causal and extrinsic relations.
The system reduces all affective plurality to a dynamic triad, to which are added variation of power, the idea of cause, temporal imagination, and social relation.
Affects do not primarily indicate the nature of the external thing, but the actual constitution of the body and the manner in which the Mind orders it through confused ideas.
Affective time is not strictly divided into present, past, and future, because memory and expectation can assume the present force of an image.
Judgments of right, wrong, sacred, profane, honorable, and shameful appear in the field of affects as effects of institution and custom, not as natural properties of acts.
The affective subject is not the free author of its passions, but the locus in which bodily power, imagination, and social causes are composed into denominated forms.
It must be false that named affects are simple and irreducible natures; otherwise the reduction to three primitives would collapse.
It must be false that an affect provides clear knowledge of an external cause, since its idea primarily indicates the constitution of the body.
It must be false that free will institutes affects from nothing, since free deliberation itself is referred to fiction.
It must be false that acts are in themselves joyful, sad, honorable, or shameful, since the cause of those affective conjunctions is placed in education and custom.
It must be false that a taxonomy of affects can be exhausted through received terms, since very many composites lack a name and it suffices for them to be known only in general.
The absence of affective doubt is not admitted as a form of certainty concerning the outcome of a particular thing.
Moral and common vocabulary is not admitted as the ultimate tribunal of the nature of affects, because the explanation of things is prior to linguistic usage.
A purely mental affect separated from the affirmation of bodily existence is not admitted, because in an affect the Mind affirms something concerning its Body.
Changed constitution of the Body → confused idea of that constitution → passion of the Mind.
Affirmed increase of power → Joy; affirmed diminution of power → Sadness.
A given idea that bears the Mind to this rather than that → Desire.
Primary affect + idea of an external, internal, or accidental cause → Love, Hate, Self-Contentment, Humility, Inclination, or Aversion.
Primary affect + image of a past or future thing + doubt or imagined exclusion → Hope, Fear, Security, Despair, Joy, Remorse of Conscience, or Longing.
Primary affect + image of another, of likeness, praise, blame, benefit, or harm → social, imitative, and comparative affects.
Composite affect + extrinsic relation + received name → denominated plurality of affects without multiplication of principles.
Exclusion from the class of passions of a positive cause, fictitious freedom, merely nominal opposition, and active virtue → boundaries of the system.
Novelty of a thing → lack of associative transition → exclusion of Wonder from the number of affects.
Exclusion of the false primitive → positing of Joy, Sadness, and Desire as the fundamental triad.
Primitive triad → idea of an external, internal, or accidental cause → denominated causal affects.
Causal affects → temporal imagination and doubt → inconstant, secure, or despairing affects.
Imagination of others and moral institution → social, comparative, and reflexive affects.
Correction of terms and exclusions → reduction of apparent species.
Derived taxonomy → general definition of passion as a confused idea of a change in bodily power.
Named affects are reclassified as relational modes of three motions, not as an inventory of independent psychological natures.
A distinction is made among the cause of an affect, the accompanying idea of the cause, and the constitution of the body that the affective idea immediately expresses.
The opposition between present and non-present is dissolved in the affective field, because past and future can acquire the force of presence through imagination.
Moral judgments are relocated from the order of properties of acts to the order of affects composed through education, custom, and religion.
Moderating virtues are distinguished from passive affects, so that moral contrariety is not confused with affective contrariety.
Surface — The text defines a series of affective names and their immediate relations to Joy, Sadness, Desire, causes, and objects.
Structural — A passive affect is explained through a confused idea of the constitution of the body, in which the power of existing and acting is increased, diminished, aided, or restrained.
Metastrategic — The argumentation retains commonly received terms, but submits their explanatory authority to the reduction of things to causes and generative relations.

Ontological/Temporal — The Mind affirms the actual existence of the body, while affective times are ordered through imagination and the absence of doubt does not pass into certainty concerning a particular thing.
The nucleus of the three affects, confused ideas, and change in bodily power suffices to restore the general law of reduction.
The distinctions of cause, time, social imagination, and institution suffice to regenerate the principal families of derived definitions.
The derivation of individual local definitions is not wholly autonomous, because several steps refer back to earlier propositions and scholia and are not demonstrated again here.
A fragile joint remains between the general corporeal definition and the social or moral species, whose reduction to variation of power is here rather presupposed than explicitly carried out.

A semantic tension remains between the principle of the nature of things and the retention of terms shaped by common usage, which the text resolves through pragmatic use rather than an exhaustive semantic rule.
The fiction of free decree and the affect of Repentance cohere only if belief in freedom is understood as an efficacious imagined cause; this connection is affirmed here, but not fully re-deduced.
The reconstruction preserves the true movement, because it proceeds from the exclusion of apparent primitives to the triad, from it to denominations, and finally to the general form of passion.

identity.title: Pars tertia - De origine et natura affectuum · passage 5

units.title: Pars quarta - De servitute humana seu de affectuum viribus · passage 1

items.text: Textus quaerit cur homo, etsi meliora cognoscere videatur, affectibus tamen regi atque deteriora sequi cogatur.
Argumentatio vocabula perfectionis, imperfectionis, boni et mali ex ordine naturæ removet et ad comparationes mentis atque usum humanum refert.
Homo constituitur pars finita Naturæ, cuius potentia causis externis infinito ordine superatur et quae se sola concipi non potest.
Affectus non error nudus, sed affirmatio positiva constitutionis corporis est; ideo veritas sola imaginationem eiusque vim non delet.
Vis passionis ex proportione causæ externæ ad potentiam hominis nascitur; hinc affectus actiones reliquas superare et pertinaciter manere potest.
Moderatio affectus non ex nuda cognitione, sed ex conflictu corporali-affectivo oritur, in quo affectus contrarius et fortior priorem excludit.

Gradus affectuum per praesentiam imaginatam, propinquitatem temporalem et modum quo existentia rei affirmatur vel secluditur ordinantur; vera cognitio boni et mali efficax fit tantum quatenus ipsa affectus est.
Deus sive Natura eadem necessitate agit qua existit, nec ullum finem externum in agendo habet.
Causa finalis non est proprietas rerum, sed appetitus humanus ut principium actionis ab hominibus consideratus.
Perfectio et imperfectio sunt modi cogitandi ex comparatione individuorum ad exemplaria universalia orti, non defectus reales Naturæ.
Realitas et perfectio in genere idem significant; mutatio perfectionis intelligitur ut augmentum vel imminutio potentiæ agendi, non ut transitus essentiae in aliam essentiam.
Bonum et malum nihil positivum rebus in se insunt, sed res secundum utilitatem vel impedimentum respectu humani exemplaris ordinant.
Virtus hominis est ipsa eius essentia seu natura quatenus potentiam habet efficiendi ea quae ex solis ipsius legibus intelliguntur.
Nulla res singularis ita potens est ut alia potentior dari non possit, a qua destrui aut superari possit.
Homo patitur quatenus est pars Naturæ cuius effectuum tantum causa partialis est; propterea mutationes externas necessario patitur.
Positivum quod idea falsa continet non tollitur praesentia veri quatenus verum est.
Vis passionis determinatur potentia causæ externæ cum potentia hominis comparata, et hanc potentiam superare potest.
Affectus coerceri aut tolli nequit nisi per affectum contrarium et fortiorem, qui existentiam prioris excludit.
Cognitio boni et mali est affectus lætitiæ vel tristitiæ quatenus eius conscii sumus; ideo cognoscere affectum regere non est nisi cognitio ipsa vim affectivam obtineat.
Natura non agit propter finem, nec res naturales secundum scopum a Natura intentum perfectæ vel imperfectæ sunt.
Imperfectio non est privatio alicuius rei propriae nec peccatum Naturæ, sed nomen ex comparatione mentis ortum.
Bonum et malum non sunt qualitates positivas rerum in se spectatarum.
Diuturnitas existendi non constituit maiorem perfectionem rei singularis.
Homo sui iuris non est quatenus affectibus obnoxius est, nec a mutationibus externis segregari potest.
Verum, quatenus verum, imaginationem positivam nec affectum ex ea ortum per se non annihilat.
Affectus non vincitur contradictione logica, sed sola oppositione affectiva quae simul contraria et fortior est.
Distantia temporalis ultra terminum imaginationis distinctæ non servatur ut differentia affectiva proportionalis.
Exclusionem finalitatis sequitur iudicia de perfectione rerum naturalium indicare praeiudicium comparativum, non statum obiectivum Naturæ.
Vocabulum boni retineri potest, sed tantum ut index medii ad potentiam humanam seu ad exemplar humanæ naturæ augendam ordinati.
Servitus humana non est lapsus contingens, sed conditio necessaria entis finiti quod in ordine causarum externarum partialiter tantum agit.
Correctio erroris potest ignorantiam tollere, manente tamen imaginatione quae praesentem corporis constitutionem exprimit.
Affectus pertinax explicatur non ex defectu voluntatis, sed ex excessu causæ externæ supra potentiam hominis.
Omnis coërcitio affectiva requirit productionem corporis affectionis contrariæ et fortioris, cui respondet idea seu affectus contrarius in mente.
Affectus rei praesentis, rei temporaliter propinquæ, rei necessariæ, aut rei possibilis cuius existentia aliquo modo ponitur, ceteris paribus intenditur.
Cognitio boni et mali affectum regere potest solum si ipsa, ut lætitia vel tristitia conscia, vim maiorem et contrariam obtinet.
Ethica reconstituitur ut analysis immanens variationum potentiæ, non ut iudicium rerum ex fine transcendente aut defectu naturali.
Virtus non opponitur causalitati Naturæ, sed designat gradum quo agere ex propria natura intelligi potest intra ordinem causarum qui hominem semper excedit.
Veritas theoretica non habet imperium automaticum super vitam affectivam, quia verum privationem erroris tollit potius quam positivam corporis affectionem.
Regimen affectuum describitur ut certamen potentiarum, in quo cognitio efficax esse debet causa affectiva et non mera repraesentatio vera.
Tempus et modalitas non sunt hic tantum formae cognitionis, sed condiciones per quas imaginatio distributionem virium affectivarum componit.
Falsum esse debet exemplar Naturæ quasi artificis qui fines concipit, exemplaria praestituit et defectus suos in rebus imperfectis relinquit.
Falsum esse debet exemplar boni et mali ut proprietatum absolutarum quae rebus ante omnem relationem ad potentiam humanam insunt.
Falsum esse debet exemplar mentis cuius cognitio vera corpus et imaginationem sine mediatione causali gubernat.
Falsum esse debet exemplar individui per se sufficientis, cuius essentia omnium mutationum quas patitur causa adæquata est.
Falsum esse debet exemplar passionis ut mera infirmitas voluntatis; passio est effectus determinatus causarum externarum cum potentia hominis comparatarum.
Argumentatio excludit possibilitatem ordinis normativi transcendentis in quo natura ipsa bonum, malum, perfectionem et finem obiective distribuat.
Argumentatio excludit liberationem quae consisteret in absoluta exemptione hominis a causalitate externa et a passionibus.
Argumentatio excludit rationem puram ut potentiam affectibus extrinsecam; ratio operari potest tantum cum in ordine affectuum vim obtinet.
Argumentatio excludit praesentiam temporis ut mensuram neutram, quia praesentia imaginata et propinquitas temporalem vim affectivam constituunt.
Necessitas Naturæ sine fine → causæ finales, perfectiones et defectus naturales ad modos cogitandi comparativos rediguntur.
Comparatio cum exemplari humano → bonum et malum functiones utilitatis et impedimenti fiunt, non entia moralia rerum.
Homo ut pars finita Naturæ → passio ut effectus cuius homo causa tantum partialis est → servitus necessaria.
Imaginatio ut affirmatio constitutionis corporis → veritas ignorantiam corrigit, sed positivam imaginationem non exstinguit.
Causa externa comparata cum potentia hominis + praesentia, propinquitas et affirmatio existentiæ imaginatæ → gradus virium affectivarum.
Affectus superans → affectus contrarius fortior → coërcitio vel sublatio prioris affectus.
Cognitio boni et mali → affectus conscius → efficacia solum si in conflictu affectuum vim contrariam maiorem habet.
Praeiudicium finalitatis et defectus Naturæ dissolvitur in comparationes, exemplaria et appetitus humanos.
→ Bonum, malum, perfectio et virtus reordinantur secundum utilitatem et potentiam agendi.
→ Homo ut pars finita et causaliter partialis ponitur, unde obnoxietas passionibus necessario sequitur.
→ Passionum vis ad causas externas et ad imaginationes corporis refertur, non ad falsitatem simplicem aut ad liberum arbitrium.
→ Praesentia, tempus, necessitas, possibilitas et contingentia distribuunt intensitates affectuum.
→ Cognitio vera subordinatur legi conflictus affectivi: efficax est tantum quatenus affectus fortior et contrarius efficitur.
Defectus Naturæ fit invisibilis ut proprietas rerum et visibilis ut effectus comparationis humanae ad exemplar conceptum.
Bonum et malum reclassificantur ex praedicatis moralibus absolutis in relationes practicas utilitatis, impedimenti, lætitiæ et tristitiæ.
Virtus reclassificatur ex merito morali in potentiam immanentem agendi quae ex natura hominis intelligi potest.
Oppositio veri et falsi desinit esse schema sufficiens ad affectus explicandos; locus causalitatis corporalis et certaminis affectivi aperitur.
Tempus futurum, praeteritum et praesens, una cum necessitate, possibilitate et contingentia, fiunt coordinatae intensitatis affectivae.
Surface — Homo affectibus obnoxius meliora cognoscere potest et tamen deteriora sequi, quia passiones eius actiones superare possunt.
Structural — Passio oritur ubi homo causa partialis est, et vis eius ex proportione potentiae externae ad potentiam hominis determinatur.
Metastrategic — Regimen affectuum mutatur ex praecepto cognitionis rectae in quaestionem de productione affectus contrarii fortioris.
Ontological/Temporal — Natura necessario agit sine fine, dum imaginatio praesentiam, distantiam temporalem et modum existentiae in differentias virium affectivarum convertit.
Series axiomatum sufficit ad restitutionem motus principalis, quia transitus a critica finalitatis ad theoriam servitutis et ad legem conflictus affectivi explicatur.
Nodus firmissimus est connexio inter finitudinem hominis, excessum causarum externarum et necessitatem passionum.
Exemplar naturae humanae ad quod bonum et malum referuntur functionem practicam obtinet, sed eius determinatio materialis in hoc loco non deducitur.
Formula boni ut id quod certo utile scitur criterium certitudinis praesupponit quod hic non constituitur, licet vis cognitionis affectivae stricte limitetur.
Tensio interna manet inter dissolutionem perfectionis obiectivae et retentionem exempli humani normativi; textus eam per distinctionem inter naturam rerum et usum humanum continet.
Lex qua affectus sola vi affectus contrari et fortioris coercetur stabilitur, sed modus quo cognitio vera talem vim obtineat ultra conditionem generalem affectus non explicatur.
Restitutio servat motum textus, quia vocabula moralia non abolentur simpliciter, sed ab ontologia finalistica ad calculus immanentem potentiarum transferuntur.

translations.title: Part Four — On Human Bondage, or the Powers of the Affects · passage 1

items.text: The text asks why a human being, although seeming to know what is better, is nevertheless compelled to be governed by affects and to pursue what is worse.
The argument removes the terms perfection, imperfection, good, and evil from the order of Nature and refers them to comparisons of the mind and to human use.
The human being is constituted as a finite part of Nature, whose power is surpassed in an infinite order by external causes and which cannot be conceived through itself alone.
An affect is not bare error, but a positive affirmation of the constitution of the body; therefore truth alone does not destroy the imagination and its force.
The force of a passion arises from the proportion of the external cause to human power; hence an affect can overcome the remaining actions and persist obstinately.
The restraint of an affect arises not from bare cognition, but from a bodily-affective conflict in which a contrary and stronger affect excludes the prior one.

The degrees of affects are ordered by imagined presence, temporal proximity, and the manner in which the existence of a thing is affirmed or excluded; true knowledge of good and evil becomes effective only insofar as it is itself an affect.
God, or Nature, acts by the same necessity by which it exists, and has no external end in acting.
A final cause is not a property of things, but human appetite considered by human beings as a principle of action.
Perfection and imperfection are modes of thinking arising from the comparison of individuals with universal models, not real defects of Nature.

Reality and perfection signify the same thing in kind; a change of perfection is understood as an increase or diminution of the power of acting, not as the transition of an essence into another essence.
Good and evil contain nothing positive in things themselves, but order things according to utility or hindrance in relation to the human model.
Human virtue is its very essence or nature insofar as it has the power to effect those things which are understood from its laws alone.
No singular thing is so powerful that another more powerful thing cannot be given by which it may be destroyed or overcome.
A human being suffers insofar as it is a part of Nature of whose effects it is only a partial cause; therefore it necessarily undergoes external changes.
The positive content contained by a false idea is not removed by the presence of the true insofar as it is true.
The force of a passion is determined by the power of the external cause compared with human power, and it can surpass this power.
An affect cannot be restrained or removed except by a contrary and stronger affect which excludes the existence of the prior one.
Knowledge of good and evil is an affect of joy or sadness insofar as we are conscious of it; therefore knowing is not governing an affect unless knowledge itself possesses affective force.
Nature does not act for the sake of an end, nor are natural things perfect or imperfect according to an aim intended by Nature.
Imperfection is not the privation of any proper thing nor a sin of Nature, but a name arising from a comparison of the mind.
Good and evil are not positive qualities of things considered in themselves.
Duration of existence does not constitute a greater perfection of a singular thing.
A human being is not its own master insofar as it is subject to affects, nor can it be separated from external changes.
The true, insofar as it is true, does not by itself annihilate positive imagination or the affect arising from it.
An affect is not conquered by logical contradiction, but only by an affective opposition which is at once contrary and stronger.
Temporal distance beyond the limit of distinct imagination is not retained as a proportional affective difference.
From the exclusion of finality it follows that judgments concerning the perfection of natural things indicate a comparative prejudice, not an objective state of Nature.
The term good may be retained, but only as an index of a means ordered toward increasing human power or the model of human nature.
Human bondage is not a contingent fall, but the necessary condition of a finite being which acts only partially within the order of external causes.
The correction of error can remove ignorance, while the imagination that expresses the present constitution of the body nevertheless remains.
A persistent affect is explained not by a defect of the will, but by the excess of the external cause over human power.
Every affective restraint requires the production of a contrary and stronger affection of the body, to which a contrary idea or affect in the mind corresponds.
An affect toward a present thing, a temporally proximate thing, a necessary thing, or a possible thing whose existence is in some manner posited, is intensified, other things being equal.
Knowledge of good and evil can govern an affect only if it itself, as conscious joy or sadness, attains a greater and contrary force.
Ethics is reconstituted as an immanent analysis of variations in power, not as a judgment of things by a transcendent end or natural defect.
Virtue is not opposed to the causality of Nature, but designates the degree to which acting from one's own nature can be understood within an order of causes that always exceeds the human being.
Theoretical truth has no automatic dominion over affective life, because the true removes the privation of error rather than the positive affection of the body.
The governance of affects is described as a contest of powers, in which knowledge must be an affective cause and not a mere true representation in order to be effective.
Time and modality are here not merely forms of cognition, but conditions through which imagination composes the distribution of affective forces.
The model of Nature as an artificer who conceives ends, pre-establishes models, and leaves its defects in imperfect things must be false.
The model of good and evil as absolute properties inherent in things prior to every relation to human power must be false.
The model of a mind whose true knowledge governs the body and imagination without causal mediation must be false.
