The model of a self-sufficient individual whose essence is the adequate cause of all the changes it undergoes must be false.
The model of passion as mere weakness of will must be false; passion is a determined effect of external causes compared with human power.
The argument excludes the possibility of a transcendent normative order in which nature itself objectively distributes good, evil, perfection, and end.
The argument excludes liberation consisting in the absolute exemption of the human being from external causality and passions.
The argument excludes pure reason as a power extrinsic to affects; reason can operate only when it obtains force within the order of affects.
The argument excludes the presence of time as a neutral measure, because imagined presence and temporal proximity constitute affective force.
Necessity of Nature without end → final causes, perfections, and natural defects are reduced to comparative modes of thinking.
Comparison with the human model → good and evil become functions of utility and hindrance, not moral entities of things.
Human being as a finite part of Nature → passion as an effect of which the human being is only a partial cause → necessary bondage.
Imagination as affirmation of the constitution of the body → truth corrects ignorance, but does not extinguish positive imagination.
External cause compared with human power + presence, proximity, and affirmation of imagined existence → degrees of affective forces.
Overcoming affect → contrary stronger affect → restraint or removal of the prior affect.
Knowledge of good and evil → conscious affect → effectiveness only if, in the conflict of affects, it has a greater contrary force.
The prejudice of finality and of defect in Nature is dissolved into comparisons, models, and human appetites.
→ Good, evil, perfection, and virtue are reordered according to utility and the power of acting.
→ The human being is posited as finite and causally partial, whence subjection to passions necessarily follows.
→ The force of passions is referred to external causes and to imaginations of the body, not to simple falsity or free will.
→ Presence, time, necessity, possibility, and contingency distribute the intensities of affects.
→ True knowledge is subordinated to the law of affective conflict: it is effective only insofar as it becomes a stronger and contrary affect.
Defect in Nature becomes invisible as a property of things and visible as an effect of human comparison with a conceived model.
Good and evil are reclassified from absolute moral predicates into practical relations of utility, hindrance, joy, and sadness.
Virtue is reclassified from moral merit into an immanent power of acting that can be understood from human nature.
The opposition of true and false ceases to be a sufficient schema for explaining affects; the domain of bodily causality and affective contest is opened.
Future, past, and present time, together with necessity, possibility, and contingency, become coordinates of affective intensity.
Surface — A human being subject to affects can know what is better and nevertheless pursue what is worse, because passions can overcome its actions.
Structural — Passion arises where the human being is a partial cause, and its force is determined by the proportion of external power to human power.
Metastrategic — The governance of affects changes from a precept of correct knowledge into a question of producing a stronger contrary affect.
Ontological/Temporal — Nature acts necessarily without end, while imagination converts presence, temporal distance, and the mode of existence into differences of affective forces.
The series of axioms suffices for restoring the principal movement, because the transition from the critique of finality to the theory of bondage and to the law of affective conflict is explained.
The strongest node is the connection between human finitude, the excess of external causes, and the necessity of passions.
The model of human nature to which good and evil are referred obtains a practical function, but its material determination is not deduced here.
The formula of good as that which is certainly known to be useful presupposes a criterion of certainty that is not established here, although the affective force of knowledge is strictly limited.

An internal tension remains between the dissolution of objective perfection and the retention of a normative human model; the text contains it through the distinction between the nature of things and human use.

The law by which an affect is restrained solely by the force of a contrary and stronger affect is established, but the manner in which true knowledge might obtain such force is not explained beyond the general condition of affect.
The reconstruction preserves the movement of the text, because moral terms are not simply abolished, but transferred from finalistic ontology to an immanent calculus of powers.

identity.title: Pars quarta - De servitute humana seu de affectuum viribus · passage 1

units.title: Pars quarta - De servitute humana seu de affectuum viribus · passage 2

items.text: Textus quaerit cur vera boni et mali cognitio, etiamsi cupiditatem activam generet, hominem a passionibus non necessario liberet.
Demonstratur cupiditatem ex cognitione ortam potentia humana tantum definiri, dum cupiditates passivae a causis externis potentioribus definiri possunt.
Praesentia et contingentia futurae rei inaequalem affectuum vim efficiunt, ita ut cognitio futuri facilius a cupiditatibus praesentibus vincatur.
Diagnosis impotentiae ad reconstructionem transit: conatus sese conservandi constituit virtutem, felicitatem et fundamentum utilitatis rationalis.
Ratio in intelligendo consistit; bonum certum ad intellectionem conducit, et summum Mentis bonum est Dei cognitio.
Conveniens natura utilitatem et compositionem potentiae producit; passiones homines dissociant, Ratio autem eos necessario in concordiam reducit.
Cupiditas sive appetitus est ipsa hominis essentia, id est conatus quo homo in suo esse perseverat.
Virtus est humana potentia ex solis legibus propriae naturae agendi, cuius primum et unicum fundamentum est conatus sese conservandi.
Cognitio boni et mali est affectus Laetitiae vel Tristitiae, quatenus homo eius est conscius.
Unusquisque ex legibus propriae naturae necessario appetit quod bonum, et aversatur quod malum esse iudicat.
Laetitia conatum et cupiditatem auget, Tristitia vero eadem minuit vel coercet.
Cupiditates ex passionibus ortae vi causarum externarum definiuntur, quae potentiam humanam indefinite superare possunt.
Cupiditas ex vera boni et mali cognitione orta, quatenus ex intellectione procedit, ad agendi potentiam propriae essentiae pertinet.
Affectus rei praesentis vehementior est affectu rei futurae imaginatae, et cognitio boni vel mali contingentis adhuc infirmius movet.
Homo ex ideis inadaequatis determinatus patitur; ex eo quod intelligit determinatus agit atque ex virtute procedit.
Ratio est Mens quatenus clare et distincte intelligit, nec utile certum iudicat nisi quod ad intelligendum conducit.
Nemo ex necessitate propriae naturae suum esse negare potest nec suum esse alterius rei causa conservare conatur.
Homo sine rebus externis suum esse conservare nequit, et individua eiusdem naturae coniuncta maiorem potentiam compositam efficiunt.
Res cuius natura a natura humana prorsus diversa est humanam agendi potentiam neque iuvare neque coercere potest.
Id quod cum natura humana convenit necessario bonum est; malum est tantum quod agendi potentiam contrarie minuit vel coercet.
Natura convenire est positive in potentia convenire, non solam finitatem, impotentiam vel negationem communicare.
Passiones a causis externis definitae homines diversificant, inconstantes faciunt et invicem opponere possunt.
Homines, quatenus ex ductu Rationis vivunt, ex natura humana ut causa proxima agunt atque necessario inter se conveniunt.
Deus est Ens absolute infinitum, sine quo nihil esse neque concipi potest, ideoque summum obiectum Mentis intellegentis.
Vera boni et mali cognitio non est vis quae passiones per se vincit.
Cupiditas ex cognitione futuri vel contingentis orta non aequat vim cupiditatis rerum suavium praesentium.
Cognitio humanae impotentiae non probat ignorantiam cognitione praestantiorem neque stultum sapienti in moderandis affectibus parem esse.
Ratio nihil contra Naturam postulat, et virtus non in negatione propriae naturae consistit.
Bonum et malum res cui natura nostra prorsus externa est attribui non possunt.
Communis finitas, imminutio vel passivitas non constituit veram naturarum convenientiam.
Neglectus conservationis sui et imminutio vitae non sunt actus qui ex sola hominis natura necessario sequuntur.
Idem obiectum amatum non est per se causa mutui damni; conflictus ex discrepantia affectuum et imaginationum oritur.
Homines non simpliciter quatenus homines, sed tantum quatenus Ratione ducuntur, necessario conveniunt.
Cupiditas ex vera boni et mali cognitione orta a cupiditatibus passionum extingui vel coerceri potest, quia hae potentia causarum externarum augeri possunt.
Cupiditas ex cognitione futuri orta facilius coercetur quam cupiditas ex cognitione rei praesentis, et cognitio contingentis adhuc facilius succumbit.
Hinc explicatur cur homines opinionibus et libidinibus magis quam vera Ratione saepe moveantur.
Cupiditas ex Laetitia orta, ceteris paribus, cupiditate ex Tristitia orta fortior est.
Ratio praecipit ut unusquisque se amet, verum utile quaerat, maiorem perfectionem appetat et suum esse, quantum potest, conservet.
Beate vivere, bene agere et bene vivere non possunt ab actu esse, agere et vivere separari.
Ex virtute agere nihil aliud est quam ex ductu Rationis agere, vivere et suum esse conservare.
Nihil certo bonum esse scitur nisi quod ad intellegendum revera conducit, nec malum nisi quod intellectionem impedit.
Dei cognitio est summum Mentis bonum et Dei cognitio summa Mentis virtus.
Quo res magis cum natura humana convenit, eo utilior et melior est; quo magis est contraria, eo magis mala est.
Passiones humanae diversitatem et oppositionem explicant, dum Ratio concordiam naturarum humanarum necessario explicat.
Homo ex ductu Rationis vivens est homini res singularis utilissima; utilitas propria rationalis in commune utile extenditur.
Servitus humana non est mera erroris conditio, sed asymmetria causalis inter potentiam finitam agentis et potentiam causarum externarum.
Bonum et malum duplicem ordinem habent: affective indicant augmentum vel diminutionem potentiae, rationaliter vero certo definiuntur per relationem ad intellectionem.
Utilitas propria et commune utile non sunt termini contrarii, quia conservatio individui rationalis per convenientiam naturarum et compositionem potentiarum augetur.
Ordinatio socialis rationalis concipitur ut compositio individuorum in quasi unum Corpus et unam Mentem, non ut imminutio conatus singularis.
Humanitas bifariam ordinatur: quatenus patitur, variat et opponitur; quatenus intelligit, convenit et mutuam utilitatem producit.
Ordo ethicus ascendit a conservatione sui per virtutem et intellectionem ad Dei cognitionem ut supremum obiectum Mentis.
Falsum esse debet cognitionem veram esse facultatem motivationalem a potentia affectuum et causis externis separatam.
Falsum esse debet ethicam fundari in mandato naturae humanae externo, in sacrificio sui, vel in recusatione amoris sui.
Falsum esse debet individuum humanum posse per se solum sufficienter subsistere aut sufficienter intelligere.
Falsum esse debet solidarietatem humanam ex communi defectu, finitate vel passivitate positive constitui.
Falsum esse debet communionem obiecti amati ipsam esse fontem oppositionis; discrepantia affectiva, non convenientia, conflictum producit.
Falsum esse debet voluntariam sui annihilationem ex sola natura hominis procedere.
Falsum esse debet bonum et malum esse proprietates rerum absolute a relatione ad humanam potentiam et intellectionem separatae.
Argumentatio libertatem absolutam, quae a nexu causarum externarum prorsus exempta sit, non admittit.
Argumentatio beatitudinem quae ab actu existere, agere et perseverare separari possit indisponibilem facit.
Argumentatio concordiam collectivam ex sola communi humanitate, sine Ratione et convenientia positiva, non permittit.
Argumentatio finem rationalem extra intellectionem et Dei cognitionem ultimum statuere non potest.
Potentia causarum externarum → passiones → cupiditates externis causis definitae → coercitio cupiditatis ex vera cognitione ortae → servitus humana.
Futurum vel contingens → affectus remissior → cupiditas cognitivi boni infirmior → maior vulnerabilitas ad suavitatem praesentem.
Conatus sese conservandi → virtus → actio ex intellectu → Ratio ut intelligere → utile certum → Dei cognitio.
Indigentia rerum externarum + convenientia naturarum → compositio potentiarum → maius esse conservandum → commune utile.
Passio → discrepantia imaginativa et affectiva → inconstantia vel conflictus; Ratio → actio ex natura humana communi → necessaria convenientia.
Vera cognitio boni et mali → cupiditas activa finita → collisio cum cupiditatibus passionum.
Praesentia rerum suavium et imminutio futuri contingentis → superior vis cupiditatum praesentium → diagnosis impotentiae.
Diagnosis impotentiae → recusatio ignorantiae → determinatio limitum Rationis in moderandis affectibus.
Conatus → virtus et felicitas → quaesitio veri utilitatis.
Ratio → intellegere → bonum certum → Dei cognitio ut summum bonum.
Communitas naturae → utilitas et compositio; contrarietas naturae → malum et imminutio potentiae.
Passiones → dissensio humana; Ratio → concordia, fides, iustitia et commune utile.
Bonum et malum a praedicatis moralibus abstractis in indices augmenti, diminutionis et ordinationis potentiae humanae transferuntur.
Virtus a sacrificio vel obedientia externa ad conatum rationalem sese conservandi reclassificatur.
Distinctio inter cognitionem veram et efficaciam affectivam visibilis fit: veritas non ex se dominationem causalem importat.
Convenientia naturarum ut relatio positiva potentiae, non ut communis defectus aut mera identitas negativa, definitur.
Alter homo ex possibili competitore in summam rem singularem utilem mutatur, sed tantum quatenus Ratione vivit.
Tempus affectivum distinguitur: praesens vim immediatam habet, futurum et contingens vim imminutam.
Surface — Textus explicat cur homines cognitionem melioris sequi non valeant, et quae dictamina Ratio de utilitate, virtute et conservatione praecipiat.
Structural — Affectus ordinantur per comparationem potentiae humanae cum causis externis, per praesentiam temporalem, et per convenientiam vel contrarietatem naturarum.
Metastrategic — Moderatio affectuum non per moralem increpationem, sed per cognitionem limitum causalium, ordinationem intellectionis et compositionem utilitatum reformulatur.
Ontological/Temporal — Essentia est conatus actualis perseverandi; Deus est terminus supremus intellectionis; futurum contingens minus efficaciter movet quam praesens imaginatum.
Axiomata sufficiunt ad restituendam seriem principalem: causae externae passionum, impotentia cupiditatis cognitivae, conatus ut virtutis fundamentum, Ratio ut intellectus, et concordia rationalis.
Firmissimum systematis nexus est inter conatum, virtutem, actionem ex intellectu et utilitatem quae ad intellegendum conducit.
Vis diagnosis pendet a distinctione inter cupiditatem ex cognitione ortam et cupiditates quas causae externae indefinitae augent.
Efficacia positiva Rationis ad affectus vincendos hic non demonstratur, sed ad tractationem separatam de potentia Rationis differtur.
Transitus ab utilitate singulari ad commune utile compositionem naturarum affirmat, sed mechanismum quo homines passionales ad talem compositionem perveniant non explicat.
Duplex definitio boni et mali, affectiva et rationaliter certa, ordines distinguit sed mediationem plenam inter eos non exhaurit.
Concordia humana non universaliter asseritur, sed conditionaliter sub ratione vivendi; hac condicione servata, motus argumentationis interne cohaeret.

translations.title: Part Four - On Human Bondage, or the Powers of the Affects · passage 2

items.text: The text asks why true knowledge of good and evil, even if it generates an active desire, does not necessarily free a human being from the passions.
It is demonstrated that desire arising from knowledge is defined only by human power, whereas passive desires can be defined by more powerful external causes.
The presence and contingency of a future thing produce unequal force in the affects, so that knowledge of the future is more easily overcome by present desires.
The diagnosis of impotence passes into reconstruction: the striving to preserve oneself constitutes virtue, happiness, and the foundation of rational utility.
Reason consists in understanding; certain good conduces to understanding, and the highest good of the Mind is the knowledge of God.
Agreement in nature produces utility and the composition of power; passions dissociate human beings, whereas Reason necessarily brings them back into concord.
Desire, or appetite, is the very essence of a human being, that is, the striving by which a human being perseveres in his being.
Virtue is the human power of acting from the laws of one's own nature alone, whose first and sole foundation is the striving to preserve oneself.
Knowledge of good and evil is an affect of Joy or Sadness, insofar as a human being is conscious of it.
Everyone necessarily, from the laws of his own nature, desires what he judges to be good and is averse to what he judges to be evil.
Joy increases striving and desire, whereas Sadness diminishes or restrains them.
Desires arising from passions are defined by the force of external causes, which can indefinitely surpass human power.
Desire arising from true knowledge of good and evil, insofar as it proceeds from understanding, pertains to the power of acting of one's own essence.
An affect of a present thing is more vehement than an affect of an imagined future thing, and knowledge of a contingent good or evil moves still more weakly.
A human being determined by inadequate ideas is passive; determined by what he understands, he acts and proceeds from virtue.
Reason is the Mind insofar as it understands clearly and distinctly, and judges nothing certainly useful except what conduces to understanding.
No one can, from the necessity of his own nature, deny his own being, nor does anyone strive to preserve his own being for the sake of another thing.
A human being cannot preserve his being without external things, and individuals of the same nature, joined together, produce a greater composite power.
A thing whose nature is wholly different from human nature can neither aid nor restrain the human power of acting.
What agrees with human nature is necessarily good; evil is only what contrarily diminishes or restrains the power of acting.
To agree in nature is to agree positively in power, not merely to share finitude, impotence, or negation.
Passions defined by external causes differentiate human beings, make them inconstant, and can set them against one another.
Human beings, insofar as they live under the guidance of Reason, act from human nature as proximate cause and necessarily agree with one another.
God is an absolutely infinite Being, without whom nothing can be or be conceived, and is therefore the highest object of the understanding Mind.
True knowledge of good and evil is not a force that overcomes the passions by itself.
Desire arising from knowledge of the future or the contingent does not equal the force of desire for pleasant present things.
Knowledge of human impotence does not prove ignorance superior to knowledge, nor that the fool equals the wise person in moderating the affects.
Reason demands nothing contrary to Nature, and virtue does not consist in the negation of one's own nature.
Good and evil cannot be attributed to a thing whose nature is wholly external to our nature.
Common finitude, diminution, or passivity does not constitute a true agreement of natures.
Neglect of self-preservation and diminution of life are not acts that necessarily follow from human nature alone.
The same beloved object is not in itself a cause of mutual harm; conflict arises from the discrepancy of affects and imaginings.
Human beings do not necessarily agree simply insofar as they are human beings, but only insofar as they are guided by Reason.
Desire arising from true knowledge of good and evil can be extinguished or restrained by desires of the passions, because these can be increased by the power of external causes.
Desire arising from knowledge of the future is more easily restrained than desire arising from knowledge of a present thing, and knowledge of the contingent succumbs still more easily.
Hence it is explained why human beings are often moved more by opinions and lusts than by true Reason.
Desire arising from Joy is, other things being equal, stronger than desire arising from Sadness.
Reason commands that everyone love himself, seek what is truly useful, desire greater perfection, and preserve his being, insofar as he can.
To live blessedly, to act well, and to live well cannot be separated from the act of being, acting, and living.
To act from virtue is nothing other than to act, live, and preserve one's being under the guidance of Reason.
Nothing is known certainly to be good except what truly conduces to understanding, nor evil except what impedes understanding.
Knowledge of God is the highest good of the Mind, and knowledge of God is the highest virtue of the Mind.
The more a thing agrees with human nature, the more useful and better it is; the more contrary it is, the more evil it is.
Human passions explain diversity and opposition, whereas Reason necessarily explains the concord of human natures.
A human being living under the guidance of Reason is the most useful singular thing for a human being; rational self-interest extends into common utility.
Human bondage is not a mere condition of error, but a causal asymmetry between the finite power of the agent and the power of external causes.
Good and evil have a twofold order: affectively they indicate an increase or diminution of power, but rationally they are certainly defined through their relation to understanding.
Self-interest and common utility are not contrary terms, because the preservation of the rational individual is increased through the agreement of natures and the composition of powers.
Rational social ordering is conceived as the composition of individuals into, as it were, one Body and one Mind, not as a diminution of singular striving.
Humanity is ordered in two ways: insofar as it is passive, it varies and is opposed; insofar as it understands, it agrees and produces mutual utility.
The ethical order ascends from self-preservation through virtue and understanding to knowledge of God as the supreme object of the Mind.
It must be false that true knowledge is a motivational faculty separate from the power of the affects and from external causes.
It must be false that ethics is founded upon a command external to human nature, upon self-sacrifice, or upon the refusal of self-love.
It must be false that the human individual can by itself alone subsist sufficiently or understand sufficiently.
It must be false that human solidarity is positively constituted from common defect, finitude, or passivity.
It must be false that sharing a beloved object is itself the source of opposition; affective discrepancy, not agreement, produces conflict.
It must be false that voluntary self-annihilation proceeds from human nature alone.
It must be false that good and evil are properties of things absolutely separate from their relation to human power and understanding.
The argument does not admit absolute freedom wholly exempt from the nexus of external causes.
The argument renders unavailable a blessedness that could be separated from the act of existing, acting, and persevering.
The argument does not permit collective concord from common humanity alone, without Reason and positive agreement.
The argument cannot establish an ultimate rational end outside understanding and knowledge of God.
Power of external causes → passions → desires defined by external causes → restraint of desire arising from true knowledge → human bondage.
Future or contingent → weaker affect → weaker desire for cognitive good → greater vulnerability to present pleasantness.
Striving to preserve oneself → virtue → action from understanding → Reason as understanding → certain utility → knowledge of God.
Need of external things + agreement of natures → composition of powers → greater being to be preserved → common utility.
Passion → imaginative and affective discrepancy → inconstancy or conflict; Reason → action from common human nature → necessary agreement.
True knowledge of good and evil → finite active desire → collision with desires of the passions.
Presence of pleasant things and diminution of the contingent future → superior force of present desires → diagnosis of impotence.
Diagnosis of impotence → rejection of ignorance → determination of the limits of Reason in moderating the affects.
Striving → virtue and happiness → pursuit of true utility.
Reason → understanding → certain good → knowledge of God as the highest good.
Community of nature → utility and composition; contrariety of nature → evil and diminution of power.
Passions → human dissension; Reason → concord, faith, justice, and common utility.
Good and evil are shifted from abstract moral predicates into indices of increase, diminution, and ordering of human power.
Virtue is reclassified from sacrifice or external obedience into rational striving to preserve oneself.
The distinction between true knowledge and affective efficacy becomes visible: truth does not of itself entail causal dominion.
Agreement of natures is defined as a positive relation of power, not as common defect or mere negative identity.
Another human being is transformed from a possible competitor into the most useful singular thing, but only insofar as he lives by Reason.
Affective time is distinguished: the present has immediate force, the future and contingent have diminished force.
Surface — The text explains why human beings cannot follow knowledge of the better, and what precepts Reason enjoins concerning utility, virtue, and preservation.
Structural — The affects are ordered through the comparison of human power with external causes, through temporal presence, and through the agreement or contrariety of natures.
Metastrategic — The moderation of the affects is reformulated not through moral reproach, but through knowledge of causal limits, the ordering of understanding, and the composition of utilities.
Ontological/Temporal — Essence is the actual striving to persevere; God is the supreme terminus of understanding; the contingent future moves less effectively than the imagined present.

The axioms suffice to restore the principal sequence: external causes of passions, the impotence of cognitive desire, striving as the foundation of virtue, Reason as understanding, and rational concord.
The strongest nexus of the system is that between striving, virtue, action from understanding, and utility that conduces to understanding.
The force of the diagnosis depends on the distinction between desire arising from knowledge and desires increased by indefinite external causes.
The positive efficacy of Reason in overcoming the affects is not demonstrated here, but deferred to a separate treatment of the power of Reason.
The transition from singular utility to common utility affirms the composition of natures, but does not explain the mechanism by which passionate human beings may arrive at such a composition.
The twofold definition of good and evil, affective and rationally certain, distinguishes orders but does not exhaust the full mediation between them.
Human concord is not asserted universally, but conditionally under the manner of living according to Reason; with this condition preserved, the movement of the argument is internally coherent.

identity.title: Pars quarta - De servitute humana seu de affectuum viribus · passage 2

units.title: Pars quarta - De servitute humana seu de affectuum viribus · passage 3

items.text: Textus quaerit quomodo conatus unuscujusque suum utile quaerendi, qui speciem egoismi conflictuosi habere potest, in utilitatem mutuam et societatem humanam convertatur.
Solutio prima ponit homines, quatenus Ratione ducuntur, natura convenire; inde virtus, utilitas propria, utilitas mutua et bonum commune eadem catena ordinantur.
Textus deinde ostendit hanc convenientiam rationalem non esse condicionem empirice dominantem, quia affectus homines externos, inconstantes et sibi contrarios efficiunt.
Ex hac discrepantia inter normam Rationis et condicionem affectivam Civitas generatur ut apparatus securitatis, cessionis juris, legis communis et coactionis per minas.
Post institutionem civilem, bonum et malum ad potentiam corporis et mentis referuntur, atque affectus per effectum suum in capacitatem agendi, concordiam et stabilitatem dijudicantur.

Argumentatio demonstrativo-reconstructiva procedit a convenientia rationali ad necessitatem civilem, et a constitutione corporis ad strategiam affectuum per amorem, generositatem et liberationem a metu.
Virtus est potentia agendi ex ductu Rationis, et suum utile rationaliter quaerere est se conservare secundum leges propriae naturae.
Homines, quatenus ex ductu Rationis vivunt, natura conveniunt; ideo utilitas rationaliter quaesita utilitatem mutuam auget.
Summum bonum virtutem sectantium est cognitio Dei, omnibus hominibus communis et ab omnibus aeque possidenda.
Cupiditas qua vir rationalis summum bonum sibi appetit idem bonum reliquis cupit, atque haec cupiditas cum cognitione Dei crescit.
Homines plerumque affectibus externis fortioribus patiuntur, et affectus non nisi affectu fortiore atque contrario coercetur; Ratio sola affectus coërcere non potest.
Jus naturale uniuscujusque ipsius potentia definitur, ita ut in statu naturali singulus ex suo ingenio bonum, malum, utile, vindictam et conservationem decernat.
Concordia civilis requirit mutuam cessionem juris naturalis et potestatem communem leges ferentem easque minis firmantem.
Peccatum, meritum, justum, injustum et dominium ex consensu atque jure Civitatis oriuntur, non ex attributis intrinsecis Mentis vel Naturae.
Utile est quod Corpus aptius reddit ad pluribus modis afficiendum, alia corpora afficiendum et Mentem ad plura percipiendum.
Forma Corporis in certa ratione motus et quietis consistit; eius conservatio capacitatem corporis servat, eius mutatio destructionem inducit.
Bonitas affectuum per augmentum vel diminutionem potentiae totius Corporis, et per proportionem qua partes Corporis afficiuntur, dijudicatur.
Odium erga homines destructionem appetit atque malum est; Amor sive Generositas Odium extinguere et in contrarium affectum convertere potest.
Spes et Metus Tristitiam ac cognitionis defectum involvunt, atque per se boni esse non possunt.
Existimatio et Despectus Rationi repugnant, et Existimatio facile Superbiam generat.
Reciprocitas ethica ex convenientia naturae humanae procedit; bruta, natura et affectibus a hominibus diversa, in eandem communitatem amicitiae non includuntur.
Utilitas propria rationalis non est egoismus competitivus, quia Rationis ductus homines natura conciliat.
Summum bonum non est res rara, exclusoria aut unius tantum possessoris capax.
Pietas et Honestitas non sunt conatus affectivus ut reliqui ex proprio ingenio vivent, sed communicatio boni communis per amicitiam.
Vita socialis empirica non praesupponitur iam rationalis, cum homines plerumque Invidia, contrarietate et affectuum imperio teneantur.
Lex civilis non fundatur in sola persuasione rationali, quia Ratio per se affectus coërcere nequit.
In statu naturali non dantur peccatum, meritum, justum, injustum neque proprietas ex consensu definita.
Bonum non coincidit cum qualibet Laetitia, nec malum cum quolibet Dolore, quia affectus localis potest potentiam totius Corporis minuere, et Dolor excessum coercere.
Mors Corporis non restringitur ad cadaver aut ad cessationem sanguinis circulationis, sed intelligitur per mutationem rationis motus et quietis.
Risus et jocus non sunt Irrisio, quia illi Laetitiam meram significare possunt, haec autem ad Odium pertinet.
Odium non habet usum moralem proprium, quamvis vindicta vel imminutio alterius interdum utilia apparere possint.
Spes, Metus, Securitas, Desperatio et Conscientiae morsus non sunt formae stabilis virtutis.
Sentire non sufficit ut bruta participes sint societatis humanae vel amicitiae rationalis.
Quanto magis unusquisque suum utile ex Ratione quaerit, tanto magis reliquis hominibus utilis efficitur.
Virtus non producit conflictum de summo bono, quia bonum quod quaeritur omnibus communicabile manet.
Incrementum cognitionis Dei incrementum cupiditatis producere debet qua reliqui eodem bono fruantur.
Conatus rationalis ad alios ducendos humaniter agere debet, quia impositio affectiva proprii ingenii contrarium impetum et odium suscitat.
Civitas stabilis non simpliciter consensu theoretico, sed per securitatem mutuam et metus majoris damni efficitur.
Poena peccatum et praemium meritum non detegunt ut res naturales, sed oboedientiam vel inoboedientiam erga ordinem civilem instituunt.
Institutum vitae moderatae, quod varietatem alimentorum, recreationum et delectationum admittit, bonum est quatenus integritatem Corporis et multiplicitatem Mentis conservat.
Concordia hominum est utilis quia conditiones vitae ex Ratione conformis producit; discordia mala est quia hanc conditionem destruit.
Generositas est strategia affectiva rationalis, qua Odium non reciproco Odio augetur sed Amore coercetur.
Vita ex Ratione tendit ad minuendam dependentiam a Spe, Metu et Fortuna, atque ad dirigendas actiones certo Rationis consilio.
Relatio ad bruta non regitur eadem reciprocitate morali quae inter homines viget, sed potentia, utilitate et diversitate naturae.
Societas duplex fundamentum habet: normam internam convenientiae rationalis et mechanismum externum coercitionis affectivae.
Systema tres ordines normativos distinguit: utile naturale ut potentiae augmentum, bonum rationale ut cognitio communis, et justum civile ut decretum publicum.
Ethica non ascetica fit, quia conservatio et multiplicatio corporis sunt conditio multiplicationis perceptionum Mentis.
Self-preservatio, quamvis ab individuo incipiat, solitariam vitam excludit, quia potentia humana per societatem, auxilium et concordiam augetur.
Ratio affectus non simpliciter eliminat, sed contrarios affectus ordinat, praecipue Amorem et Generositatem, ut vires destructivas superet.
Identitas corporis non in sola apparentia vitae, memoria vel circulatione sanguinis, sed in perseverantia relationis structurae corporalis ponitur.
Argumentatio tacite requirit bonum rationalem non esse structuram rivalitatis; aliter utilitas propria et utilitas mutua non coinciderent.
Argumentatio negat Intellectum nudum sufficientem esse ad regimen vitae affectivae; actio rationalis vim affectivam contrariam assumere debet.
Argumentatio excludit ordinem juridicum aut moralem naturaliter datum ante Civitatem, quia culpa, meritum, dominium et justitia institutionem publicam postulant.
Argumentatio excludit aestimationem affectuum per sola nomina positiva vel negativa, quia Laetitia localis nocere et Dolor limitate prodesse potest.
Argumentatio excludit universalem communionem omnium viventium sentientium, quia convenientia naturae humanae, non sola sensibilitas, fundamentum relationis ethicae constituit.
Argumentatio excludit identitatem corporis absolute permanentem, quia mutatio relationis constitutivae corpus in naturam aliam transferre potest.
Nulla justitia naturalis transcendentis ordinis admittitur inter jus ut potentiam et jus ut decretum Civitatis.
Nulla Civitas stabilis ex sola illuminatione rationali supponitur, quia affectuum potentia institutionem coactivam necessario interponit.
Nulla universalitas ethica indifferens ad differentias naturae ponitur, quia communitas boni et amicitiae ad convenientiam humanam limitatur.
Nulla definitio mortis per solum signum biologicum admittitur, quia destructio dicitur mutatio formae relationis corporalis.

Conatus propriae utilitatis → Virtus sive potentia rationalis → Convenientia naturae humanae → Utilitas reciproca → Cognitio Dei communis → Cupiditas ut omnes eodem bono fruantur → Pietas et Honestitas.
Heteronomia affectuum → Contrarietas inter homines mutuo indigentes → Necessitas securitatis → Cessio juris naturalis → Potestas communis → Leges minis firmatae → Civitas, Cives et normae juridicae.

Ratio motus et quietis → Integritas formae corporalis → Multiplex aptitudo ad afficiendum et afficiendum → Amplior perceptio Mentis → Discrimen affectuum bonorum et malorum → Moderatio, Laetitia integra, Amor et Generositas.
Convenientia naturae humanae → Amicitia et reciprocitas → Communitas rationalis; diversitas naturae brutorum → Relatio instrumentaliter utilitatis, non societas ethica.
Utilitas propria rationalis → Virtus → Convenientia humana → Bonum commune non-rivale → Communicatio cognitionis Dei → Amicitia et Generositas.
Imperium affectuum → Insecuritas et conflictus → Cessio juris → Coercitio communis → Civitas → Peccatum, meritum, justum et injustum ut effectus juridici.
Conservatio formae corporis → Augmentum capacitatis → Laetitia ordinata → Reiectio Odii et affectuum impotentiae → Amor, moderatio et actio ex consilio Rationis.
Oppositio inter utilitatem propriam et utilitatem communem dissolvitur pro hominibus quatenus Ratione ducuntur.
Summum bonum reclassificatur ut bonum communicabile, non ut obiectum possessionis exclusoriae.
Distinctio constituitur inter ductum rationalem aliorum et imperium affectivum quo quis reliquos ad proprium ingenium cogere conatur.
Civitas describitur non ut simplex expressio moralis consensus, sed ut machina securitatis quae categorias juridicas efficit.
Affectus ordinantur non secundum nomen, sed secundum effectum in potentiam integratam Corporis, aptitudinem Mentis et concordiam socialem.
Vita bona reclassificatur ut moderata multiplicatio corporalis et mentalis capacitatis, non ut fuga delectationis vel cultus Tristitiae.
Limes societatis ethicae inter homines et bruta collocatur in convenientia naturae et reciprocitate, non in sola facultate sentiendi.
Surface — Textus bonum et malum, Laetitiam et Tristitiam, Odium et Amorem, Spem et Metum, justum et injustum formaliter distinguit.
Structural — Corpus per rationem motus et quietis, affectus per potentiam, et Civitas per securitatem atque minas describuntur.
Metastrategic — Ratio non solum veritatem cognoscit, sed affectuum regimen per Generositatem, institutionem civilem et ordinatam vitae moderationem constituit.
Ontological/Temporal — Jus cum potentia, identitas corporis cum relatione structurae, et normae civiles cum institutione temporali Civitatis conectuntur.
Axiomata sufficiunt ad restituendum transitum a convenientia rationali ad bonum commune, et ab affectuum conflictu ad necessitatem Civitatis.
Cardo firmissimus systematis est nexus inter bonum commune non-rivale et cupiditatem rationalem qua idem bonum reliquis communicatur.
Commissura fragilis manet inter Civitatem per minas firmatam et concordiam quae ex vita rationali definita est, quia coactio securitatem explicat sed rationem viventem non plene producit.
Systema postulat consensum vel cessionem juris naturalis, sed mechanismum quo singuli affectibus dominati hanc cessionem primitus stabilem efficiant non ulterius deducit.
Tensionem continet duplex normativitas: bonum naturale per potentiam definitur, dum justum et injustum sola institutione civili constituuntur.
Limes inter homines et bruta structuram systematis servat, sed convenientiam naturae humanae tamquam condicionem decisivam assumit potius quam in hoc loco ulterius demonstrat.
Criterium mortis per mutationem rationis motus et quietis systematice cohaeret, sed gradum determinatum quo mutatio corpus in naturam aliam transfert indeterminatum relinquit.
Restitutio motum textus servat, si ordo duplicis machinae retinetur: Ratio bonum commune demonstrat, affectus autem necessitatem institutionis et contrarii affectus imponunt.

translations.title: Part Four - On Human Bondage, or the Powers of the Affects · passage 3

items.text: The text asks how each person's striving to seek his own advantage, which may appear as a form of conflictual egoism, is transformed into mutual advantage and human society.
The first solution posits that human beings, insofar as they are guided by Reason, agree by nature; hence virtue, self-advantage, mutual advantage, and the common good are ordered in the same chain.
The text then shows that this rational agreement is not an empirically dominant condition, because affects render human beings external, inconstant, and opposed to one another.
From this discrepancy between the norm of Reason and the affective condition, the State is generated as an apparatus of security, surrender of right, common law, and coercion through threats.
After the civil institution, good and evil are referred to the power of body and mind, and affects are judged by their effect upon the capacity to act, concord, and stability.

The argument proceeds demonstratively and reconstructively from rational agreement to civil necessity, and from the constitution of the body to a strategy of affects through love, generosity, and liberation from fear.
Virtue is the power of acting under the guidance of Reason, and rationally seeking one's own advantage is preserving oneself according to the laws of one's own nature.
Human beings, insofar as they live under the guidance of Reason, agree by nature; therefore advantage rationally sought increases mutual advantage.
The supreme good of those who pursue virtue is the knowledge of God, common to all human beings and to be possessed equally by all.
The desire by which a rational person seeks the supreme good for himself desires the same good for others, and this desire increases with the knowledge of God.
Human beings are for the most part acted upon by stronger external affects, and an affect is restrained only by a stronger and contrary affect; Reason alone cannot restrain affects.

The natural right of each person is defined by his own power, so that in the state of nature each individual decides, according to his own disposition, concerning good, evil, advantage, revenge, and preservation.
Civil concord requires the mutual surrender of natural right and a common power that makes laws and upholds them through threats.
Sin, merit, justice, injustice, and ownership arise from the consent and right of the State, not from intrinsic attributes of Mind or Nature.
Useful is that which renders the Body more apt to be affected in many ways, to affect other bodies, and the Mind to perceive more things.
The form of the Body consists in a certain ratio of motion and rest; its preservation preserves the body's capacity, while its alteration induces destruction.
The goodness of affects is judged by the increase or decrease of the power of the whole Body, and by the proportion in which the parts of the Body are affected.
Hatred toward human beings seeks destruction and is evil; Love or Generosity can extinguish Hatred and transform it into a contrary affect.
Hope and Fear involve Sadness and a defect of knowledge, and cannot in themselves be good.
Esteem and Contempt are contrary to Reason, and Esteem easily produces Pride.
Ethical reciprocity proceeds from the agreement of human nature; beasts, differing from human beings in nature and affects, are not included in the same community of friendship.
Rational self-advantage is not competitive egoism, because the guidance of Reason reconciles human beings by nature.
The supreme good is not a rare or exclusionary thing, or one capable of having only a single possessor.
Piety and Honesty are not an affective striving that others should live according to their own disposition, but the communication of the common good through friendship.
Empirical social life is not presupposed to be already rational, since human beings are for the most part held by Envy, contrariety, and the dominion of affects.
Civil law is not founded upon rational persuasion alone, because Reason by itself cannot restrain affects.
In the state of nature there are no sin, merit, justice, injustice, or property defined by consent.
Good does not coincide with every Joy, nor evil with every Pain, because a local affect can diminish the power of the whole Body, and Pain can restrain excess.
The death of the Body is not restricted to a corpse or to the cessation of blood circulation, but is understood through a change in the ratio of motion and rest.
Laughter and jest are not Mockery, because the former can signify pure Joy, whereas the latter pertains to Hatred.
Hatred has no proper moral use, although revenge or the diminution of another may sometimes appear useful.
Hope, Fear, Security, Despair, and remorse of conscience are not forms of stable virtue.
Feeling is not sufficient for beasts to be participants in human society or rational friendship.
The more each person seeks his own advantage from Reason, the more useful he becomes to other human beings.
Virtue does not produce conflict over the supreme good, because the good sought remains communicable to all.
An increase in the knowledge of God must produce an increase in the desire that others enjoy the same good.
The rational striving to lead others must act humanely, because affective imposition of one's own disposition arouses a contrary impulse and hatred.
A stable State is effected not simply by theoretical consent, but through mutual security and fear of greater harm.
Punishment does not disclose sin, nor reward merit, as natural things, but establishes obedience or disobedience toward the civil order.
A regimen of moderate life, which admits a variety of foods, recreations, and pleasures, is good insofar as it preserves the integrity of the Body and the multiplicity of the Mind.
Human concord is useful because it produces the conditions of a life conforming to Reason; discord is evil because it destroys this condition.
Generosity is a rational affective strategy by which Hatred is not increased by reciprocal Hatred but restrained by Love.
Life according to Reason tends to diminish dependence on Hope, Fear, and Fortune, and to direct actions by the certain counsel of Reason.
The relation to beasts is not governed by the same moral reciprocity that prevails among human beings, but by power, advantage, and diversity of nature.
Society has a twofold foundation: the internal norm of rational agreement and the external mechanism of affective coercion.
The system distinguishes three normative orders: natural usefulness as increase of power, rational good as common knowledge, and civil justice as public decree.
Ethics becomes non-ascetic, because the preservation and multiplication of the body are conditions for the multiplication of the Mind's perceptions.
Self-preservation, although it begins with the individual, excludes a solitary life, because human power is increased through society, assistance, and concord.
Reason does not simply eliminate affects, but orders contrary affects, especially Love and Generosity, so as to overcome destructive forces.
The identity of the body is located not in the mere appearance of life, memory, or blood circulation, but in the persistence of the relation of bodily structure.
The argument tacitly requires rational good not to be a structure of rivalry; otherwise self-advantage and mutual advantage would not coincide.
The argument denies that bare Intellect is sufficient for the governance of affective life; rational action must assume a contrary affective force.
The argument excludes a juridical or moral order naturally given prior to the State, because guilt, merit, ownership, and justice require public institution.
The argument excludes the evaluation of affects by positive or negative names alone, because local Joy can harm and Pain can beneficially limit.
The argument excludes a universal communion of all sentient living beings, because agreement of human nature, not sensibility alone, constitutes the foundation of ethical relation.
The argument excludes an absolutely permanent identity of the body, because a change in its constitutive relation can transfer the body into another nature.
No natural justice of a transcendent order is admitted between right as power and right as decree of the State.
No stable State is supposed to arise from rational illumination alone, because the power of affects necessarily interposes a coercive institution.
No ethical universality indifferent to differences of nature is posited, because the community of good and friendship is limited to human agreement.
No definition of death through a biological sign alone is admitted, because destruction is said to be a change in the form of bodily relation.
Striving for one's own advantage → Virtue or rational power → Agreement of human nature → Reciprocal advantage → Common knowledge of God → Desire that all enjoy the same good → Piety and Honesty.

Heteronomy of affects → Contrariety among mutually needy human beings → Necessity of security → Surrender of natural right → Common power → Laws upheld by threats → State, Citizens, and juridical norms.

Ratio of motion and rest → Integrity of bodily form → Multiple aptitude for affecting and being affected → Broader perception of the Mind → Distinction between good and evil affects → Moderation, integral Joy, Love, and Generosity.
Agreement of human nature → Friendship and reciprocity → Rational community; diversity of the nature of beasts → Instrumentally useful relation, not ethical society.
Rational self-advantage → Virtue → Human agreement → Non-rival common good → Communication of the knowledge of God → Friendship and Generosity.
Dominion of affects → Insecurity and conflict → Surrender of right → Common coercion → State → Sin, merit, justice, and injustice as juridical effects.
Preservation of bodily form → Increase of capacity → Ordered Joy → Rejection of Hatred and affects of impotence → Love, moderation, and action from the counsel of Reason.
The opposition between self-advantage and common advantage is dissolved for human beings insofar as they are guided by Reason.
The supreme good is reclassified as a communicable good, not as an object of exclusive possession.
A distinction is established between rational guidance of others and affective dominion by which someone seeks to compel others to conform to his own disposition.
The State is described not as a simple expression of moral consensus, but as a machine of security that produces juridical categories.
Affects are ordered not according to their name, but according to their effect on the integrated power of the Body, the aptitude of the Mind, and social concord.
The good life is reclassified as the moderate multiplication of bodily and mental capacity, not as the flight from pleasure or the cult of Sadness.
The boundary of ethical society between human beings and beasts is placed in agreement of nature and reciprocity, not in the mere faculty of feeling.
Surface — The text formally distinguishes good and evil, Joy and Sadness, Hatred and Love, Hope and Fear, justice and injustice.
Structural — The Body is described through the ratio of motion and rest, affects through power, and the State through security and threats.
Metastrategic — Reason not only knows truth, but establishes the governance of affects through Generosity, civil institution, and the ordered moderation of life.
Ontological/Temporal — Right is connected with power, the identity of the body with the relation of structure, and civil norms with the temporal institution of the State.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the transition from rational agreement to the common good, and from the conflict of affects to the necessity of the State.
The firmest hinge of the system is the connection between the non-rival common good and the rational desire by which the same good is communicated to others.
A fragile joint remains between the State upheld by threats and the concord defined by rational life, because coercion explains security but does not fully produce rational living.
The system requires consent or surrender of natural right, but does not further deduce the mechanism by which individuals dominated by affects first make this surrender stable.
It contains the tension of a twofold normativity: natural good is defined through power, while justice and injustice are constituted by civil institution alone.
The boundary between human beings and beasts preserves the structure of the system, but assumes agreement of human nature as the decisive condition rather than further demonstrating it at this point.

The criterion of death through a change in the ratio of motion and rest is systematically coherent, but leaves indeterminate the determinate degree at which change transfers a body into another nature.

The reconstruction preserves the movement of the text if the order of the double machine is retained: Reason demonstrates the common good, whereas affects impose the necessity of institution and of a contrary affect.

identity.title: Pars quarta - De servitute humana seu de affectuum viribus · passage 3

units.title: Pars quarta - De servitute humana seu de affectuum viribus · passage 4

items.text: Textus quaerit quibus affectibus homo ratione ductus uti possit, quos excludere debeat, et qua ratione eadem actio vel servilis vel libera fieri possit.
Thesis principalis statuit virtutem non ex tristitia, metu, paenitentia aut commiseratione oriri, sed ex ratione quae potentiam agendi intelligit et dirigit.
Argumentatio simul diagnostica et reconstructiva est: passiones per earum dependentiam, partialitatem et temporalem caecitatem diagnoscit, deinde actionem rationalem sine passionibus restituit.
Motus procedit ab affectuum moralium reclassificatione ad distinctionem inter actionem et causam actionis, inde ad utilitatem totius hominis et ad ordinem temporalem rationis.
Contrapositio finalis hominem affectu vel opinione actum servum, hominem ratione ductum liberum constituit; libertas est vita directe ex proprio utili et cognitione ducta.
Terminus argumenti tendit ad condicionem in qua libertas ipsa conceptus boni et mali superfluos reddit, quia hi ex comparatione et impedimento nascuntur.
Ex ratione agere est ex necessitate naturae humanae, quatenus per se et adequate intelligitur, agere.
Vera hominis agendi potentia, seu virtus, est ipsa ratio.
Tristitia potentiam agendi minuit vel coercet et, quatenus hominem ad minorem perfectionem transfert, passio est.
Laetitia cum ratione convenit quatenus agendi potentiam auget; passio manet quatenus homo se suasque actiones adequate non concipit.
Affectus passivi ad laetitiam, tristitiam aut cupiditatem reducuntur, et cupiditates ex passionibus ortae caecae sunt.
Commiseratio est tristitia ex alterius miseria orta.
Actio in se spectata neque bona neque mala est; eius valor ex affectu vel cognitione qua determinatur pendet.
Cupiditas ex affectu ad unam corporis partem relato utilitatem totius hominis non considerat.
Ratio res sub specie necessitatis et aeternitatis concipit, non differenter prout futurae, praeteritae vel praesentes imaginantur.
Cupiditas ex ratione orta essentiam humanam actu agentem exprimit et propterea excessum habere nequit.
Metus ad tristitiam pertinet; qui bonum agit ut malum fugiat, non ratione ducitur.
Cognitio mali est cognitio tristitiae conscia et ideo cognitio inadæquata.
Bonum et malum relationes comparativae sunt; ratio maius bonum et minus malum eligit.
Cognitio humana durationis et temporum existentiae est inadæquata atque imaginatione potius quam ratione ordinatur.
Homo ratione ductus bonum directe appetit, malum autem solum indirecte fugit.
Affectus non rationales, quamvis virtutes non sint, homines raro ratione viventes ad ordinem socialem et ad futuram libertatem disponere possunt.
Commiseratio non est virtus rationalis, et liberatio alterius ex commiseratione orta non est ipsa causa rationalis beneficentiae.
Homo rationalis non definitur per insensibilitatem erga alios, quia auxilium alteri praestare potest ex solo rationis dictamine.
Humilitas et paenitentia non sunt formae virtutis, quia ex tristitia et impotentiae contemplatione oriuntur.
Indignatio non est iustitia rationalis; poena publica rationalis tantum est si ex amore salutis publicae, non ex odio, procedit.
Gloria vulgi opinione sustentata non est vera acquiescentia, quia cum opinione externa perit.
Nulla actio passionem requirit ut fieri possit, quia eadem actio ex imaginibus confusis vel ideis adequatis determinari potest.
Metus non est forma inferior prudentiae rationalis, sed signum actionis ab avoidance mali potius quam a cognitione boni motae.
Bonum et malum non sunt proprietates absolutae rerum aut actionum.
Cogitatio mortis non est centrum sapientiae liberae; sapientia libera meditationem vitae constituit.
Commiseratio in homine ratione ducto per se mala et inutilis est, quia tristitia est, dum beneficentia quam comitari videtur ex ratione sola produci potest.
Homo rationalis conatur ne commiseratione tangatur, non ut auxilium neget, sed ut bene agendi causam a tristitia ad rationem transferat.
Favor et acquiescentia in se ipso cum ratione convenire possunt, quia ab intellectu propriae vel alienae potentiae agentis oriri possunt.
Humilitas et paenitentia impotentiam duplicant: primum actum pravum non removent, deinde tristitiam superaddunt.
Maxima superbia et maxima abjectio non sunt contrariae libertati diversis modis, sed communes formae maximae sui ignorantiae et animi impotentiae.
Eadem corporalis actio ex ira, odio, ratione vel idea clara procedere potest; distinctio ethica igitur ad determinationem causalem, non ad motum externum, refertur.
Cupiditates passionum nullam actionem unice necessariam efficiunt, quia ratio ad omnes actiones quas passio determinat determinare potest.
Cupiditas passionis plerumque praesentem corporis statum conservat sine ratione integrae valetudinis aut futuri.
Ratio, si sola spectatur, maius bonum futurum minori bono praesenti anteponit et minus malum praesens pro maiore bono futuro suscipit.
Cupiditas rationalis bonum prosequitur ex laetitia activa, non ex tristitia mali vitandi; propterea nec excessum nec formam metuendi habet.
Cognitio mali, quia inadæquata est, rationem non instruit per malum ut obiectum positivum, sed tantum per comparationem bonorum et impedimentorum.
Servitus est agere ea quae homo maxime ignorat ex affectu vel opinione; libertas est sibi soli obtemperare in iis quae ad vivendum et conservandum esse maxime cognoscuntur.
Systema ethicum actiones non per species exteriores distribuit, sed per transitum a causis externis et imaginariis ad causam internam adequate intellectam.
Virtus reorganizatur ut augmentum et ordinatio potentiae agendi, non ut tolerantia tristitiae, imminutio sui, metus poenae aut dolor paenitentialis.
Ratio temporaliter totalizat utilitatem sub specie aeternitatis, dum passio localiter et praesentaneae parti corporis inservit.
Ordo politicus affectibus uti potest ut homines ad disciplinam et tandem ad libertatem disponantur, sed affectus ipsi fundamentum libertatis fieri nequeunt.
Conceptus boni et mali statum comparativum et imperfectum exprimunt; libertas perfecta tendit ad ordinem in quo haec vocabula formari desinunt.
Falsum esse debet passionem irreducibilem fontem actionis utilis esse, quia ratio omnes actiones quas passio producit producere potest.
Falsum esse debet malum positivam rem adequate cognosci posse, quia cognitio mali ad tristitiam et ideam inadæquatam reducitur.
Falsum esse debet affectum localem spontaneam cognitionem utilitatis totius hominis praebere.
Falsum esse debet iudicium vulgi stabilem mensuram perfectionis propriae constituere.
Falsum esse debet libertatem consistere in fuga mali aut morte vitanda; libertas bonum et vitam directe affirmat.
Falsum esse debet sui imminutio veram sui cognitionem exprimere, quia cognitio rationalis essentiam et potentiam, non impotentiam, percipit.
Argumentatio excludit moralitatem cuius vis directiva in metu, prohibitione et fuga mali consistit.
Argumentatio excludit commiserationem ut supremam formam relationis humanae, quia rationalis communitas ex beneficentia activa et favore, non ex tristitia communicata, constituitur.
Argumentatio excludit subiectum quod per defectum, culpam aut abiectionem se ipsummet vere cognoscere possit.
Argumentatio circumagit condicionem libertatis in qua bonum et malum, ut conceptus comparativi servitutis, nullam amplius functionem cognitivam habent.
Affectus → laetitia / tristitia / cupiditas → examen per augmentum vel diminutionem potentiae agendi.
Tristitia vel imaginatio partialis → passio → cognitio inadæquata → cupiditas caeca et praesentis temporis capta.
Actio exterior eadem → causae affectivae vel causae rationales diversae → valor ad modum determinationis, non ad figuram actus, refertur.
Ratio → cognitio adequata potentiae → laetitia activa → cupiditas sine excessu → bonum directe appetitum.
Ratio sub specie aeternitatis → comparatio bonorum et malorum → electio maioris boni et minoris mali etiam trans tempora.
Raritas vitae rationalis → usus transitorius affectuum ad disciplinam socialem → transitus possibilis ad libertatem → imminutio functionis boni et mali.
Commiseratio ut tristitia → separatio auxilii ab affectu miserendi → virtus ut ratio et potentia agendi → reiectio humilitatis, paenitentiae et metus → actio a causa affectiva seiungitur.
Partialitas corporis et praesentis imaginationis → cupiditas caeca → ratio aeternitatem et comparationem bonorum introducit → electio utilitatis integrae et futurae.
Actio ex opinione et affectu → servitus → actio ex cognitione proprii utilis → libertas → vita potius quam mors meditanda.
Libertas continua → imminutio comparationum boni et mali → prospectus condicionis in qua haec concepta non formantur.
Affectus reclassificantur non per approbationem moralem vulgarem, sed per relationem ad potentiam agendi, adecquationem cognitionis et utilitatem totius.
Oppositio actus boni et actus mali dissolvitur, atque substituitur oppositio eiusdem actus ex passione vel ex ratione determinati.
Misericordia, humilitas, paenitentia et metus e regione virtutis transferuntur ad passiones quae interdum disciplinarem, non autem rationalem, functionem habent.
Utilitas individualis non iam cum satisfactione partis corporis aut cum commodo praesenti identificatur, sed cum conservatione et perfectione totius hominis per tempora ordinata.
Gloria et vituperium ab indicibus valoris intrinseci ad machinas opinionis externae et servitutis affectivae transferuntur.
Libertas a facultate eligendi inter bona et mala ad activitatem ex sola ratione, vitae affirmationem et proprii utilis cognitionem reconfiguratur.
Surface — Textus iudicat commiserationem, favorem, acquiescentiam, humilitatem, paenitentiam, superbiam, gloriam, metum et cupiditatem.
Structural — Affects distribuuntur secundum potentiam agendi, adequationem idearum, relationem corporis partis ad totum et dependentiam ab opinionibus externis.
Metastrategic — Textus separat virtutem rationalem a mechanismis quibus multitudo affectibus continetur, dum hos mechanismos transitui ad libertatem conditionaliter reservat.
Ontological/Temporal — Ratio res necessario et aeternaliter concipit, passio autem imaginatione temporali, praesentia et duratione inadæquate cognita ordinatur.
Ontological/Temporal — Libertas significat hominem ut causam ex propria natura agentem; sub hoc horizonte bonum et malum status comparativi, non entia absoluta, fiunt.
Axiomata de ratione ut actione adequata, de virtute ut potentia, de tristitia ut diminutione, et de actione ut causaliter qualificata sufficiunt ad nucleum argumenti restituendum.
Axiomata de partialitate affectuum, de imaginatione temporali et de ratione sub specie aeternitatis explicant transitum a diagnostica passionum ad electionem rationalem bonorum.
Systema maxime cohaeret ubi eandem actionem a causa passionis separat et sic beneficentiam a commiseratione, poenam publicam ab indignatione, atque salutem a metu distinguit.
Commissura fragilis manet inter normam rationis, quae bonum futurum aeque ac praesens ponderat, et conditionem humanam, quae durationem rerum necessario inadæquate cognoscit.
Tensio interna manet quia humilitas, paenitentia et metus rationi adversa declarantur, sed eadem affecta instrumenta utilia fiunt ad multitudinem ad rationem ducendam.
Distinctio inter virtutem et signum virtutis necessaria est ut pudor, tristitia et disciplina affectiva aliquo sensu utiles dicantur sine eo quod fontes rationales virtutis fiant.
Prospectus quo homines liberi nullum boni et mali conceptum formarent in fine tantum enuntiatur; demonstratio eius plena in hoc fonte nondum perficitur.

translations.title: Part Four - On Human Bondage, or the Powers of the Affects · passage 4

items.text: The text asks which affects a person guided by reason may employ, which they ought to exclude, and how the same action may be either servile or free.
The principal thesis establishes that virtue arises not from sadness, fear, repentance, or pity, but from reason, which understands and directs the power of acting.
The argument is at once diagnostic and reconstructive: it diagnoses passions through their dependence, partiality, and temporal blindness, then restores rational action without passions.
The movement proceeds from the moral reclassification of affects to the distinction between action and the cause of action, thence to the utility of the whole person and to reason's temporal order.
The final opposition constitutes the person driven by affect or opinion as a slave, and the person guided by reason as free; freedom is life directed immediately by one's own advantage and knowledge.
The terminus of the argument tends toward a condition in which freedom itself renders the concepts of good and evil superfluous, because these arise from comparison and impediment.
To act from reason is to act from the necessity of human nature insofar as it is understood through itself and adequately.
The true power of acting of a human being, or virtue, is reason itself.
Sadness diminishes or restrains the power of acting and, insofar as it transfers a human being to lesser perfection, is a passion.
Joy agrees with reason insofar as it increases the power of acting; it remains a passion insofar as a person does not adequately conceive himself and his actions.
Passive affects are reduced to joy, sadness, or desire, and desires arising from passions are blind.
Pity is sadness arising from another's misery.
An action considered in itself is neither good nor evil; its value depends on the affect or knowledge by which it is determined.
Desire arising from an affect related to one part of the body does not consider the advantage of the whole person.
Reason conceives things under the aspect of necessity and eternity, not differently according as they are imagined as future, past, or present.
Desire arising from reason expresses human essence actually acting and therefore cannot have excess.
Fear belongs to sadness; one who does good in order to flee evil is not guided by reason.
Knowledge of evil is conscious knowledge of sadness and therefore inadequate knowledge.
Good and evil are comparative relations; reason chooses the greater good and the lesser evil.
Human knowledge of duration and of the temporal existence of things is inadequate and is ordered by imagination rather than reason.
A person guided by reason directly seeks good, but flees evil only indirectly.
Non-rational affects, although they are not virtues, can dispose persons rarely living by reason toward social order and future freedom.
Pity is not a rational virtue, and another's deliverance arising from pity is not itself the rational cause of beneficence.
The rational person is not defined by insensibility toward others, because he can render assistance to another from the dictate of reason alone.
Humility and repentance are not forms of virtue, because they arise from sadness and the contemplation of impotence.
Indignation is not rational justice; public punishment is rational only if it proceeds from love of the public welfare, not from hatred.
Glory sustained by popular opinion is not true self-contentment, because it perishes with external opinion.
No action requires a passion in order to be possible, because the same action can be determined by confused images or adequate ideas.
Fear is not an inferior form of rational prudence, but a sign of action moved by the avoidance of evil rather than by knowledge of good.
Good and evil are not absolute properties of things or actions.
Thought of death is not the center of free wisdom; free wisdom consists in meditation on life.
Pity in a person guided by reason is in itself evil and useless, because it is sadness, whereas the beneficence it seems to accompany can be produced by reason alone.
The rational person strives not to be touched by pity, not in order to deny assistance, but in order to transfer the cause of doing good from sadness to reason.
Favor and self-contentment can agree with reason, because they can arise from understanding one's own or another's active power.
Humility and repentance double impotence: first, they do not remove the wrongful act; then, they add sadness.
The greatest pride and the greatest abjection are not contrary to freedom in different ways, but are common forms of the greatest ignorance of oneself and impotence of mind.
The same bodily action can proceed from anger, hatred, reason, or a clear idea; ethical distinction therefore refers to causal determination, not to external movement.
Desires of the passions render no action uniquely necessary, because reason can determine to all the actions to which passion determines.
The desire of passion generally preserves the present state of the body without regard for integral health or the future.
Reason, if considered alone, prefers a greater future good to a lesser present good and accepts a lesser present evil for the sake of a greater future good.
Rational desire pursues good from active joy, not from the sadness of avoiding evil; therefore it has neither excess nor a form of fearing.
Knowledge of evil, because it is inadequate, does not instruct reason through evil as a positive object, but only through comparison of goods and impediments.

Bondage is acting from affect or opinion in those things that a person most greatly does not know; freedom is obeying oneself alone in those things that are most greatly known to pertain to living and preserving oneself.
The ethical system distributes actions not according to external kinds, but according to the transition from external and imaginary causes to an internal cause adequately understood.
Virtue is reorganized as the increase and ordering of the power of acting, not as endurance of sadness, diminution of oneself, fear of punishment, or penitential pain.
Reason temporally totalizes utility under the aspect of eternity, whereas passion serves locally and the present part of the body.
The political order can employ affects so that persons may be disposed toward discipline and finally toward freedom, but the affects themselves cannot become the foundation of freedom.
The concepts of good and evil express a comparative and imperfect state; perfect freedom tends toward an order in which these terms cease to be formed.
It must be false that passion is an irreducible source of useful action, because reason can produce all actions that passion produces.
It must be false that evil can be adequately known as a positive thing, because knowledge of evil is reduced to sadness and an inadequate idea.
It must be false that a local affect provides spontaneous knowledge of the advantage of the whole person.
It must be false that the judgment of the crowd constitutes a stable measure of one's own perfection.
It must be false that freedom consists in flight from evil or avoidance of death; freedom directly affirms good and life.
It must be false that self-diminution expresses true self-knowledge, because rational knowledge perceives essence and power, not impotence.
The argument excludes a morality whose directive force consists in fear, prohibition, and flight from evil.
The argument excludes pity as the supreme form of human relation, because rational community is constituted from active beneficence and favor, not from shared sadness.
The argument excludes a subject who could truly know himself through defect, guilt, or abjection.
The argument turns around a condition of freedom in which good and evil, as comparative concepts of bondage, no longer have any cognitive function.
Affects → joy / sadness / desire → examination through increase or diminution of the power of acting.
Sadness or partial imagination → passion → inadequate knowledge → blind desire captive to the present time.
Same external action → different affective causes or rational causes → value refers to the mode of determination, not to the form of the act.
Reason → adequate knowledge of power → active joy → desire without excess → good directly sought.
Reason under the aspect of eternity → comparison of goods and evils → choice of the greater good and the lesser evil even across times.
Rarity of rational life → transitory use of affects for social discipline → possible transition to freedom → diminution of the function of good and evil.
Pity as sadness → separation of assistance from the affect of pitying → virtue as reason and power of acting → rejection of humility, repentance, and fear → action separated from affective cause.
Partiality of the body and of present imagination → blind desire → reason introduces eternity and comparison of goods → choice of integral and future advantage.
Action from opinion and affect → bondage → action from knowledge of one's own advantage → freedom → life rather than death to be meditated upon.
Continuous freedom → diminution of comparisons of good and evil → prospect of a condition in which these concepts are not formed.
Affects are reclassified not by ordinary moral approval, but by their relation to the power of acting, the adequacy of knowledge, and the advantage of the whole.
The opposition of good action and evil action is dissolved, and is replaced by the opposition of the same action determined by passion or by reason.
Mercy, humility, repentance, and fear are transferred from the region of virtue to passions that sometimes have a disciplinary, but not a rational, function.
Individual advantage is no longer identified with the satisfaction of a part of the body or with present convenience, but with the preservation and perfection of the whole person ordered across time.
Glory and blame are transferred from indicators of intrinsic value to mechanisms of external opinion and affective bondage.
Freedom is reconfigured from the faculty of choosing between goods and evils into activity from reason alone, affirmation of life, and knowledge of one's own advantage.
Surface — The text judges pity, favor, self-contentment, humility, repentance, pride, glory, fear, and desire.
Structural — Affects are distributed according to the power of acting, the adequacy of ideas, the relation of a part of the body to the whole, and dependence on external opinions.

Metastrategic — The text separates rational virtue from the mechanisms by which the multitude is restrained through affects, while conditionally reserving these mechanisms for the transition to freedom.
Ontological/Temporal — Reason conceives things necessarily and eternally, whereas passion is ordered by temporal imagination, the present, and inadequately known duration.
Ontological/Temporal — Freedom signifies a person as a cause acting from his own nature; under this horizon, good and evil become comparative states, not absolute entities.
The axioms concerning reason as adequate action, virtue as power, sadness as diminution, and action as causally qualified suffice to reconstruct the core of the argument.
The axioms concerning the partiality of affects, temporal imagination, and reason under the aspect of eternity explain the transition from the diagnosis of passions to the rational choice of goods.
The system is most coherent where it separates the same action from the cause of passion and thus distinguishes beneficence from pity, public punishment from indignation, and welfare from fear.
A fragile joint remains between the norm of reason, which weighs future good equally with present good, and the human condition, which necessarily knows the duration of things inadequately.
An internal tension remains because humility, repentance, and fear are declared contrary to reason, yet the same affects become useful instruments for leading the multitude toward reason.

The distinction between virtue and a sign of virtue is necessary so that shame, sadness, and affective discipline may be called useful in some sense without thereby becoming rational sources of virtue.
The prospect in which free persons would form no concept of good and evil is stated only at the end; its full demonstration is not yet completed in this source.

identity.title: Pars quarta - De servitute humana seu de affectuum viribus · passage 4

units.title: Pars quarta - De servitute humana seu de affectuum viribus · passage 5

items.text: Textus quaerit quomodo libertas humana, sub necessitate Naturae et inter homines plerumque affectibus ductos, effici possit sine exemptionis causalis fictione.
Libertas perfecte concepta statuitur ut terminus hypotheticus: homo sola Ratione ductus ideis adequatis fruitur atque boni malique conceptus transcendit.
Argumentatio diagnostica servitutem ex cognitione mutilata, affectuum imperio et causarum externarum potentia derivat; libertatem ex actione rationali et affectuum moderatione restituit.
Motus practicus a periculis, beneficiis, gratitudine et fide transit ad conclusionem politicam quod homo Ratione ductus in Civitate liberior sit quam in solitudine.
Appendix conatum, rationem boni, corporis conservationem, societatem, oeconomiam et acquiescentiam in ordine Naturae in unam rationem vitae rationalis conectit.
Homo liber eatenus est, quatenus sola Ratione ducitur et ideis adequatis agit.
Libertas integra, qua homo libere nascitur et liber manet, homini ut parti Naturae considerato non competit, sed tantum hypothetice concipi potest.
Omnis humanus conatus seu Cupiditas ex necessitate naturae humanae, sive ex ordine totius Naturae, sequitur.
Cupiditates ex ideis adequatis ortae actiones sunt et potentiam humanam indicant; ex cognitione inadequata ortae passiones sunt et potentia externa definiuntur.
Actiones Ratione definitae semper bonae sunt; reliquae Cupiditates bonitatem aut malitiam tantum relative habere possunt.
Bonum est quod vitam rationalem et perfectionem intellectus promovet; beatitudo est acquiescentia ex cognitione Dei intuitiva orta.
Potentia causarum externarum humanam potentiam infinite superat; malum homini, quatenus patitur, ab externis causis provenit.
Affectus coerceri aut tolli non potest nisi affectu contrario et fortiore.
Conservatio rationalis sui simul utilitatem communem postulat, quia homo Ratione ductus bonum sibi cupitum reliquis hominibus etiam cupit.
Dolus malus non potest esse regula rationalis, quia, si universalis esset, fidem, foedera et iura communia destrueret.
