Homo Ratione ductus libertatem suam amplius in communibus Civitatis iuribus quam in solitudine invenit.
Ius Naturae homini concedit removendi quae eius vitam rationalem impediunt et utendi rebus quas ad conservationem utileis iudicat.
Corporis aptitudo ad plures affectiones et operationes Mentis aptitudinem ad plura concipienda auget; corpus variis alimentis et rebus indiget.
Laetitia potentiam humanam auget, sed, nisi Ratione et vigilantia moderetur, in excessum et in praesentis suavitatis praeiudicium cadit.
Homines plerumque non ex Ratione, sed ex varietate ingeniorum, invidia, odio, vindicta et aliis affectibus agunt.
Concordia stabilis iustitia, aequitate, honestate, amore et generositate alitur; metus concordiam sine fide tantum parit.
Intellegere omnia ex necessitate Naturae sequi partem meliorem Mentis ad acquiescentiam ordinatam disponit.
Libertas non est immunitas empirica ab affectibus, a causis externis aut ab ordine totius Naturae.
Bonum et malum non sunt proprietates absolutae rerum, sed relationes ad vitam rationalem, cognitionem et humanam utilitatem.
Fortitudo non est periculum semper aggredi; fuga tempestiva eandem animi praesentiam postulare potest ac pugna.
Beneficium ab ignaro acceptum non est officium simplex neque vinculum per se rationale, quia aestimatio affectiva benefactoris odium parere potest.
Gratia non est mercatura, aucupium aut corruptibilitas per dona; imminutio donationum nocivarum non est ingratitudo.
Fides civilis non ex dolo malo, perfidia aut conventione verbali cum inimicitia reali constitui potest.
Civitas rationalis non est mera coactio metu fundata, neque libertas rationalis est solitudo sibi soli obtemperans.
Concordia non est adulatio, abiectio, falsa pietas, libido meretricia aut affectus tristitiae specie religiosus.
Tristitia, superstitio, metus et commiseratio non sunt principia vitae rationalis, quamvis aliquando pietatis aut honestatis imaginem gerant.
Pecunia non est finis rationis vitae, sed instrumentum ad mutuas operas et corporis sustentationem reductibile.
Acquiescentia in necessitate Naturae non est potestas externa omnia ad usum humanum redigendi.
Eadem fortitudo requiritur ad periculum prudenter declinandum ac ad idem superandum, quia utrumque contra affectus caecos ordinari debet.
Homo liber beneficia ignarorum, quantum potest, declinat, sed ea recipere et secundum ingenium benefactoris recompensare potest, ubi necessitas humana aut cautio socialis id postulat.
Gratia vera inter homines liberos tantum stabilis est, quia eorum mutua utilitas, amicitia et beneficentia ex Ratione procedunt.
Homo liber semper cum fide agit, quia dolus malus, si ratio conservationis esset, condicionem ipsam societatis rationalis destrueret.
Obedientia legibus communibus, ubi ad communem vitam et utilitatem ordinantur, non libertatem minuit sed libertatem rationalem perficit.
Cura egentium ad societatem integram pertinet, quia facultas privata neque universali necessitati neque stabili amicitiae sufficere potest.
Res non humanae conservari, destrui aut ad usum adaptari possunt, quatenus corpus conservant, Mentem adiuvent et vitam rationalem non impediant.
Mutuae operae et pecunia ex indigentia corporali et diversitate necessitatum oriuntur, sed pecunia mentem vulgi capere potest, ubi a vero usu separatur.
Inter homines affectibus obnoxios, virtus politica est affectus aliorum non imitari, vitia non exprobrare, et amorem ad vitam rationalem incitandam conciliare.
Eventus externos inevitabiles aequo animo ferre licet, ubi intellectus cognoscit se officium suum fecisse et potentiam finitam ultra limites suos non extendi posse.
Libertas non est proprietas interior individui solitarii, sed gradus agendi qui simul ex cognitione, affectionum dispositione, corporali potentia, societate et iure civili constituitur.
Virtus reclassificatur ut potentia rationaliter ordinata ad conservandum, intelligendum et cum aliis concorditer agendum, non ut obedientia legi morali externae.
Ordo politicus rationalis fidem, amorem, iustitiam et curam publicam indigentium requirit, quia beneficentia privata et metus neque sufficientiam materialem neque concordiam fidelem producunt.
Corpus, cognitio et oeconomia constituunt unam infrastructuram libertatis: varietas corporalis postulat res externas, res externas mutua opera, mutuas operas media commutationis.
Ius Naturae usum rerum ex potentia et utilitate iudicata describit; Ratio autem hunc usum ad corporis conservationem, cognitionem et societatem stabilem ordinat.
Necessitas Naturae libertatem non delet, sed libertatem ab imperio externorum ad intellectam participationem in ordine necessario transfert.
Falsum esse debet hominem esse causam sui actus penitus indeterminatam, si omnis Cupiditas ex natura propria et ordine Naturae necessario sequitur.
Falsum esse debet bonum et malum esse genera absoluta rerum, si eorum ratio a potentia, cognitione et vita rationali dependet.
Falsum esse debet individuum sibi sufficere posse, si humana utilitas maxima ex hominibus Ratione ductis, mutuis operis et iure communi provenit.
Falsum esse debet Mentem rationalem a conditionibus corporis et rerum externarum separari posse, si corporis aptitudo mentis aptitudinem ad cogitandum auget.
Falsum esse debet metum, poenam, adulationem aut dolum fundamentum stabile societatis esse, si concordia rationalis fidem et generositatem requirit.
Falsum esse debet Ratio sine affectuum ordinatione operari posse, si affectus tantum per affectus contrarios et fortiores coerceri possunt.
Falsum esse debet societatem fidelem ex universali perfidia constitui posse, si perfidia generalis iura communia et cooperationem inanes facit.
Systema omnem prospectum humanum extra Naturam excludit: homo semper pars totius est, cuius ordinem sequi cogitur.
Systema possibilitatem libertatis humanae absolutae et perpetuae excludit, dum figuram hominis perfecte liberi retinet ut terminum normativum.
Systema bonum ultimum mere privatum excludit, quia bonum rationaliter quaesitum simul aliis communicari et per societatem sustineri debet.
Systema communitatem sine mediationibus affectivis, iuridicis et materialibus excludit, quia homines non plerumque ex sola Ratione vivunt.
Necessitas Naturae → conatus et Cupiditates → distinctio actionum ex cognitione adequata et passionum ex cognitione inadequata.
Actiones rationales → bonum ut vita rationalis → perfectio intellectus → beatitudo ut acquiescentia cognitiva.
Potentia externa superior + affectuum servitus → imminutio libertatis → necessitas affectuum contrariorum, fortitudinis et vigilantiae.
Conservatio rationalis sui → bonum commune → amicitia, gratia, fides → exclusio doli mali.
Utilitas communis + pluralitas affectiva hominum → ius civile, iustitia, amor et generositas → libertas maior in Civitate.
Corpus multiplex + rerum externarum necessitas → usus Naturae, mutua opera et pecunia → moderatio cupiditatis et Laetitiae.
Eventus inevitabiles extra potentiam humanam → cognitio necessitatis → acquiescentia Mentis in ordine totius Naturae.
Libertas hypothetica perfecta → fortitudo in periculis → prudentia circa beneficia ignarorum → gratia et fides inter liberos → libertas civilis maior quam solitudo.
Conatus necessarius → actio/passio → bonum ut vita rationalis → conservatio corporis et Mentis → societas, ius et oeconomia → moderatio affectuum → acquiescentia in necessitate Naturae.
Libertas e figura arbitrii privati in modum agendi ex Ratione, legibus communibus et relationibus utilibus constitutum transfertur.
Fuga tempestiva e genere timiditatis in genus fortitudinis reclassificatur, si eadem animi praesentia qua pugna eligitur.
Beneficium, gratia et ingratitudo a codice morali simplici ad structuram affectivam, rationalem et socialem distinguendam transferuntur.
Civitas non opponitur libertati; Civitas rationaliter ordinata fit medium quo libertas singularis actu maior efficitur.
Affectus sociales dividuntur in eos qui concordiam fidelem augent et eos qui tantum speciem concordiae per metum, captationem, servitutem aut tristitiam fingunt.
Corpus, res externae, nutritio, labor et pecunia non sunt adiuncta extrinseca, sed condiciones cognitivas et sociales vitae rationalis constituunt.
Necessitas Naturae non amplius apparet ut fatum libertati extrinsecum, sed ut ordo cui intellectus finitus consentiendo libertatem relativam exercet.
Surface — Textus regulas de periculis, beneficiis, gratia, fide, civitate, matrimonio, pudore, pecunia et toleratione eventuum exponit.
Structural — Hae regulae ex distinctione inter actionem et passionem, ex superioritate causarum externarum et ex interdependentia corporali ac sociali procedunt.
Metastrategic — Textus certamen morale in artem ordinandi affectus, instituendi fidem, conciliandi amorem et construendi condiciones cooperationis convertit.
Ontological/Temporal — Homo pars Naturae necessario ordinatae est; affectus praesentem suavitatem prae futuro aestimat, Ratio autem necessitatem intellegens stabilem Mentis acquiescentiam quaerit.
Axiomata satis sunt ad seriem principalem restituendam: necessitas Naturae, adequatio, actio et passio, utilitas rationalis, societas civilis et acquiescentia.
Firmissimus nexus systematis est transitus ab impotentia affectiva ad necessitatem cooperationis rationalis: homo finitus nec solus nec dolo stabiliter conservari potest.
Figura hominis perfecte liberi simul norma argumenti et hypothesis falsa manet; transitus ab hoc termino hypothetico ad hominem actualem graduatim liberum non plene formalizatur.
Systema Civitatem libertatis medium facit, sed discrimen inter Civitatem ex communi decreto viventem et Civitatem re vera metu aut cupiditate gubernatam hic non plene resolvit.
Ius utendi rebus externis late definitur, dum eius moderatio per utilitatem rationalem affirmatur; criterium quo utilitas singularis et communis in casu conflictus componantur non explicatur.
Affectus per affectus coercendos esse textus statuit, sed vis concreta qua Ratio affectum contrarium efficacem producit in hoc loco praesupponitur potius quam demonstratur.
Bonum et malum in figura hominis perfecte liberi evanescunt, sed in ratione vitae finitae necessaria manent; distinctio perspectivarum implicatur, non autem explicite sistematizatur.
Restitutio motum verum servat, quia ab ideali libertatis ad fortitudinem, societatem, condiciones materiales et tandem ad intellectam necessitatem Naturae procedit.

translations.title: Part Four — On Human Bondage, or the Powers of the Affects · passage 5

items.text: The text asks how human freedom can be achieved, under the necessity of Nature and among people for the most part led by affects, without the fiction of causal exemption.
Perfectly conceived freedom is posited as a hypothetical limit: a human being led by Reason alone enjoys adequate ideas and transcends the concepts of good and evil.
The diagnostic argument derives bondage from mutilated cognition, the dominion of affects, and the power of external causes; it restores freedom through rational action and the moderation of affects.
The practical movement passes from dangers, benefits, gratitude, and faith to the political conclusion that a human being led by Reason is freer in the State than in solitude.
The appendix connects conatus, the account of good, the preservation of the body, society, economy, and acquiescence in the order of Nature into a single account of rational life.
A free human being is free insofar as he is led by Reason alone and acts from adequate ideas.
Complete freedom, by which a human being is born free and remains free, does not belong to a human being considered as a part of Nature, but can be conceived only hypothetically.
Every human conatus or Desire follows from the necessity of human nature, or from the order of the whole of Nature.
Desires arising from adequate ideas are actions and indicate human power; those arising from inadequate cognition are passions and are determined by external power.
Actions determined by Reason are always good; the remaining Desires can possess goodness or badness only relatively.
Good is what advances rational life and the perfection of the intellect; blessedness is acquiescence arising from the intuitive knowledge of God.
The power of external causes infinitely surpasses human power; evil befalls a human being, insofar as he suffers, from external causes.
An affect cannot be restrained or removed except by a contrary and stronger affect.
Rational self-preservation at the same time demands common advantage, because a human being led by Reason also desires for other human beings the good he desires for himself.
Malicious deceit cannot be a rational rule, because, if it were universal, it would destroy trust, agreements, and common rights.
A human being led by Reason finds his freedom more fully in the common rights of the State than in solitude.
Natural right grants a human being the right to remove what hinders his rational life and to use things which he judges useful for preservation.
The body's aptitude for a greater number of affections and operations increases the Mind's aptitude for conceiving more things; the body requires diverse foods and things.
Joy increases human power, but unless it is moderated by Reason and vigilance, it falls into excess and into the prejudice of present sweetness.
People for the most part act not from Reason but from diversity of dispositions, envy, hatred, revenge, and other affects.
Stable concord is nourished by justice, fairness, honesty, love, and generosity; fear produces only concord without trust.
Understanding that all things follow from the necessity of Nature disposes the better part of the Mind toward ordered acquiescence.
Freedom is not empirical immunity from affects, external causes, or the order of the whole of Nature.
Good and evil are not absolute properties of things, but relations to rational life, knowledge, and human utility.
Fortitude is not always confronting danger; timely flight can require the same presence of mind as combat.
A benefit received from an ignorant person is neither a simple obligation nor in itself a rational bond, because the benefactor's affective estimation can generate hatred.
Gratitude is not commerce, solicitation, or corruptibility through gifts; diminishing harmful gifts is not ingratitude.
Civil trust cannot be constituted from malicious deceit, perfidy, or verbal agreement with real hostility.
A rational State is not mere coercion founded on fear, nor is rational freedom solitude obeying itself alone.
Concord is not flattery, abjection, false piety, meretricious lust, or an affect religious in the guise of sadness.
Sadness, superstition, fear, and compassion are not principles of rational life, even though they may at times bear the appearance of piety or honesty.
Money is not the end of rational life, but is reducible to an instrument for reciprocal services and bodily sustenance.
Acquiescence in the necessity of Nature is not an external power to reduce all things to human use.
The same fortitude is required to avoid danger prudently as to overcome it, because both must be ordered against blind affects.

A free human being avoids, as far as he can, the benefits of ignorant persons, but can receive them and recompense them according to the disposition of the benefactor where human necessity or social caution requires it.
True gratitude is stable only among free human beings, because their reciprocal utility, friendship, and beneficence proceed from Reason.
A free human being always acts in good faith, because malicious deceit, if it were a principle of preservation, would destroy the very condition of rational society.
Obedience to common laws, where they are ordered to common life and utility, does not diminish freedom but perfects rational freedom.
Care for the needy belongs to society as a whole, because private means can suffice neither for universal necessity nor for stable friendship.
Non-human things can be preserved, destroyed, or adapted to use insofar as they preserve the body, assist the Mind, and do not hinder rational life.
Reciprocal services and money arise from bodily need and the diversity of necessities, but money can captivate the mind of the multitude where it is separated from true use.
Among people subject to affects, political virtue is not to imitate the affects of others, not to reproach vices, and to win over love for the encouragement of rational life.
Inevitable external events may be borne with equanimity where the intellect knows that it has done its duty and that finite power cannot extend beyond its limits.
Freedom is not an interior property of the solitary individual, but a degree of acting constituted simultaneously by knowledge, the disposition of affects, bodily power, society, and civil right.
Virtue is reclassified as power rationally ordered toward preserving, understanding, and acting harmoniously with others, not as obedience to an external moral law.
Rational political order requires trust, love, justice, and public care for the needy, because private beneficence and fear produce neither material sufficiency nor faithful concord.
Body, knowledge, and economy constitute one infrastructure of freedom: bodily diversity demands external things, external things reciprocal service, reciprocal service means of exchange.
Natural right describes the use of things in terms of power and judged utility; Reason, however, orders this use toward bodily preservation, knowledge, and stable society.
The necessity of Nature does not abolish freedom, but transfers freedom from the dominion of externals to understood participation in necessary order.
It must be false that a human being is a wholly undetermined cause of his action, if every Desire necessarily follows from his own nature and the order of Nature.
It must be false that good and evil are absolute genera of things, if their account depends on power, knowledge, and rational life.
It must be false that an individual can be self-sufficient, if the greatest human utility derives from human beings led by Reason, reciprocal services, and common right.
It must be false that the rational Mind can be separated from the conditions of the body and external things, if the body's aptitude increases the Mind's aptitude for thinking.
It must be false that fear, punishment, flattery, or deceit can be the stable foundation of society, if rational concord requires trust and generosity.
It must be false that Reason can operate without the ordering of affects, if affects can be restrained only through contrary and stronger affects.
It must be false that a faithful society can be constituted from universal perfidy, if general perfidy renders common rights and cooperation empty.
The system excludes every human standpoint outside Nature: a human being is always a part of the whole, whose order he is compelled to follow.
The system excludes the possibility of absolute and perpetual human freedom, while retaining the figure of the perfectly free human being as a normative limit.
The system excludes a merely private highest good, because the good rationally sought must at once be shared with others and sustained through society.
The system excludes community without affective, juridical, and material mediations, because people do not for the most part live from Reason alone.
Necessity of Nature → conatus and Desires → distinction of actions from adequate cognition and passions from inadequate cognition.
Rational actions → good as rational life → perfection of the intellect → blessedness as cognitive acquiescence.
Superior external power + bondage to affects → diminution of freedom → necessity of contrary affects, fortitude, and vigilance.
Rational self-preservation → common good → friendship, gratitude, trust → exclusion of malicious deceit.
Common utility + affective plurality of human beings → civil right, justice, love, and generosity → greater freedom in the State.
Complex body + necessity of external things → use of Nature, reciprocal service, and money → moderation of Desire and Joy.
Inevitable events beyond human power → knowledge of necessity → acquiescence of the Mind in the order of the whole of Nature.
Perfect hypothetical freedom → fortitude in dangers → prudence concerning the benefits of ignorant persons → gratitude and trust among free persons → civil freedom greater than solitude.
Necessary conatus → action/passion → good as rational life → preservation of body and Mind → society, right, and economy → moderation of affects → acquiescence in the necessity of Nature.
Freedom is transferred from the figure of private choice to a mode of acting constituted by Reason, common laws, and useful relations.
Timely flight is reclassified from the genus of timidity into that of fortitude, if it is chosen with the same presence of mind as combat.
Benefit, gratitude, and ingratitude are transferred from a simple moral code to an affective, rational, and social structure requiring distinction.
The State is not opposed to freedom; a rationally ordered State becomes the means through which individual freedom is actually made greater.
Social affects are divided into those that increase faithful concord and those that merely feign the appearance of concord through fear, solicitation, bondage, or sadness.
The body, external things, nourishment, labor, and money are not extrinsic adjuncts, but constitute the cognitive and social conditions of rational life.
The necessity of Nature no longer appears as a fate extrinsic to freedom, but as an order to which the finite intellect, by assenting, exercises relative freedom.
Surface — The text sets out rules concerning dangers, benefits, gratitude, trust, the State, marriage, modesty, money, and the endurance of events.
Structural — These rules proceed from the distinction between action and passion, from the superiority of external causes, and from bodily and social interdependence.
Metastrategic — The text transforms moral struggle into an art of ordering affects, establishing trust, reconciling love, and constructing the conditions of cooperation.

Ontological/Temporal — A human being is a part of necessarily ordered Nature; affect values present sweetness above the future, whereas Reason, understanding necessity, seeks stable acquiescence of the Mind.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the principal sequence: necessity of Nature, adequacy, action and passion, rational utility, civil society, and acquiescence.
The system's strongest connection is the transition from affective impotence to the necessity of rational cooperation: a finite human being can be preserved stably neither alone nor by deceit.

The figure of the perfectly free human being remains at once the norm of the argument and a false hypothesis; the transition from this hypothetical limit to the actually gradually free human being is not fully formalized.
The system makes the State a means of freedom, but does not fully resolve here the distinction between a State living by common decree and a State in fact governed by fear or Desire.

The right to use external things is broadly defined, while its moderation through rational utility is affirmed; the criterion by which individual and common utility are to be reconciled in a case of conflict is not explained.
The text posits that affects must be restrained by affects, but the concrete force by which Reason produces an effective contrary affect is here presupposed rather than demonstrated.
Good and evil vanish in the figure of the perfectly free human being, but remain necessary in the account of finite life; the distinction of perspectives is implied but not explicitly systematized.
The reconstruction preserves the true movement, because it proceeds from the ideal of freedom to fortitude, society, material conditions, and finally to the understood necessity of Nature.

identity.title: Pars quarta - De servitute humana seu de affectuum viribus · passage 5

units.title: Pars quinta - De potentia intellectus seu de libertate humana · passage 1

items.text: Libertas humana quaeritur non ut imperium voluntatis absolutum in affectus, sed ut mensura qua Mens, per Rationem, minus ab affectibus patitur et eos moderatur.
Argumentatio polemica opinionem Stoicam et Cartesianam dissolvit, quia voluntas neque causam claram neque potentiam mensurabilem habet qua motus Corporis et passiones absolute regat.
Potentia Mentis in sola intelligentia reponitur; ideo affectus non voluntate reprimendi, sed ordine idearum reformandi sunt.
Cognitio clara, intellectus necessitatis, et affectuum ad causas plurimas ordinatio passivitatem minuunt atque affectus rationales stabiliores faciunt.
Ordinatio imaginum et memoria praeceptorum vitae efficiunt ut Mens affectus futuros anticipet, eosque ad actiones rationales et laetitiam dirigat.
Omnes Corporis affectiones ad ideam Dei referri possunt; ex intellectu sui affectuum nascitur Amor Dei, dum Deus ipse omni passione et amore reciproco caret.
Motus ad enuntiationem pervenit qua nemo Deum odio habere potest, sed demonstratio huius termini in fonte dato nondum exhibetur.
Mentis potentia sola intelligentia definitur, id est cogitatione et formatione idearum adaequatarum.
Ordo et concatenatio idearum in Mente ordine et concatenationi affectionum Corporis respondent.
Affectus, quatenus passio est, idea confusa est; clara et distincta idea eius facit ut, quatenus ad Mentem refertur, passio esse desinat.
Omnis Corporis affectio aliquem conceptum clarum et distinctum involvit; ideo omnis affectus saltem ex parte clare intelligi potest.
Amor et Odium constant Laetitia vel Tristitia cum idea causae externae; remoto illo nexu causali, forma eorum destruitur.
Res simpliciter vel libera imaginata affectum maximum excitat, quia causae quibus determinatur ignorantur.
Mens, quatenus res ut necessarias et infinito causarum nexu determinatas intelligit, minus ab affectibus patitur.
Affectus ex Ratione ortus ad proprietates communes semper praesentes refertur et ideo affectibus temporalibus contrariis stabilior est.
Affectus a pluribus causis simul concurrentibus excitatus fortior est.
Affectus ad plures causas vel obiecta relatus Mentem minus impedit, minus passivam facit, et erga singulas causas minus intense afficit.
Imago pluribus imaginibus coniuncta frequentius excitatur; imagines ad res clare intellectas pertinentes facilius in tales nexus ingrediuntur.
Dum affectus naturae contrarii Mentem non impediunt, Mens Corporis affectiones secundum ordinem ad intellectum ordinare et concatenare potest.
Praecepta vitae memoriae mandata et imaginibus rerum particularium adiuncta parant affectus rationales ad occursus futuros.
Mens omnes Corporis affectiones ad ideam Dei referre potest.
Clara cognitio sui et affectuum Laetitiam cum idea Dei producit, atque hinc Amorem Dei; quia hic Amor omnibus affectionibus iungitur, Mentem maxime occupat.
Deus expers est passionum, nec proprie loquendo amat aut odio habet.
Eadem Cupiditas passio est si ex ideis inadaequatis oritur, virtus autem si ex ideis adaequatis generatur.
Libertas non est imperium absolutum voluntatis in affectus.
Mens non explicatur ut res a Corpore separata quae glandulam pinealem voluntate moveat et sic passiones mechanice regat.
Remedium affectuum non est ars medica Corporis neque ars perficiendi Intellectum, sed cognitio qua Mens affectus intelligit et ordinat.
Affectus non est vis caeca cognitioni penitus externa, quia omnis affectus conceptum clarum et distinctum involvere dicitur.
Affectuum imminutio non procedit ex rerum contingentia vel libertate imaginata, sed ex intellectu necessitatis earum.
Moderatio affectuum non consistit in contemplatione vitiorum, obtrectatione hominum, aut falsa specie libertatis.
Amor Dei non est relatio reciproca inter Deum passibilem et hominem, quia Deus neque Laetitia neque Tristitia, amore neque odio afficitur.
Cognitio affectus passivitatem minuit, quia affectus quatenus clare intelligitur desinit esse passio, et nullus affectus omnino cognitioni clarae subtrahitur.
Amor, Odium, et fluctuationes ex eis ortae dissolvi possunt, si affectus ab idea causae externae segregatur et veris cogitationibus coniungitur.
Intellectus necessitatis transformat dolorem rerum singularium amissarum, quia impedit ne res ut vitium Naturae, iniuria, vel casus evitabilis imaginetur.
Affectus rationalis, quia ad communia semper praesentia refertur, affectibus contrariis externis non continuo sustentatis paulatim dominatur.

Architectura affectuum tres operationes distinguit: concursus causarum affectum auget, distributio eius inter plura obiecta noxam minuit, et multiplicatio nexuum imaginativorum eius frequentiam auget.
Praemeditatio praeceptorum rationalium fit dispositio corporalis et imaginativa, quia ideae memoriter firmatae affectiones Corporis secundum intellectum concatenant.
Eadem actio vel Cupiditas non ex obiecto suo, sed ex genere ideae a qua oritur, ut passio aut virtus classificanda est.
Amor Dei fit affectus maxime occupans, quia omnis affectio Corporis ad Deum referri potest et sic plures causae eundem amorem fovent.
Libert as non est imminutio causalitatis, sed imminutio passivitatis per reordinationem idearum, affectionum Corporis, memoriae, et imaginum.
Necessitas Naturae non parit fatalismum, sed rationem praevidendi et mitigandi affectus, quia intellectus causarum imminutam passivitatem cum praeparatione practica coniungit.
Ethica affectuum transit a iudicio de obiectis desideratis ad iudicium de causis ideationalibus ex quibus desiderium generatur.
Praxis rationalis non tantum affectus hostiles reprimit, sed laetitiam, virtutes, utilitatem communem, et imagines bonorum ita multiplicat ut contrarii affectus minus locum obtineant.
Theologia affectiva fit asymmetrica: Mens Deum amat quia affectus suos intelligit, sed Deus nec amorem nec odium erga homines habet.
Falsum esse debet affectum esse residuum cognitioni impervium; aliter cognitio clara passionem mutare non posset.
Falsum esse debet Mentem posse extra ordinem causarum stare atque voluntate nuda Corpore imperare.
Falsum esse debet desideria per se virtutes aut vitia esse; eorum status ex adaequatione vel inadaequatione causae mentis pendet.
Falsum esse debet necessitatem rerum omnem agendi potentiam destruere; eadem necessitas intellecta affectus mitigat et ordinationem rationalem permittit.
Falsum esse debet Deum affectibus humanis analogis moveri; aliter Amor Dei in mutuam passionum commutationem redigeretur.
Excluditur possibilitas libertatis ut absolutae autonomia singularis, quia Mentis imperium in affectus ex parte tantum obtinet et condicionibus conflictus affectivi subiacet.
Excluditur punctum extra seriem causarum ex quo homo affectus suos libere eligere possit; cognitio liberans ipsa intellectus ordinis necessarii est.
Excluditur forma religionis in qua Deus responderet odio, amore, praemio, aut offensa; relatio ad Deum est ordinatio Mentis, non mutua affectio Dei.
Ignorantia causarum → res ut simpliciter libera imaginatur → affectus maximus excitatur.
Affectus confusus cum idea causae externae → passio, Amor, Odium, et fluctuationes animi producuntur.
Conceptus clarus affectus + intellectus necessitatis → imminutio passivitatis et imminutio affectus erga causam singularem.
Ordo idearum → ordo affectionum Corporis → nexus imaginum rationalium → memoria praeceptorum → responsio affectiva praeparata.
Cupiditas ex idea inadaequata → passio; eadem Cupiditas ex idea adaequata → actio sive virtus.
Omnes affectiones ad ideam Dei referuntur → Amor Dei omnibus affectibus fovetur → Mens maxime occupatur, sine reciproca Dei passione.

Imperium voluntatis absolutum negatur → potentia Mentis in intelligentia collocatur → affectus ut ideae confusae intelliguntur → cognitio clara et necessitatis passivitatem minuit → imagines et praecepta in ordinem rationalem concatenantur → Amor Dei universaliter fovetur → impassibilitas Dei relationem theologicam non reciprocam constituit.
Amor Dei maxime occupans → enuntiatio impossibilitatis odii erga Deum, cuius demonstratio in segmento dato suspenditur.
Affectus reclassificatur ut structura ideationalis et corporalis ordinabilis, non ut impetus voluntati extrinsecus oppositus.
Libertas reclassificatur ut graduata imminutio passivitatis, non ut exemptio a necessitate causarum.
Distinctio passionis et virtutis transfertur ab obiecto Cupiditatis ad originem eius in ideis inadaequatis vel adaequatis.
Memoria, imaginatio, et habitus fiunt instrumenta Rationis, quia nexus imaginum affectus futuros vel fovent vel moderantur.
Amor Dei describitur ut effectus cognitionis universalis et nexus affectuum, non ut commercium cum Deo affective respondente.
Surface — Quaeritur quomodo affectus coerceri, moderari, et ad actiones vitae dirig i possint.
Structural — Mechanismus operatur per correspondentiam ordinis idearum et affectionum Corporis, per claritatem idearum, et per concatenationem imaginum in memoria.
Metastrategic — Certamen contra affectus transfertur a repulsione negativa ad praeoccupationem imaginativam per dogmata vitae, virtutes, Laetitiam, et cognitionem veri utilis.
Ontological/Temporal — Rerum necessitas, concatenatio infinita causarum, constantia proprietatum communium, et impassibilitas Dei determinant condiciones sub quibus libertas graduata intelligitur.
Axiomata sufficiunt ad restituendum nucleum argumenti: Mentis potentia est intelligentia, affectus passivus est cognitio confusa, et libertas est imminutio passivitatis per ordinationem rationalem.
Commissura firmissima est nexus inter ideam claram, intellectum necessitatis, et imminutam vim affectuum, quia hic nexus doctrinam, remedium, et praxim simul sustinet.

Commissura fragilis manet inter propositionem quod omnis affectio aliquem conceptum clarum involvat et conclusionem quod affectus ipse clare et distincte intelligi possit; quantitas cognitionis requisitae non plene determinatur.

Tensio interna inter augmentum affectus per plures causas et imminutam noxam affectus ad plures causas relati servanda est; textus eam distinguit per concursus causalis, distributionem obiectivam, et frequentiam imaginativam, sed distinctionem formaliter non universaliter explicat.
Imperium Mentis non est absolutum: exercitium ordinationis valet dum affectus naturae contrarii Mentem non impediunt, et cognitio affectuum saepe tantum ex parte obtinetur.

Transitus ad Amorem Dei nititur principio importato quo omnes affectiones ad ideam Dei referri possunt; intra segmentum datum haec relatio asseritur et demonstratur per remissum ad Partem I, non ex novo fundamento evolvitur.
Enuntiatio finalis de impossibilitate odii erga Deum motum argumenti claudit, sed restitutio demonstrativa eius non potest compleri, quia demonstratio Prop. XVIII in fonte dato interrompitur.

translations.title: Part Five - On the Power of the Intellect, or on Human Freedom · passage 1

items.text: Human freedom is sought not as the absolute dominion of the will over the affects, but as the measure by which the Mind, through Reason, suffers less from the affects and moderates them.

The polemical argument dismantles the Stoic and Cartesian opinion, because the will has neither a clear cause nor a measurable power by which it absolutely governs the motions of the Body and the passions.
The power of the Mind is situated in understanding alone; therefore affects are to be reformed not by the will, but by the ordering of ideas.
Clear knowledge, understanding of necessity, and the ordering of affects according to a plurality of causes diminish passivity and render rational affects more stable.
The ordering of images and the memory of precepts of life bring it about that the Mind anticipates future affects and directs them toward rational actions and joy.
All affections of the Body can be referred to the idea of God; from understanding oneself and one's affects there arises the Love of God, while God himself lacks every passion and reciprocal love.
The movement arrives at the proposition that no one can hate God, but the demonstration of this conclusion is not yet presented in the given source.
The power of the Mind is defined by understanding alone, that is, by thought and the formation of adequate ideas.
The order and connection of ideas in the Mind correspond to the order and connection of the affections of the Body.
An affect, insofar as it is a passion, is a confused idea; a clear and distinct idea of it makes it, insofar as it is referred to the Mind, cease to be a passion.
Every affection of the Body involves some clear and distinct conception; therefore every affect can at least in part be clearly understood.
Love and Hate consist in Joy or Sadness together with the idea of an external cause; once that causal connection is removed, their form is destroyed.
A thing imagined simply as free excites the greatest affect, because the causes by which it is determined are unknown.
The Mind, insofar as it understands things as necessary and determined by an infinite nexus of causes, suffers less from the affects.
An affect arising from Reason is referred to common properties that are always present and is therefore more stable than contrary temporal affects.
An affect excited by several simultaneously concurrent causes is stronger.
An affect referred to several causes or objects impedes the Mind less, makes it less passive, and affects it less intensely toward each individual cause.
An image joined to several images is excited more frequently; images pertaining to things clearly understood enter such connections more easily.
So long as affects contrary in nature do not impede the Mind, the Mind can order and connect the affections of the Body according to an order directed toward understanding.
Precepts of life committed to memory and joined to images of particular things prepare rational affects for future occurrences.
The Mind can refer all affections of the Body to the idea of God.
Clear knowledge of oneself and one's affects produces Joy together with the idea of God, and hence the Love of God; because this Love is joined to all affections, it most greatly occupies the Mind.
God is devoid of passions, and, properly speaking, neither loves nor hates.
The same Desire is a passion if it arises from inadequate ideas, but a virtue if it is generated from adequate ideas.
Freedom is not the absolute dominion of the will over the affects.
The Mind is not explained as a thing separate from the Body that moves the pineal gland by the will and thus mechanically governs the passions.
The remedy for the affects is neither the medical art of the Body nor the art of perfecting the Intellect, but the knowledge by which the Mind understands and orders the affects.
An affect is not a blind force wholly external to knowledge, because every affect is said to involve a clear and distinct conception.
The diminution of affects does not proceed from imagined contingency or freedom of things, but from the understanding of their necessity.
The moderation of affects does not consist in contemplation of vices, detraction of persons, or a false appearance of freedom.
The Love of God is not a reciprocal relation between a passible God and a human being, because God is affected neither by Joy nor by Sadness, neither by love nor by hate.
Knowledge of an affect diminishes passivity, because an affect, insofar as it is clearly understood, ceases to be a passion, and no affect is wholly excluded from clear knowledge.
Love, Hate, and the fluctuations arising from them can be dissolved if the affect is separated from the idea of an external cause and joined to true thoughts.
Understanding necessity transforms the pain of lost singular things, because it prevents one from imagining a thing as a defect of Nature, an injury, or an avoidable accident.
A rational affect, because it is referred to common things always present, gradually prevails over contrary external affects not continuously sustained.

The architecture of affects distinguishes three operations: the concurrence of causes increases an affect, its distribution among several objects diminishes its harm, and the multiplication of imaginative connections increases its frequency.
Premeditation of rational precepts becomes a bodily and imaginative disposition, because ideas firmly retained in memory connect the affections of the Body according to understanding.
The same action or Desire is to be classified as a passion or a virtue not from its object, but from the kind of idea from which it arises.
The Love of God becomes the affect that most occupies, because every affection of the Body can be referred to God and thus several causes foster the same love.
Freedom is not a diminution of causality, but a diminution of passivity through the reordering of ideas, affections of the Body, memory, and images.
The necessity of Nature does not produce fatalism, but a means of foreseeing and mitigating affects, because the understanding of causes joins diminished passivity with practical preparation.
The ethics of affects passes from judgment concerning desired objects to judgment concerning the ideational causes from which desire is generated.
Rational practice not only represses hostile affects, but multiplies joy, virtues, common utility, and images of goods in such a way that contrary affects have less room.
Affective theology becomes asymmetrical: the Mind loves God because it understands its affects, but God has neither love nor hate toward human beings.
It must be false that an affect is a residue impervious to knowledge; otherwise clear knowledge could not transform passion.
It must be false that the Mind can stand outside the order of causes and command the Body by bare will.
It must be false that desires are in themselves virtues or vices; their status depends on the adequacy or inadequacy of the cause in the mind.
It must be false that the necessity of things destroys every power of acting; that same necessity, when understood, mitigates affects and permits rational ordering.
It must be false that God is moved by affects analogous to human ones; otherwise the Love of God would be reduced to a mutual exchange of passions.

The possibility of freedom as the absolute autonomy of the individual is excluded, because the Mind's dominion over the affects obtains only in part and is subject to the conditions of affective conflict.
A point outside the series of causes from which a human being could freely choose his affects is excluded; liberating knowledge itself is understanding of the necessary order.
A form of religion in which God would respond with hate, love, reward, or offense is excluded; the relation to God is an ordering of the Mind, not a mutual affection of God.
Ignorance of causes → a thing is imagined as simply free → the greatest affect is excited.
Confused affect together with the idea of an external cause → passion, Love, Hate, and fluctuations of mind are produced.
Clear conception of an affect + understanding of necessity → diminution of passivity and diminution of the affect toward a singular cause.
Order of ideas → order of affections of the Body → nexus of rational images → memory of precepts → prepared affective response.
Desire from an inadequate idea → passion; the same Desire from an adequate idea → action or virtue.
All affections are referred to the idea of God → the Love of God is fostered by all affects → the Mind is most greatly occupied, without reciprocal divine passion.

Absolute dominion of the will is denied → the power of the Mind is located in understanding → affects are understood as confused ideas → clear knowledge and understanding of necessity diminish passivity → images and precepts are connected into a rational order → the Love of God is universally fostered → the impassibility of God establishes a non-reciprocal theological relation.
The Love of God most occupying → proposition of the impossibility of hatred toward God, the demonstration of which is suspended in the given segment.
An affect is reclassified as an orderable ideational and bodily structure, not as an impulse extrinsically opposed to the will.
Freedom is reclassified as a graduated diminution of passivity, not as exemption from the necessity of causes.
The distinction between passion and virtue is transferred from the object of Desire to its origin in inadequate or adequate ideas.
Memory, imagination, and habit become instruments of Reason, because connections of images either foster or moderate future affects.
The Love of God is described as an effect of universal knowledge and the nexus of affects, not as commerce with an affectively responsive God.
Surface — It is asked how affects can be restrained, moderated, and directed toward the actions of life.
Structural — The mechanism operates through the correspondence of the order of ideas and affections of the Body, through the clarity of ideas, and through the connection of images in memory.
Metastrategic — The contest against affects is transferred from negative repulsion to imaginative preoccupation through doctrines of life, virtues, Joy, and knowledge of the true useful.

Ontological/Temporal — The necessity of things, the infinite connection of causes, the constancy of common properties, and the impassibility of God determine the conditions under which graduated freedom is understood.

The axioms suffice to reconstruct the core of the argument: the power of the Mind is understanding, a passive affect is confused knowledge, and freedom is the diminution of passivity through rational ordering.
The strongest joint is the nexus between a clear idea, understanding of necessity, and the diminished force of affects, because this nexus simultaneously sustains doctrine, remedy, and practice.

A fragile joint remains between the proposition that every affection involves some clear conception and the conclusion that the affect itself can be clearly and distinctly understood; the quantity of knowledge required is not fully determined.

The internal tension between the increase of an affect through several causes and the diminished harm of an affect referred to several causes must be retained; the text distinguishes it through causal concurrence, objective distribution, and imaginative frequency, but does not formally explain the distinction universally.
The dominion of the Mind is not absolute: the exercise of ordering is effective so long as affects contrary in nature do not impede the Mind, and knowledge of affects is often obtained only in part.

The transition to the Love of God rests on the imported principle that all affections can be referred to the idea of God; within the given segment this relation is asserted and demonstrated by reference back to Part I, not developed from a new foundation.

The final proposition concerning the impossibility of hatred toward God closes the movement of the argument, but its demonstrative reconstruction cannot be completed, because the demonstration of Prop. XVIII is interrupted in the given source.

identity.title: Pars quinta - De potentia intellectus seu de libertate humana · passage 1

units.title: Pars quinta - De potentia intellectus seu de libertate humana · passage 2

items.text: Textus potentiam Mentis adversus affectus et libertatem quaerit, distinguens id quod tempori et Corpori adstrictum est ab eo quod Mentis essentiae aeternum manet.
Argumentatio demonstrativa et reconstructiva affectuum remedia ex gradu cognitionis derivat, non ex voluntaria affectuum repressione.
Idea Dei adaequata primum amorem divinum ab odio, tristitia, invidia et zelotypia segregat.
Potentia Mentis dein ad proportionem idearum adaequatarum et inadaequatarum reducitur atque per ordinationem affectuum explicatur.
Imaginatio, memoria et passiones ad durationem Corporis referuntur; essentia Corporis in Deo concepta ad aeternitatem Mentis refertur.
Cognitio tertii generis ex aeternitate Mentis procedens summam laetitiam et Amorem Dei intellectualem producit.
Amor intellectualis ut pars amoris infiniti Dei libertatem, beatitudinem, imminutam mortis metum et maiorem Mentis partem aeternam constituit.
Contemplatio Dei ex idea in nobis adaequata est actio Mentis cui tristitia non concomitatur.
Deus, qui a finito amatur, ex humana cupiditate in naturam mutabilem vel non-divinam transire non potest.
Amor rationalis erga Deum est summum bonum omnibus commune et per imaginationem gaudii communis augetur.
Vis affectus ex comparatione causae externae cum nostra, potentia Mentis ex sola cognitione, passio autem ex cognitionis privatione definitur.
Mens cognitione affectus a confusa cogitatione causae externae separat eosque secundum ordinem intellectus ordinare et concatenare potest.
Affectus ad res intellectas, proprietates communes vel Deum relati, pluribus causis fulti, affectus ex cognitione confusa ortos superant.
Imaginatio, memoria, conceptio rerum sub duratione et passiones ad actualem Corporis existentiam pertinent.
In Deo necessario datur idea essentiae cuiusque Corporis humani, quae ad essentiam Mentis humanae pertinet et aeterna est.
Tertium cognitionis genus procedit ab idea adaequata attributorum Dei ad cognitionem adaequatam essentiarum rerum singularium.
Cupiditas res tertio cognitionis genere cognoscendi ex primo cognitionis genere oriri non potest, sed ex secundo oritur.
Mens, quatenus aeternam Corporis essentiam concipit, Dei cognitionem habet et causa formalis cognitionis tertii generis est.
Ex cognitione tertii generis oritur summa Mentis laetitia cum idea Dei tamquam causae.
Amor Dei intellectualis, qui ex tertio cognitionis genere oritur, est aeternus.
Amor intellectualis Mentis erga Deum pars est amoris infiniti quo Deus se ipsum amat.
Nihil in Natura datur quod Amori Dei intellectuali contrarium sit aut eum tollere possit.
Quo Mens plura secundo et tertio cognitionis genere intelligit, eo minus ab affectibus malis patitur et eo minus mortem timet.
Corpus plurimis actionibus aptum Mentem disponit ad affectiones secundum intellectum ordinandas et ad maiorem Mentis partem aeternam constituendam.
Tristitia cum idea Dei consistere non potest; ideo Deus odio haberi nequit et Amor erga Deum in odium verti nequit.
Amor Dei non includit conatum ut Deus amantem contra amet, quia talis cupiditas Deum non-Deum esse vellet.
Amor Dei rationalis nec invidia nec zelotypia inquinatur, quia summum bonum commune non per participationem minuitur.
Cognitio clara et distincta passiones non necessario omnes absolute tollit; eas tamen minimam Mentis partem efficit.
Mens sine Corpore nihil imaginari, rerum praeteritarum recordari aut passionibus obnoxia esse potest.
Aeternitas per durationem explicari neque ad tempus referri potest.
Cognitio mutilata et confusa primi generis cupiditatem cognitionis tertii generis gignere non potest.
Nullus Amor praeter Amorem intellectualem aeternus est.
Nullum verum contrarium Amori intellectuali dari potest, quia eius destructio veritatem in falsitatem converteret.
Idea Dei adaequata Deum ab obiecto tristitiae et odii in obiectum actionis et amoris convertit.
Qui Deum amat, non potest desiderare ut Deus ipsum reciproce amet, quia amor iste mutationem divinae naturae postularet.
Communicatio Amoris Dei non est imminutio boni sed causa incrementi amoris; plures homines eodem bono fruentes amorem unius augent.
Magnitudo affectus non per se indicat potentiam Mentis, quia affectuum conflictus a viribus externis, Mentis actio autem ab ideis adaequatis aestimatur.
Animi aegritudines ex nimio amore rerum mutabilium et incompossibilium oriuntur; cognitio causalis affectus reordinat, et Amor in rem immutabilem atque vere possidendam transfert.
Cum Corpore desinunt imaginatio, memoria et passiones; manet tamen id Mentis quod per aeternam ideam essentiae Corporis in Deo concipitur.
Actualitas bifariam concipitur: vel sub certo tempore et loco, vel in Deo ex necessitate divinae naturae; sola secunda conceptio res sub specie aeternitatis exhibet.
Quo Mens aptior est cognitioni tertii generis, eo magis res eodem cognitionis genere cognoscere cupit; progressio eius ab adequate cognito procedit, non ex confusione.
Cognitio rerum singularium tertio genere Mentem efficacius afficit quam cognitio universalis secundi generis, quia ex ipsa singulari essentia dependentia a Deo concipitur.
Cognitio tertii generis summam laetitiam producit, quae cum idea Dei causae Amorem Dei intellectualem constituit atque aeternitatem eius sequitur.
Amor intellectualis Mentis erga Deum et Amor Dei erga homines idem Amor sunt, quatenus infinitus amor divinus per essentiam Mentis humanae explicatur.
Amor intellectualis, quia ex veritate aeterna necessario sequitur, non ab affectu contrario destrui potest; amoribus imaginativis et corporalibus sola temporalitas competit.
Incrementum cognitionis adaequatae et aptitudo Corporis ad plura agendum minuunt passiones malas, mortis metum et proportionem Mentis pereuntem.
Libertas non est exemptio a causalitate neque vacuitas affectuum, sed stabilis praevalentia actionum cognitivae originis super passiones ex ideis inadaequatis ortas.
Aeternitas Mentis non est proprietas indivisa totius personae empiricae, sed proportio eius quod Mentem ad essentiam aeternam referentem constituit.
Summum bonum rationaliter intellectum structuram non-rivalem habet: communicatio eius non divisionem inducit, sed causam sui incrementi.
Cognitio intuitiva rerum singularium non est applicatio secundaria universalis cognitionis, sed locus in quo dependentia divina affective efficax fit.
Corpus non est simplex impedimentum aeternitatis, sed condicio strategica qua Mens ad ordinationem affectionum et ad maiorem partem aeternam disponitur.
Falsum esse debet libertatem consistere in imperio voluntatis quod omnes affectus omnino exstinguat; systema libertatem in mutatione proportionis inter actionem et passionem ponit.
Falsum esse debet aeternitatem esse continuationem memoriae, imaginationis aut narrationis personalis post mortem; haec omnia ad durationem Corporis pertinent.
Falsum esse debet Deum esse alterum externum, cuius amor reciproce petitur aut cui tristitia passive imputatur; Deus intelligitur causa immanens, non obiectum mutuae negotiationis affectivae.
Falsum esse debet omnes cognitionis gradus aequaliter ad cognitionem intuitivam ducere; primum genus est structuraliter sterile respectu cupiditatis tertii generis.
Falsum esse debet beatitudinem esse bonum scarce distributum, cuius participatio alterius felicitatem minuere possit.
Praecluditur subiectum finitum extra Deum subsistens, quod Deum tamquam obiectum extrinsecum amet; Amor intellectualis est determinatio amoris divini ipsius.
Praecluditur mensura temporalis qua aeternitas, salus aut beatitudo aestimari possint; principium, duratio et recordatio ad ordinem aeternum non transferuntur.
Praecluditur possibilitas ut veritas aeterna actionis intellectualis per vim oppositam naturalem annihiletur; destructio amoris intellectualis falsitatem veri postularet.
Idea inadaequata + imaginatio Corporis sub duratione + amor rei mutabilis → passio, anxietas, conflictus et vulnerabilitas affectiva.
Cognitio causae + separatio ab externo confuse imaginato + ordinatio affectionum → imminutio passionis et praevalentia actionis Mentis.
Actualitas Corporis temporalis / essentia Corporis in Deo aeterna → distinctio memoriae pereuntis et partis Mentis aeternae.
Mens quatenus aeterna → cognitio Dei → cognitio tertii generis → summa laetitia → Amor Dei intellectualis aeternus.
Amor intellectualis ut pars amoris Dei + absentia contrarii → beatitudo stabilis, imminutio mortis metus et libertas affectiva.
Aptitudo Corporis ad plura agendum → ordinatio plurium affectionum → relatio earum ad ideam Dei → maior pars Mentis aeterna.
Idea Dei adaequata → actio sine tristitia → impossibilitas odii et conversionis Amoris Dei in odium.
Summum bonum commune → imminutio invidiae et zelotypiae → Amor Dei per participationem aliorum auctus.
Potentia ut cognitio → remedia per cognitionem causalem et ordinationem affectuum → imminutio passionum, non absoluta earum abolitio.
Corpus durans → imaginatio et memoria temporales; essentia Corporis in Deo → pars Mentis aeterna.
Mens aeterna → tertium cognitionis genus → summa laetitia → Amor Dei intellectualis aeternus.
Amor intellectualis ut amor divinus partialiter explicatus → nulla destructio contraria → beatitudo, libertas et imminutio mortis metus.
Affectus a scala intensitatis psychologicae ad proportionem inter causas externas, cognitionem adaequatam et cognitionis privationem reclassificantur.
Actualitas dividitur in actualitatem temporalem imaginabilem et actualitatem aeternam in Deo conceptam.
Amor Dei ab amore reciproco, possessivo et rivalitario ad laetitiam intellectualem causae divinae refertur.
Genera cognitionis in structuram asymmetricam disponuntur: primum genus tertium non generat, secundum transitum aperit, tertium essentias singulares intuetur.
Corpus ab altero aeternitatis ad instrumentum dispositionis Mentis reclassificatur.
Surface — Deus odio haberi nequit, Amor Dei intellectualis aeternus est, et Mens quatenus Corpus actu durat imaginatur atque recordatur.
Structural — Potentia Mentis ex cognitione, passio ex ideis inadaequatis, et remedia ex causali affectuum reordinatione oriuntur.
Metastrategic — Libertatis quaestio a dominio voluntario affectuum ad productionem actionum intellectualium et ad mutationem proportionis Mentis reconstituitur.
Ontological/Temporal — Duratio pertinet ad existentiam actualem Corporis, aeternitas ad essentiam eius in Deo conceptam, et Amor intellectualis ad ordinem aeternum huius essentiae.
Systema extractum argumentationem restituit, si definitiones externae idearum adaequatarum, passionis, conatus et generum cognitionis iam concessae sunt.
Catena firmissima est nexus inter ideam Dei adaequatam, actionem Mentis, cognitionem tertii generis, laetitiam et Amorem intellectualem aeternum.
Compressio relinquit indeterminatum quomodo notiones adaequationis, inadaequationis et causae formalis intra hunc locum sola constitui possint, quia textus eas ex Partibus prioribus accipit.
Commissura fragilis manet inter absentiam memoriae ante Corpus et assertionem quod nos aeternos sentimus ac experimur; transitio a demonstratione ad experientiam hic non independenter mechanizatur.

Tensio temporalis manet inter Amorem intellectualem sine principio et narrationem qua Mens paulatim aptior ad cognitionem tertii generis fit; textus hanc tensionem per fictionem expositionis temporalis administrat, non removet.

Commissura inter aptitudinem Corporis et maiorem partem Mentis aeternam pendet a longa catena ordinationis affectionum, relationis ad Deum et amoris crescentis, cuius nexus non hic separatim demonstratur.
Restitutio motum textus servat: remedia affectuum → distinctio durationis et aeternitatis → cognitio intuitiva → Amor Dei intellectualis → libertas et imminutio mortis metus.

translations.title: Part Five - On the Power of the Intellect, or on Human Freedom · passage 2

items.text: The text investigates the power of the Mind over the affects and freedom, distinguishing what is bound to time and the Body from what remains eternal to the essence of the Mind.
Demonstrative and reconstructive argument derives remedies for the affects from the degree of knowledge, not from voluntary repression of the affects.
An adequate idea of God first separates divine love from hatred, sadness, envy, and jealousy.
The power of the Mind is then reduced to the proportion of adequate and inadequate ideas and explained through the ordering of the affects.
Imagination, memory, and passions are referred to the duration of the Body; the essence of the Body conceived in God is referred to the eternity of the Mind.
Knowledge of the third kind, proceeding from the eternity of the Mind, produces the highest joy and the intellectual Love of God.
Intellectual Love, as a part of God's infinite love, constitutes freedom, blessedness, diminished fear of death, and the greater eternal part of the Mind.
Contemplation of God from an adequate idea in us is an action of the Mind not accompanied by sadness.
God, who is loved by a finite being, cannot, through human desire, pass into a mutable or non-divine nature.
Rational love toward God is the highest good common to all and is increased through the imagination of common joy.
The force of an affect is defined by comparison of the external cause with our own, the power of the Mind by knowledge alone, and passion by the privation of knowledge.
By knowledge the Mind separates an affect from the confused thought of an external cause and can order and connect affects according to the order of the intellect.
Affects referred to things understood, common properties, or God, supported by several causes, overcome affects arising from confused knowledge.
Imagination, memory, the conception of things under duration, and passions pertain to the actual existence of the Body.
In God there is necessarily given an idea of the essence of each human Body, which pertains to the essence of the human Mind and is eternal.
The third kind of knowledge proceeds from an adequate idea of God's attributes to the adequate knowledge of the essences of singular things.
The desire to know things by the third kind of knowledge cannot arise from the first kind of knowledge, but arises from the second.
The Mind, insofar as it conceives the eternal essence of the Body, has knowledge of God and is the formal cause of knowledge of the third kind.
From knowledge of the third kind arises the Mind's highest joy, together with the idea of God as cause.
The intellectual Love of God, which arises from the third kind of knowledge, is eternal.
The intellectual Love of the Mind toward God is a part of the infinite love by which God loves himself.
Nothing is given in Nature that is contrary to the intellectual Love of God or can remove it.
The more the Mind understands by the second and third kinds of knowledge, the less it suffers from evil affects and the less it fears death.
A Body suited to very many actions disposes the Mind to order affections according to the intellect and to constitute a greater eternal part of the Mind.
Sadness cannot coexist with the idea of God; therefore God cannot be hated, and Love toward God cannot be turned into hatred.
Love of God does not include the striving that God should love the lover in return, because such desire would will God to be non-God.
Rational Love of God is polluted by neither envy nor jealousy, because the common highest good is not diminished through participation.
Clear and distinct knowledge does not necessarily abolish all passions absolutely; nevertheless, it makes them the smallest part of the Mind.
Without the Body the Mind can imagine nothing, recall past things, or be subject to passions.
Eternity can neither be explained through duration nor referred to time.
Mutilated and confused knowledge of the first kind cannot generate the desire for knowledge of the third kind.
No Love other than intellectual Love is eternal.
No truth contrary to intellectual Love can be given, because its destruction would convert truth into falsehood.
An adequate idea of God transforms God from an object of sadness and hatred into an object of action and love.
One who loves God cannot desire that God love him in return, because that love would require a change in divine nature.
The sharing of Love of God is not a diminution of good but a cause of the increase of love; more people enjoying the same good increase the love of one.

The magnitude of an affect does not in itself indicate the power of the Mind, because the conflict of affects is assessed from external forces, whereas the action of the Mind is assessed from adequate ideas.
Ailments of the mind arise from excessive love of mutable and incompatible things; causal knowledge reorders affects and transfers Love to an immutable thing that can truly be possessed.
With the Body, imagination, memory, and passions cease; yet there remains that of the Mind which is conceived through the eternal idea of the essence of the Body in God.
Actuality is conceived in two ways: either under a determinate time and place, or in God from the necessity of divine nature; only the second conception presents things under the aspect of eternity.
The more suited the Mind is to knowledge of the third kind, the more it desires to know things by the same kind of knowledge; its progress proceeds from what is adequately known, not from confusion.

Knowledge of singular things by the third kind affects the Mind more efficaciously than universal knowledge of the second kind, because from the singular essence itself dependence on God is conceived.
Knowledge of the third kind produces the highest joy, which, together with the idea of God as cause, constitutes the intellectual Love of God and entails its eternity.
The intellectual Love of the Mind toward God and God's Love toward human beings are the same Love, insofar as infinite divine love is explained through the essence of the human Mind.
Intellectual Love, because it necessarily follows from eternal truth, cannot be destroyed by a contrary affect; imaginative and bodily loves belong to temporality alone.
The increase of adequate knowledge and the aptitude of the Body for doing more things diminish evil passions, fear of death, and the perishing proportion of the Mind.
Freedom is neither exemption from causality nor emptiness of affects, but the stable predominance of actions of cognitive origin over passions arising from inadequate ideas.
The eternity of the Mind is not an undivided property of the entire empirical person, but the proportion of that which constitutes the Mind as referring to eternal essence.
The highest good, rationally understood, has a non-rivalrous structure: its sharing does not introduce division but the cause of its own increase.
Intuitive knowledge of singular things is not a secondary application of universal knowledge, but the locus in which divine dependence becomes affectively efficacious.
The Body is not a mere impediment to eternity, but a strategic condition by which the Mind is disposed to the ordering of affections and to a greater eternal part.
It must be false that freedom consists in a command of the will that wholly extinguishes all affects; the system places freedom in a change of proportion between action and passion.
It must be false that eternity is a continuation of memory, imagination, or personal narrative after death; all these pertain to the duration of the Body.

It must be false that God is an external other, whose love is reciprocally sought or to whom sadness is passively imputed; God is understood as immanent cause, not as an object of mutual affective negotiation.
It must be false that all degrees of knowledge equally lead to intuitive knowledge; the first kind is structurally sterile with respect to the desire of the third kind.
It must be false that blessedness is a scarce-distributed good, participation in which could diminish another's happiness.
A finite subject subsisting outside God, which loves God as an extrinsic object, is precluded; intellectual Love is a determination of divine love itself.
A temporal measure by which eternity, salvation, or blessedness could be assessed is precluded; beginning, duration, and recollection are not transferred to the eternal order.
The possibility that the eternal truth of intellectual action be annihilated by an opposed natural force is precluded; the destruction of intellectual Love would require the falsehood of truth.
Inadequate idea + imagination of the Body under duration + love of a mutable thing → passion, anxiety, conflict, and affective vulnerability.
Knowledge of the cause + separation from the externally and confusedly imagined + ordering of affections → diminution of passion and predominance of the Mind's action.
Temporal actuality of the Body / eternal essence of the Body in God → distinction between perishing memory and the eternal part of the Mind.
Mind insofar as eternal → knowledge of God → knowledge of the third kind → highest joy → eternal intellectual Love of God.
Intellectual Love as part of God's love + absence of a contrary → stable blessedness, diminution of fear of death, and affective freedom.
Aptitude of the Body for doing more things → ordering of more affections → their relation to the idea of God → greater eternal part of the Mind.
Adequate idea of God → action without sadness → impossibility of hatred and of the conversion of Love of God into hatred.
Common highest good → diminution of envy and jealousy → Love of God increased through the participation of others.
Power as knowledge → remedies through causal knowledge and ordering of affects → diminution of passions, not their absolute abolition.
Durable Body → temporal imagination and memory; essence of the Body in God → eternal part of the Mind.
Eternal Mind → third kind of knowledge → highest joy → eternal intellectual Love of God.
Intellectual Love as partially explained divine love → no contrary destruction → blessedness, freedom, and diminution of fear of death.
Affects are reclassified from a scale of psychological intensity to a proportion among external causes, adequate knowledge, and privation of knowledge.
Actuality is divided into imaginable temporal actuality and eternal actuality conceived in God.
Love of God is referred away from reciprocal, possessive, and rivalrous love to intellectual joy in the divine cause.
The kinds of knowledge are arranged in an asymmetric structure: the first kind does not generate the third, the second opens the transition, and the third intuits singular essences.
The Body is reclassified from the other of eternity to an instrument for disposing the Mind.
Surface — God cannot be hated, intellectual Love of God is eternal, and the Mind, insofar as the Body actually endures, imagines and remembers.
Structural — The power of the Mind arises from knowledge, passion from inadequate ideas, and remedies from the causal reordering of affects.
Metastrategic — The question of freedom is reconstituted from voluntary mastery of affects to the production of intellectual actions and to a change in the proportion of the Mind.
Ontological/Temporal — Duration pertains to the actual existence of the Body, eternity to its essence conceived in God, and intellectual Love to the eternal order of this essence.
The extracted system restores the argumentation if the external definitions of adequate ideas, passion, conatus, and the kinds of knowledge have already been granted.
The firmest chain is the connection among the adequate idea of God, the action of the Mind, knowledge of the third kind, joy, and eternal intellectual Love.
The compression leaves indeterminate how the notions of adequacy, inadequacy, and formal cause can be constituted solely within this passage, because the text receives them from the prior Parts.

A fragile joint remains between the absence of memory before the Body and the assertion that we feel and experience ourselves to be eternal; the transition from demonstration to experience is not independently mechanized here.

A temporal tension remains between intellectual Love without beginning and the narrative by which the Mind gradually becomes more suited to knowledge of the third kind; the text manages this tension through the fiction of temporal exposition, rather than removing it.

The joint between the aptitude of the Body and the greater eternal part of the Mind depends upon a long chain of ordering affections, relation to God, and increasing love, whose connection is not separately demonstrated here.

The restoration preserves the movement of the text: remedies for affects → distinction of duration and eternity → intuitive knowledge → intellectual Love of God → freedom and diminution of fear of death.

identity.title: Pars quinta - De potentia intellectus seu de libertate humana · passage 2

units.title: Pars quinta - De potentia intellectus seu de libertate humana · passage 3

items.text: Textus variationem corporis et mentis constituit ut condicionem ex qua felicitas, infelicitas et ordinatio vitae intelligendae sunt.
Capacitas corporis ad plura agendum cum ampliore mentis conscientia sui, Dei et rerum conectitur, ita ut transformatio corporis ad intellectum dirigatur.
Perfectio ex gradu agendi et imminutis passionibus definitur; hinc intellectus aeternus imaginatione pereunte perfectior demonstratur.
Fundamentum virtutis ab cognitione immortalitatis removetur et in rationali quaesitione proprii utilis collocatur.
Beatitudo non consequens disciplinae affectuum, sed amor intellectualis Dei, virtus ipsa et fons potestatis affectus coercendi constituitur.
Textus oppositionem inter ignarum externis causis et libidine actum atque sapientem ex necessitate aeterna intelligentem concludit.
Res eo perfectior est quo magis agit et quo minus patitur; perfectio, realitas et potentia agendi eundem gradum exprimunt.
Intellectus est pars mentis aeterna, imaginatio autem pars quae perire dicitur.
Mens per intellectum agit et per imaginationem patitur.
Unicum fundamentum virtutis seu recte vivendi est proprium utile ratione quaerere.
Praecepta rationis de pietate, religione, animositate et generositate ex cognitione aeternitatis mentis non dependent.
Beatitudo consistit in amore erga Deum qui ex tertio cognitionis genere oritur.
Amor intellectualis Dei, quatenus ad mentem agentem refertur, ipsa virtus est.
Quo mens beatitudine magis gaudet, eo plus intelligit, maiorem in affectus potentiam habet et minus ab affectibus malis patitur.
Corpus ad plura aptum menti respondet quae amplius sui, Dei et rerum conscia est; vita igitur ad hanc aptitudinem, quantum natura fert, ordinari potest.
Mens, quatenus intelligit, est modus cogitandi aeternus ab aliis modis aeternis in infinitum determinatus.
Virtus non definitur per spem praemii post mortem nec per metum supplicii post mortem.
Pietas, religio, animositas et generositas non sunt onera servilia quae solum compensatione ultramortali tolerari possint.
Beatitudo non est praemium virtutis neque effectus posterior coercitionis libidinum.
Libertas non est licentia libidini parendi neque imminutio iuris ex sola observantia legis externa recepta.
Pars mentis imaginativa non est locus eius perfectionis quae post corporis existentiam considerari potest.
Sapientia non consistit in evadenda necessitate, sed in eius aeternae cognitionis forma.
Pars mentis quae manet perfectior est reliqua, quia per intellectum agit, dum imaginatio peritura passionum sedes manet.
Ratio pietatem et fortitudinem exigere potest etiam sub ignorantia aeternitatis mentis, quia earum norma est utile rationale, non destinatio post mortem.
Coercitio libidinum non producit beatitudinem; beatitudo, intellectum augens, ipsam coercendi potentiam producit.
Vita rationalis non requirit oppugnationem affectuum ut finem primarium, sed incrementum intellectus ex quo imminutio passionum sequitur.
Institutio vitae tendit ad corpus aptius et mentem magis consciam, ut memoria et imaginatio respectu intellectus minorem vim obtineant.
Stabilitas animi sapientis oritur ex intellectione necessitatis, dum ignorantia externarum causarum et libidinum imperio mentem fluctuantem relinquit.
Ordo ethicus a ratione mercedis differtur ad immanentiam: virtus suum effectum constitutivum, beatitudinem, intra ipsum exercitium habet.
Ordo liberationis est epistemicus et affectivus simul: cognitio non affectibus extrinsece additur, sed potentiam activam qua affectus ordinantur efficit.
Discrimen sapientis et ignari non in possessione futuri praemii, sed in diverso modo praesentis existentiae consistit: alter agit et intelligit, alter patitur et quasi inscius vivit.
Corpus non est mera sarcina mortalitatis, sed condicio practica qua mens ad ampliorem conscientiam et ad intellectus praevalentiam disponi potest.
Identitas mentis perfectioris non cum memoria, imaginatione aut historia singulari corporis coincidit.
Bonum vivere non pendet ex promissione compensationis quae vitam praesentem post mortem iustificet.
Affectuum dominium non est actus voluntatis nudae, quia humana potentia ad eos coercendos in solo intellectu ponitur.
Externae causae, quatenus mentem passive determinant, veram animi acquiescentiam producere non possunt.
Necessitas causalis non destruit libertatem sapientis, sed arbitrium indeterminatum tamquam condicionem libertatis excludit.
Textus excludit oeconomiam moralem in qua virtus sine promisso praemio aut comminatione poenae caret ratione exercendi.
Textus excludit conceptionem libertatis ut exemptio a causatione, quia mens intelligens in serie infinita modorum aeternorum determinatur.
Textus excludit mortem corporis ut principium absolutum quo omnis esse mentis, omnis veritas vitae et omnis ratio virtutis aboleri debeant.
Variatio corporis → diversus gradus aptitudinis → diversus gradus conscientiae mentis → directio practica ad corpus aptius et intellectum praevalentem.
Perfectio-realitas → maior actio et minor passio → intellectus ut pars activa → eius perfectio prae imaginatione peritura.
Utile rationale → praecepta virtutis → independentia a doctrina immortalitatis → exclusio spei et metus ut fundamentorum moralium.
Cognitio tertii generis → amor Dei → beatitudo-virtus → augmentum intellectus → imminutio passionum et potentia coercendi libidines.
Intellectus necessitatis aeternae → imminutio agitationis → vera animi acquiescentia → figura sapientis contra ignorantem.

Variatio corporis et mentis → aptitudo ad intelligendum → distinctio intellectus et imaginationis → perfectio ut actio → virtus sine praemio ultramortali → beatitudo ut virtus → libertas sapientis sub necessitate.
Spes-metúsque vulgares → falsa ratio pietatis → separatio virtutis ab eschatologia → amor intellectualis Dei → imminutio passionum → animi acquiescentia.
Perfectio a qualitate morali externa ad rationem activitatis et passionis reclassificatur.
Pietas et religio a regimine praemii-poenae ad normam rationis et proprii utilis transferuntur.
Beatitudo a termino posteriore disciplinae ad causam immanentem virtutis et potentiae affectivae transfertur.
Libertas a licentia libidinis et ab exemptionis causalitate imagine ad stabilitatem intellectus sub necessitate aeterna reordinatur.
Corpus a mero correlato mortalitatis ad condicionem mutabilem progressionis intellectualis reclassificatur.
Surface — Textus declarat partem mentis aeternam perfectiorem esse, virtutem ex immortalitate non pendere, et beatitudinem ipsam virtutem esse.
Structural — Intellectus, imaginatio, actio, passio, aptitudo corporis et causae externae constituunt mechanismum quo diversae formae vitae producuntur.
Metastrategic — Argumentatio mutat modum affectus regendi: non metus aut imminutio voluntaria, sed cognitio et beatitudo sunt principium transformationis.
Ontological/Temporal — Mens intelligens in ordine aeterno modorum cogitandi ponitur, dum imaginatio, memoria et corporis existentia ad ordinem transitorium referuntur.
Axiomata sufficiunt ad restitutionem catenae principalis: perfectio → actio → intellectus → beatitudo → virtus → imminutio passionum.
Nexus inter aptitudinem corporis et ampliorem conscientiam mentis affirmatur, sed mechanismus eius intra hunc locum non plene explicatur.
Independentia virtutis ab immortalitate cohaeret cum fundamento utilitatis rationalis, quamvis textus simul cognitionem aeternitatis ad summam sapientis formam pertinere servet.
Structura firmissima est ubi beatitudo causaliter, non remunerative, explicatur ut principium potentiae in affectus.
Commissura fragilis manet inter partem mentis aeternam et singularitatem vitae imaginativae, quia quantitas et modus transitus inter has rationes hic non determinantur.
