πάθος λέγεται ἕνα μὲν τρόπον ποιότης καθʼ ἣν ἀλλοιοῦσθαι ἐνδέχεται, οἷον τὸ λευκὸν καὶ τὸ μέλαν, καὶ γλυκὺ καὶ πικρόν, καὶ βαρύτης καὶ κουφότης, καὶ ὅσα ἄλλα τοιαῦτα· ἕνα δὲ αἱ τούτων ἐνέργειαι καὶ ἀλλοιώσεις ἤδη. ἔτι τούτων μᾶλλον αἱ βλαβεραὶ ἀλλοιώσεις καὶ κινήσεις, καὶ μάλιστα αἱ λυπηραὶ βλάβαι. ἔτι τὰ μεγέθη τῶν συμφορῶν καὶ λυπηρῶν πάθη λέγεται.

στέρησις λέγεται ἕνα μὲν τρόπον ἂν μὴ ἔχῃ τι τῶν πεφυκότων ἔχεσθαι, κἂν μὴ αὐτὸ ᾖ πεφυκὸς ἔχειν, οἷον φυτὸν ὀμμάτων ἐστερῆσθαι λέγεται· ἕνα δὲ ἂν πεφυκὸς ἔχειν, ἢ αὐτὸ ἢ τὸ γένος, μὴ ἔχῃ, οἷον ἄλλως ἄνθρωπος ὁ τυφλὸς ὄψεως ἐστέρηται καὶ ἀσπάλαξ, τὸ μὲν κατὰ τὸ γένος τὸ δὲ καθʼ αὑτό. ἔτι ἂν πεφυκὸς καὶ ὅτε πέφυκεν ἔχειν μὴ ἔχῃ· ἡ γὰρ τυφλότης στέρησίς τις, τυφλὸς δʼ οὐ κατὰ πᾶσαν ἡλικίαν, ἀλλʼ ἐν ᾗ πέφυκεν ἔχειν, ἂν μὴ ἔχῃ. ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἐν ᾧ ἂν ᾖ πεφυκὸς καὶ καθʼ ὃ καὶ πρὸς ὃ καὶ ὥς, ἂν μὴ ἔχῃ . ἔτι ἡ βιαία ἑκάστου ἀφαίρεσις στέρησις λέγεται. καὶ ὁσαχῶς δὲ αἱ ἀπὸ τοῦ α ἀποφάσεις λέγονται, τοσαυταχῶς καὶ αἱ στερήσεις λέγονται· ἄνισον μὲν γὰρ τῷ μὴ ἔχειν ἰσότητα πεφυκὸς λέγεται, ἀόρατον δὲ καὶ τῷ ὅλως μὴ ἔχειν χρῶμα καὶ τῷ φαύλως, καὶ ἄπουν καὶ τῷ μὴ ἔχειν ὅλως πόδας καὶ τῷ φαύλους. ἔτι καὶ τῷ μικρὸν ἔχειν, οἷον τὸ ἀπύρηνον·  τοῦτο δʼ ἐστὶ τὸ φαύλως πως ἔχειν.

ἔτι τῷ μὴ ῥᾳδίως ἢ τῷ μὴ καλῶς, οἷον τὸ ἄτμητον οὐ μόνον τῷ μὴ τέμνεσθαι ἀλλὰ καὶ τῷ μὴ ῥᾳδίως ἢ μὴ καλῶς. ἔτι τῷ πάντῃ μὴ ἔχειν· τυφλὸς γὰρ οὐ λέγεται ὁ ἑτερόφθαλμος ἀλλʼ ὁ ἐν ἀμφοῖν μὴ ἔχων ὄψιν· διὸ οὐ πᾶς ἀγαθὸς ἢ κακός, ἢ δίκαιος ἢ ἄδικος, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ μεταξύ.

τὸ ἔχειν λέγεται πολλαχῶς, ἕνα μὲν τρόπον τὸ ἄγειν κατὰ τὴν αὑτοῦ φύσιν ἢ κατὰ τὴν αὑτοῦ ὁρμήν, διὸ λέγεται πυρετός τε ἔχειν τὸν ἄνθρωπον καὶ οἱ τύραννοι τὰς πόλεις καὶ τὴν ἐσθῆτα οἱ ἀμπεχόμενοι· ἕνα δʼ ἐν ᾧ ἄν τι ὑπάρχῃ ὡς δεκτικῷ, οἷον ὁ χαλκὸς ἔχει τὸ εἶδος τοῦ ἀνδριάντος καὶ τὴν νόσον τὸ σῶμα· ἕνα δὲ ὡς τὸ περιέχον τὰ περιεχόμενα· ἐν ᾧ γάρ ἐστι περιέχοντι, ἔχεσθαι ὑπὸ τούτου λέγεται, οἷον τὸ ἀγγεῖον ἔχειν τὸ ὑγρόν φαμεν καὶ τὴν πόλιν ἀνθρώπους καὶ τὴν ναῦν ναύτας, οὕτω δὲ καὶ τὸ ὅλον ἔχειν τὰ μέρη. ἔτι τὸ κωλῦον κατὰ τὴν αὑτοῦ ὁρμήν τι κινεῖσθαι ἢ πράττειν ἔχειν λέγεται τοῦτο αὐτό, οἷον καὶ οἱ κίονες τὰ ἐπικείμενα βάρη, καὶ ὡς οἱ ποιηταὶ τὸν Ἄτλαντα ποιοῦσι τὸν οὐρανὸν ἔχειν ὡς συμπεσόντʼ ἂν ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν, ὥσπερ καὶ τῶν φυσιολόγων τινές φασιν· τοῦτον δὲ τὸν τρόπον καὶ τὸ συνέχον λέγεται ἃ συνέχει ἔχειν, ὡς διαχωρισθέντα ἂν κατὰ τὴν αὑτοῦ ὁρμὴν ἕκαστον.
καὶ τὸ ἔν τινι δὲ εἶναι ὁμοτρόπως λέγεται καὶ ἑπομένως τῷ ἔχειν.

τὸ ἔκ τινος εἶναι λέγεται ἕνα μὲν τρόπον ἐξ οὗ ἐστὶν ὡς ὕλης, καὶ τοῦτο διχῶς, ἢ κατὰ τὸ πρῶτον γένος ἢ κατὰ τὸ ὕστατον εἶδος, οἷον ἔστι μὲν ὡς ἅπαντα τὰ τηκτὰ ἐξ ὕδατος, ἔστι δʼ ὡς ἐκ χαλκοῦ ὁ ἀνδριάς· ἕνα δʼ ὡς ἐκ τῆς πρώτης κινησάσης ἀρχῆς (οἷον ἐκ τίνος ἡ μάχη; ἐκ λοιδορίας, ὅτι αὕτη ἀρχὴ τῆς μάχης)· ἕνα δʼ ἐκ τοῦ συνθέτου ἐκ τῆς ὕλης καὶ τῆς μορφῆς, ὥσπερ ἐκ τοῦ ὅλου τὰ μέρη καὶ ἐκ τῆς Ἰλιάδος τὸ ἔπος καὶ ἐκ τῆς οἰκίας οἱ λίθοι· τέλος μὲν γάρ ἐστιν ἡ μορφή, τέλειον δὲ τὸ ἔχον τέλος. τὰ δὲ ὡς ἐκ τοῦ μέρους τὸ εἶδος, οἷον ἅνθρωπος ἐκ τοῦ δίποδος καὶ ἡ συλλαβὴ ἐκ τοῦ στοιχείου· ἄλλως γὰρ τοῦτο καὶ ὁ ἀνδριὰς ἐκ χαλκοῦ·  ἐκ τῆς αἰσθητῆς γὰρ ὕλης ἡ συνθετὴ οὐσία, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ εἶδος ἐκ τῆς τοῦ εἴδους ὕλης. τὰ μὲν οὖν οὕτω λέγεται, τὰ δʼ ἐὰν κατὰ μέρος τι τούτων τις ὑπάρχῃ τῶν τρόπων, οἷον ἐκ πατρὸς καὶ μητρὸς τὸ τέκνον καὶ ἐκ γῆς τὰ φυτά, ὅτι ἔκ τινος μέρους αὐτῶν.

ἕνα δὲ μεθʼ ὃ τῷ χρόνῳ, οἷον ἐξ ἡμέρας νὺξ καὶ ἐξ εὐδίας χειμών, ὅτι τοῦτο μετὰ τοῦτο· τούτων δὲ τὰ μὲν τῷ ἔχειν μεταβολὴν εἰς ἄλληλα οὕτω λέγεται, ὥσπερ καὶ τὰ νῦν εἰρημένα, τὰ δὲ τῷ κατὰ τὸν χρόνον ἐφεξῆς μόνον, οἷον ἐξ ἰσημερίας ἐγένετο ὁ πλοῦς ὅτι μετʼ ἰσημερίαν ἐγένετο, καὶ ἐκ Διονυσίων Θαργήλια ὅτι μετὰ τὰ Διονύσια.

μέρος λέγεται ἕνα μὲν τρόπον εἰς ὃ διαιρεθείη ἂν τὸ ποσὸν ὁπωσοῦν (ἀεὶ γὰρ τὸ ἀφαιρούμενον τοῦ ποσοῦ ᾗ ποσὸν μέρος λέγεται ἐκείνου, οἷον τῶν τριῶν τὰ δύο μέρος λέγεταί πως), ἄλλον δὲ τρόπον τὰ καταμετροῦντα τῶν τοιούτων μόνον· διὸ τὰ δύο τῶν τριῶν ἔστι μὲν ὡς λέγεται μέρος, ἔστι δʼ ὡς οὔ. ἔτι εἰς ἃ τὸ εἶδος διαιρεθείη ἂν ἄνευ τοῦ ποσοῦ, καὶ ταῦτα μόρια λέγεται τούτου· διὸ τὰ εἴδη τοῦ γένους φασὶν εἶναι μόρια. ἔτι εἰς ἃ διαιρεῖται ἢ ἐξ ὧν σύγκειται τὸ ὅλον, ἢ τὸ εἶδος ἢ τὸ ἔχον τὸ εἶδος, οἷον τῆς σφαίρας τῆς χαλκῆς ἢ τοῦ κύβου τοῦ χαλκοῦ καὶ ὁ χαλκὸς μέρος (τοῦτο δʼ ἐστὶν ἡ ὕλη ἐν ᾗ τὸ εἶδος) καὶ ἡ γωνία μέρος. ἔτι τὰ ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τῷ δηλοῦντι ἕκαστον, καὶ ταῦτα μόρια τοῦ ὅλου· διὸ τὸ γένος τοῦ εἴδους καὶ μέρος λέγεται, ἄλλως δὲ τὸ εἶδος τοῦ γένους μέρος.

ὅλον λέγεται οὗ τε μηθὲν ἄπεστι μέρος ἐξ ὧν λέγεται ὅλον φύσει, καὶ τὸ περιέχον τὰ περιεχόμενα ὥστε ἕν τι εἶναι ἐκεῖνα· τοῦτο δὲ διχῶς· ἢ γὰρ ὡς ἕκαστον ἓν ἢ ὡς ἐκ τούτων τὸ ἕν. τὸ μὲν γὰρ καθόλου, καὶ τὸ ὅλως λεγόμενον  ὡς ὅλον τι ὄν, οὕτως ἐστὶ καθόλου ὡς πολλὰ περιέχον τῷ κατηγορεῖσθαι καθʼ ἑκάστου καὶ ἓν ἅπαντα εἶναι ὡς ἕκαστον, οἷον ἄνθρωπον ἵππον θεόν, διότι ἅπαντα ζῷα· τὸ δὲ συνεχὲς καὶ πεπερασμένον, ὅταν ἕν τι ἐκ πλειόνων ᾖ, ἐνυπαρχόντων μάλιστα μὲν δυνάμει, εἰ δὲ μή, ἐνεργείᾳ. τούτων δʼ αὐτῶν μᾶλλον τὰ φύσει ἢ τέχνῃ τοιαῦτα, ὥσπερ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἐλέγομεν, ὡς οὔσης τῆς ὁλότητος ἑνότητός τινος.  ἔτι τοῦ ποσοῦ ἔχοντος δὲ ἀρχὴν καὶ μέσον καὶ ἔσχατον, ὅσων μὲν μὴ ποιεῖ ἡ θέσις διαφοράν, πᾶν λέγεται, ὅσων δὲ ποιεῖ, ὅλον.

ὅσα δὲ ἄμφω ἐνδέχεται, καὶ ὅλα καὶ πάντα· ἔστι δὲ ταῦτα ὅσων ἡ μὲν φύσις ἡ αὐτὴ μένει τῇ μεταθέσει, ἡ δὲ μορφὴ οὔ, οἷον κηρὸς καὶ ἱμάτιον· καὶ γὰρ ὅλον καὶ πᾶν λέγεται· ἔχει γὰρ ἄμφω. ὕδωρ δὲ καὶ ὅσα ὑγρὰ καὶ ἀριθμὸς πᾶν μὲν λέγεται, ὅλος δʼ ἀριθμὸς καὶ ὅλον ὕδωρ οὐ λέγεται, ἂν μὴ μεταφορᾷ. πάντα δὲ λέγεται ἐφʼ οἷς τὸ πᾶν ὡς ἐφʼ ἑνί, ἐπὶ τούτοις τὸ πάντα ὡς ἐπὶ διῃρημένοις· πᾶς οὗτος ὁ ἀριθμός, πᾶσαι αὗται αἱ μονάδες.

κολοβὸν δὲ λέγεται τῶν ποσῶν οὐ τὸ τυχόν, ἀλλὰ μεριστόν τε δεῖ αὐτὸ εἶναι καὶ ὅλον. τά τε γὰρ δύο οὐ κολοβὰ θατέρου ἀφαιρουμένου ἑνός (οὐ γὰρ ἴσον τὸ καλόβωμα καὶ τὸ λοιπὸν οὐδέποτʼ ἐστίν) οὐδʼ ὅλως ἀριθμὸς οὐδείς· καὶ γὰρ τὴν οὐσίαν δεῖ μένειν· εἰ κύλιξ κολοβός, ἔτι εἶναι κύλικα· ὁ δὲ ἀριθμὸς οὐκέτι ὁ αὐτός. πρὸς δὲ τούτοις κἂν ἀνομοιομερῆ ᾖ, οὐδὲ ταῦτα πάντα (ὁ γὰρ ἀριθμὸς ἔστιν ὡς καὶ ἀνόμοια ἔχει μέρη, οἷον δυάδα τριάδα), ἀλλʼ ὅλως ὧν μὴ ποιεῖ ἡ θέσις διαφορὰν οὐδὲν κολοβόν, οἷον ὕδωρ ἢ πῦρ, ἀλλὰ δεῖ τοιαῦτα εἶναι ἃ κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν θέσιν ἔχει. ἔτι συνεχῆ· ἡ γὰρ ἁρμονία ἐξ ἀνομοίων μὲν καὶ θέσιν ἔχει, κολοβὸς δὲ οὐ γίγνεται. πρὸς δὲ τούτοις οὐδʼ ὅσα ὅλα, οὐδὲ ταῦτα ὁτουοῦν μορίου στερήσει κολοβά.

οὐ γὰρ δεῖ οὔτε τὰ κύρια τῆς οὐσίας οὔτε τὰ ὁπουοῦν ὄντα· οἷον ἂν τρυπηθῇ ἡ κύλιξ, οὐ κολοβός, ἀλλʼ ἂν τὸ οὖς ἢ ἀκρωτήριόν τι, καὶ ὁ ἄνθρωπος οὐκ ἐὰν σάρκα ἢ τὸν σπλῆνα, ἀλλʼ ἐὰν ἀκρωτήριόν τι, καὶ τοῦτο οὐ πᾶν ἀλλʼ ὃ μὴ ἔχει γένεσιν ἀφαιρεθὲν ὅλον. διὰ τοῦτο οἱ φαλακροὶ οὐ κολοβοί.

γένος λέγεται τὸ μὲν ἐὰν ᾖ ἡ γένεσις συνεχὴς τῶν τὸ εἶδος ἐχόντων τὸ αὐτό, οἷον λέγεται ἕως ἂν ἀνθρώπων γένος ᾖ, ὅτι ἕως ἂν ᾖ ἡ γένεσις συνεχὴς αὐτῶν· τὸ δὲ ἀφʼ οὗ ἂν ὦσι πρώτου κινήσαντος εἰς τὸ εἶναι· οὕτω γὰρ λέγονται Ἕλληνες τὸ γένος οἱ δὲ Ἴωνες, τῷ οἱ μὲν ἀπὸ Ἕλληνος οἱ δὲ ἀπὸ Ἴωνος εἶναι πρώτου γεννήσαντος· καὶ μᾶλλον οἱ ἀπὸ τοῦ γεννήσαντος ἢ τῆς ὕλης (λέγονται γὰρ καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ θήλεος τὸ γένος, οἷον οἱ ἀπὸ Πύρρας).  ἔτι δὲ ὡς τὸ ἐπίπεδον τῶν σχημάτων γένος τῶν ἐπιπέδων καὶ τὸ στερεὸν τῶν στερεῶν· ἕκαστον γὰρ τῶν σχημάτων τὸ μὲν ἐπίπεδον τοιονδὶ τὸ δὲ στερεόν ἐστι τοιονδί· τοῦτο δʼ ἐστὶ τὸ ὑποκείμενον ταῖς διαφοραῖς. ἔτι ὡς ἐν τοῖς λόγοις τὸ πρῶτον ἐνυπάρχον, ὃ λέγεται ἐν τῷ τί ἐστι, τοῦτο γένος, οὗ διαφοραὶ λέγονται αἱ ποιότητες.

τὸ μὲν οὖν γένος τοσαυταχῶς λέγεται, τὸ μὲν κατὰ γένεσιν συνεχῆ τοῦ αὐτοῦ εἴδους, τὸ δὲ κατὰ τὸ πρῶτον κινῆσαν ὁμοειδές, τὸ δʼ ὡς ὕλη· οὗ γὰρ ἡ διαφορὰ καὶ ἡ ποιότης ἐστί, τοῦτʼ ἔστι τὸ ὑποκείμενον, ὃ λέγομεν ὕλην. ἕτερα δὲ τῷ γένει λέγεται ὧν ἕτερον τὸ πρῶτον ὑποκείμενον καὶ μὴ ἀναλύεται θάτερον εἰς θάτερον μηδʼ ἄμφω εἰς ταὐτόν, οἷον τὸ εἶδος καὶ ἡ ὕλη ἕτερον τῷ γένει, καὶ ὅσα καθʼ ἕτερον σχῆμα κατηγορίας τοῦ ὄντος λέγεται (τὰ μὲν γὰρ τί ἐστι σημαίνει τῶν ὄντων τὰ δὲ ποιόν τι τὰ δʼ ὡς διῄρηται πρότερον)· οὐδὲ γὰρ ταῦτα ἀναλύεται οὔτʼ εἰς ἄλληλα οὔτʼ εἰς ἕν τι.

τὸ ψεῦδος λέγεται ἄλλον μὲν τρόπον ὡς πρᾶγμα ψεῦδος, καὶ τούτου τὸ μὲν τῷ μὴ συγκεῖσθαι ἢ ἀδύνατον εἶναι συντεθῆναι (ὥσπερ λέγεται τὸ τὴν διάμετρον εἶναι σύμμετρον ἢ τὸ σὲ καθῆσθαι· τούτων γὰρ ψεῦδος τὸ μὲν ἀεὶ τὸ δὲ ποτέ· οὕτω γὰρ οὐκ ὄντα ταῦτἀ, τὰ δὲ ὅσα ἔστι μὲν ὄντα, πέφυκε μέντοι φαίνεσθαι ἢ μὴ οἷα) ἐστιν ἢ ἃ μὴ ἔστιν (οἷον ἡ σκιαγραφία καὶ τὰ ἐνύπνια· ταῦτα γὰρ ἔστι μέν τι, ἀλλʼ οὐχ ὧν ἐμποιεῖ τὴν φαντασίαν)·—πράγματα μὲν οὖν ψευδῆ οὕτω λέγεται, ἢ τῷ μὴ εἶναι αὐτὰ ἢ τῷ τὴν ἀπʼ αὐτῶν φαντασίαν μὴ ὄντος εἶναι· λόγος δὲ ψευδὴς ὁ τῶν μὴ ὄντων, ᾗ ψευδής, διὸ πᾶς λόγος ψευδὴς ἑτέρου ἢ οὗ ἐστὶν ἀληθής, οἷον ὁ τοῦ κύκλου ψευδὴς τριγώνου.

ἑκάστου δὲ λόγος ἔστι μὲν ὡς εἷς, ὁ τοῦ τί ἦν εἶναι, ἔστι δʼ ὡς πολλοί, ἐπεὶ ταὐτό πως αὐτὸ καὶ αὐτὸ πεπονθός, οἷον Σωκράτης καὶ Σωκράτης μουσικός (ὁ δὲ ψευδὴς λόγος οὐθενός ἐστιν ἁπλῶς λόγος)· διὸ Ἀντισθένης ᾤετο εὐήθως μηθὲν ἀξιῶν λέγεσθαι πλὴν τῷ οἰκείῳ λόγῳ, ἓν ἐφʼ ἑνός· ἐξ ὧν συνέβαινε μὴ εἶναι ἀντιλέγειν, σχεδὸν δὲ μηδὲ ψεύδεσθαι. ἔστι δʼ ἕκαστον λέγειν οὐ μόνον τῷ αὐτοῦ λόγῳ ἀλλὰ καὶ τῷ ἑτέρου, ψευδῶς μὲν καὶ παντελῶς, ἔστι δʼ ὡς καὶ ἀληθῶς, ὥσπερ τὰ ὀκτὼ διπλάσια τῷ τῆς δυάδος λόγῳ.  τὰ μὲν οὖν οὕτω λέγεται ψευδῆ, ἄνθρωπος δὲ ψευδὴς ὁ εὐχερὴς καὶ προαιρετικὸς τῶν τοιούτων λόγων, μὴ διʼ ἕτερόν τι ἀλλὰ διʼ αὐτό, καὶ ὁ ἄλλοις ἐμποιητικὸς τῶν τοιούτων λόγων, ὥσπερ καὶ τὰ πράγματά φαμεν ψευδῆ εἶναι ὅσα ἐμποιεῖ φαντασίαν ψευδῆ. διὸ ὁ ἐν τῷ Ἱππίᾳ λόγος παρακρούεται ὡς ὁ αὐτὸς ψευδὴς καὶ ἀληθής.

τὸν δυνάμενον γὰρ ψεύσασθαι λαμβάνει ψευδῆ (οὗτος δʼ ὁ εἰδὼς καὶ ὁ φρόνιμος)· ἔτι τὸν ἑκόντα φαῦλον βελτίω. τοῦτο δὲ ψεῦδος λαμβάνει διὰ τῆς ἐπαγωγῆς—ὁ γὰρ ἑκὼν χωλαίνων τοῦ ἄκοντος κρείττων—τὸ χωλαίνειν τὸ μιμεῖσθαι λέγων, ἐπεὶ εἴ γε χωλὸς ἑκών, χείρων ἴσως, ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἤθους, καὶ οὗτος.

συμβεβηκὸς λέγεται ὃ ὑπάρχει μέν τινι καὶ ἀληθὲς εἰπεῖν, οὐ μέντοι οὔτʼ ἐξ ἀνάγκης οὔτε ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολύ, οἷον εἴ τις ὀρύττων φυτῷ βόθρον εὗρε θησαυρόν. τοῦτο τοίνυν συμβεβηκὸς τῷ ὀρύττοντι τὸν βόθρον, τὸ εὑρεῖν θησαυρόν· οὔτε γὰρ ἐξ ἀνάγκης τοῦτο ἐκ τούτου ἢ μετὰ τοῦτο, οὔθʼ ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ ἄν τις φυτεύῃ θησαυρὸν εὑρίσκει. καὶ μουσικός γʼ ἄν τις εἴη λευκός· ἀλλʼ ἐπεὶ οὔτε ἐξ ἀνάγκης οὔθʼ ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ τοῦτο γίγνεται, συμβεβηκὸς αὐτὸ λέγομεν. ὥστʼ ἐπεὶ ἔστιν ὑπάρχον τι καὶ τινί, καὶ ἔνια τούτων καὶ ποὺ καὶ ποτέ, ὅ τι ἂν ὑπάρχῃ μέν, ἀλλὰ μὴ διότι τοδὶ ἦν ἢ νῦν ἢ ἐνταῦθα, συμβεβηκὸς ἔσται. οὐδὲ δὴ αἴτιον ὡρισμένον οὐδὲν τοῦ συμβεβηκότος ἀλλὰ τὸ τυχόν· τοῦτο δʼ ἀόριστον. συνέβη τῳ εἰς Αἴγιναν ἐλθεῖν, εἰ μὴ διὰ τοῦτο ἀφίκετο ὅπως ἐκεῖ ἔλθῃ, ἀλλʼ ὑπὸ χειμῶνος ἐξωσθεὶς ἢ ὑπὸ λῃστῶν ληφθείς.

γέγονε μὲν δὴ ἢ ἔστι τὸ συμβεβηκός, ἀλλʼ οὐχ ᾗ αὐτὸ ἀλλʼ ᾗ ἕτερον· ὁ γὰρ χειμὼν αἴτιος τοῦ μὴ ὅπου ἔπλει ἐλθεῖν, τοῦτο δʼ ἦν Αἴγινα. λέγεται δὲ καὶ ἄλλως συμβεβηκός, οἷον ὅσα ὑπάρχει ἑκάστῳ καθʼ αὑτὸ μὴ ἐν τῇ οὐσίᾳ ὄντα, οἷον τῷ τριγώνῳ τὸ δύο ὀρθὰς ἔχειν. καὶ ταῦτα μὲν ἐνδέχεται ἀΐδια εἶναι, ἐκείνων δὲ οὐδέν. λόγος δὲ τούτου ἐν ἑτέροις.

A principle is called, in one sense, that from which one might first move in respect of the thing, as, for example, this is a principle of length and of a road from this end, while from the opposite end another. In another sense, that from which each thing might come about best; thus, even in learning, one must sometimes begin not from what is first and from the principle of the thing, but from where one might learn most easily. In another sense, that from which a thing first comes to be, being present in it, as the keel of a ship and the foundation of a house; and among animals some suppose it to be the heart, others the brain, and others whatever thing of this sort they happen upon. In another sense, that from which a thing first comes to be, not being present in it, and from which motion and change are naturally first initiated, as a child from father and mother, and a fight from abuse. In another sense, that by whose choice things moved are moved, and things changing change; thus the offices in cities, and dynasties, kingships, and tyrannies are called principles, and so are the arts, especially the architectonic among them.

Further, that from which a thing is first known is called a principle of the thing also, as the hypotheses of demonstrations. Causes too are spoken of in as many ways; for all causes are principles. It is common, then, to all principles to be that from which a thing either is, comes to be, or is known; and of these, some are present in the thing, others external. Hence nature is a principle, as are an element, thought, choice, substance, and that for the sake of which; for in many cases the good and the beautiful are principles both of knowing and of motion.

A cause is called, in one sense, that from which something comes to be, being present in it, as bronze is the cause of a statue and silver of a bowl, and the genera of these. In another sense, the form and the paradigm; and this is the account of what-it-was-to-be, and the genera of this (as, for the octave, the ratio of two to one, and in general number), and the parts in the account. Further, that from which the first principle of change or of rest comes, as the one who deliberated is a cause, and the father is cause of the child, and in general the maker of what is made and the changer of what is changed. Further, as the end; this is that for the sake of which, as health is the end of walking. For why does he walk? we say. In order that he may be healthy. And having spoken thus, we think that we have given the cause. And whatever comes about intermediate to the end through the motion of another, as, for health, emaciation or purgation or drugs or instruments: for all these are for the sake of the end, though they differ from one another in that some are instruments and others works.

Causes, then, are spoken of in approximately this many ways; but, since causes are spoken of in many ways, it happens that there are also many causes of the same thing, and not accidentally (as both the art of statue-making and bronze are causes of a statue, not in respect of something else but insofar as it is a statue; though not in the same way, but the one as matter and the other as that from which the motion comes). And things are causes of one another (as exertion is cause of good condition, and this of exertion; though not in the same way, but the one as end and the other as a principle of motion). Further, the same thing is cause of contraries; for what, when present, is cause of this, we sometimes blame, when absent, as cause of the contrary—for example, the absence of the steersman for the capsizing, whose presence was cause of preservation. Both, presence and privation, are causes as movers.—But all the causes now mentioned fall under the four most evident modes.

For the elements of syllables, the matter of manufactured things, fire and earth and all such things among bodies, the parts of a whole, and the hypotheses of a conclusion, are causes as that from which a thing is. Of these, some are as the underlying subject, such as the parts, and others as the what-it-was-to-be, namely the whole, the composition, and the form. Seed, physician, deliberator, and in general the maker, are all that from which comes the principle of change or rest. Others are as the end and the good of the others; for that for the sake of which tends to be the best and the end of the others; and let it make no difference whether one calls it good or apparent good.—Such, and so many in form, are the causes; but the modes of causes are many in number, though when summed up these too are fewer.

For causes are spoken of in many ways, and even among those of the same form one is prior and another posterior: for example, for health, the physician and the expert; and for the octave, the double and number; and always the encompassing universals in relation to any particular. Further, they are spoken of as the accidental and the genera of these: for a statue, Polycleitus in one way and statue-maker in another, because it is accidental to the statue-maker to be Polycleitus; and also the things encompassing the accident, as man is cause of the statue, or indeed animal in general, because Polycleitus is a man and man an animal. Among accidents too, some are more remote and others nearer than others, as if the white man and the musical man were said to be causes of the statue, and not merely Polycleitus or man. Besides all the causes spoken of properly and accidentally, some are spoken of as capable and others as active: for example, of the house's being built, a builder, or a builder building.

Similarly, the things of which the causes are causes will be spoken of in the ways stated: for example, of this statue, or of a statue, or of an image in general; and of this bronze, or bronze, or matter in general; and likewise in the case of accidents. Further, both these and those will be spoken of in combination: for example, not Polycleitus nor statue-maker, but Polycleitus the statue-maker. Yet all these are six in number, and are spoken of in two ways: for either as the particular or as the genus, or as the accident or as the genus of the accident, or as these combined or as spoken of simply; and all either as active or in potentiality. They differ to this extent: active causes and particular causes exist and do not exist simultaneously with the things of which they are causes, as this physician treating this patient being healed, and this builder with this thing being built; but potential causes do not always do so, for the house and the builder do not perish at the same time.

An element is called that first constituent thing, present in a compound, which is indivisible in form into another form; for example, the elements of speech are those from which speech is composed and into which it is ultimately divided, while they are no longer divisible into other sounds differing in form from them; but even if they are divided, their parts are of the same form, as a part of water is water, but not so a part of a syllable. Similarly, those who speak of the elements of bodies mean those into which bodies are ultimately divided, while these are no longer divided into others differing in form; and whether there be one or more such things, these they call elements. In a similar way, the elements of diagrams, and in general of demonstrations, are spoken of; for the first demonstrations, which are present in several demonstrations, are called elements of demonstrations; and such are the primary syllogisms from three terms through one middle term.

By transference from this, they call an element whatever, being one and small, is useful for many things; hence even what is small and simple and indivisible is called an element. From this it has followed that the most universal things are elements, because each of them, being one and simple, is present in many things, either in all or in the greatest number; and the one and the point seem to some to be principles. Since, then, the things called genera are universal and indivisible (for there is no account of them), some call the genera elements, more so than the differentia, because the genus is more universal; for where the differentia belongs, the genus follows, but where the genus belongs, the differentia does not belong in every case. Common to all is that the element of each thing is the first constituent present in each thing.

Nature is called, in one sense, the coming-to-be of growing things, as if one were to pronounce the υ with an extended sound; in another, that from which what grows first grows, being present in it. Further, that from which the first motion in each of the things that are by nature is present in it, insofar as it is itself. Things are said to grow when they have increase through another by touching and growing together or adhering, as embryos do. Growing together differs from touching: in the latter case there need be nothing other than the touch, but in things that have grown together there is some one and the same thing in both which makes them, instead of merely touching, grow together and be one in respect of continuity and quantity, but not in respect of quality.

Further, nature is called that from which something that is by nature either is or comes to be first, it being unarranged and unchangeable from its own potentiality; for example, bronze is called the nature of a statue and of bronze implements, and wood that of wooden things; and likewise in the other cases. For each thing is from these, the primary matter being preserved. In this way they also say that the elements of things that are by nature are nature, some naming fire, others earth, others air, others water, others something else of this sort; some naming certain of these, others all of them. Further, in another way nature is called the substance of things that are by nature, as those who say that nature is the first composition, or as Empedocles says that
there is no nature of any of the things that are,
but only mixture and separation of things mixed
exist; and ‘nature’ is a name applied to them by men.

Empedocles Fr. 8 Therefore, even things that are or come to be by nature, when that from which they are naturally fitted to come to be or be is already present, we do not yet say have their nature unless they have form and shape. What is by nature, then, is that which is from both of these, as animals and their parts are. Nature is both the primary matter (and this in two ways: either what is primary in relation to the thing itself, or what is primary without qualification—for example, for works in bronze, bronze is first in relation to them, but perhaps water is first without qualification, if all meltable things are water) and the form and substance; and this is the end of coming-to-be. By transference, moreover, every substance is called nature because of this, since nature too is a kind of substance. From what has been said, then, the first nature, and that called nature in the primary sense, is the substance of things that have in themselves a principle of motion insofar as they are themselves. For matter is called nature because it is receptive of this, and generations and growing are called nature because they are motions from this. And this is the principle of motion of things that are by nature, being present in them somehow, either in potentiality or in actuality.

Necessary is called that without which it is impossible to live, as a joint cause (for example, breathing and nourishment are necessary for an animal, since it is impossible for it to be without them); and those things without which the good cannot either be or come to be, or evil be cast off or removed (for example, drinking the medicine is necessary in order not to be ill, and sailing to Aegina in order to recover one's money). Further, the compulsory and compulsion; and this is what impedes and prevents contrary to impulse and choice. For the compulsory is called necessary, and hence painful (as Evenus says, “For every necessary thing is naturally grievous”), and compulsion is a kind of necessity (as Sophocles says, “But force compels me to do these things”); and necessity seems to be something not open to persuasion, rightly so, for it is contrary to motion according to choice and according to reasoning.

Further, we say that what cannot be otherwise is necessarily so; and according to this necessary, all the other things too are in some way called necessary. For the compulsory is said to be necessary to do or suffer when one cannot act according to one's impulse because of what compels one, as though this were a necessity through which it cannot be otherwise; and similarly in the case of the joint causes of living and of the good. For when the good in one case, and life and being in another, cannot be without certain things, these things are necessary, and this cause is a kind of necessity. Further, demonstration concerns necessary things, because, if it has been demonstrated without qualification, it cannot be otherwise; and the causes of this are the first things, if the things from which the syllogism proceeds cannot be otherwise. For some things have another cause of their being necessary, but others have none; rather, because of these others are from necessity. Therefore, what is first and properly necessary is the simple; for this cannot be in more than one way, and hence not otherwise and otherwise; for it would then already be in more than one way.
If, then, there are certain eternal and unmoved things, nothing is compulsory or contrary to nature for them.

One is called either accidentally or in itself. Accidentally, for example, Coriscus and the musical, and musical Coriscus (for it is the same thing to say Coriscus and the musical, and musical Coriscus); and the musical and the just, and musical Coriscus and just Coriscus. For all these are called one accidentally: the just and the musical because they are accidents of one substance, and the musical and Coriscus because one is an accident of the other. In a certain way, similarly, musical Coriscus is one with Coriscus because one of the parts in the account is an accident of the other, as the musical is of Coriscus; and musical Coriscus is one with just Coriscus because a part of each is an accident of the same one thing.

Similarly, even if the accident is said of a genus or of some universal name, as when man is said to be the same as musical man: either because the musical is an accident of the one substance, man, or because both are accidents of some particular, as of Coriscus. Yet the two do not belong in the same way: one perhaps as genus and in the substance, the other as a state or affection of the substance.—Such, then, is the way in which things are called one accidentally. Of things called one in themselves, some are so called because they are continuous, as a bundle by a binding and pieces of wood by glue; and a line, even if it is bent, provided it is continuous, is called one, as is each of the parts, such as a leg or an arm. Of these themselves, things continuous by nature are more one than those continuous by art. A continuous thing is one whose motion is one in itself and cannot be otherwise; and a motion is one if it is indivisible, and indivisible in time.

Things are continuous in themselves when they are one not by contact; for if one were to place pieces of wood touching one another, one would not say that they are one—neither one piece of wood nor one body nor anything else continuous. Things wholly continuous, then, are called one even if they have a bend, and still more those without a bend, as shin or thigh are parts of a leg, because the motion of the leg may fail to be one. And the straight is more one than the bent. We say that the bent thing having an angle is both one and not one, because its motion can be both not simultaneous and simultaneous; but that of the straight is always simultaneous, and no part having magnitude is at rest while another moves, as happens with the bent.

Further, one is called in another way because the underlying subject is undifferentiated in form; and things are undifferentiated whose form is indivisible to perception. The underlying subject is either the first or the last in relation to the end. For wine is called one, and water one, insofar as they are indivisible in form; and all liquids are called one (as oil and wine), as are all meltable things, because the ultimate underlying subject of all is the same; for all these are water or air. Things are also called one when their genus is one, differing by opposed differentiae—and all these are called one because the genus underlying the differentiae is one (as horse, man, and dog are one thing because all are animals), and in a manner similar to matter being one. These are sometimes called one in this way; but sometimes the higher genus is said to be the same—when they are ultimate species of the genus—as that which is above them: for example, isosceles and equilateral are the same and one figure because both are triangles; but they are not the same triangles.

Further, one is said of those things whose account stating the what-it-was-to-be is indivisible in relation to another account declaring the thing (for every account is in itself divisible). For in this way too the increasing and diminishing thing is one, because the account is one, just as in the case of planes the account of the species is one. And in general, those things whose thought, in thinking the what-it-was-to-be, is indivisible and cannot separate them either in time or in place or in account, are most of all one, and among these, as many as are substances. For universally, as many things as have no division, insofar as they do not have it, are said to be one: for example, if, insofar as it is a man, it has no division, it is one man; if insofar as it is an animal, one animal; and if insofar as it is a magnitude, one magnitude. Most things, then, are said to be one by doing or having or undergoing something else that is one, or by being relative to something one; but those primarily said to be one are those whose substance is one, and it is one either by continuity or by species or by account. For we count as many either things that are not continuous, or things whose species is not one, or things whose account is not one.

Further, in one way we say that anything whatever is one if it is a quantity and continuous, but in another way not, if it is not some whole; and this will be so if it does not have one species. For example, we would not say in the same way, on seeing the parts of a shoe put together in any fashion, that they are one, unless on account of continuity; rather, only if they are so arranged as to be a shoe and already have some one species. Hence also the circular line is most of all one among lines, because it is whole and complete.—To be one is to be a principle of some number; for the first measure is a principle, since that by which we first know is the first measure of each genus. Thus the one is the principle, in each case, of what is known. But the one is not the same in all genera: in one case it is a diesis, in another the vowel or the mute; and there is one for weight and another for motion. But everywhere the one is indivisible either in quantity or in species.

Of what is indivisible in respect of quantity, that which is indivisible in every way and has no position is called a unit; that which is indivisible in every way and has position, a point; that which is divisible in one way, a line; that which is divisible in two ways, a plane; and that which is divisible in every way and in three ways in respect of quantity, a body. And, reversing the order, what is divisible in two ways is a plane, what is divisible in one way a line, and what is in no way divisible in respect of quantity a point and a unit—the unit being without position, and the point having position. Further, some things are one in number, others in species, others in genus, and others by analogy: in number, those whose matter is one; in species, those whose account is one; in genus, those having the same figure of category; and by analogy, all things which stand as one thing to another. The later always follow upon the earlier: things one in number are also one in species, but not all things one in species are one in number; yet all things one in species are one in genus, but not all things one in genus are one in species, but by analogy; and not all things one by analogy are one in genus.

It is clear also that the many will be spoken of in opposition to the one: some by not being continuous, some by having matter divisible in species, whether the first or the last, and some by having several accounts stating the what-it-was-to-be.

Being is said in one way accidentally, and in another in itself. Accidentally, for example, when we say that the just man is musical, and that the man is musical, and the musical man a man; speaking in a manner similar to saying that the musical man builds because it has happened that the builder is musical or the musical man a builder (for this thing's being that thing signifies that that has happened to this). So too in the cases mentioned: when we call the man musical and the musical man a man, or the white thing musical or this thing white, in one case it is because both have happened to the same thing, in another because it has happened to what is, and in another because musical has happened to this man (and in this way too non-white is said to be, because that to which it has happened is). Thus things said to be accidentally are so said either because both belong to the same being, or because one belongs to that being, or because it is itself that to which belongs that of which it is predicated. Things are said to be in themselves in as many ways as the figures of the

categories signify; for in however many ways they are spoken of, in so many ways does being signify. Since, then, of predicates some signify what a thing is, others quality, others quantity, others relation, others acting or being acted upon, others where, and others when, being signifies the same thing as each of these. For it makes no difference whether one says “a man is healthy” or “a man is in health,” nor whether “a man is walking” or cutting and “a man walks” or cuts; and likewise in the other cases. Further, being and is signify that something is true, and not being that it is not true but false, alike in affirmation and negation: for example, “Socrates is musical,” because this is true; or “Socrates is not white,” because this is true; but “the diagonal is not commensurable,” because it is false.

Further, being and what is signify, among the things stated, what is potential in one way and what is in actuality in another. For we say that both what sees potentially and what sees actually see; likewise, that both what can use knowledge and what is using it know; and that both that in which rest already belongs and that which can be at rest are at rest. Likewise also in the case of substances: for we say that Hermes is in the stone, and the half of the line, and that grain not yet ripe is grain. But when a thing is potential and when it is not yet so must be determined elsewhere.

Substance is said of the simple bodies, such as earth and fire and water and things of this kind; and in general of bodies and of the things composed of these—animals and divine beings and the parts of these. All these are called substances because they are not said of a subject, but other things are said of them. In another way, it is said of whatever is the cause of being, present in such things as are not said of a subject, for example the soul in an animal. Further, it is said of whatever parts are present in such things, delimit them, and signify a this-something, upon whose removal the whole is removed—for example, a body in relation to a plane, as some say, and a plane in relation to a line. And in general number seems to some to be such a thing (for when it is removed, they say, nothing exists, and it delimits all things). Further, the what-it-was-to-be, whose account is a definition, is also called the substance of each thing.

It follows, then, that substance is said in two ways: both the ultimate subject, which is no longer said of another, and whatever, being a this-something, is separable; and such is the form and species of each thing.

The same is said accidentally in some cases: for example, the white and the musical are the same because both have happened to the same thing; and man and musical, because one of them has happened to the other; and the musical is a man because musical has happened to the man. And each of these is the same as the other and as this: for both man and musical are said to be the same as the musical man, and that is said to be the same as these. Hence none of all these is said universally; for it is not true to say that every man is the same as the musical. For universals belong in themselves, whereas accidents do not belong in themselves; but in the case of particulars it is said without qualification, since Socrates and musical Socrates seem to be the same. But “Socrates” is not said of many, and hence “every Socrates” is not said as “every man” is.—Some things, then, are said to be the same in this way; others in themselves, in as many ways as the one is said. For things whose matter is one either in species or in number, and things whose substance is one, are called the same; so that it is clear that sameness is a certain unity either of more than one thing in being or

when it is treated as more than one, for example when one says that a thing is the same as itself; for one treats it as two.—Other things are said to be different when either their species or their matter or the account of their substance is more than one; and in general the different is spoken of in opposition to the same.

Things are called different when, being other things, they are the same in some respect, not only in number but also in species or genus or analogy; further, things whose genus is different, contraries, and things that have otherness in their substance. Things are called like both when they have undergone the same thing in every respect, and when they have undergone more of the same things than different things, and when their quality is one. And among contraries in respect of which alteration is possible, that which has more, or the more dominant, is like that other. Unlike things are spoken of in opposition to like things.

Opposites are called contradiction, contraries, relatives, privation and possession, and the terminal points from which and into which generations and corruptions occur; and whatever cannot be present together in that which is receptive of both is said to be opposed, either themselves or the things from which they are. For grey and white do not belong to the same thing at the same time; hence the things from which they are are opposed. Contraries are called both things, differing in genus, that cannot be present together in the same thing, and things differing most among those in the same genus, and things differing most among those in the same recipient, and things differing most among those under the same capacity, and things whose difference is greatest either without qualification or in genus or in species. Other things are called contraries, some because they have such things, some because they are receptive of such things, some because they are productive or affected in respect of such things, or produce or undergo them, or are losses or acquisitions, or are possessions or privations of such things.

Since the one and being are said in many ways, it is necessary that the other things said in accordance with these also follow; thus the same, the different, and the contrary are different in each category.—Things are said to be different in species when, being of the same genus, they are not subordinate to one another; and when, being in the same genus, they have a difference; and when they have contrariety in substance. Contraries too are different in species from one another, either all contraries or those primarily so called; and so are things whose accounts are different in the ultimate species of the genus—for example, man and horse are indivisible in genus, but their accounts are different—and things which, being in the same substance, have a difference. The same in species are things spoken of oppositely to these.

Prior and posterior are said in some cases by being nearer to some first thing and principle in each genus, whether to a principle determined simply and by nature, or relatively, or somewhere, or by certain people. For some things are prior in place by being nearer either by nature to some determined place, such as the middle or the extremity, or to a chance point, while what is farther away is posterior; others are prior in time—for things farther from the now, as in the case of things that have occurred, are prior, since the Trojan events are prior to the Median because they are more distant from the now; while things nearer the now, as in the case of future things, are prior, since the Nemean games are prior to the Pythian because they are nearer the now, using the now as principle and first; others are prior in motion, for what is nearer to the first mover is prior, as a boy is prior to a man; and this too is in some way a principle simply; others in capacity, for what exceeds in capacity and is more capable is prior. Such is that upon whose choice the other, the posterior, necessarily follows, so that, if it does not move, the other does not move, and if it moves, the other moves; and choice is a principle. Others are prior in order: these are things that are arranged at different distances from some one determined thing according to a certain account, for example, the second-from-last is prior to the third-from-last, and the paranētē to the nētē; for in one case the leader, and in the other the middle, is the principle.—These, then, are called prior in this way; but in another way, what is prior in knowledge is also prior without qualification. Of these, things prior in account and things prior in perception differ. For in account universals are prior, but in perception particulars; and in account the accident is prior to the whole, for example musical to musical man, since the whole account will not exist without the part, although musical cannot exist if no musical thing exists. Further, the attributes of prior things are called prior, for example straightness is prior to smoothness; for the former is an attribute of a line in itself, the latter of a surface.

and if it moves, the other moves; and choice is a principle. Others are prior in order: these are things that are arranged at different distances from some one determined thing according to a certain account, for example, the second-from-last is prior to the third-from-last, and the paranētē to the nētē; for in one case the leader, and in the other the middle, is the principle.—These, then, are called prior in this way; but in another way, what is prior in knowledge is also prior without qualification. Of these, things prior in account and things prior in perception differ. For in account universals are prior, but in perception particulars; and in account the accident is prior to the whole, for example musical to musical man, since the whole account will not exist without the part, although musical cannot exist if no musical thing exists. Further, the attributes of prior things are called prior, for example straightness is prior to smoothness; for the former is an attribute of a line in itself, the latter of a surface.

Some things, then, are called prior and posterior in these ways; others are so called in nature and substance: those which can be without other things, while those other things cannot be without them—a division which Plato employed. (Since being is said in many ways, first the subject is prior, and hence substance is prior; then, in another way, things are prior in potentiality and in actuality: for some are prior potentially, others actually—for example, potentially the half is prior to the whole, the part to the whole, and matter to substance, but actually they are posterior; for only when the whole has been dissolved will they be actually.) In a certain way, all things called prior and posterior are so called in accordance with these. For some can be without others in generation, for example the whole without the parts, while others can be without others in destruction, for example the part without the whole. Likewise also the rest.

Capacity is called, in one sense, a principle of motion or change in another thing or insofar as it is another; for the capacity for building is one that is not present in the thing being built, whereas the medical capacity, though present in the thing being treated, may be present in it, but not insofar as it is being treated. Thus capacity is called, in general, a principle of change or motion in another thing or insofar as it is another; and also a principle of being changed by another thing or insofar as it is another (for in virtue of that by which the patient undergoes something, we sometimes say that it is capable of undergoing it if it undergoes anything whatever, but sometimes not in respect of every affection, but only if it is toward the better). Further, it is the capacity for accomplishing this well or according to choice; for we sometimes do not say that people who merely walk or speak, but do not do so well or as they chose, are able to speak or walk. Likewise in the case of being affected.

Further, such states as render things altogether unaffected or unchangeable, or not readily changeable for the worse, are called capacities. For things are broken, crushed, bent, and in general destroyed not through being capable but through not being capable and through lacking something; and things are unaffected by such things when they are affected only with difficulty and slightly, through capacity and through being capable and being disposed in some way.

Since capacity is spoken of in so many ways, the capable too will be spoken of in one way as that which has a principle of motion or change (for even what is capable of being at rest is something capable) in another thing or insofar as it is another; in another way, if something else has in it such a capacity; in another, if it has a capacity to change into anything whatever, whether for the worse or for the better. For even what is perishing seems capable of perishing, since it would not have perished if it were incapable; but as it is, it has some disposition and cause and principle of such an affection. Sometimes it seems to be such by having something, sometimes by being deprived of something; but if privation is in some way a state, everything would be so by having something, so that a thing is capable both by having some state and principle and by having the privation of this, if it is possible to have privation; but if not, homonymously. In another way, it is capable by not having another, or another insofar as it is another, capacity or principle destructive of it. Further, all these are capable either because the event may merely occur or not occur, or because it may occur well.

For such a capacity is present even in inanimate things, for example in instruments: they say that one lyre can sound, but another cannot, if it is not tuneful. Incapacity is a privation of capacity and of such a principle as has been stated, either absolutely or in what is naturally fitted to have it, or even when it is already naturally fitted to have it. For they would not say in the same way that a child, a man, and a eunuch are incapable of begetting. Further, there is an opposed incapacity corresponding to each capacity, both to the merely motive capacity and to the capacity to move well.

And “impossible” is said in one way in accordance with this impossibility, and in another way as are “possible” and “impossible”: impossible is that whose contrary is necessarily true (for example, that the diagonal is commensurable is impossible, because such a thing is false, whose contrary is not only true but also necessary; therefore, being commensurable is not only false but necessarily false); and its contrary, the possible, is when the contrary is not necessarily false, for example, that a human being is seated is possible; for it is not necessarily false that he is not seated. Thus the possible, in one way, as has been said, signifies what is not necessarily false; in another, what is true; and in another, what admits of being true. By metaphor, power is also spoken of in geometry. These, then, are possibles not in respect of power; but all things said in respect of power are said in relation to the primary sense; and this is a principle of change in another thing, or in the same thing qua other.

For the other things are called capable because some of them have something else possessing such a power, others do not have it, and others have it in such-and-such a way. Likewise also the incapables. Hence the proper definition of the primary power would be: a principle productive of change in another thing, or in the same thing qua other.

Quantity is said to be that which is divisible into inherent things, each or either of which is naturally one and a this. A plurality, then, is a quantity if it is numerable, and a magnitude if it is measurable. Plurality is said to be what is potentially divisible into non-continuous things, magnitude what is divisible into continuous things; and of magnitude, what is continuous in one direction is length, in two breadth, and in three depth. Of these, finite plurality is number, length is line, breadth surface, and depth body. Further, some things are called quantities in themselves, others incidentally; for example, a line is a quantity in itself, but the musical is so incidentally. Of things that are quantities in themselves, some are so according to substance, for example, a line is a quantity (for quantity belongs in the account stating what it is); others are affections and states of such substance, for example, much and little, long and short, broad and narrow, deep and shallow, heavy and light, and the other such things.

Further, great and small, greater and lesser, are affections of quantity both when said in themselves and when said in relation to one another; these names, however, are also transferred to other things. Of quantities said incidentally, some are so called in the way stated, because the musical and the white are quantities through the thing in which they inhere being a quantity; others are so called as motion and time are. For these too are called quantities of a sort and continuous, because those things of which they are affections are divisible. I mean not the thing in motion, but that which was moved; for motion is quantitative because that is quantitative, and time because of this.

Quality is said in one way to be the difference of substance: for example, a human being is an animal of a certain quality because it is two-footed, a horse because it is four-footed, and a circle is a figure of a certain quality because it is without angles, since the difference according to substance is a quality. —Thus, then, quality is said in this one way as a difference of substance; in another way, as the immovable things and mathematical objects are, as numbers are certain qualities, for example composite numbers and numbers not merely existing in one dimension, but of which the plane and the solid are imitations (these are numbers-times-numbers, or numbers-times-numbers-times-numbers), and in general whatever belongs in substance besides quantity. For the substance of each is what it is once, for example, in the case of six, not what they are twice or three times, but what it is once; for six is once six. Further, there are all the affections of moving substances, such as heat and coldness, whiteness and blackness, heaviness and lightness, and all such things, in accordance with which bodies, when they change, are said also to be altered. Further, there is quality according to virtue and vice, and in general the bad and the good.

Thus quality might be said in approximately two ways, and of these one is the most proper. For the primary quality is the difference of substance (and the quality in numbers is in some way a part of this; for it is a certain difference of substances, but either of things not moved or not qua moved); the others are affections of moving things qua moving, and differences of motions. Virtue and vice are a certain part of affections; for they signify differences of motion and activity, in accordance with which things in motion act or are acted upon well or badly. For what is capable of being moved or acting in this way is good, and what is so capable in this way and contrariwise is bad. But quality signifies the good and bad most especially in living things, and among these especially in those having choice.

Relatives are said in one way as double to half, and triple to a third; and in general multiple to submultiple, and exceeding to exceeded; in another, as what heats to what is heated, and what cuts to what is cut, and in general what produces to what is affected; and in another, as what is measurable to measure, what is knowable to knowledge, and what is perceptible to perception.

The first of these are said according to number, either simply or determinate, in relation either to themselves or to one: for example, double is a determinate number in relation to one, while multiple is according to number in relation to one, but not a determinate number, such as this or that; sesquialteral is according to a determinate number in relation to a determinate number, while superparticular is according to an indeterminate number, as multiple is in relation to one; and exceeding in relation to exceeded is wholly indeterminate according to number. For number is commensurate, but number is not spoken of in relation to the incommensurate; whereas the exceeding in relation to the exceeded is so much and more, and this is indeterminate; for whichever happens to be the case, it is either equal or unequal. Thus all these relatives are said according to number and are affections of number; and further, equal, similar, and same are said in another way (for all are said according to one: things are the same whose substance is one, similar whose quality is one, and equal whose quantity is one; and one is the principle and measure of number,

so that all these are called relatives according to number, though not in the same way). Productive and affective things, on the other hand, are relatives according to productive and affective power and the activities of the powers: for example, what heats is relative to what can be heated because it is capable, and again what is heating is relative to what is being heated, and what is cutting to what is being cut, as being active. But among things according to number there are no activities, except in the way stated in the other cases; activities according to motion are not present. Of things according to power, some are already called relatives also according to times, such as what has made in relation to what has been made, and what will make in relation to what will be made. For it is thus that a father is called father of a son; for the one is something that has acted, the other something that has been affected. Further, some are relatives according to privation of power, such as the incapable and whatever is so spoken of, for example the invisible.

Things called relatives according to number and power are all relatives because what they are is said of another, but not because another is said in relation to them. But the measurable, the knowable, and the thinkable are called relatives because another is said in relation to them. For the thinkable signifies that there is thought of it, but thought is not said in relation to that of which it is thought (for then the same thing would have been said twice); similarly too sight is sight of something, not of that of which it is sight (although it is true to say this), but of colour or something else of that sort. In that other way, however, the same thing will be said twice: that it is that of which sight is sight.

Of things called relatives in themselves, some are called so in this way, while others are so if their genera are such; for example, medicine is among relatives because its genus, knowledge, seems to be a relative. Further, they are so according to those things which possess them are called relatives; for example, equality, because the equal is relative, and similarity, because the similar is relative. Others are relatives incidentally, for example, a human being is a relative because it happens to be double, and this is among relatives; or the white, if it happens that the same thing is both double and white.

Complete is said in one way of that outside which it is not possible to take even one part: for example, this is the complete time of each thing, outside which it is not possible to take any time that is a part of this time. It is also said of what, in respect of virtue and excellence, has no excess in relation to its kind: for example, a complete physician and a complete flute-player, when they lack nothing in the form of their proper virtue. Thus, by transference, we also speak of a complete informer and a complete thief in the case of bad things, since we call them good too, for example, a good thief and a good informer; and virtue is a kind of completion. For each thing is then complete, and every substance is then complete, when according to the form of its proper virtue it lacks no part of its natural magnitude. Further, things to which the end belongs, being something serious, are called complete; for they are complete by having the end. Hence, since the end is something ultimate, by transference we also say that things have been completely destroyed and completely corrupted when they lack nothing of

corruption and evil but are at the ultimate point. Hence too death is metaphorically called an end, because both are ultimate; and the final cause is also ultimate. Thus things called complete in themselves are said in these many ways: some because they lack nothing in respect of excellence and have neither excess nor anything outside; others generally because they have no excess in each kind and there is nothing outside. The other things are now called complete in accordance with these, because they either produce something such, possess it, are fitted to it, or are somehow or other spoken of in relation to things primarily called complete.

Limit is said to be both the extremity of each thing, and that outside of which nothing of the first thing can be taken and inside of which is everything of the first thing; and whatever is the form of a magnitude or of something having magnitude; and the end of each thing (such is that toward which motion and action are directed, and not that from which they proceed—though sometimes it is both, both that from which and that toward which, as well as that for the sake of which); and the substance of each thing and the what-it-was-to-be for each thing. For this is the limit of knowledge; and if of knowledge, then also of the thing. Hence it is clear that limit is said in as many ways as principle, and in still more ways; for principle is a certain limit, but not every limit is a principle.

That according to which is said in many ways: in one way, the form and substance of each thing, for example, that according to which something is good is the good itself; in another, that in which it is naturally fitted first to come to be, for example, colour in a surface. Thus what is primarily called that according to which is the form, and secondarily the matter of each thing and what is first underlying each thing. In general, that according to which will belong in as many ways as cause; for “on account of what did he come?” or “for the sake of what did he come?” is said, and “on account of what has he reasoned falsely or reasoned syllogistically?” or “what is the cause of the syllogism or false inference?” Further, that according to which also signifies position: that according to which something stands or that according to which it walks; for all these signify place and position. Hence also per se must be said in many ways. For in one way, per se is the what-it-was-to-be for each thing: for example, Callias is per se Callias, and the what-it-was-to-be for Callias. In another way, it is whatever belongs in what a thing is: for example, Callias is an animal per se; for animal is present in the account, since Callias is a certain animal.

Further, it is what has been received first in itself or in some part of itself: for example, a surface is white per se, and a human being lives per se; for the soul is a certain part of the human being, in which life is first present. Further, it is that of which there is no other cause. For there are many causes of a human being—animal and two-footed—but nevertheless the human being is per se human. Further, whatever belongs to a thing alone, and qua alone is separated through itself, is per se.
Disposition is said to be the arrangement of that which has parts, whether according to place, power, or form; for there must be some positioning, as the name disposition also indicates.

Having is said in one way to be a kind of actuality of what has and what is had, as a kind of action or motion (for when the one acts and the other is acted upon, there is production between them; similarly, between the one having a garment and the garment that is had, there is having). It is clear, then, that it is not possible to have this sort of having (for there will be an infinite regress if there is to be a having of what is had). In another way, having is called a disposition in accordance with which the thing disposed is disposed either well or badly, either in itself or in relation to another, as health is a certain having; for it is such a disposition. Further, having is said if it is a part of such a disposition; hence the virtue of the parts too is a certain having.

Affection is said in one way to be a quality in accordance with which alteration is possible, such as white and black, sweet and bitter, heaviness and lightness, and all other such things; in another, the actualities and already actual alterations of these. Further, more especially, it is harmful alterations and motions, and most especially painful injuries. Further, the magnitudes of misfortunes and painful things are called affections.

Privation is said in one way when a thing does not have something which things are naturally fitted to have, even if it itself is not naturally fitted to have it, as a plant is said to be deprived of eyes. In another way, it is when either the thing itself or its genus is naturally fitted to have something but does not have it; for example, a human being and a mole are deprived of sight in different ways, the latter according to its genus, the former in itself. Further, it is when a thing naturally fitted to have something does not have it at the time when it is naturally fitted to have it; for blindness is a certain privation, but one is not blind at every age, but when one is naturally fitted to have sight and does not have it. Likewise also in that in which, according to which, in relation to which, and in the way in which it is naturally fitted to have something, if it does not have it. Further, the forcible removal of anything is called privation. And in as many ways as negations formed with a- are spoken of, privations too are spoken of in as many ways. For unequal is said of what, though naturally fitted to have equality, does not have it; invisible is said both of what has no colour at all and of what has it badly; and footless is said both of what has no feet at all and of what has bad feet. Further, it is said also of what has something only slightly, as seedless; and this is to be in some way badly disposed.

Further, it is said of what is not easy or not good: for example, uncuttable is said not only of what cannot be cut but also of what cannot be cut easily or well. Further, it is said of what does not have something in every respect; for one-eyed is not called blind, but only what has no sight in both eyes. Hence not everything is either good or bad, or just or unjust, but there is also the intermediate.

Having is said in many ways. In one way, it is to lead according to one's own nature or impulse; hence fever is said to have a human being, tyrants cities, and those who are clothed a garment. In another, it is that in which something is present as in a recipient: for example, bronze has the form of a statue, and the body has disease. In another, it is as the containing has what is contained; for that which is in a container is said to be held by it: for example, we say that a vessel has liquid, a city has human beings, and a ship has sailors; and likewise the whole has its parts. Further, that which prevents something from being moved or acting according to its own impulse is said to have that thing, as columns have the weights laid upon them, and as poets make Atlas hold the heaven, which otherwise would fall upon the earth, as some of the natural philosophers also say. In this way too, what holds together is said to have the things which it holds together, since each would be separated according to its own impulse if they were separated.
And being in something is said in a similar way and consequently to having.

“To be from something” is said in one way of that from which a thing is as from matter, and this in two ways: either according to the first genus or according to the ultimate species; for example, all fusible things are from water in one way, while the statue is from bronze in another. In one way it is said with reference to the first moving principle (for example, from what is a battle? From abuse, because this is a principle of the battle). In one way it is said from the composite of matter and form, as the parts are from the whole, the verse from the Iliad, and the stones from the house; for the form is an end, and that which has an end is complete. Some things are said to be from the part as the species, for example, man from the two-footed and a syllable from an element; for this is otherwise than the statue from bronze. For the composite substance is from sensible matter, but the form too is from the matter of the form. Some things, then, are said thus; others, if someone of these modes belongs to them in part—for example, the child is from father and mother, and plants from earth, because they are from some part of them.

In one way it is said of that which is after something in time, as night from day and winter from fair weather, because this is after that. Of these, some are so said because they have change into one another, as also the things just mentioned; others only because of temporal succession, as a voyage took place from the equinox because it took place after the equinox, and the Thargelia from the Dionysia because they are after the Dionysia.

A part is said, in one way, to be that into which a quantity may be divided in any manner whatsoever (for what is taken away from a quantity, qua quantity, is always called a part of it; for example, two of three is in some way called a part). In another way, it is said only of those things which measure out such quantities; hence two of three is in one sense said to be a part, and in another sense not.

Again, those into which the form may be divided apart from quantity are called parts of it; hence they say that the species are parts of the genus. Again, the things into which the whole, or the form, or that which has the form, is divided, or from which it is composed; for example, of the bronze sphere or the bronze cube, both bronze is a part (this is the matter in which the form is) and the angle is a part. Again, the things in the account which makes each thing clear are also parts of the whole; hence the genus too is called a part of the species, though in another way the species is a part of the genus.

A whole is said to be that from which no part is absent of those things from which it is naturally called a whole; and that which contains the things contained so that they are some one thing. This is in two ways: either as each is one, or as the one is from these. For the universal, and that which is spoken of simply as being some whole, is universal in this way: as containing many by being predicated of each, and as all being one as each—for example, man, horse, god, because all are animals. But the continuous and limited is a whole whenever some one thing is from several, especially when they are present potentially, or, if not, actually. Of these things themselves, those which are such by nature are more so than those which are such by art, as we said also in the case of the one, since wholeness is a certain unity.

Again, among quantities having a beginning, middle, and end, those in which position makes no difference are called “all,” while those in which it does make a difference are called “whole.”

Whatever admits of both is called both whole and all. Such are those whose nature remains the same upon transposition, but whose form does not, for example wax and a garment; for both “whole” and “all” are said of them, since they possess both. Water, and all liquids, and number are called “all,” but “whole number” and “whole water” are not said, except metaphorically. But where “all” is said as of one thing, in these cases “all things” is said as of things divided: this whole number, these all units.

Mutilated is said not of any quantity whatever, but it must both be divisible and be a whole. For two is not mutilated if one of the two is removed (for the mutilation and what remains are never equal), nor is any number whatever mutilated; for the substance too must remain: if a cup is mutilated, it is still a cup, but the number is no longer the same. Further, even if things have unlike parts, not all such things are mutilated (for number too has, as it were, unlike parts, for example a two and a three); rather, in general, nothing is mutilated among things in which position makes no difference, such as water or fire, but they must be such things as have position in accordance with their substance. Again, they must be continuous; for harmony consists of unlike things and has position, yet does not become mutilated. Further, not even all wholes are mutilated by the privation of any part whatever.

For the missing parts must be neither the principal parts of the substance nor parts of any sort whatsoever. For example, if a cup is pierced, it is not mutilated; but it is if its handle or some projection is removed. And a man is not mutilated if he loses flesh or the spleen, but if he loses some extremity; and not every extremity, but one which, when removed entire, does not grow again. Therefore bald men are not mutilated.

Genus is said, in one way, when the generation of things having the same species is continuous—for example, it is said that there is a genus of men so long as their generation is continuous. In another way, it is that from which they come as from the first mover into being; for thus the Greeks and the Ionians are called a genus, because the former are from Hellen and the latter from Ion, as the first begetter; and they are so called more from the begetter than from the matter (for they are also called a genus from the female, for example those from Pyrrha).

Again, plane is the genus of plane figures and solid of solid figures; for each figure is either such-and-such a plane figure or such-and-such a solid figure; and this is the substrate of the differences. Again, as that which is first present in the accounts, which is stated in the what-it-is, is genus, whose differences are said to be the qualities.

Thus genus is said in as many ways: according to the continuous generation of the same species, according to the first mover of like kind, and as matter; for that of which the difference and quality are, this is the substrate, which we call matter. Things are said to differ in genus whose first substrates are different and neither is resolved into the other nor both into the same thing; for example, form and matter differ in genus, as do all things spoken of according to a different figure of the categories of being (for some beings signify what a thing is, others a certain quality, and others according to the divisions previously made); for neither are these resolved either into one another or into some one thing.

The false is said in one way as a false thing; and of this, one kind is false because it is not compounded or is impossible to compound (as is said that the diagonal is commensurable, or that you are sitting; for of these, one is false always and the other sometimes, since in this way these are not beings); another kind consists in things which are, but are naturally apt to appear either not as they are or as things which are not—for example, a painting in shadow-colours and dreams; for these are something, but not the things of which they produce an appearance. Things, then, are called false in these ways: either because they do not exist, or because the appearance from them is of what does not exist. A false account is an account of things that are not, insofar as it is false; hence every false account is false of something other than that of which it is true—for example, the account of a circle is false of a triangle.

The account of each thing is in one way one, namely the account of its what-it-was-to-be, but in another way many, since in a way the thing itself and the thing itself as affected are the same—for example, Socrates and musical Socrates (but a false account is, simply, the account of nothing). Hence Antisthenes thought, naively, that nothing should be predicated except by its proper account, one account of one thing; from which it followed that there is no contradiction, and almost that it is impossible to speak falsely. But it is possible to state each thing not only by its own account but also by that of another, falsely indeed and altogether, but in a way also truly, as eight is double by the account of two.

Thus, then, false things are so called; but a false man is one readily and deliberately disposed to such accounts, not because of anything else but for their own sake, and one who produces such accounts in others, just as we call false those things which produce a false appearance. Hence the argument in the Hippias is deceptive in taking the same man to be false and true.

For it takes as false the one capable of speaking falsely (and this is the one who knows and is prudent); again, it takes the voluntarily bad man to be better. But this is false by induction—for the man who limps voluntarily is superior to one who limps involuntarily—understanding limping to mean imitation; since, if he were voluntarily lame, he would perhaps be worse, as in the case of character, and so would this man.

An accident is said to be what belongs to something and may truly be asserted, yet neither of necessity nor for the most part; for example, if someone digging a hole for a plant finds a treasure. Thus, finding a treasure is an accident to the one digging the hole; for this does not follow from that, or after that, by necessity, nor does one for the most part find a treasure when planting. And a musician may be white; but since this occurs neither necessarily nor for the most part, we call it an accident. Consequently, since there is something that belongs, and belongs to something, and some of these belong somewhere and at some time, whatever belongs but not because this was this thing, or now, or here, will be an accident. There is no determinate cause of an accident, but only the chance one; and this is indeterminate. It happened to someone to come to Aegina if he did not arrive for the purpose of getting there, but was driven out by a storm or captured by pirates.

An accident has come to be or is, then, but not qua itself, rather qua something else; for the storm is the cause of his arriving not where he was sailing, and that was Aegina. Accident is also said in another way, namely, of whatever belongs to each thing in itself without being in its substance—for example, having angles equal to two right angles belongs to a triangle. And these may be eternal, whereas none of the former may be. The account of this is elsewhere.
