The healthy thing comes to be when [the practitioner] has thought as follows: since this is health, if [the patient] is to be healthy, this must belong, for example uniformity; and if this, warmth. And thus he thinks continually, until he leads [the process] to that which he himself is able to make last. Then the motion from this point onward is called production, [the motion] toward being healthy.

Consequently, in a way it follows that health comes to be from health, and a house from a house—the one having matter from the one without matter; for medicine and housebuilding are the form of health and of house. By substance without matter I mean the what-it-was-to-be.

Of comings-to-be and motions, one is called thought and the other production: thought begins from the principle and the form, production from the last point of the thought. Likewise each of the other intermediate [stages] comes to be. I mean, for example, if [someone] is to be healthy, he must be made uniform. What then is being made uniform? This; and this will be if he is heated. And what is this? This. But this is present potentially; and this is already up to him.

The producing cause, then, and that from which the motion toward being healthy begins, if it is from art, is the form in the soul; but if it is spontaneous, it begins from that which at any time initiates production for the producer acting from art, just as in medical treatment perhaps the beginning is from heating (and this it produces by rubbing). Thus the warmth in the body is either a part of health, or something of such a sort follows upon it which is a part of health, whether through several intervening steps or not. This is the last [stage], that which produces the part of health—and likewise [what produces] the part of a house (for example, the stones) and of the other things. Hence, as is said, it is impossible for something to come to be if nothing pre-exists. That some part must necessarily pre-exist is clear; for matter is a part (for it is present and comes to be). But is it also [a part] of the account? We speak in both ways of what bronze circles are, stating both the matter, that it is bronze, and the form, that it is such-and-such a shape; and this is the genus into which it is first placed.

The bronze circle, then, has matter in its account.—But from that out of which some things come to be as matter, when they have come to be they are said to be not that thing but made of that thing; for example, a statue is not stone but stone-made. But the man who is becoming healthy is not said to be that from which [he comes to be]. The reason is that he comes to be both from the privation and from the underlying subject, which we call matter (for both the man and the sick man become healthy); yet he is said rather to come to be from the privation, for example, healthy from sick rather than from man. Hence the healthy [man] is not called sick, but man, and the man is healthy. But where the privation is obscure and nameless, as [the privation] of any sort of shape in bronze, or of a house in bricks and timber, [the product] seems to come to be from these, as there [the healthy man seems to come to be] from sick. Hence, just as in the former case that from which this [comes to be] is not called that [thing], so here too the statue is not timber, but is derivatively called wooden; and bronze, but not bronze [itself]; and stone-made, but not stone; and the house brick-made, but not bricks. For neither would one say without qualification, if one looked closely, that a statue comes to be from timber or a house
from bricks, because that from which [a thing comes to be] must change, not remain. It is for this reason, then, that it is so spoken of.

Since what comes to be comes to be by something (by which I mean that from which the principle of its coming-to-be derives), and from something (let this not be the privation but the matter—for the way in which we use this expression has already been distinguished), and something comes to be (and this is either a sphere or a circle or any of the other things whatsoever), just as [the producer] does not make the underlying subject, the bronze, so neither does he make the sphere, except accidentally, because the bronze sphere is a sphere and he makes that. For to make this particular thing out of the underlying subject simply is to make this particular thing. I mean that making the bronze round is not making the round or the sphere, but something else, namely this form in something else. For if he makes [the form], he will make it out of something else; for this was the underlying subject. For example, he makes a bronze sphere, and he does this in the sense that from this, which is bronze, he makes this, which is a sphere. If, then, he also makes this itself, it is clear that he will make [it] in the same way, and comings-to-be will proceed to infinity.

It is clear, then, that neither the form—nor whatever one ought to call the shape in the perceptible thing—comes to be, nor is there a coming-to-be of it, nor [of] the what-it-was-to-be (for this is what comes to be in something else, either by art or by nature or by capacity). But he makes [the thing] be a bronze sphere; for he makes it from bronze and sphere. For he makes [it] into this form, and this is a bronze sphere. But if there is to be a coming-to-be of being-a-sphere simpliciter, something will come to be from something. For what comes to be must always be divisible, and one part must be this and another that—I mean, the one matter and the other form. If, then, a sphere is a figure equal [in all directions] from the middle, one part of it will be that in which what produces will be, another that in the former, and the whole will be the thing that has come to be, for example the bronze sphere.

It is clear from what has been said, then, that what is spoken of as form or substance does not come to be, but the concrete whole spoken of in accordance with it comes to be; and that in everything generated matter is present, and one part is this and another that.—Is there then some sphere besides these [particular spheres], or some house besides the bricks? Or rather, if that were so, a particular thing would never come to be; but [the form] signifies such-and-such, and is not a particular and determinate thing; rather, [one] makes and generates from this such-and-such a thing, and when it has been generated, it is a particular such-and-such thing. But the whole particular thing, Callias or Socrates, is as this particular bronze sphere, while man and animal are as bronze sphere simpliciter. It is clear, then, that the cause of the Forms, as some are accustomed to call the Forms, if there are any besides particulars, is of no use with regard to comings-to-be and substances; nor would they, at least for this reason, be substances in themselves.

In some cases it is also clear that what begets is such as what is begotten, though it is not the same thing nor one in number, but one in form—as among natural things; for man begets man—unless something comes to be contrary to nature, as a horse begets a mule. (And these cases are similar too; for whatever would be common to horse and ass, the nearest genus, has not been named; but perhaps it would be both, for example mule.) Hence it is clear that there is no need to posit a Form as a paradigm (for they would most of all be sought in these cases; for these are substances most of all); rather, the begetter is sufficient to make [the offspring] and to be the cause of the form in the matter. And the whole [thing] is now such-and-such a form in these flesh and bones, Callias and Socrates; and they are different because of their matter (for it is different), but the same in form (for the form is indivisible).

One might raise the difficulty why some things come to be both by art and spontaneously, for example health, while others do not, for example a house. The reason is that, among the matters which govern the coming-to-be in producing and coming-to-be something by art, and in which there is present some part of the thing, one kind is such as to be moved by itself, while another is not; and of the former, one is capable of being moved in this way, while another is incapable. For many things are capable of being moved by themselves, but not in this way—for example, of dancing. Thus things whose matter is of such a kind, for example stones, cannot be moved in this way unless by another, though in another way they can; and likewise fire. For this reason, some things will not be [produced] without one who possesses the art, while others will be; for they will be moved by things that do not possess the art, though [those things] are capable of being moved by other things not possessing the art, or by a part [of themselves].

It is also clear from what has been said that, in a way, all things come to be from a homonymous thing, as natural things do, or from a part which is homonymous—for example, a house from a house, insofar as [it is produced] by intellect; for the art is the form—or from something having some part [of it], unless it comes to be accidentally. For the cause of producing is, primarily and in itself, a part. For the warmth in the motion produced warmth in the body; and this is either health or a part [of health], or some part of health or health itself follows upon it. Hence it too is said to produce, because it produces that upon which [health] follows and to which it has happened. Therefore, just as in syllogisms, substance is the principle of all things; for syllogisms proceed from what a thing is, and here comings-to-be [proceed from it]. Natural compounds are similarly disposed.

For seed produces as things from art do (for it has the form potentially, and that from which the seed comes is in a way homonymous—not that one must always seek [the relation] in the way that man [comes] from man; for woman too [comes] from man—unless it is a mutilation; hence a mule does not come from a mule). Things that come to be spontaneously, as in the former case, are those whose matter can also move itself with the motion which the seed moves; but those whose [matter] cannot [do so] cannot come to be otherwise than from themselves.—And the argument shows not only concerning substance that the form does not come to be, but the same account applies commonly and similarly to all the primary things, such as quantity, quality, and the other categories. For a bronze sphere comes to be, but not sphere or bronze; and similarly in the case of bronze, if it comes to be (for matter and form must always pre-exist); and likewise in the case of what a thing is, and of quality and quantity and the other categories alike. For it is not the quality that comes to be, but qualified wood; nor the quantity, but quantified wood or animal.

But from these points one may grasp a peculiarity of substance: it is necessary that another substance, being in actuality, pre-exist and produce, for example an animal if an animal comes to be; but in the case of a quality or quantity this is not necessary, but only [something] potentially [such].

Since a definition is an account, and every account has parts, and as the account stands to the thing so the part of the account likewise stands to the part of the thing, there is now a difficulty whether the account of the parts must be present in the account of the whole or not. For in some cases they seem to be present, and in others not. For the account of the circle does not contain that of the segments, whereas that of the syllable contains that of the letters; yet the circle too is divided into segments just as the syllable is into letters. Further, if the parts are prior to the whole, and the acute angle is a part of the right angle and the finger a part of the animal, the acute angle would be prior to the right angle and the finger to man. Yet those [wholes] seem to be prior; for [the parts] are defined from those, and they are prior in being also, since they can be without one another.—Or is “part” said in many ways, one way being what measures in respect of quantity? But let this be set aside; we must consider the things from which substance consists as parts.

If, then, one thing is matter, another form, and another that which is from these, and if both matter and form and that which is from these are substance, then in one way matter too is said to be a part of something, while in another way it is not; rather, [the parts are] those from which the account of the form consists. For flesh is not a part of concavity (for it is the matter in which it comes to be), but it is a part of snubness; and bronze is a part of the concrete statue, but not of the statue spoken of as form (for one must speak of the form, and each thing insofar as it has form; but the material thing must never be spoken of in itself). Hence the account of the circle does not contain that of the segments, whereas that of the syllable contains that of the letters; for the letters are parts of the account, parts of the form, and not matter, whereas the segments are parts as matter in which [the form] supervenes; though they are closer to the form than bronze is when roundness comes to be in bronze.

Yet in one way not all the letters of the syllable will be present in the account, for example these particular letters in wax or those in air; for these too are already parts of the syllable as perceptible matter. Nor is it because a line, if divided into its halves, is destroyed, or a man into bones and sinews and flesh, that they are for this reason composed of these as parts that are parts of the substance; rather, [they are composed] as of matter, and these are parts of the concrete whole, but no longer of the form and of that of which there is an account; hence they are not in the accounts either. Thus, in some accounts the account of such parts will be present, while in others it need not be present, unless [the account] is of the compound. For this reason some things consist of these as principles into which they perish, while others do not.

Whatever things are jointly taken as form and matter, such as the snub or the bronze circle, are perishable into these, and matter is a part of them; but whatever things are not jointly taken with matter but are without matter, whose accounts are of the form alone, these are not perishable, either without qualification or at least not in this way. Thus these are principles and parts of the former, but neither parts nor principles of the form. And for this reason the clay statue is perishable into clay, and the sphere into bronze, and Callias into flesh and bones, and further the circle into its segments; for there is a certain circle which is jointly taken with matter. For “circle” is said homonymously both of that spoken of simply and of the particular circle, because there is no special name for the particulars.—What is true has now been stated; nevertheless, let us state it still more clearly by taking it up again.

For whatever are parts of the account, and into which the account is divided, are prior, either all or some of them; but the account of the right angle is not divided into an account of the acute angle, but that of the acute angle into the right angle; for one defining the acute employs the right angle, since the acute is less than a right angle. Similarly also with the circle and the semicircle; for the semicircle is defined by the circle, and the finger by the whole, since such-and-such a part of a human being is a finger. Hence whatever are parts as matter and into which things are divided as into matter are posterior; but whatever are parts as parts of the account and of the substance according to the account are prior, either all or some of them.

And since the soul of animals (for this is the substance of the animate thing) is the substance according to the account, and the form and the what-it-was-to-be for such-and-such a body (at any rate, if each part is to be defined well, it will not be defined without its function, which will not belong to it without perception), it follows that the parts of this are prior, either all or some of them, to the composite animal, and similarly in each particular case; but the body and its parts are posterior to this substance, and not the substance but the composite is divided into these as into matter.—Thus in one way these are prior to the composite, but in another way they are not (for they cannot exist when separated; for it is not a finger in every condition that is a finger of an animal, but the dead one is homonymous); while some are simultaneous, namely those which are dominant and in which the account and the substance are primarily present, for example, whether this be the heart or the brain; for it makes no difference which such thing it is.

But man and horse and things thus spoken of in the case of particulars, though universally, are not substance but some composite of this account and this matter taken universally; whereas Socrates, already, is from the ultimate matter a particular, and similarly in the other cases.—There is, then, a part both of the form (and by form I mean the what-it-was-to-be) and of the composite composed of form and matter, and of matter itself. But only the parts of the form are parts of the account, and the account is of the universal; for being-a-circle and circle are the same, and being-a-soul and soul are the same. But of the composite, for example this particular circle and any particular thing, whether sensible or intelligible—I call intelligible such things as mathematical objects, and sensible such things as bronze and wooden ones—of these there is no definition; rather, they are known with thought or perception, and when they have departed from actuality it is not clear whether they are or are not; but they are always spoken of and known by the universal account.

Matter in itself is unknowable. Matter is of two kinds, sensible and intelligible: sensible matter, for example, bronze and wood and all movable matter; intelligible matter, that which belongs to sensibles not insofar as they are sensible, for example mathematical objects. How things stand concerning whole and part, and concerning prior and posterior, has been stated; but in answer to the question, when someone asks whether the right angle and the circle and the animal are prior, or the parts into which they are divided and from which they consist, one must answer that it is not so without qualification.

For if the soul too is an animal or an animate thing, or each thing is its own essence, and if circle is being-a-circle, and right angle is being-a-right-angle and the substance of the right angle, then one must say that something is posterior to something, for example to the things in the account and to some right angle (for there is both the right angle with matter, the bronze right angle, and that in particular lines); but the one without matter is posterior to the things in the account and prior to the particular parts, though it must not be said simply. But if the soul is different and is not an animal, then in this way too some things must be affirmed and others not, as has been stated.

It is reasonably disputed which parts are parts of the form and which are not, but are parts of the composite. Yet unless this is clear, it is not possible to define each thing; for the definition is of the universal and the form. Therefore, unless it is evident which parts are as matter and which are not, neither will the account of the thing be evident. Now whatever appear to come to be upon things differing in form, such as a circle in bronze, stone, and wood, these seem clearly not to be anything of the substance of the circle—neither bronze nor stone—because they are separable from it. But regarding whatever are not seen as separable, nothing prevents their being similarly related to these, just as if all circles that were seen were bronze; for bronze would be none the less nothing of the form. But it is difficult to remove it in thought.

For example, the form of a human being always appears in flesh and bones and such parts. Are these then also parts of the form and of the account? Or are they not, but matter; yet because it does not also come to be in other things, are we unable to separate them? And since this seems possible but it is unclear when, some already raise the difficulty even concerning the circle and triangle, as though it were not proper to define them by lines and the continuous, but as though all these too were spoken of in the same way as flesh and bones are of a human being, and bronze and stone of a statue. And they reduce all things to numbers, and say that the account of a line is that of two. And among those who posit the Forms, some say that the Dyad itself is the line itself, while others say it is the form of the line; for in some cases the form and that of which it is the form are the same, such as the Dyad and the form of the Dyad, but no longer in the case of a line.

It follows, then, that there is one form of many things whose form appears different—which was also the consequence for the Pythagoreans—and that it is possible to make one thing itself the form of all things, with the others not being forms; yet in this way all things will be one.

That matters concerning definitions involve a certain difficulty, and for what cause, has been stated. Hence it is superfluous to reduce all things in this way and remove matter; for perhaps some things are this in this, or are such-and-such things disposed in such-and-such a way. And the comparison concerning the animal which the younger Socrates used to make is not sound; for it leads away from the truth and makes one suppose it possible for man to be without his parts, just as a circle is without bronze. But the case is not similar; for an animal is something sensible, and it cannot be defined without motion, and therefore not without parts disposed in a certain way. For a hand is not in every condition a part of a human being, but only if it is capable of accomplishing its function, and thus is animate; if not animate, it is not a part. But why, in mathematical things, are the accounts not parts of the accounts, for example the semicircles of the circle? Is it because these are not sensible?

Or does it make no difference? For there will be matter even of some things that are not sensible; indeed, there is some matter of everything which is not the what-it-was-to-be and form itself in itself, but a this-something. Thus there will not be parts of the universal circle, but these will be parts of particular circles, as was stated before; for matter is of two kinds, sensible and intelligible. It is clear also that the soul is primary substance, the body matter, and man or animal, taken universally, that which is from both; but Socrates and Coriscus, if the soul too is Socrates, are twofold (for some take them as soul, others as the composite), whereas if they are simply this soul and this body, they are as the universal and the particular. Whether there is, besides matter, some other substance of such substances, and whether one should seek some different substance, such as numbers or something of that sort, must be examined later.

For it is for this reason that we are attempting to determine the matter concerning sensible substances, since inquiry concerning sensible substances is, in a way, the work of natural philosophy and second philosophy. For the natural philosopher must know not only about matter but also, and more so, about the substance according to the account. But how the items in the account are parts in definitions, and why the definition is one account—for it is clear that the thing is one, but by what is the thing one, since it has parts?—must be examined later.

What the what-it-was-to-be is, then, and how it is in itself, has been stated universally concerning everything; and also why, in the case of some things, the account of the what-it-was-to-be contains the parts of the thing defined, while in other cases it does not; and that in the account of substance the parts that are thus as matter will not be present—for they are not parts of that substance, but of the composite substance. Of this composite there is in a way an account and in a way there is not: with matter there is not, for it is indeterminate, but according to the primary substance there is, for example the account of the soul in the case of man. For substance is the form that is present, from which and matter the composite substance is called substance, for example concavity (for from this and the nose there are a snub nose and snubness). But in the composite substance, for example a snub nose or Callias, matter too will be present. And the what-it-was-to-be and each thing are the same in some cases, namely in the case of primary substances, such as curvature and being-curvature, if it is primary (and by primary I mean that which is not said by being-other-in-other and in a subject as matter); but whatever are as
matter or as jointly taken with matter are not the same, not even if they are one accidentally, such as Socrates and the musical; for these are the same accidentally.

But now let us speak first to the extent that definition has not been discussed in the Analytics; for the difficulty stated there is useful for the discussions concerning substance. I mean this difficulty: why is that whose account we say is a definition one, for example, in the case of man, animal two-footed? For let this be his account. Why then is this one and not many, animal and two-footed? For in the case of man and white they are many when neither belongs to the other, but one when it belongs and the subject, man, undergoes something—for then one thing comes to be, the white man. But here neither partakes of the other; for the genus does not seem to partake of the differentiae (for then the same thing would at once partake of contraries, since the differentiae by which the genus differs are contraries). But even if it does partake, the same account applies, if the differentiae are more than one, for example footed, two-footed, wingless.

For why are these one and not many? Not because they are inherent; for in that way one thing will be made out of all things. But all the items in the definition must be one; for definition is some one account and an account of substance, so it must be an account of something one; for substance signifies something one and a this-something, as we say.—But one must first examine definitions according to divisions. For there is nothing else in the definition besides the first genus spoken and the differentiae; the other genera are the first genus and, together with it, the differentiae taken in combination, for example the first is animal, the next animal two-footed, and again animal two-footed wingless; and similarly even if it is spoken through more terms. And in general it makes no difference whether it is spoken through many or through few, and consequently neither through few nor through two. Of the two, one is the differentia and the other the genus; for example, in “animal two-footed,” animal is genus and the other is differentia.

If, then, the genus simply is not apart from the species as species of a genus, or if it is but is as matter (for sound is genus and matter, while the differentiae make the forms and elements from it), it is clear that the definition is the account composed of the differentiae. Yet one must divide by the differentia of the differentia, for example the differentia of animal is footed; again, the differentia of the footed animal must be that by which it is footed. Thus one must not say that of the footed, one kind is winged and another wingless, if one is to speak correctly—though because of inability one will do this—but rather that one kind is cloven-footed and another uncloven-footed; for these are differentiae of foot: cloven-footedness is a certain kind of footedness. And in this way one always wishes to proceed until one comes to what is without difference; then there will be as many species of foot as there are differentiae, and the footed animals will be equal in number to the differentiae.

If this is so, it is clear that the last differentia will be the substance of the thing and the definition, if one must not say the same things repeatedly in the definitions; for that is superfluous. Yet this does happen: when one says “animal footed two-footed,” one has said nothing other than “animal having feet, having two feet”; and if one divides this by the proper division, one will say it more often, and as many times as there are differentiae. Thus, if there comes to be a differentia of a differentia, the last will be one, the form and the substance; but if it is accidental, for example if one divides the footed into white and black, there will be as many as there are divisions. Hence it is clear that definition is an account composed of differentiae, and, correctly speaking, of the last of these. This would be evident if someone transposed such definitions, for example that of man, saying “animal two-footed footed”; for “footed” is superfluous when “two-footed” has been said.

But there is no order in substance; for how must one conceive the one as later and the other as prior? Let this suffice, then, as a first account of definitions according to divisions, of what sort they are.

Since the inquiry is concerning substance, let us return again. Substance is said to be, as it were, the subject, the what-it-was-to-be, that which is from these, and the universal. Now concerning two of these we have spoken—for concerning both the what-it-was-to-be and the subject: that the subject underlies in two ways, either as a this-something, as the animal underlies its affections, or as matter underlies actuality. But the universal also seems to some to be especially a cause and to be a principle; therefore let us consider this too. For it seems impossible that any of the things spoken of universally should be substance. First, the substance of each thing is its own, belonging to that thing, and does not belong to another; but the universal is common, for that is called universal which is naturally fitted to belong to many things. Of what, then, will this be the substance? Either of all or of none; but it cannot be of all. And if it is of one, the others will also be that one; for things whose substance is one and whose what-it-was-to-be is one are themselves one.

Further, substance is said to be what is not said of a subject, whereas the universal is always said of some subject. But perhaps it is not possible in this way, as the what-it-was-to-be, but it is present in this, for example animal in man and horse? Then clearly there is some account of it. And it makes no difference even if there is not an account of all the things in the substance; for it will no less be the substance of something, as man is the substance of the man in whom it is present, so that the same consequence will occur again: for it will be the substance of that, for example animal, in which it is present as its own. Further, it is both impossible and absurd that a this-something and a substance, if it is composed of certain things, should not be composed of substances or of this-somethings, but of a quality; for then non-substance and quality will be prior to substance and this-something. But this is impossible; for neither in account nor in time nor in generation can affections be prior to substance, since they would then be separable too. Further, there will be substance in Socrates as substance, so that there will be a substance of two things.

In general, it follows that, if man and whatever is spoken of in this way is substance, none of the things in the account is the substance of anything, nor does it exist separately from them or in something else; I mean, for example, that there is no animal apart from the particular animals, nor anything else among the things in the accounts. From these considerations it is evident to those who examine them that none of the universals that belong is substance, and that none of the things commonly predicated signifies a this something, but rather a such something. Otherwise, many other consequences follow, including the Third Man.

Further, it is clear also in this way. For it is impossible for a substance to be composed of substances existing in actuality; for two things that are thus actual are never one thing in actuality, though if they are two potentially, they will be one (for example, the double is potentially composed of two halves; for actuality separates them). Hence, if substance is one, it will not be composed of substances existing in it, and in this way Democritus speaks correctly; for he says that it is impossible for one thing to come from two, or two from one; for he makes the indivisible magnitudes the substances.

Similarly, then, it is clear that the case will be the same with number, if number is a composition of units, as some say; for either the dyad is not one, or there is not a unit in it in actuality.—But the consequence involves a difficulty. For if no substance can be composed from universals, because they signify a such something and not a this something, and if no composite substance can be composed of substances in actuality, every substance would be non-composite; hence there would be no account of any substance. Yet it seems to everyone, and it was said long ago, that either substance alone has a definition, or has one most of all; but now not even substance does. Therefore there will be a definition of nothing; or in one way there will be and in another way there will not. What is being said will become clearer from what follows.

From these very considerations the consequence is also evident for those who say that the Forms are separate substances and at the same time make the Form out of the genus and the differentiae. For if there are Forms, and animal is in man and horse, then it is either one and the same numerically, or different. For in account it is clearly one; since the speaker will set out the same account in each case. If, then, there is some man himself, in his own right, a this something and separate, necessarily the things from which he is composed, such as animal and biped, also signify a this something and are separate and substances; and hence so too is animal.

If, then, what is in horse and in man is the same and one, as you are one with yourself, how will the one be separately one in things that are, and why will this animal not also be separate from itself? Further, if it will partake of biped and many-footed, something impossible follows; for contraries will belong to it simultaneously, though it is one and a this something. But if not, what is the manner in which someone will say that animal is biped or footed? Perhaps, then, it is compounded, or connected, or mixed; but all these alternatives are absurd. But it is different in each case. Then there will be, so to speak, infinitely many things whose substance is animal; for man is not from animal accidentally. Further, animal-itself will be many things. For the animal in each case is substance (for it is not spoken of in virtue of something else; otherwise man will be from that, and that will be his genus), and again all the things out of which man is composed will be Forms. Therefore there will not be a Form of one thing and a substance of another (for that is impossible); consequently, animal-itself will be one thing in each of the animals.

Further, from what is this, and how is it from animal-itself? Or how can animal, whose substance is animal-itself, exist apart from animal-itself? Further, in the case of sensibles these consequences occur, and consequences more absurd than these. If, then, it is impossible for things to be so, it is clear that there are no Forms of them in the way some assert.

But since substance is one thing, and the concrete whole and the account another (by the former I mean substance when the account is taken together with the matter, and by the latter the account simply), those spoken of in the former way are subject to destruction—for they also come to be—whereas the account is not subject to destruction in this way (for neither does it come to be: it is not being-a-house that comes to be, but being this particular house); rather, they are and are not without coming to be and passing away; for it has been shown that no one generates or makes these.

For this reason there is neither definition nor demonstration of the particular sensible substances, because they have matter whose nature is such as to admit both of being and of not being; hence all their particulars are perishable.

If, then, demonstration is of necessary things and definition is scientific, and if, just as knowledge cannot at one time be knowledge and at another time ignorance—such a condition belongs rather to opinion—so too neither demonstration nor definition can be such, but opinion is of what admits of being otherwise, it is clear that there could be neither definition nor demonstration of these things. For perishable things are unclear to those who possess knowledge, when they have departed from perception; and even if the same accounts are preserved in the soul, there will no longer be either a definition or a demonstration. Therefore, when someone defines any particular among things directed toward a definition, he must not fail to recognize that it is always possible to destroy it; for it is not possible to define it.

Nor indeed is it possible to define any Form. For the Form is of particulars, as they say, and is separate; but the account must consist of names, and the definer will not coin a name (for it would be unknown), while the established names are common to all. Therefore these names must also belong to something else. For example, if someone were to define you, he will say “a thin animal,” or “a white animal,” or something else that will also belong to another. But if someone should say that nothing prevents all these predicates from belonging separately to many things, but together to this one thing alone, it must first be said that they belong to both, for example, “biped animal” belongs to animal and biped (and in the case of eternal things this must be so, since they are prior and parts of the composite; indeed, they are also separate, if man is separate—for either neither is separate, or both are; if neither, the genus will not exist apart from the Forms, while if it does, the differentia will too); and then, that they are prior in being. But these are not reciprocally destroyed.

Further, if Forms are composed of Forms (for the things out of which they are composed are more non-composite), then the things out of which the Form is composed, such as animal and biped, must also be predicated of many things. Otherwise, how will they be known? For there will be some Form which it is impossible to predicate of more than one thing. But this does not seem so; rather, every Form seems to be participable.

Thus, as has been said, it escapes notice that it is impossible to define eternal things, especially those that are unique, such as the sun or moon. For they err not only by adding such things that, if removed, the sun will still be sun, such as “moving around the earth” or “concealed at night” (for if it stands still or is visible, it will no longer be sun; but this is absurd, if it is not sun; for sun signifies a certain substance); further, they add things that can belong to another, for example, if another thing should come to be such, it is clear that it will be a sun. The account, then, is common; but the sun was one of the particulars, like Cleon or Socrates. Again, why does none of them offer a definition of their Form? For if they tried, it would become clear that what has now been said is true.

It is also clear that most of the things thought to be substances are potentials: the parts of animals (for none of them exists separately; and when they are separated, then too they all exist as matter), and earth, fire, and air. For none of these is one, but rather like a heap, before it has been concocted and some one thing has come to be from them. One might especially suppose that the parts of living things and the things close to soul are both actual and potential, because they have principles of motion from some source in their joints; hence some animals live when divided. But nevertheless all will be potentially such whenever they are one and naturally continuous, and not by force or by growing together; for such a condition is a mutilation.

But since one is spoken of in the same ways as being, and the substance of the one is one, and things whose substance is one numerically are one numerically, it is clear that neither one nor being can be the substance of things, just as neither can being an element or a principle. Rather, we seek what the principle is, in order that we may reduce it to something more knowable.

Being and one, then, are substance to a greater degree than principle, element, and cause; but not even these are substance, if indeed no other common thing is substance either. For substance belongs to nothing except itself and that which has it, of which it is the substance. Further, the one could not be simultaneously in many places, whereas the common belongs simultaneously in many places. Hence it is clear that none of the universals exists separately apart from particulars.

But those who posit the Forms speak correctly in separating them, if they are substances; but incorrectly in calling a Form one over many. The reason is that they cannot say what such imperishable substances are, apart from the particular and sensible ones. They therefore make them the same in form as the perishable things (for these are familiar to us), man-itself and horse-itself, adding to sensibles the word “itself.”

And yet, even if we had not seen the stars, there would nonetheless, I think, be eternal substances besides those we knew. Thus, even now, if we do not know what they are, it is perhaps necessary that there be some. It is clear, then, that none of the things spoken of universally is substance, and that no substance is composed of substances.

But what we ought to say substance is, and what sort of thing it is, let us say again, making, as it were, another beginning; for perhaps from these considerations it will be clear also concerning that substance which is separate from sensible substances. Since, then, substance is a certain principle and cause, we must proceed from this point. For the question “why?” is always sought in this way: why does one thing belong to another? For to ask why a musical man is a musical man is either to ask the question already stated, why a man is musical, or something else. Now, to ask why a thing itself is itself is to ask nothing (for the that and the being must be present and manifest—I mean, for example, that the moon is eclipsed); but why it is itself has one account and one cause in all cases—why man is man, or the musical is musical—unless someone says that each thing is indivisible in relation to itself, and that this was being one; but this is common to all things and is a short answer. One might rather ask why man is an animal of such-and-such a kind.

This, then, is clear: he is not asking why whoever is a man is a man. He asks, then, why something belongs to something (and that it belongs must be clear; for if not, he asks nothing); for example, why does it thunder? Why does a noise arise in the clouds? For what is sought in this way is one thing of another. And why are these things—bricks and stones, for example—a house? It is clear, then, that he seeks the cause. This is, to speak logically, the what-it-was-to-be, which in some cases is that for the sake of which, perhaps in the case of a house or a bed, and in other cases what first moved; for this too is a cause. But the latter sort of cause is sought in connection with coming to be and passing away, the other also in connection with being.

What is sought escapes notice especially in things not spoken of one of another; for example, “what is man?” is sought because it is spoken simply and does not distinguish that this is this. But one must articulate the question before seeking; otherwise, there comes to be no difference between seeking nothing and seeking something.

Since being must be present and belong, it is clear that he seeks why the matter is some particular thing. For example, why are these things a house? Because that which was being a house belongs to them. And why is this a man, or why is this body, having this character, a man? Thus the cause of the matter is sought (and this is the form), by which it is something; and this is the substance.

It is clear, then, that in the case of simple things there is no inquiry or teaching, but another manner of inquiry concerning such things.—But since a thing composed of something is such that the whole is one, not like a heap but like a syllable—and a syllable is not its elements, nor is ba the same as b and a, nor is flesh fire and earth (for when they are dissolved, the former things, such as flesh and the syllable, no longer exist, whereas the elements do exist, both fire and earth)—there is, then, something that the syllable is, not merely its elements, vowel and consonant, but something else; and flesh is not merely fire and earth, or hot and cold, but something else.

If, then, that other thing must itself be either an element or composed of elements, if it is an element, the same argument will recur (for flesh will be composed of this and fire and earth and yet another thing, and so the process will proceed to infinity); but if it is composed of elements, it is clear that it will not be composed of one but of several, or else it will be that thing itself, so that again we shall give the same account in its case as in that of flesh or syllable.

This would seem to be something and not an element, and indeed the cause of this being flesh and that being a syllable; and similarly in the other cases. And this is the substance of each thing (for this is the first cause of being). But since some things are not substances, whereas those things are substances which are constituted according to nature and by nature, this nature would appear to be substance, which is not an element but a principle.—An element is that into which a thing is divided, being present in it as matter, as a and b are elements of a syllable.
