καίτοι χρῶνται καὶ λέγουσι μέγα μικρόν, πολὺ ὀλίγον, ἐξ ὧν οἱ ἀριθμοί, μακρὸν βραχύ, ἐξ ὧν τὸ μῆκος, πλατὺ στενόν, ἐξ ὧν τὸ ἐπίπεδον, βαθὺ ταπεινόν, ἐξ ὧν οἱ ὄγκοι· καὶ ἔτι δὴ πλείω εἴδη λέγουσι τοῦ πρός τι· τούτοις δὴ τί αἴτιον τοῦ πολλὰ εἶναι;—ἀνάγκη μὲν οὖν, ὥσπερ λέγομεν, ὑποθεῖναι τὸ δυνάμει ὂν ἑκάστῳ (τοῦτο δὲ προσαπεφήνατο ὁ ταῦτα λέγων, τί τὸ δυνάμει τόδε καὶ οὐσία, μὴ ὂν δὲ καθʼ αὑτό, ὅτι τὸ πρός τι, ὥσπερ εἰ εἶπε τὸ ποιόν, ὃ οὔτε δυνάμει ἐστὶ τὸ ἓν ἢ τὸ ὂν οὔτε ἀπόφασις τοῦ ἑνὸς οὐδὲ τοῦ ὄντος ἀλλʼ ἕν τι τῶν ὄντων), πολύ τε μᾶλλον, ὥσπερ ἐλέχθη, εἰ ἐζήτει πῶς πολλὰ τὰ ὄντα, μὴ τὰ ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ κατηγορίᾳ ζητεῖν, πῶς πολλαὶ οὐσίαι ἢ πολλὰ ποιά, ἀλλὰ πῶς πολλὰ τὰ ὄντα· τὰ μὲν γὰρ οὐσίαι τὰ δὲ πάθη τὰ δὲ πρός τι.

ἐπὶ μὲν οὖν τῶν ἄλλων κατηγοριῶν ἔχει τινὰ καὶ ἄλλην ἐπίστασιν πῶς πολλά (διὰ γὰρ τὸ μὴ χωριστὰ εἶναι τῷ τὸ ὑποκείμενον πολλὰ γίγνεσθαι καὶ εἶναι ποιά τε πολλὰ  καὶ ποσά· καίτοι δεῖ γέ τινα εἶναι ὕλην ἑκάστῳ γένει, πλὴν χωριστὴν ἀδύνατον τῶν οὐσιῶν)· ἀλλʼ ἐπὶ τῶν τόδε τι ἔχει τινὰ λόγον πῶς πολλὰ τὸ τόδε τι, εἰ μή τι ἔσται καὶ τόδε τι καὶ φύσις τις τοιαύτη· αὕτη δέ ἐστιν ἐκεῖθεν μᾶλλον ἡ ἀπορία, πῶς πολλαὶ ἐνεργείᾳ οὐσίαι ἀλλʼ οὐ μία. ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ εἰ μὴ ταὐτόν ἐστι τὸ τόδε καὶ τὸ ποσόν, οὐ λέγεται πῶς καὶ διὰ τί πολλὰ τὰ ὄντα, ἀλλὰ πῶς ποσὰ πολλά. ὁ γὰρ ἀριθμὸς πᾶς ποσόν τι σημαίνει, καὶ ἡ μονάς, εἰ μὴ μέτρον καὶ τὸ κατὰ τὸ ποσὸν ἀδιαίρετον. εἰ μὲν οὖν ἕτερον τὸ ποσὸν καὶ τὸ τί ἐστιν, οὐ λέγεται τὸ τί ἐστιν ἐκ τίνος οὐδὲ πῶς πολλά·  εἰ δὲ ταὐτό, πολλὰς ὑπομένει ὁ λέγων ἐναντιώσεις.—ἐπιστήσειε δʼ ἄν τις τὴν σκέψιν καὶ περὶ τῶν ἀριθμῶν πόθεν δεῖ λαβεῖν τὴν πίστιν ὡς εἰσίν.

τῷ μὲν γὰρ ἰδέας τιθεμένῳ παρέχονταί τινʼ αἰτίαν τοῖς οὖσιν, εἴπερ ἕκαστος τῶν ἀριθμῶν ἰδέα τις ἡ δʼ ἰδέα τοῖς ἄλλοις αἰτία τοῦ εἶναι ὃν δή ποτε τρόπον (ἔστω γὰρ ὑποκείμενον αὐτοῖς τοῦτο)· τῷ δὲ τοῦτον μὲν τὸν τρόπον οὐκ οἰομένῳ διὰ τὸ τὰς ἐνούσας δυσχερείας ὁρᾶν περὶ τὰς ἰδέας ὥστε διά γε ταῦτα μὴ ποιεῖν ἀριθμούς, ποιοῦντι δὲ ἀριθμὸν τὸν μαθηματικόν, πόθεν τε χρὴ πιστεῦσαι ὡς ἔστι τοιοῦτος ἀριθμός, καὶ τί τοῖς ἄλλοις χρήσιμος; οὐθενὸς γὰρ οὔτε φησὶν ὁ λέγων αὐτὸν εἶναι, ἀλλʼ ὡς αὐτήν τινα λέγει καθʼ αὑτὴν φύσιν οὖσαν, οὔτε φαίνεται ὢν αἴτιος· τὰ γὰρ θεωρήματα τῶν ἀριθμητικῶν πάντα καὶ κατὰ τῶν αἰσθητῶν ὑπάρξει, καθάπερ ἐλέχθη.

οἱ μὲν οὖν τιθέμενοι τὰς ἰδέας εἶναι, καὶ ἀριθμοὺς αὐτὰς εἶναι, τῷ κατὰ τὴν ἔκθεσιν ἑκάστου παρὰ τὰ πολλὰ λαμβάνειν  ἕν τι ἕκαστον πειρῶνταί γε λέγειν πως διὰ τί ἔστιν, οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ ἐπεὶ οὔτε ἀναγκαῖα οὔτε δυνατὰ ταῦτα, οὐδὲ τὸν ἀριθμὸν διά γε ταῦτα εἶναι λεκτέον· οἱ δὲ Πυθαγόρειοι διὰ τὸ ὁρᾶν πολλὰ τῶν ἀριθμῶν πάθη ὑπάρχοντα τοῖς αἰσθητοῖς σώμασιν, εἶναι μὲν ἀριθμοὺς ἐποίησαν τὰ ὄντα, οὐ χωριστοὺς δέ, ἀλλʼ ἐξ ἀριθμῶν τὰ ὄντα· διὰ τί δέ; ὅτι τὰ πάθη τὰ τῶν ἀριθμῶν ἐν ἁρμονίᾳ ὑπάρχει καὶ ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ καὶ ἐν πολλοῖς ἄλλοις. τοῖς δὲ τὸν μαθηματικὸν μόνον λέγουσιν εἶναι ἀριθμὸν οὐθὲν τοιοῦτον ἐνδέχεται λέγειν κατὰ τὰς ὑποθέσεις, ἀλλʼ ὅτι οὐκ ἔσονται αὐτῶν αἱ ἐπιστῆμαι ἐλέγετο. ἡμεῖς δέ φαμεν εἶναι, καθάπερ εἴπομεν πρότερον. καὶ δῆλον ὅτι οὐ κεχώρισται τὰ μαθηματικά· οὐ γὰρ ἂν κεχωρισμένων τὰ πάθη ὑπῆρχεν ἐν τοῖς σώμασιν.

οἱ μὲν οὖν Πυθαγόρειοι κατὰ μὲν τὸ τοιοῦτον οὐθενὶ ἔνοχοί εἰσιν, κατὰ μέντοι τὸ ποιεῖν ἐξ ἀριθμῶν τὰ φυσικὰ σώματα, ἐκ μὴ ἐχόντων βάρος μηδὲ κουφότητα ἔχοντα κουφότητα καὶ βάρος, ἐοίκασι περὶ ἄλλου οὐρανοῦ λέγειν καὶ σωμάτων ἀλλʼ οὐ τῶν αἰσθητῶν· οἱ δὲ χωριστὸν ποιοῦντες, ὅτι ἐπὶ τῶν αἰσθητῶν οὐκ ἔσται τὰ ἀξιώματα, ἀληθῆ δὲ τὰ λεγόμενα καὶ σαίνει τὴν ψυχήν, εἶναί τε ὑπολαμβάνουσι καὶ χωριστὰ εἶναι· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ τὰ μεγέθη τὰ μαθηματικά.  δῆλον οὖν ὅτι καὶ ὁ ἐναντιούμενος λόγος τἀναντία ἐρεῖ, καὶ ὃ ἄρτι ἠπορήθη λυτέον τοῖς οὕτω λέγουσι, διὰ τί οὐδαμῶς ἐν τοῖς αἰσθητοῖς ὑπαρχόντων τὰ πάθη ὑπάρχει αὐτῶν ἐν τοῖς αἰσθητοῖς. εἰσὶ δέ τινες οἳ ἐκ τοῦ πέρατα εἶναι καὶ ἔσχατα τὴν στιγμὴν μὲν γραμμῆς, ταύτην δʼ ἐπιπέδου, τοῦτο δὲ τοῦ στερεοῦ, οἴονται εἶναι ἀνάγκην τοιαύτας φύσεις εἶναι. δεῖ δὴ καὶ τοῦτον ὁρᾶν τὸν λόγον, μὴ λίαν ᾖ μαλακός.

οὔτε γὰρ οὐσίαι εἰσὶ τὰ ἔσχατα ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον πάντα ταῦτα πέρατα (ἑπεὶ καὶ τῆς βαδίσεως καὶ ὅλως κινήσεως ἔστι τι πέρας· τοῦτʼ οὖν ἔσται τόδε τι καὶ οὐσία τις· ἀλλʼ ἄτοπον)·—οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ εἰ καὶ εἰσί, τῶνδε τῶν αἰσθητῶν ἔσονται πάντα (ἐπὶ τούτων γὰρ ὁ λόγος εἴρηκεν)· διὰ τί οὖν χωριστὰ ἔσται;—ἔτι δὲ ἐπιζητήσειεν ἄν τις μὴ λίαν εὐχερὴς ὢν περὶ μὲν τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ παντὸς καὶ τῶν μαθηματικῶν τὸ μηθὲν συμβάλλεσθαι ἀλλήλοις τὰ πρότερα τοῖς ὕστερον (μὴ ὄντος γὰρ τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ οὐθὲν ἧττον τὰ μεγέθη ἔσται τοῖς τὰ μαθηματικὰ μόνον εἶναι φαμένοις, καὶ τούτων μὴ ὄντων ἡ ψυχὴ καὶ τὰ σώματα τὰ αἰσθητά· οὐκ ἔοικε δʼ ἡ φύσις ἐπεισοδιώδης οὖσα ἐκ τῶν φαινομένων, ὥσπερ μοχθηρὰ τραγῳδία)· τοῖς δὲ τὰς ἰδέας τιθεμένοις τοῦτο μὲν ἐκφεύγει—ποιοῦσι γὰρ τὰ μεγέθη ἐκ τῆς ὕλης καὶ ἀριθμοῦ, ἐκ μὲν τῆς δυάδος τὰ μήκη, ἐκ τριάδος δʼ ἴσως τὰ ἐπίπεδα, ἐκ δὲ τῆς τετράδος τὰ στερεὰ ἢ καὶ ἐξ ἄλλων ἀριθμῶν· διαφέρει γὰρ οὐθέν—,

ἀλλὰ ταῦτά γε πότερον ἰδέαι ἔσονται, ἢ τίς ὁ τρόπος αὐτῶν, καὶ τί συμβάλλονται τοῖς οὖσιν; οὐθὲν γάρ, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ τὰ μαθηματικά, οὐδὲ ταῦτα συμβάλλεται. ἀλλὰ μὴν οὐδʼ ὑπάρχει γε κατʼ αὐτῶν οὐθὲν θεώρημα, ἐὰν μή τις βούληται κινεῖν τὰ μαθηματικὰ καὶ ποιεῖν ἰδίας τινὰς δόξας. ἔστι δʼ οὐ χαλεπὸν ὁποιασοῦν ὑποθέσεις λαμβάνοντας μακροποιεῖν καὶ συνείρειν. οὗτοι μὲν οὖν ταύτῃ προσγλιχόμενοι ταῖς ἰδέαις τὰ μαθηματικὰ διαμαρτάνουσιν· οἱ δὲ πρῶτοι δύο τοὺς ἀριθμοὺς ποιήσαντες, τόν τε τῶν εἰδῶν καὶ τὸν μαθηματικόν, οὔτʼ εἰρήκασιν οὔτʼ ἔχοιεν ἂν εἰπεῖν πῶς καὶ ἐκ τίνος ἔσται ὁ μαθηματικός. ποιοῦσι γὰρ αὐτὸν μεταξὺ τοῦ εἰδητικοῦ καὶ τοῦ αἰσθητοῦ.

εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἐκ τοῦ μεγάλου καὶ μικροῦ, ὁ αὐτὸς ἐκείνῳ ἔσται τῷ τῶν ἰδεῶν (ἐξ ἄλλου δέ τινος μικροῦ καὶ μεγάλου τὰ  μεγέθη ποιεῖ)·  εἰ δʼ ἕτερόν τι ἐρεῖ, πλείω τὰ στοιχεῖα ἐρεῖ· καὶ εἰ ἕν τι ἑκατέρου ἡ ἀρχή, κοινόν τι ἐπὶ τούτων ἔσται τὸ ἕν, ζητητέον τε πῶς καὶ ταῦτα πολλὰ τὸ ἓν καὶ ἅμα τὸν ἀριθμὸν γενέσθαι ἄλλως ἢ ἐξ ἑνὸς καὶ δυάδος ἀορίστου ἀδύνατον κατʼ ἐκεῖνον. πάντα δὴ ταῦτα ἄλογα, καὶ μάχεται καὶ αὐτὰ ἑαυτοῖς καὶ τοῖς εὐλόγοις, καὶ ἔοικεν ἐν αὐτοῖς εἶναι ὁ Σιμωνίδου μακρὸς λόγος· γίγνεται γὰρ ὁ μακρὸς λόγος ὥσπερ ὁ τῶν δούλων ὅταν μηθὲν ὑγιὲς λέγωσιν. φαίνεται δὲ καὶ αὐτὰ τὰ στοιχεῖα τὸ μέγα καὶ τὸ μικρὸν βοᾶν ὡς ἑλκόμενα· οὐ δύναται γὰρ οὐδαμῶς γεννῆσαι τὸν ἀριθμὸν ἀλλʼ ἢ τὸν ἀφʼ ἑνὸς διπλασιαζόμενον.—ἄτοπον δὲ καὶ γένεσιν ποιεῖν ἀϊδίων ὄντων, μᾶλλον δʼ ἕν τι τῶν ἀδυνάτων.

οἱ μὲν οὖν Πυθαγόρειοι πότερον οὐ ποιοῦσιν ἢ ποιοῦσι γένεσιν οὐδὲν δεῖ διστάζειν· φανερῶς γὰρ λέγουσιν ὡς τοῦ ἑνὸς συσταθέντος, εἴτʼ ἐξ ἐπιπέδων εἴτʼ ἐκ χροιᾶς εἴτʼ ἐκ σπέρματος εἴτʼ ἐξ ὧν ἀποροῦσιν εἰπεῖν, εὐθὺς τὸ ἔγγιστα τοῦ ἀπείρου ὅτι εἵλκετο καὶ ἐπεραίνετο ὑπὸ τοῦ πέρατος. ἀλλʼ ἐπειδὴ κοσμοποιοῦσι καὶ φυσικῶς βούλονται λέγειν, δίκαιον αὐτοὺς ἐξετάζειν τι περὶ φύσεως, ἐκ δὲ τῆς νῦν ἀφεῖναι μεθόδου· τὰς γὰρ ἐν τοῖς ἀκινήτοις ζητοῦμεν ἀρχάς, ὥστε καὶ τῶν ἀριθμῶν τῶν τοιούτων ἐπισκεπτέον τὴν γένεσιν.

τοῦ μὲν οὖν περιττοῦ γένεσιν οὔ φασιν, ὡς δηλονότι τοῦ ἀρτίου οὔσης γενέσεως· τὸν δʼ ἄρτιον πρῶτον ἐξ ἀνίσων τινὲς κατασκευάζουσι τοῦ μεγάλου καὶ μικροῦ ἰσασθέντων. ἀνάγκη οὖν πρότερον ὑπάρχειν τὴν ἀνισότητα αὐτοῖς τοῦ ἰσασθῆναι· εἰ δʼ ἀεὶ ἦσαν ἰσασμένα, οὐκ ἂν ἦσαν ἄνισα πρότερον (τοῦ γὰρ ἀεὶ οὐκ ἔστι πρότερον οὐθέν), ὥστε φανερὸν ὅτι οὐ τοῦ θεωρῆσαι ἕνεκεν ποιοῦσι τὴν γένεσιν τῶν ἀριθμῶν.—ἔχει δʼ ἀπορίαν καὶ εὐπορήσαντι ἐπιτίμησιν πῶς ἔχει πρὸς τὸ ἀγαθὸν καὶ τὸ καλὸν τὰ στοιχεῖα καὶ αἱ ἀρχαί· ἀπορίαν μὲν ταύτην, πότερόν ἐστί τι ἐκείνων οἷον βουλόμεθα λέγειν αὐτὸ τὸ ἀγαθὸν καὶ τὸ ἄριστον, ἢ οὔ, ἀλλʼ ὑστερογενῆ.

παρὰ μὲν γὰρ τῶν θεολόγων ἔοικεν ὁμολογεῖσθαι τῶν νῦν τισίν, οἳ οὔ φασιν, ἀλλὰ προελθούσης τῆς τῶν ὄντων φύσεως καὶ τὸ ἀγαθὸν καὶ τὸ καλὸν ἐμφαίνεσθαι (τοῦτο δὲ ποιοῦσιν εὐλαβούμενοι ἀληθινὴν δυσχέρειαν ἣ συμβαίνει τοῖς λέγουσιν, ὥσπερ ἔνιοι, τὸ ἓν ἀρχήν·  ἔστι δʼ ἡ δυσχέρεια οὐ διὰ τὸ τῇ ἀρχῇ τὸ εὖ ἀποδιδόναι ὡς ὑπάρχον, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸ τὸ ἓν ἀρχὴν καὶ ἀρχὴν ὡς στοιχεῖον καὶ τὸν ἀριθμὸν ἐκ τοῦ ἑνός),—οἱ δὲ ποιηταὶ οἱ ἀρχαῖοι ταύτῃ ὁμοίως, ᾗ βασιλεύειν καὶ ἄρχειν φασὶν οὐ τοὺς πρώτους, οἷον νύκτα καὶ οὐρανὸν ἢ χάος ἢ ὠκεανόν, ἀλλὰ τὸν Δία· οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ τούτοις μὲν διὰ τὸ μεταβάλλειν τοὺς ἄρχοντας τῶν ὄντων συμβαίνει τοιαῦτα λέγειν, ἐπεὶ οἵ γε μεμιγμένοι αὐτῶν  τῷ μὴ μυθικῶς πάντα λέγειν, οἷον Φερεκύδης καὶ ἕτεροί τινες, τὸ γεννῆσαν πρῶτον ἄριστον τιθέασι, καὶ οἱ Μάγοι, καὶ τῶν ὑστέρων δὲ σοφῶν οἷον Ἐμπεδοκλῆς τε καὶ Ἀναξαγόρας, ὁ μὲν τὴν φιλίαν στοιχεῖον ὁ δὲ τὸν νοῦν ἀρχὴν ποιήσας.

τῶν δὲ τὰς ἀκινήτους οὐσίας εἶναι λεγόντων οἱ μέν φασιν αὐτὸ τὸ ἓν τὸ ἀγαθὸν αὐτὸ εἶναι· οὐσίαν μέντοι τὸ ἓν αὐτοῦ ᾤοντο εἶναι μάλιστα.—ἡ μὲν οὖν ἀπορία αὕτη, ποτέρως δεῖ λέγειν· θαυμαστὸν δʼ εἰ τῷ πρώτῳ καὶ ἀϊδίῳ καὶ αὐταρκεστάτῳ τοῦτʼ αὐτὸ πρῶτον οὐχ ὡς ἀγαθὸν ὑπάρχει, τὸ αὔταρκες καὶ ἡ σωτηρία. ἀλλὰ μὴν οὐ διʼ ἄλλο τι ἄφθαρτον ἢ διότι εὖ ἔχει, οὐδʼ αὔταρκες, ὥστε τὸ μὲν φάναι τὴν ἀρχὴν τοιαύτην εἶναι εὔλογον ἀληθὲς εἶναι, τὸ μέντοι ταύτην εἶναι τὸ ἕν, ἢ εἰ μὴ τοῦτο, στοιχεῖόν γε καὶ στοιχεῖον ἀριθμῶν, ἀδύνατον. συμβαίνει γὰρ πολλὴ δυσχέρεια—ἣν ἔνιοι φεύγοντες ἀπειρήκασιν, οἱ τὸ ἓν μὲν ὁμολογοῦντες ἀρχὴν εἶναι πρώτην καὶ στοιχεῖον, τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ δὲ τοῦ μαθηματικοῦ —ἅπασαι γὰρ αἱ μονάδες γίγνονται ὅπερ ἀγαθόν τι, καὶ πολλή τις εὐπορία ἀγαθῶν.

ἔτι εἰ τὰ εἴδη ἀριθμοί, τὰ εἴδη πάντα ὅπερ ἀγαθόν τι· ἀλλὰ μὴν ὅτου βούλεται τιθέτω τις εἶναι ἰδέας· εἰ μὲν γὰρ τῶν ἀγαθῶν μόνον, οὐκ ἔσονται οὐσίαι αἱ ἰδέαι, εἰ δὲ καὶ τῶν οὐσιῶν, πάντα τὰ ζῷα καὶ τὰ φυτὰ ἀγαθὰ καὶ τὰ μετέχοντα. ταῦτά τε δὴ συμβαίνει ἄτοπα, καὶ τὸ ἐναντίον στοιχεῖον, εἴτε πλῆθος ὂν εἴτε τὸ ἄνισον καὶ μέγα καὶ μικρόν, τὸ κακὸν αὐτό (διόπερ ὁ μὲν ἔφευγε τὸ ἀγαθὸν προσάπτειν τῷ ἑνὶ ὡς ἀναγκαῖον ὄν, ἐπειδὴ ἐξ ἐναντίων ἡ γένεσις, τὸ κακὸν τὴν τοῦ πλήθους φύσιν εἶναι· οἱ δὲ λέγουσι τὸ ἄνισον τὴν τοῦ κακοῦ φύσιν)· συμβαίνει δὴ πάντα τὰ ὄντα μετέχειν τοῦ κακοῦ ἔξω ἑνὸς αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἑνός, καὶ μᾶλλον ἀκράτου μετέχειν τοὺς ἀριθμοὺς ἢ τὰ μεγέθη,  καὶ τὸ κακὸν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ χώραν εἶναι, καὶ μετέχειν καὶ ὀρέγεσθαι τοῦ φθαρτικοῦ· φθαρτικὸν γὰρ τοῦ ἐναντίου τὸ ἐναντίον.

καὶ εἰ ὥσπερ ἐλέγομεν ὅτι ἡ ὕλη ἐστὶ τὸ δυνάμει ἕκαστον, οἷον πυρὸς τοῦ ἐνεργείᾳ τὸ δυνάμει πῦρ, τὸ κακὸν ἔσται αὐτὸ τὸ δυνάμει ἀγαθόν. ταῦτα δὴ πάντα συμβαίνει, τὸ μὲν ὅτι ἀρχὴν πᾶσαν στοιχεῖον ποιοῦσι, τὸ δʼ ὅτι τἀναντία ἀρχάς, τὸ δʼ ὅτι τὸ ἓν ἀρχήν, τὸ δʼ ὅτι τοὺς ἀριθμοὺς τὰς πρώτας οὐσίας καὶ χωριστὰ καὶ εἴδη.

εἰ οὖν καὶ τὸ μὴ τιθέναι τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἐν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς καὶ τὸ τιθέναι οὕτως ἀδύνατον, δῆλον ὅτι αἱ ἀρχαὶ οὐκ ὀρθῶς ἀποδίδονται οὐδὲ αἱ πρῶται οὐσίαι. οὐκ ὀρθῶς δʼ ὑπολαμβάνει οὐδʼ εἴ τις παρεικάζει τὰς τοῦ ὅλου ἀρχὰς τῇ τῶν ζῴων καὶ φυτῶν, ὅτι ἐξ ἀορίστων ἀτελῶν τε ἀεὶ τὰ τελειότερα, διὸ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν πρώτων οὕτως ἔχειν φησίν, ὥστε μηδὲ ὄν τι εἶναι τὸ ἓν αὐτό. εἰσὶ γὰρ καὶ ἐνταῦθα τέλειαι αἱ ἀρχαὶ ἐξ ὧν ταῦτα· ἄνθρωπος γὰρ ἄνθρωπον γεννᾷ, καὶ οὐκ ἔστι τὸ σπέρμα πρῶτον. ἄτοπον δὲ καὶ τὸ τόπον ἅμα τοῖς στερεοῖς τοῖς μαθηματικοῖς ποιῆσαι (ὁ μὲν γὰρ τόπος τῶν καθʼ ἕκαστον ἴδιος, διὸ χωριστὰ τόπῳ, τὰ δὲ μαθηματικὰ οὐ πού), καὶ τὸ εἰπεῖν μὲν ὅτι ποὺ ἔσται, τί δέ ἐστιν ὁ τόπος μή.—ἔδει δὲ τοὺς λέγοντας ἐκ στοιχείων εἶναι τὰ ὄντα καὶ τῶν ὄντων τὰ πρῶτα τοὺς ἀριθμούς, διελομένους πῶς ἄλλο ἐξ ἄλλου ἐστίν, οὕτω λέγειν τίνα τρόπον ὁ ἀριθμός ἐστιν ἐκ τῶν ἀρχῶν.

πότερον μίξει; ἀλλʼ οὔτε πᾶν μικτόν, τό τε γιγνόμενον ἕτερον, οὐκ ἔσται τε χωριστὸν τὸ ἓν οὐδʼ ἑτέρα φύσις· οἱ δὲ βούλονται. ἀλλὰ συνθέσει, ὥσπερ συλλαβή; ἀλλὰ θέσιν τε ἀνάγκη ὑπάρχειν, καὶ χωρὶς ὁ νοῶν νοήσει τὸ ἓν καὶ τὸ πλῆθος. τοῦτʼ οὖν ἔσται ὁ ἀριθμός, μονὰς καὶ πλῆθος, ἢ τὸ ἓν καὶ ἄνισον. καὶ ἐπεὶ τὸ ἐκ τινῶν εἶναι ἔστι μὲν ὡς ἐνυπαρχόντων ἔστι δὲ ὡς οὔ, ποτέρως ὁ ἀριθμός; οὕτως γὰρ ὡς ἐνυπαρχόντων οὐκ ἔστιν ἀλλʼ ἢ ὧν γένεσις ἔστιν. ἀλλʼ ὡς ἀπὸ σπέρματος; ἀλλʼ οὐχ οἷόν τε τοῦ ἀδιαιρέτου τι ἀπελθεῖν. ἀλλʼ ὡς ἐκ τοῦ ἐναντίου μὴ ὑπομένοντος; ἀλλʼ ὅσα οὕτως ἔστι, καὶ ἐξ ἄλλου τινός ἐστιν ὑπομένοντος. ἐπεὶ τοίνυν τὸ ἓν ὁ μὲν τῷ πλήθει ὡς ἐναντίον τίθησιν,  ὁ δὲ τῷ ἀνίσῳ, ὡς ἴσῳ τῷ ἑνὶ χρώμενος, ὡς ἐξ ἐναντίων εἴη ἂν ὁ ἀριθμός· ἔστιν ἄρα τι ἕτερον ἐξ οὗ ὑπομένοντος καὶ θατέρου ἐστὶν ἢ γέγονεν.

ἔτι τί δή ποτε τὰ μὲν ἄλλʼ ὅσα ἐξ ἐναντίων ἢ οἷς ἔστιν ἐναντία φθείρεται κἂν ἐκ παντὸς ᾖ, ὁ δὲ ἀριθμὸς οὔ; περὶ τούτου γὰρ οὐθὲν λέγεται. καίτοι καὶ ἐνυπάρχον καὶ μὴ ἐνυπάρχον φθείρει τὸ ἐναντίον, οἷον τὸ νεῖκος τὸ μῖγμα (καίτοι γε οὐκ ἔδει· οὐ γὰρ ἐκείνῳ γε ἐναντίον).—οὐθὲν δὲ διώρισται οὐδὲ ὁποτέρως οἱ ἀριθμοὶ αἴτιοι τῶν οὐσιῶν καὶ τοῦ εἶναι, πότερον ὡς ὅροι (οἷον αἱ στιγμαὶ τῶν μεγεθῶν, καὶ ὡς Εὔρυτος ἔταττε τίς ἀριθμὸς τίνος, οἷον ὁδὶ μὲν ἀνθρώπου ὁδὶ δὲ ἵππου, ὥσπερ οἱ τοὺς ἀριθμοὺς ἄγοντες εἰς τὰ σχήματα τρίγωνον καὶ τετράγωνον, οὕτως ἀφομοιῶν ταῖς ψήφοις τὰς μορφὰς τῶν φυτῶν), ἢ ὅτι  λόγος ἡ συμφωνία ἀριθμῶν, ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἄνθρωπος καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἕκαστον; τὰ δὲ δὴ πάθη πῶς ἀριθμοί, τὸ λευκὸν καὶ γλυκὺ καὶ τὸ θερμόν; ὅτι δὲ οὐχ οἱ ἀριθμοὶ οὐσία οὐδὲ τῆς μορφῆς αἴτιοι, δῆλον· ὁ γὰρ λόγος ἡ οὐσία, ὁ δʼ ἀριθμὸς ὕλη.

οἷον σαρκὸς ἢ ὀστοῦ ἀριθμὸς ἡ οὐσία οὕτω, τρία πυρὸς γῆς δὲ δύο· καὶ ἀεὶ ὁ ἀριθμὸς ὃς ἂν ᾖ τινῶν ἐστιν, ἢ πύρινος ἢ γήϊνος ἢ μοναδικός, ἀλλʼ ἡ οὐσία τὸ τοσόνδʼ εἶναι πρὸς τοσόνδε κατὰ τὴν μῖξιν· τοῦτο δʼ οὐκέτι ἀριθμὸς ἀλλὰ λόγος μίξεως ἀριθμῶν σωματικῶν ἢ ὁποιωνοῦν. οὔτε οὖν τῷ ποιῆσαι αἴτιος ὁ ἀριθμός, οὔτε ὅλως ὁ ἀριθμὸς οὔτε ὁ μοναδικός, οὔτε ὕλη οὔτε λόγος καὶ εἶδος τῶν πραγμάτων. ἀλλὰ μὴν οὐδʼ ὡς τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα.

ἀπορήσειε δʼ ἄν τις καὶ τί τὸ εὖ ἐστὶ τὸ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀριθμῶν τῷ ἐν ἀριθμῷ εἶναι τὴν μῖξιν, ἢ ἐν εὐλογίστῳ ἢ ἐν περιττῷ. νυνὶ γὰρ οὐθὲν ὑγιεινότερον τρὶς τρία ἂν ᾖ τὸ μελίκρατον κεκραμένον, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ὠφελήσειεν ἂν ἐν οὐθενὶ λόγῳ ὂν ὑδαρὲς δὲ ἢ ἐν ἀριθμῷ ἄκρατον ὄν. ἔτι οἱ λόγοι ἐν προσθέσει ἀριθμῶν εἰσὶν οἱ τῶν μίξεων, οὐκ ἐν ἀριθμοῖς, οἷον τρία πρὸς δύο ἀλλʼ οὐ τρὶς δύο. τὸ γὰρ αὐτὸ δεῖ γένος εἶναι ἐν ταῖς πολλαπλασιώσεσιν, ὥστε δεῖ μετρεῖσθαι τῷ τε Α τὸν στοῖχον ἐφʼ οὗ ΑΒΓ καὶ τῷ Δ τὸν ΔΕΖ· ὥστε τῷ αὐτῷ πάντα. οὔκουν ἔσται πυρὸς ΒΕΓΖ καὶ ὕδατος ἀριθμὸς δὶς τρία.  —εἰ δʼ ἀνάγκη πάντα ἀριθμοῦ κοινωνεῖν, ἀνάγκη πολλὰ συμβαίνειν τὰ αὐτά, καὶ ἀριθμὸν τὸν αὐτὸν τῷδε καὶ ἄλλῳ.

ἆρʼ οὖν τοῦτʼ αἴτιον καὶ διὰ τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ πρᾶγμα, ἢ ἄδηλον; οἷον ἔστι τις τῶν τοῦ ἡλίου φορῶν ἀριθμός, καὶ πάλιν τῶν τῆς σελήνης, καὶ τῶν ζῴων γε ἑκάστου τοῦ βίου καὶ ἡλικίας· τί οὖν κωλύει ἐνίους μὲν τούτων τετραγώνους εἶναι ἐνίους δὲ κύβους, καὶ ἴσους τοὺς δὲ διπλασίους; οὐθὲν γὰρ κωλύει, ἀλλʼ ἀνάγκη ἐν τούτοις στρέφεσθαι, εἰ ἀριθμοῦ πάντα ἐκοινώνει. ἐνεδέχετό τε τὰ διαφέροντα ὑπὸ τὸν αὐτὸν ἀριθμὸν πίπτειν· ὥστʼ εἴ τισιν ὁ αὐτὸς ἀριθμὸς συνεβεβήκει, ταὐτὰ ἂν ἦν ἀλλήλοις ἐκεῖνα τὸ αὐτὸ εἶδος ἀριθμοῦ ἔχοντα, οἷον ἥλιος καὶ σελήνη τὰ αὐτά. ἀλλὰ διὰ τί αἴτια ταῦτα; ἑπτὰ μὲν φωνήεντα, ἑπτὰ δὲ χορδαὶ ἡ ἁρμονία, ἑπτὰ δὲ αἱ πλειάδες, ἐν ἑπτὰ δὲ ὀδόντας βάλλει (ἔνιά γε, ἔνια δʼ οὔ), ἑπτὰ δὲ οἱ ἐπὶ Θήβας.

ἆρʼ οὖν ὅτι τοιοσδὶ ὁ ἀριθμὸς πέφυκεν, διὰ τοῦτο ἢ ἐκεῖνοι ἐγένοντο ἑπτὰ ἢ ἡ πλειὰς ἑπτὰ ἀστέρων ἐστίν; ἢ οἱ μὲν διὰ τὰς πύλας ἢ ἄλλην τινὰ αἰτίαν, τὴν δὲ ἡμεῖς οὕτως ἀριθμοῦμεν, τὴν δὲ ἄρκτον γε δώδεκα, οἱ δὲ πλείους· ἐπεὶ καὶ τὸ ΞΨΖ συμφωνίας φασὶν εἶναι, καὶ ὅτι ἐκεῖναι τρεῖς, καὶ ταῦτα τρία· ὅτι δὲ μυρία ἂν εἴη τοιαῦτα, οὐθὲν μέλει (τῷ γὰρ Γ καὶ Ρ εἴη ἂν ἓν σημεῖον)· εἰ δʼ ὅτι διπλάσιον τῶν ἄλλων ἕκαστον, ἄλλο δʼ οὔ, αἴτιον δʼ ὅτι τριῶν ὄντων τόπων ἓν ἐφʼ ἑκάστου ἐπιφέρεται τῷ σίγμα, διὰ τοῦτο τρία μόνον ἐστὶν ἀλλʼ οὐχ ὅτι αἱ συμφωνίαι τρεῖς, ἐπεὶ πλείους γε αἱ συμφωνίαι, ἐνταῦθα δʼ οὐκέτι δύναται. ὅμοιοι δὴ καὶ οὗτοι τοῖς ἀρχαίοις Ὁμηρικοῖς, οἳ μικρὰς ὁμοιότητας ὁρῶσι μεγάλας δὲ παρορῶσιν.

λέγουσι δέ τινες ὅτι πολλὰ τοιαῦτα, οἷον αἵ τε μέσαι ἡ μὲν ἐννέα ἡ δὲ ὀκτώ, καὶ τὸ ἔπος δεκαεπτά, ἰσάριθμον τούτοις, βαίνεται δʼ ἐν μὲν τῷ δεξιῷ ἐννέα συλλαβαῖς, ἐν δὲ τῷ ἀριστερῷ ὀκτώ·  καὶ ὅτι ἴσον τὸ διάστημα ἔν τε τοῖς γράμμασιν ἀπὸ τοῦ Α πρὸς τὸ Ω, καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ βόμβυκος ἐπὶ τὴν ὀξυτάτην  ἐν αὐλοῖς, ἧς ὁ ἀριθμὸς ἴσος τῇ οὐλομελείᾳ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ. ὁρᾶν δὲ δεῖ μὴ τοιαῦτα οὐθεὶς ἂν ἀπορήσειεν οὔτε λέγειν οὔθʼ εὑρίσκειν ἐν τοῖς ἀϊδίοις, ἐπεὶ καὶ ἐν τοῖς φθαρτοῖς.

ἀλλʼ αἱ ἐν τοῖς ἀριθμοῖς φύσεις αἱ ἐπαινούμεναι καὶ τὰ τούτοις ἐναντία καὶ ὅλως τὰ ἐν τοῖς μαθήμασιν, ὡς μὲν λέγουσί τινες καὶ αἴτια ποιοῦσι τῆς φύσεως, ἔοικεν οὑτωσί γε σκοπουμένοις διαφεύγειν (κατʼ οὐδένα γὰρ τρόπον τῶν διωρισμένων περὶ τὰς ἀρχὰς οὐδὲν αὐτῶν αἴτιον)· ἔστιν ὡς μέντοι ποιοῦσι φανερὸν ὅτι τὸ εὖ ὑπάρχει καὶ τῆς συστοιχίας ἐστὶ τῆς τοῦ καλοῦ τὸ περιττόν, τὸ εὐθύ, τὸ ἰσάκις ἴσον, αἱ δυνάμεις ἐνίων ἀριθμῶν· ἅμα γὰρ ὧραι καὶ ἀριθμὸς τοιοσδί· καὶ τὰ ἄλλα δὴ ὅσα συνάγουσιν ἐκ τῶν μαθηματικῶν θεωρημάτων πάντα ταύτην ἔχει τὴν δύναμιν.

διὸ καὶ ἔοικε συμπτώμασιν· ἔστι γὰρ συμβεβηκότα μέν, ἀλλʼ οἰκεῖα ἀλλήλοις πάντα, ἓν δὲ τῷ ἀνάλογον· ἐν ἑκάστῃ γὰρ τοῦ ὄντος κατηγορίᾳ ἐστὶ τὸ ἀνάλογον, ὡς εὐθὺ ἐν μήκει οὕτως ἐν πλάτει τὸ ὁμαλόν, ἴσως ἐν ἀριθμῷ τὸ περιττόν, ἐν δὲ χροιᾷ τὸ λευκόν.—ἔτι οὐχ οἱ ἐν τοῖς εἴδεσιν ἀριθμοὶ αἴτιοι τῶν ἁρμονικῶν καὶ τῶν τοιούτων (διαφέρουσι γὰρ ἐκεῖνοι ἀλλήλων οἱ ἴσοι εἴδει· καὶ γὰρ αἱ μονάδες)· ὥστε διά γε ταῦτα εἴδη οὐ ποιητέον. τὰ μὲν οὖν συμβαίνοντα ταῦτά τε κἂν ἔτι πλείω συναχθείη· ἔοικε δὲ τεκμήριον εἶναι τὸ πολλὰ κακοπαθεῖν περὶ τὴν γένεσιν αὐτῶν καὶ μηδένα τρόπον δύνασθαι συνεῖραι τοῦ μὴ χωριστὰ εἶναι τὰ μαθηματικὰ τῶν αἰσθητῶν, ὡς ἔνιοι λέγουσι, μηδὲ ταύτας εἶναι τὰς ἀρχάς.

Let so much then have been said about this substance. But all make the principles contraries, as in the case of natural things, and likewise in the case of immovable substances. Yet if it is impossible for anything to be prior to the principle of all things, it would be impossible for the principle, being something else, to be a principle; as if someone were to say that white is a principle, not insofar as it is something else but insofar as it is white, while nevertheless it belongs to a substrate and, being something else, is white; for that other thing will be prior. But all things come to be from contraries as from some substrate; therefore this must belong most of all to contraries.

Therefore all contraries are always predicated of a substrate, and none is separate; but, as also appears, nothing is contrary to substance, and the argument bears witness to this.

Therefore none of the contraries is, properly speaking, a principle of all things, but some other thing is.—But some make one of the contraries matter: some set the unequal against the one, as being the nature of plurality; others set plurality against the one (for numbers are generated, according to some, from the dyad of the unequal, the great and the small, and according to others from plurality, both being under the substance of the one). For he too who calls the unequal and the one the elements, and the unequal a dyad composed of great and small, says that the unequal and the great and the small are one, though he does not distinguish that they are one in account but not in number. But neither do they rightly render the principles which they call elements: some say that the great and the small together with the one are three elements of numbers, the two being matter and the one form; others say the many and the few, because the great and the small are more proper in nature to magnitude; and others still state the more universal terms in these cases, the exceeding and the exceeded.

These differ, one may say, in nothing with respect to some of the consequences, but only with respect to logical difficulties, which they guard against because they themselves conduct logical demonstrations. Yet it belongs to the same argument to make the exceeding and the exceeded principles, rather than the great and the small, and to make number prior to the dyad from the elements; for both are more universal. But now they state the one and not the other. Some oppose the different and the other to the one; others oppose plurality and the one. But if beings are, as they wish, from contraries, and if nothing is contrary to the one—or, if anything is to be, plurality—while the unequal is contrary to the equal, and the different to the same, and the other to itself, those who oppose the one to plurality have most hold of some plausible view; yet not even these sufficiently. For the one will be few; for plurality is opposed to fewness, and the many to the few.—That the one signifies a measure is clear.

And in every case there is some other underlying thing: for example, in harmony a diesis; in magnitude a finger or a foot or something of that sort; in rhythms a foot or a syllable. Likewise, in weight there is some determinate weight; and in all cases in the same way: among qualities, some quality; among quantities, some quantity; and the measure is indivisible, in one case according to the form, in another with respect to perception, as though the one were not some substance existing by itself. And this is reasonable; for the one signifies that it is the measure of some plurality, and number that it is a measured plurality and a plurality of measures (and therefore it is reasonably not the one that is number; for neither is the measure measures, but both the measure and the one are a principle). But the measure must always be something the same for all things: for example, if they are horses, the measure is a horse; and if men, a man. But if there are a man and a horse and a god, perhaps the measure is an animal, and their number will be animals.

But if there are a man and white and walking, there is least of all a number of these, because all belong to the same thing and are one in number; nevertheless, their number will be of genera, or of some other such designation.

But those who make the unequal one thing, and the indefinite dyad of great and small, speak very far from what seems and is possible. For these are affections and attributes rather than substrates of numbers and magnitudes: the many and few of number, and the great and small of magnitude, just as even and odd, smooth and rough, straight and curved. Further, besides this error, the great and small and things of this sort must be relatives; and the relative is least of all a certain nature or substance, and is posterior to quality and quantity. And the relative is, as was said, an affection of quantity, but not matter—if indeed it is something different both from the relative in general and from its parts and species. For there is nothing that is either great or small, or many or few, or in general relative, which is not, being something else, many or few or great or small or relative.

A sign that the relative is least of all a substance and a being is that it alone has neither generation nor destruction nor motion, as in quantity there are increase and diminution, in quality alteration, in place locomotion, and in substance simple generation and destruction—but there is none according to relation. For without itself being moved, a thing will at one time be greater, at another lesser or equal, another thing having been moved quantitatively.

And the matter of each thing must be that which is potentially such, and therefore also in the case of substance; but the relative is neither potentially substance nor actually. It is absurd, or rather impossible, then, to make what is not a substance an element of substance and prior to it; for all the categories are posterior. Further, the elements are not predicated of the things of which they are elements; but many and few are predicated separately and together of number, and long and short of a line, and a plane is broad and narrow.

But if there is indeed some plurality of which few is always predicated, such as the dyad (for if it were many, the one would be few), and if there can be something simply many, such as ten, if there is no greater number than this, or ten thousand: how then will number thus be composed from few and many? For either both ought to be predicated or neither; but now only one of them is predicated.

But one must consider in general whether eternal things can be composed of elements. For they will have matter; for everything composed of elements is composite. If, then, it is necessary that that from which a thing is—even if it always is—should be that from which it comes to be, if it comes to be, and everything comes to be from that which is potentially the thing that comes to be (for it could not come to be from the impossible, nor could it be), and what is possible admits both of being actual and of not being actual, then, even if number or anything else having matter exists always as much as possible, it would admit of not being, just as does that which lasts one day and that which lasts however many years; and if so, also that which lasts for a time without limit. They would not then be eternal, if that which admits of not being is not eternal, as it has happened to us to establish in other discussions. But if what is now said is universally true, that no substance is eternal unless it is actuality, while the elements are matter of substance, there could be no elements, inherent in it, from which any eternal substance is composed.

There are some who make the indefinite dyad, together with the one, an element, but object to the unequal, reasonably, on account of the impossible consequences. They have removed from the difficulties only as many as necessarily follow for those who make the unequal and the relative an element because they do so; but whatever difficulties are apart from this opinion must necessarily belong to them too, whether they make the ideal number from these or the mathematical number.—There are many causes of their turning aside toward these causes, but most of all their having been perplexed in an archaic manner. For it seemed to them that all beings would be one, being itself, unless someone should solve and confront Parmenides' saying:

for never shall this prevail, that things which are not are;
but it is necessary to show that what is not is.

For thus, from being and something else, beings will exist, if they are many.

And yet, first, if being is said in many ways (for it signifies substance in one way, quality in another, quantity in another, and likewise the other categories), in what sense will all beings be one if not-being is not to be? Will substances be one, or affections and likewise the other things, or all of them, so that this and such and so much and all the other things which signify some one thing will be one? But it is absurd, or rather impossible, that one nature, having come to be, should be the cause of being's being this in one case, such in another, so much in another, and somewhere in another. Further, from what not-being and being are beings many? For not-being too is said in many ways, since being is; and not being a man signifies not being this, not straight signifies not being such, and not three cubits signifies not being so much.

From what being and not-being, then, are beings many? He wishes, indeed, to call not-being falsity and this nature, from which, together with being, beings are many; hence it was also said that one must posit some falsity, just as geometers posit that what is not a foot long is a foot long. But this cannot be so. For geometers posit no falsity (for the proposition is not in the syllogism), nor do beings come to be or perish from not-being in this sense. But since not-being according to the cases is spoken of in as many ways as the categories, and besides this there is the not-being that is spoken of as false and that which is according to potentiality, generation is from the latter: a man comes from what is not a man but is potentially a man, and a white thing from what is not white but is potentially white, alike whether one thing or many things come to be.—But the inquiry appears to concern how being, in the sense of substances, is many; for the things generated are numbers and lengths and bodies.

It is absurd, then, to inquire how being, that which it is, is many, but not how qualities or quantities are many. For surely neither the indefinite dyad nor the great and the small is the cause of there being two white things, or many colors or flavors or figures; for these too would then be numbers and units. But if they had pursued these matters, they would have seen the cause also in those cases; for the cause is the same and analogous. For this divergence is also the cause of their, in seeking what is opposed to being and the one, from which beings arise, positing the relative and the unequal, which is neither contrary nor a negation of them, but one nature among beings, just as what-it-is and quality are. And they should have inquired also how relatives are many and not one; but now they inquire how there are many units besides the first one, but no longer how there are many unequals besides the unequal.

And yet they employ and speak of great and small, from which numbers arise; long and short, from which length arises; broad and narrow, from which plane arises; deep and shallow, from which solids arise; and they speak of yet more species of the relative. What, then, is the cause in these cases of their being many?—It is necessary, then, as we say, to posit for each a being potentially (and the speaker of these things further declared what is potentially this and substance, but is not-being in itself: namely, the relative, as though he had said quality, which is neither potentially the one or being nor a negation of the one or of being, but one of the beings); and much more, as was said, if he was inquiring how beings are many, he should not inquire about those in the same category—how there are many substances or many qualities—but how beings are many; for some are substances, others affections, others relatives.

In the case of the other categories, then, there is some other account of how they are many (for, because they are not separate, qualities and quantities become and are many through the substrate becoming many; though there must be some matter for each genus, except that it is impossible for it to be separate from substances). But in the case of this something there is some account of how this something is many, unless there is both this something and some such nature; rather, the difficulty is chiefly there: how there are many substances in actuality rather than one. Yet if this something and quantity are not the same, it is not stated how and why beings are many, but how quantities are many. For every number signifies some quantity, and the unit too, unless it is a measure and indivisible in respect of quantity. If, then, quantity and what-it-is are different, it is not stated from what or how what-it-is is many; but if they are the same, the speaker maintains many contradictions.—One might also pause the inquiry concerning numbers: whence must one obtain conviction that they exist?

For one who posits Ideas has some cause furnished for beings, if each of the numbers is an Idea and the Idea is for the other things a cause of being in whatever way it may be (let this be assumed for them). But for one who does not think this in this way, because he sees the inherent difficulties concerning the Ideas, so that for these reasons he does not make numbers thus, but makes mathematical number, from what source should one be convinced that such a number exists, and what use is it to other things? For the person who says it exists does not say that it is the number of anything, but says that it is some nature existing by itself; nor does it appear to be a cause. For all the theorems of arithmetic will also belong to sensible things, as was said.

Those, then, who posit that Ideas exist and that they are numbers, by taking each one thing besides the many according to the exposition of each, at least attempt to say somehow why it exists; yet since these things are neither necessary nor possible, one must not say that number exists on these grounds. But the Pythagoreans, because they saw many properties of numbers belonging to sensible bodies, made beings to be numbers—not separate numbers, but beings constituted from numbers. Why? Because the properties of numbers are present in harmony and in the heaven and in many other things. But those who say that only mathematical number exists can say nothing of this sort in accordance with their hypotheses; rather, it was said that their sciences would not exist. But we say that they do exist, as we said before. And it is clear that mathematical objects are not separate; for if they were separate, their attributes would not belong to bodies.

The Pythagoreans, then, are not liable to criticism in this respect; but in making natural bodies from numbers—things having weight and lightness from things having neither weight nor lightness—they seem to speak about another heaven and other bodies, not the sensible ones. But those who make them separate suppose them to exist and to be separate because the axioms will not hold of sensible things, whereas the statements are true and delight the soul; and likewise with mathematical magnitudes.

It is clear, then, that the opposing argument will say the contrary, and that those who speak thus must solve the difficulty just raised: why, though the properties are in no way present in sensible things, their properties are present in sensible things. There are some who think it necessary that such natures exist because a point is the limit and extremity of a line, this of a plane, and this of a solid. One must therefore examine this argument too, lest it be excessively weak.

For the extremities are not substances, but rather all these things are limits (since even walking and motion in general have some limit; that, then, will be a this-something and a substance—but that is absurd). Yet even if they are, they will all belong to these sensible things (for the argument has spoken of these); why, then, will they be separate?—Further, one who is not too readily satisfied might inquire, concerning every number and mathematical object, that the prior contributes nothing to the posterior (for even if number did not exist, magnitudes would nonetheless exist for those who say that only mathematical objects exist, and if these did not exist, soul and sensible bodies would exist; yet nature does not appear from the phenomena to be episodic, like a poor tragedy). But those who posit Ideas escape this—for they make magnitudes from matter and number: lengths from the dyad, planes perhaps from the triad, solids from the tetrad, or even from other numbers; for it makes no difference—,

But are these, then, going to be Forms, or what is their mode, and what do they contribute to the things that are? For they contribute nothing, any more than mathematical objects do. Nor, indeed, does any theorem hold of them, unless one wishes to set mathematical objects in motion and make up certain peculiar doctrines. And it is not difficult, by assuming any sort of hypotheses, to spin out a long argument and string things together. These men, then, by attaching themselves in this way to the Forms, go astray concerning mathematical objects; while the first two, who made two kinds of number, that of the Forms and the mathematical, have neither said nor could say how and from what the mathematical number will be. For they place it between the ideal and the sensible.

For if it is from the Great and the Small, it will be the same as that number of the Forms (but he makes magnitudes from some other Great and Small); whereas if he names something else, he will name more elements. And if the principle of each kind is some one thing, the One will be something common to these, and it must be investigated how these too are many; yet, according to that doctrine, it is impossible for number to come to be otherwise than from the One and the indefinite dyad. All these things, then, are irrational, and conflict both with themselves and with reasonable accounts; and Simonides' “long discourse” seems to be present in them. For the long discourse comes about, like that of slaves, when they say nothing sound. And the elements themselves, the Great and the Small, seem to cry out as though being dragged; for they can in no way generate number except that which is doubled from one.—It is also absurd to make a coming-to-be of things that are eternal, or rather it is one of the impossibilities.

As for the Pythagoreans, whether they do not make a coming-to-be or do make one, there is no need to hesitate; for they clearly say that, when the One had been constituted, whether from planes or from colour or from seed or from things which they are at a loss to state, immediately the nearest part of the unlimited was drawn in and limited by the limit. But since they are making a cosmos and wish to speak physically, it is just to examine them concerning nature, but to leave them aside from the present inquiry. For we are seeking the principles among immovable things, so that we must examine also the coming-to-be of numbers of this sort.

They do not, then, assert a coming-to-be of the odd, evidently because there is a coming-to-be of the even; and some construct the first even out of unequal Great and Small when these have been equalized. Therefore inequality must belong to them prior to their being equalized; but if they had always been equalized, they would not have been unequal before (for of that which always is there is nothing prior), so that it is clear that they do not make the coming-to-be of numbers for the sake of theoretical inquiry.—There is also a difficulty, and a reproach even for one who has found an answer, as to how the elements and principles stand in relation to the good and the beautiful: namely, whether any one of them is such as we mean when we speak of the Good Itself and the Best, or not, but whether these are later-born.

For among the theologians there seems to be agreement with certain of the present thinkers, who say that they are not so, but that, after the nature of beings had advanced, both the good and the beautiful are manifested. They do this from caution before a genuine difficulty which confronts those who, like some thinkers, say that the One is a principle; and the difficulty is not due to their attributing good to the principle as belonging to it, but to their making the One a principle, and a principle as an element, and number out of the One.—The ancient poets likewise agree in this respect, in that they say that not the first things, such as Night and Heaven or Chaos or Ocean, reign and rule, but Zeus. Yet these poets come to say such things because the rulers of beings change; whereas those among them who are mixed in so as not to say everything mythically, such as Pherecydes and certain others, posit that which first generated as best; so too do the Magi, and among the later wise men Empedocles and Anaxagoras, the former making Love an element, the latter Intellect a principle.

Of those who say that there are immovable substances, some say that the One Itself is the Good Itself; yet they supposed that its substance was pre-eminently the One.—This, then, is the difficulty: how one ought to speak. Yet it would be strange if the first, eternal, and most self-sufficient thing did not possess this very thing primarily as a good, namely self-sufficiency and preservation. But surely it is not imperishable, nor self-sufficient, for any other reason than because it is well. Thus to say that the principle is such is reasonably true; but that it is the One, or, failing that, an element, and an element of numbers, is impossible. For a great difficulty follows—one which some, seeking to avoid, have renounced: those who grant that the One is the first principle and element, but only of mathematical number—for all units become what is some good, and there is a great abundance of goods.

Further, if the Forms are numbers, all the Forms are what is some good. Yet let one posit Forms of whatever things he wishes. For if they are Forms of goods only, the Forms will not be substances; but if they are also Forms of substances, all animals and plants and all things participating in them will be good. Both these absurdities follow, and also that the contrary element—whether it is plurality or the unequal, Great and Small—is Evil Itself. Hence one man avoided attaching the good to the One, on the ground that, since coming-to-be is from contraries, the nature of plurality must be evil; while others say that the unequal is the nature of evil. It follows, then, that all beings participate in evil except the One Itself alone, and that numbers participate in a more unmixed evil than magnitudes do; that evil is the place of the good; and that it participates in and desires what is destructive. For the contrary is destructive of its contrary.

And if, as we said, matter is each thing potentially—for example, potentially fire is the matter of fire actually—evil will be the potentially good itself. All these consequences follow: one because they make every principle an element; another because they make contraries principles; another because they make the One a principle; another because they make numbers the primary substances, separate and Forms.

If, then, both not placing the good among the principles and placing it there in this way are impossible, it is clear that the principles and the primary substances are not correctly assigned. Nor does one suppose correctly if one compares the principles of the whole to those of animals and plants, on the ground that the more complete things always come from indefinite and incomplete things, and therefore says that the same holds also of the first things, so that the One Itself is not even something that is. For here too the principles from which these things come are complete: a human being generates a human being, and seed is not first. It is also absurd to make place exist simultaneously with mathematical solids (for place is peculiar to individual things, which is why they are separate in place, whereas mathematical objects are not somewhere), and to say that they will be somewhere, but not to say what place is.—Those who say that beings are from elements, and that numbers are the first among beings, ought, after distinguishing how one thing is from another, thus to say in what way number is from the principles.

Is it by mixture? But not everything is mixed, and what comes to be is different; nor will the One be separate, nor have another nature—which, however, they wish. Or is it by composition, as a syllable? But position must then belong to them, and the thinker will think the One and the plurality separately. Number, then, will be this: a unit and plurality, or the One and the unequal. And since being from certain things is in one way from things present in it, and in another way from things not present in it, in which way is number from them? For in the way of things present in it, only things that have coming-to-be are so. But is it as from seed? Yet it is not possible for anything to depart from the indivisible. Or as from a contrary that does not remain? But all things that are in this way are also from some other thing which remains. Since, therefore, one man posits the One as contrary to plurality, another as contrary to the unequal, treating the One as equal, number would be from contraries. Therefore there is some other thing from which, while it remains, number is or has come to be, together with the other contrary.

Further, why ever is it that all other things that are from contraries, or have contraries, perish even if they are from all of them, whereas number does not? For nothing is said about this. Yet a contrary destroys both what is present in a thing and what is not present, as Strife destroys the mixture—though it ought not to do so, since it is not contrary to that.—Nor has it been determined in what way numbers are causes of substances and of being: whether as limits (as points are limits of magnitudes, and as Eurytus assigned what number belonged to what thing—for example, this number to a human being, that to a horse—likening the forms of plants to pebbles, just as those who make numbers into figures make a triangle and a square); or because a concord is a ratio of numbers, and likewise a human being and each of the other things? But how are the attributes numbers—white, sweet, and hot? That numbers are neither substance nor causes of form is clear; for the ratio is the substance, while number is matter.

For example, the substance of flesh or bone is number in this sense: three parts fire and two earth; and the number, whatever it may be, is always a number of certain things, either fiery or earthy or of units; but the substance is being so much to so much according to the mixture. And this is no longer number, but a ratio of a mixture of bodily numbers, or of numbers of whatever sort. Therefore number, neither number in general nor unit-number, is not a cause by making, nor matter, nor the ratio and form of things. Nor, indeed, is it a cause as that for the sake of which.

One might also inquire what the benefit is that comes from mixtures being in a number, whether in a readily calculable number or in an odd number. For at present a honey-and-water mixture would be no more healthful if mixed three times three; rather, if watery, it would be more beneficial with no ratio at all than if it were unmixed in a number. Further, the ratios of mixtures are in the addition of numbers, not in numbers—for example, three to two, not three times two. For in multiplications the genus must be the same, so that the line on which A B C is must be measured by A, and the line D E Z by D; hence all must be measured by the same thing. Therefore B E G Z will not be a number of fire and twice three a number of water. —But if everything must participate in number, it is necessary that many things be the same, and that the same number belong to this thing and to another.

Is this, then, the cause, and is the thing so because of this, or is it unclear? For example, there is some number of the courses of the sun, and again of those of the moon, and of the life and age of each animal. What, then, prevents some of these from being squares, others cubes, some equal, and others double? Nothing prevents it; indeed, it is necessary to move among such things if all things participate in number. And different things could fall under the same number; so that, if the same number happened to belong to certain things, those things having the same species of number would be the same as one another—for example, the sun and moon would be the same. But why are these causes? There are seven vowels, seven strings in the scale, seven Pleiades, at seven months some animals cast teeth (though some do not), and seven against Thebes.

Is it then because number is naturally of such a kind that those men were seven, or that the Pleiad is seven stars? Or were the former seven because of the gates or some other cause, while we count the Pleiad in this way, whereas we count the Bear as twelve, and others count more? For they even say that ΞΨΖ are concords, and because those are three, these too are three; but they do not care that there could be ten thousand such cases—for Γ and Ρ could be one sign. And if the cause is that each of the others is double while this one is not, and that, because there are three places, one sigma is added in each case, this is why there are only three and not because the concords are three—since there are in fact more concords, but here they can no longer be so. These men, then, resemble the ancient Homeric scholars, who see small likenesses but overlook great ones.

Some say that there are many such facts: for example, the two middle strings, one having nine and the other eight, and the epic verse, having seventeen, equal in number to these; and that it is scanned in nine syllables on the right and eight on the left. And they say that the interval is equal both in the letters from Α to Ω and from the lowest note to the highest on flutes, whose number is equal to the complete melody of the heaven. But one should see that no one would be at a loss either to state or to discover such things among eternal things, since they occur even among perishable things.

But the much-praised natures in numbers, and their contraries, and in general the things in mathematical studies, which, as some say, they make causes of nature, appear to escape anyone who examines them in this way—for none of them is a cause in any of the ways distinguished concerning principles. Yet in one sense they evidently make clear that the good belongs to things, and that the odd, the straight, the square, and the powers of certain numbers belong to the column of the beautiful; for seasons and number of such a kind occur together. And all the other things which they collect from mathematical theorems have this same force.

Therefore they seem to be coincidences. For they are accidental, but all are akin to one another and are one by analogy. For in each category of being there is the analogous: as the straight is in length, so the level is in breadth; perhaps the odd is in number, and white in colour.—Further, the numbers in the Forms are not causes of harmonies and things of that sort (for those numbers equal in species differ from one another; the units too differ). Hence Forms should not be posited on these grounds. Such, then, are the consequences, and still more could be collected. But the fact that they suffer many difficulties concerning their generation, and are unable in any way to connect things so as to show that mathematical objects are not separate from sensible things, as some say, nor that these are the principles, seems to be evidence.

items.text: Ζητεῖται ποία τῶν αἰτιῶν καὶ ἀρχῶν θεωρία σοφία ἐστὶ καὶ τίνα σκοπὸν ἡ περὶ αὐτὴν μέθοδος διώκει.
Ἡ σοφία τίθεται θεωρητικὴ ἐπιστήμη τῶν πρώτων ἀρχῶν καὶ αἰτιῶν, αὑτῆς ἕνεκα αἱρετὴ καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἐπιστημῶν ἀρχική.
Ἡ θέσις γεννᾶται διὰ τῆς ἀνόδου ἀπὸ αἰσθήσεως εἰς μνήμην, ἐμπειρίαν, καθόλου ὑπόληψιν καὶ αἰτιώδη ἐπιστήμην.
Ὁ συλλογισμὸς διαγνωστικῶς μὲν ἐκ τῶν περὶ τοῦ σοφοῦ ὑπολήψεων, γενεαλογικῶς δὲ διὰ τῆς τῶν προτέρων φιλοσοφούντων ἐξετάσεως προβαίνει.
Ἡ τετραχὴ διαίρεσις τῶν αἰτίων γίνεται κανὼν πρὸς τὸ τάττειν, συγκρίνειν καὶ ἐλέγχειν τὰς προτέρας θεωρίας.
Ἡ κίνησις ἀπὸ τῆς φυσικῆς ὀρέξεως τοῦ εἰδέναι διὰ τοῦ διορισμοῦ τῆς σοφίας εἰς τὴν τῶν αἰτίων κατάταξιν καὶ ἐκεῖθεν εἰς τὰς ὑπολειπομένας ἀπορίας καταλήγει.
Πάντες ἄνθρωποι τοῦ εἰδέναι ὀρέγονται φύσει.
Ἡ μετὰ τῆς αἰσθήσεως μνήμη τὴν μάθησιν καὶ φρόνησιν δυνατωτέραν ποιεῖ.
Αἱ πολλαὶ μνῆμαι τοῦ αὐτοῦ πράγματος μιᾶς ἐμπειρίας δύναμιν ἀποτελοῦσιν.
Τέχνη γίνεται ὅταν ἐκ πολλῶν ἐμπείρων ἐννοημάτων μία καθόλου περὶ τῶν ὁμοίων ὑπόληψις γένηται.
Αἱ πράξεις καὶ αἱ γενέσεις περὶ τὸ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον εἰσίν, διὸ ἡ ἐμπειρία πολλάκις πρακτικῶς τοῦ ἄνευ ἐμπειρίας λόγου μᾶλλον ἐπιτυγχάνει.
Ἡ τοῦ διότι καὶ τῆς αἰτίας γνῶσις μᾶλλον εἰδέναι ποιεῖ ἢ ἡ τοῦ ὅτι μόνον γνῶσις.
Τὸ δύνασθαι διδάσκειν σημεῖόν ἐστι τῆς κατὰ τὰς αἰτίας γνώσεως.
Ὁ μάλιστα τὴν καθόλου ἐπιστήμην ἔχων οἶδέ πως πάντα τὰ ὑποκείμενα, καίπερ μὴ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον ἐπιστάμενος.
Αἱ τῶν πρώτων καὶ ἐλαττόνων ἀρχῶν ἐπιστῆμαι ἀκριβέστεραι καὶ διδασκαλικώτεραι τῶν ἐκ προσθέσεως γιγνομένων εἰσίν.
Ἡ δι᾽ αὑτὴν καὶ τοῦ εἰδέναι χάριν αἱρετὴ ἐπιστήμη μᾶλλον σοφία ἐστὶ τῆς διὰ τὰ ἀποβαίνοντα αἱρετῆς.
Ἡ τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα καὶ τἀγαθὸν γνωρίζουσα ἐπιστήμη ἀρχικωτέρα τῆς ὑπηρετούσης ἐστίν.
Αἱ κοινὰς περὶ τοῦ σοφοῦ ὑπολήψεις ἐπὶ τὴν αὐτὴν τῶν πρώτων ἀρχῶν καὶ αἰτιῶν ἐπιστήμην συμπίπτουσιν.
Ἡ φιλοσοφία ἐκ τοῦ θαυμάζειν καὶ τῆς ἰδίας ἀγνοίας αἰσθήσεως ἄρχεται, διὸ τοῦ εἰδέναι καὶ οὐ χρήσεώς τινος ἕνεκα ζητεῖται.
Τότε ἕκαστον εἰδέναι λεγόμεθα, ὅταν τὴν πρώτην αὐτοῦ αἰτίαν γνωρίζειν οἰώμεθα.
Τὰ αἴτια τετραχῶς λέγεται, ὡς οὐσία καὶ τί ἦν εἶναι, ὡς ὕλη καὶ ὑποκείμενον, ὡς ὅθεν ἡ κίνησις, καὶ ὡς οὗ ἕνεκα καὶ τἀγαθόν.
Κατὰ τὴν ἐπαγωγὴν τοῦ λόγου οὐδεὶς τῶν προτέρων ἔξω τῶν τεττάρων αἰτίων ἀρχὴν ἔθετο, πάντες δὲ ἀμυδρῶς καὶ μερικῶς αὐτῶν ἥψαντο.
Αἰτία ὀνομαζομένη ἀλλὰ μὴ πρὸς τὴν γένεσιν, τὴν κίνησιν, τὴν οὐσίαν ἢ τὸ τέλος ἱκανῶς καὶ ὁμολογουμένως χρησιμοποιουμένη οὐ πλήρης ἐξήγησίς ἐστιν.
Οὐδεμία αἴσθησις σοφία ἐστίν, ἐπειδὴ τὸ ὅτι δηλοῖ, τὸ δὲ διὰ τί οὐ λέγει.
Ἡ ἐμπειρία οὐκ ἔχει καθ᾽ αὑτὴν τὴν τοῦ καθόλου καὶ τῆς αἰτίας γνῶσιν.
Ἡ περὶ τὰ καθ᾽ ἕκαστα πρακτικὴ ἐπιτυχία οὐκ ἀποτελεῖ μόνη τὸ εἰδέναι ἢ τὴν σοφίαν.
Ἡ ζητουμένη σοφία οὐ ποιητικὴ οὐδὲ πρὸς ἑτέραν χρείαν τεταγμένη ἐστίν.
Τὸ θεῖον οὐκ ἐνδέχεται φθονερὸν εἶναι, ὥστε ἡ θεία ἐπιστήμη οὐκ ἀπαγορευτέα τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐστίν.
Τὸ ὑποκείμενον καὶ ἡ ὕλη οὐ ποιεῖ καθ᾽ αὑτὸ ἑαυτὸ μεταβάλλειν.
Τὸ αὐτόματον καὶ ἡ τύχη οὐχ ἱκανῶς αἰτιῶνται τὴν τάξιν καὶ τὸ καλῶς ἔχειν τῶν ὄντων.
Μία σωματικὴ ὕλη οὐ δύναται τῶν ἀσωμάτων, τῆς κινήσεως καὶ τοῦ τί ἐστιν ἅμα αἰτία εἶναι.
Ἀριθμοὶ καὶ ἐναντιώσεις ἄνευ λόγου κινήσεως οὐ γεννῶσι τὴν τῶν αἰσθητῶν φύσιν.
Ἡ μέθεξις καὶ ἡ μίμησις, ἐὰν μόνα ὀνόματα μένωσιν, οὐ δηλοῦσι πῶς τὰ εἴδη αἴτια τῶν αἰσθητῶν ἐστίν.
Τὰ χωριστὰ εἴδη οὔτε κινήσεως οὔτε γενέσεως οὔτε τοῦ εἶναι τῶν μετεχόντων ἱκανῶς αἴτια δείκνυται.
Τὰ στοιχεῖα πάντων τῶν ὄντων ἀδιακρίτως ζητεῖν οὐ δυνατόν ἐστιν, ἐπειδὴ τὸ ὂν πολλαχῶς λέγεται.
Ἡ ἀπὸ τῆς αἰσθήσεως εἰς τὴν τέχνην μετάβασις γίνεται διὰ διατηρήσεως, πολλαπλασιασμοῦ καὶ καθολικῆς συνάψεως τῶν καθ᾽ ἕκαστα γνωσμάτων.
Ἡ πρακτικὴ ἐπιτυχία καὶ ἡ αἰτιώδης ἐπιστήμη δύνανται χωρίζεσθαι, ἐπειδὴ ἡ μὲν τῶν καθ᾽ ἕκαστα ἅπτεται, ἡ δὲ τὸ διότι γνωρίζει.
Ἡ διδασκαλία τὴν καθόλου αἰτίαν ἀπαιτεῖ, διότι τὸ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον ὡς τοιοῦτον οὔτε κοινὸν λόγον οὔτε μεταδοτὴν ἐπιστήμην παρέχει.
Ἡ ζητουμένη σοφία ἐστὶν ἡ τῶν πρώτων καὶ καθόλου αἰτίων ἀκριβεστάτη, διδασκαλικωτάτη καὶ ἀρχικωτάτη θεωρία.
Ἡ σοφία ἐλευθέρα καλεῖται, ἐπειδὴ αὑτῆς ἕνεκα ὑπάρχει καὶ οὐχ ὡς ὄργανον ἑτέρας χρείας.
Ἡ πρώτη φιλοσοφία δεῖ πᾶν αἴτιον ἐξετάζειν κατὰ τὸ εἶδος ᾧ τὴν πρώτη τοῦ πράγματος ἐξήγησιν παρέχει.
Ἡ ὑλικὴ ἀρχὴ ἀναγκάζει ζητεῖν ἑτέραν ἀρχὴν κινήσεως, ἐπειδὴ τὸ ὑποκείμενον οὐχ ἱκανῶς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ μεταβολὴν αἰτιᾶται.
Ἡ τῶν προτέρων ἐξέτασις ἅμα βεβαιοῖ τὴν τετραχὴν διαίρεσιν καὶ φανερὰς ποιεῖ τὰς ἀσυνεπείας τῆς ἐλλιποῦς χρήσεως τῶν αἰτίων.
Ἡ γνωστικὴ ἄνοδος οὐχ ἁπλῆ πρόσθεσις γνωσμάτων ἐστίν, ἀλλὰ μετάθεσις ἀπὸ τοῦ ὅτι καὶ τοῦ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον εἰς τὸ διότι καὶ τὸ καθόλου.
Ἡ ἀξία τῆς σοφίας οὐ μετρεῖται τῇ ἀμέσῳ πρακτικῇ δυνάμει, ἀλλὰ τῷ βαθμῷ καθ᾽ ὃν τὰς αἰτίας καὶ τὸ τέλος γνωρίζει.
Ἡ ἐλευθερωτάτη ἐπιστήμη γίνεται ἅμα ἀρχικωτάτη, διότι ἡ μὴ ὑπηρετοῦσα ἑτέρῳ τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα τῶν ἄλλων δύναται γνωρίζειν.
Ἡ ἱστορία τῶν προτέρων φιλοσόφων μετατίθεται εἰς ἐνδογενῆ γένεσιν τῶν αἰτίων, καθ᾽ ἣν τὰ ἀνεξήγητα φαινόμενα ἀναγκάζει τὴν διάνοιαν νέαν ἀρχὴν ζητεῖν.
Ἡ τετραχὴ αἰτιότης ἐντὸς τοῦ λόγου λειτουργεῖ ὡς ὅρος πληρότητος, ἐπειδὴ πᾶσα προτέρα θεωρία ἢ εἰς ταύτην ἀνάγεται ἢ διὰ παραλείψεώς τινος αὐτῆς ἐλέγχεται.
Ἡ χωριστὴ οὐσία, ἐὰν μήτε ἐνυπάρχῃ μήτε κινῇ μήτε τέλος παρέχῃ, τὸ αἰτιώδης εἶναι μόνον ὀνόματι διασῴζει.
Ἡ φυσικὴ ὄρεξις τοῦ εἰδέναι οὐκ ἀνάγεται ὅλη εἰς τὴν τῶν χρησίμων ζήτησιν.
Ἡ σώρευσις τῶν ὅτι οὐ μεταβάλλεται αὐτομάτως εἰς ἐπιστήμην, ἐὰν μὴ μία καθόλου αἰτία συναγάγῃ αὐτά.
Τὸ καθόλου οὐ καθ᾽ αὑτὸ σοφία ἐστίν, ἐὰν μὴ τὴν αἰτίαν τῶν καθ᾽ ἕκαστα δηλοῖ.
Ἀρχὴ λεγομένη ἀλλὰ σπανίως ἢ ἀντιφατικῶς χρησιμοποιουμένη οὐκ ἔχει πλήρη αἰτιώδη δύναμιν.
Ἡ παράθεσις πλειόνων οὐσιῶν οὐ λύει τὸ ζήτημα τῆς αἰτίας, ἐὰν ἡ πρὸς τὰ φαινόμενα σχέσις αὐτῶν μένῃ ἄδηλος.
Τὸ αἰσθητὸν οὐκ ἐξαντλεῖ τὸ γένος τοῦ ὄντος, ἐπειδὴ ἡ περὶ τῶν ἀρχῶν ζήτησις καὶ ἀσώματα ὄντα προϋπολαμβάνει.
Ἡ τῶν πάντων ἐπιστήμη οὐ σημαίνει χωριστὴν καθ᾽ ἕκαστον ἐπιστήμην πάντων, ἀλλὰ τὴν διὰ τῶν καθόλου ἀρχῶν γνώσιν.
Ἡ κριτικὴ τῶν προτέρων οὐ δεῖ προσέχειν τοῖς ψελλιζομένοις μόνον, ἀλλὰ τῇ διανοίᾳ ἣν ἀναγκαῖον ἦν ἐκ τῶν λεγομένων ἀκολουθεῖν.
Ἡ ἀρχὴ ὅτι φύσει ὀρεγόμεθα τοῦ εἰδέναι προαποκλείει τὴν παντελῆ ἀδυναμίαν τῆς γνώσεως.
Τὸ σύστημα οὔτε τὴν αἴσθησιν ἄνευ καθόλου λόγου οὔτε τὸ χωριστὸν καθόλου ἄνευ σχέσεως πρὸς τὰ αἰσθητὰ δέχεται ὡς αὐτάρκη ἐπιστήμην.
Ἡ ἐξήγησις τῆς τάξεως ἀπαγορεύεται νὰ καταλήγῃ εἰς ψιλὴν τύχην, ἀλλ᾽ οὐ διὰ τοῦτο ἡ ἀταξία καὶ τὸ κακὸν ἐκβάλλεται ἐκ τῆς φύσεως.
Οὐδεμία ὑπηρετικὴ ἐπιστήμη δύναται τὴν ἀνωτάτην σοφίαν ἐπιτάττειν, ἐπειδὴ ἐκείνη τὸ τέλος καὶ τἀγαθὸν γνωρίζει.
Τὸ σύστημα προαποκλείει πέμπτον γένος αἰτίας, οὐ δι᾽ ἰδίαν ἀπόδειξιν ἀδυνατότητος, ἀλλὰ διὰ τῆς ἀναγωγῆς πασῶν τῶν προτέρων θεωριῶν εἰς τὰ τέτταρα γένη.
Ἡ ζητουμένη σοφία οὐ παραδίδοται ἤδη ὡς τετελεσμένη θεωρία, ἀλλὰ μόνον τὸ γένος, ὁ σκοπὸς καὶ αἱ ἀπορίαι αὐτῆς προορίζονται.
Ἡ δι᾽ αὑτὰς αἵρεσις τῶν αἰσθήσεων τεκμηριοῖ τὴν φυσικὴν ὄρεξιν τοῦ εἰδέναι.
Ἡ αἴσθησις διὰ μνήμης πολλαπλασιαζομένη μίαν ἐμπειρίαν περὶ τῶν καθ᾽ ἕκαστα γεννᾷ.
Ἡ ἐμπειρία διὰ συναγωγῆς τῶν ὁμοίων μίαν καθόλου ὑπόληψιν καὶ τέχνην γεννᾷ.
Ἡ σύγκρισις τοῦ ὅτι πρὸς τὸ διότι μεταθέτει τὸ κριτήριον τοῦ εἰδέναι ἀπὸ τῆς ἐπιτυχίας εἰς τὴν αἰτίαν καὶ τὴν διδασκαλίαν.
Αἱ κοινὰς ὑπολήψεις περὶ τοῦ σοφοῦ συνάγονται εἰς μίαν ἐπιστήμην τῶν πρώτων καὶ καθόλου αἰτίων.
Ἡ γένεσις τῆς φιλοσοφίας ἐκ θαύματος ἀποδεικνύει ὅτι ἡ ζητουμένη ἐπιστήμη θεωρητικὴ καὶ αὑτῆς ἕνεκεν ἐστίν.
Ἡ πρώτη αἰτιώδης γνώσις διαιρεῖται εἰς οὐσίαν, ὕλην, ἀρχὴν κινήσεως καὶ τέλος.
Αἱ προγενέστεραι θεωρίαι εἰς ταῦτα τὰ γένη ἀναγόμεναι ἢ ἁρμόττουσι μερικῶς ἢ διὰ παραλείψεων καὶ ἀντιφάσεων νέας ἀπορίας γεννῶσιν.
Ἡ φυσικὴ ὄρεξις τοῦ εἰδέναι διὰ τῆς αἰσθήσεως εἰς μνήμην καὶ ἐμπειρίαν προβαίνει.
Ἡ ἐμπειρία διὰ καθολικῆς συναγωγῆς τέχνην καὶ αἰτιώδη λόγον γεννᾷ.
Ἡ διάκρισις τοῦ ὅτι καὶ τοῦ διότι τὴν σοφίαν ὑπὲρ τὴν ψιλὴν πρακτικὴν ἐπιτυχίαν τάττει.
Αἱ περὶ τοῦ σοφοῦ ὑπολήψεις τὸ ζήτημα εἰς τὴν θεωρίαν τῶν πρώτων ἀρχῶν καὶ αἰτιῶν μετατιθέασιν.
Ἡ τετραχὴ διαίρεσις τῶν αἰτίων τὰς προτέρας φιλοσοφίας εἰς ὕλην, κίνησιν, οὐσίαν καὶ τέλος κατατάσσει.
Ἡ ἀσυνεπὴς ἢ ἐλλιπὴς χρῆσις τῶν αἰτίων τὴν ἱστορικὴν κατάταξιν εἰς προπαρασκευὴν τῶν ὑστέρων ἀποριῶν μεταβάλλει.
Ἡ χώρα τῆς γνώσεως διαιρεῖται οὐ κατὰ πλῆθος γνωσμάτων μόνον, ἀλλὰ κατὰ βαθμοὺς αἰτιώδους καθολικότητος.
Ἡ πρακτικὴ δύναμις καὶ ἡ σοφία παύονται ταὐτὸν εἶναι, ἐπειδὴ ἡ μὲν τὸ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον, ἡ δὲ τὸ διότι δύναται ἔχειν.
Αἱ ἐπιστῆμαι κατατάσσονται ἐκ νέου κατὰ τὸ εἶναι ὑπηρετικαί, ποιητικαί, θεωρητικαὶ ἢ ἀρχικαί.
Ἡ τῶν φιλοσόφων διαδοχὴ παύει ψιλὴ χρονολογικὴ παράθεσις εἶναι καὶ γίνεται χάρτης τῶν μερικῶς ἀνευρισκομένων αἰτίων.
Τὸ ὂν καθίσταται θεωρητὸν διὰ τεσσάρων ἀλλήλοις μὴ ἀντικαθισταμένων ἐρωτήσεων, τί ἐστιν, ἐξ οὗ ἐστιν, ὑφ᾽ οὗ κινεῖται καὶ οὗ ἕνεκα ἐστίν.
Τὰ χωριστὰ εἴδη μετατίθενται ἀπὸ φερομένης καθολικῆς λύσεως εἰς μερικὴν θεωρίαν τοῦ τί ἐστιν, ἧς ἡ πρὸς τὰ αἰσθητὰ αἰτιότης μένει ἀνεξήγητος.
Τὸ θαυμάζειν μετατίθεται ἀπὸ μόνιμον πάθος εἰς ἀφετηρίαν, ἧς τέλος ἐστὶν ἡ διὰ τῆς αἰτίας ἀναίρεσις τοῦ θαύματος.
Κατὰ τὸν ἐπιφανειακὸν βαθμὸν ἐξετάζονται αἱ γνωστικαὶ δυνάμεις, αἱ κοινὰς ὑπολήψεις περὶ σοφίας καὶ αἱ δόξαι τῶν προτέρων φιλοσόφων.
Κατὰ τὸν τῆς διατάξεως βαθμὸν ἐνεργοῦσιν ἡ ἀπὸ αἰσθήσεως εἰς αἰτίαν τάξις καὶ ἡ τετραχὴ διαίρεσις τῆς αἰτιότητος.
Κατὰ τὸν ὑπερστρατηγικὸν βαθμὸν ἡ ἱστορία τῶν δοξῶν γίνεται ὄργανον βεβαιώσεως τοῦ αἰτιώδους σχήματος καὶ παραγωγῆς ἀποριῶν.
Κατὰ τὸν περὶ ὄντος καὶ χρόνου βαθμὸν τὸ γιγνόμενον νοεῖται διὰ προτέρων τῇ φύσει αἰτίων, ἡ δὲ ἱστορικῶς ὑστέρα θεωρία ἐπανέρχεται ἐπὶ τὰ ὀντολογικῶς πρῶτα.
Τὰ ἐξῃρημένα ἀξιώματα ἱκανὰ ἐστὶ πρὸς ἀνασύστασιν τῆς ἀνόδου ἀπὸ τῆς αἰσθήσεως εἰς τὴν τῶν πρώτων αἰτίων σοφίαν.
Ἰσχυροτάτη ἡ διάταξις ἐστὶν ὅπου ἡ διάκρισις τοῦ ὅτι καὶ τοῦ διότι συνδέεται πρὸς τὴν αἰτίαν, τὴν διδασκαλίαν καὶ τὴν καθολικότητα.
Ἡ φαινομένη ἀντίφασις, καθ᾽ ἣν ὁ ἔμπειρος πράττει βέλτιον ὁ δὲ τεχνίτης σοφώτερός ἐστι, λύεται διὰ τῆς διακρίσεως πρακτικῆς ἐπιτυχίας καὶ αἰτιώδους γνώσεως.
Ἀδιοριστότερον μένει πῶς ἡ καθόλου ἐπιστήμη οἶδέ πως πάντα ἄνευ τῆς καθ᾽ ἕκαστον γνώσεως καὶ πῶς αὕτη συμβιβάζεται πρὸς τὴν ἀνάγκην προγιγνωσκομένων.
Ἡ πληρότης τῆς τετραχῆς διαιρέσεως στηρίζεται ἐπὶ προτέρᾳ φυσικῇ θεωρίᾳ καὶ ἐπὶ τῇ ἐπαγωγῇ ὅτι οὐδεὶς τῶν προτέρων ἄλλης αἰτίας ἥψατο.
Ἡ ἐλευθερία καὶ θειότης τῆς σοφίας στηρίζεται ἐπὶ τῇ ἀναλογίᾳ τοῦ ἐλευθέρου ἀνθρώπου καὶ ἐπὶ ταῖς κοινὰς περὶ τοῦ σοφοῦ ὑπολήψεσιν.
Ἡ τελικὴ αἰτία ἀναγκαίως μὲν εἰσάγεται διὰ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ καὶ τῆς τάξεως, ἀμυδρότερον δὲ ἢ ἡ ὕλη καὶ ἡ κίνησις ἐκ τῆς τῶν προτέρων ἐξετάσεως βεβαιοῦται.
Ὁ τῶν εἰδῶν ἔλεγχος δείκνυσιν ὅτι ἡ χωριστὴ οὐσία οὐχ ἱκανῶς αἰτιᾶται τὰ αἰσθητά, οὐ μέντοι ἐνταῦθα πλήρως ἀποδίδωσι πῶς ἡ οὐσία ἐνυπάρχει τοῖς πράγμασιν.
Αἱ περὶ τῶν παλαιοτάτων, τῶν ποιητῶν καὶ τῆς προτεραιότητος ἑκάστου ἀποδόσεις διατηροῦνται ὡς εἰκότα ἢ λεγόμενα καὶ οὐχ ὡς ἀναγκαῖαι βεβαιώσεις.

Ἡ ἀνασύστασις σῴζει τὴν ἀληθῆ κίνησιν τοῦ λόγου, ὅτι ἀπὸ τῆς τοῦ εἰδέναι ὀρέξεως εἰς τὸν διορισμὸν τῆς σοφίας, ἐκεῖθεν δὲ εἰς τὴν τετραχὴν αἰτιότητα, τὸν ἔλεγχον τῶν προτέρων καὶ τὰς ὑστέρους ἀπορίας προβαίνει.
The question is which study of causes and principles is wisdom and what aim the method concerning it pursues.
Wisdom is posited as a theoretical science of first principles and causes, choiceworthy for its own sake and governing over the other sciences.
The position arises through the ascent from perception to memory, experience, universal conception, and causal science.
The argument proceeds diagnostically from the opinions concerning the wise person, and genealogically through examination of earlier philosophers.
The fourfold division of causes becomes a rule for arranging, comparing, and testing the earlier theories.
The movement concludes from the natural desire to know, through the definition of wisdom, in the classification of causes and thence in the remaining aporiai.
All human beings by nature desire to know.
Memory together with perception makes learning and practical wisdom more powerful.
Many memories of the same thing constitute the capacity of a single experience.
Art arises when, from many experiential conceptions, one universal conception concerning similar things comes to be.
Actions and generations concern particulars; hence experience often succeeds more in practice than discourse without experience.
Knowledge of the why and of the cause makes one know more than knowledge of the that alone.
The ability to teach is a sign of knowledge according to causes.
One who has universal science to the greatest degree knows somehow all the things subordinate to it, although not knowing each individually.
The sciences of first and fewer principles are more exact and more teachable than those produced by addition.
The science choiceworthy for its own sake and for the sake of knowing is more wisdom than that choiceworthy for its outcomes.
The science that knows the final cause and the good is more governing than the serving science.
Common opinions concerning the wise person converge upon the same science of first principles and causes.
Philosophy begins from wonder and awareness of one's own ignorance; hence it is sought for the sake of knowing and not for the sake of any use.
Then we say that we know each thing when we suppose that we know its first cause.
Causes are spoken of in four ways: as substance and what-it-was-to-be, as matter and substrate, as that from which motion comes, and as that for the sake of which and the good.
According to the induction of the argument, none of the earlier thinkers posited a principle outside the four causes, but all touched upon them dimly and partially.
What is called a cause but is not adequately and consistently employed in relation to generation, motion, substance, or end is not a complete explanation.
No perception is wisdom, because it indicates the that but does not state the why.
Experience does not possess by itself knowledge of the universal and of the cause.
Practical success concerning particulars does not by itself constitute knowing or wisdom.
The wisdom sought is neither productive nor ordered toward another use.
The divine cannot be envious, so that divine science is not to be forbidden to a human being.
The substrate and matter do not by themselves make themselves change.
The spontaneous and chance do not adequately account for the order and good condition of beings.
One bodily matter cannot simultaneously be the cause of incorporeal things, motion, and what something is.
Numbers and oppositions without an account of motion do not generate the nature of sensibles.
Participation and imitation, if they remain mere names, do not show how forms are causes of sensibles.
Separate forms are shown to be adequate causes neither of motion nor of generation nor of the being of participants.
It is not possible to seek the elements of all beings indiscriminately, because being is spoken of in many ways.
The transition from perception to art occurs through the preservation, multiplication, and universal connection of particular cognitions.
Practical success and causal science can be separated, because the former concerns particulars whereas the latter knows the why.
Teaching requires the universal cause, because the particular as such supplies neither a common account nor communicable science.
The wisdom sought is the most exact, most teachable, and most governing theory of first and universal causes.
Wisdom is called free because it exists for its own sake and not as an instrument of another need.
First philosophy must examine every cause according to the form in which it provides the first explanation of the thing.
The material principle compels the seeking of another principle of motion, because the substrate does not adequately account for its own change.
Examination of the earlier thinkers at once confirms the fourfold division and makes manifest the inconsistencies of deficient use of causes.
The cognitive ascent is not a simple addition of cognitions, but a transition from the that and the particular to the why and the universal.
The worth of wisdom is not measured by immediate practical power, but by the degree to which it knows causes and the end.
The freest science becomes at the same time the most governing, because what does not serve another can know the final cause of the others.
The history of earlier philosophers is transformed into an endogenous generation of causes, in which unexplained phenomena compel the intellect to seek a new principle.
Fourfold causality functions within the account as a condition of completeness, because every earlier theory is either reduced to it or tested through some omission of it.
Separate substance, if it neither inheres nor moves nor supplies an end, preserves being causal in name alone.
The natural desire to know is not wholly reducible to the pursuit of useful things.
The accumulation of thats does not automatically turn into science unless one universal cause gathers them together.
The universal is not by itself wisdom unless it discloses the cause of particulars.
What is called a principle but used rarely or contradictorily does not possess complete causal power.
The positing of several substances does not solve the question of cause if their relation to phenomena remains unclear.
The sensible does not exhaust the genus of being, because inquiry concerning principles presupposes incorporeal beings as well.
Knowledge of all things does not signify separate particular knowledge of all things, but knowledge through universal principles.
Criticism of earlier thinkers should not attend only to what is stammered out, but to the thought that it was necessary to follow from what was said.
The principle that we naturally desire to know precludes in advance the complete impossibility of knowledge.
The system accepts neither perception without a universal account nor the separate universal without relation to sensibles as self-sufficient science.
The explanation of order is forbidden to end in bare chance, yet disorder and evil are not thereby expelled from nature.
No serving science can command the highest wisdom, because that wisdom knows the end and the good.
The system precludes in advance a fifth kind of cause, not through a separate proof of impossibility, but through the reduction of all earlier theories to the four kinds.
The wisdom sought is not yet delivered as a completed theory, but only its genus, aim, and aporiai are set forth in advance.
The choice of perceptions for their own sake furnishes evidence for the natural desire to know.
Perception multiplied through memory generates one experience concerning particulars.
Experience, through collection of similar things, generates one universal conception and art.
Comparison of the that with the why shifts the criterion of knowing from success to cause and teaching.
Common opinions concerning the wise person are gathered into one science of first and universal causes.
The genesis of philosophy from wonder proves that the science sought is theoretical and for its own sake.
First causal knowledge is divided into substance, matter, principle of motion, and end.
Earlier theories, reduced to these kinds, either fit partially or generate new aporiai through omissions and contradictions.
The natural desire to know proceeds through perception to memory and experience.
Experience through universal collection generates art and causal account.
The distinction between the that and the why places wisdom above bare practical success.
Opinions concerning the wise person transfer the inquiry to the theory of first principles and causes.
The fourfold division of causes classifies earlier philosophies under matter, motion, substance, and end.
Inconsistent or deficient use of causes transforms historical classification into preparation for later aporiai.
The domain of knowledge is divided not according to the quantity of cognitions alone, but according to degrees of causal universality.
Practical capacity and wisdom cease to be the same, because the former can possess the particular while the latter can possess the why.
The sciences are classified anew according to whether they are serving, productive, theoretical, or governing.
The succession of philosophers ceases to be a bare chronological juxtaposition and becomes a map of partially discovered causes.
Being becomes an object of theory through four non-interchangeable questions: what it is, from what it is, by what it is moved, and for the sake of what it is.
Separate forms are shifted from an alleged universal solution to a partial theory of what something is, whose causality with respect to sensibles remains unexplained.
Wonder is shifted from a permanent affection to a starting-point, whose end is the removal of wonder through the cause.
At the surface level, cognitive capacities, common opinions concerning wisdom, and the beliefs of earlier philosophers are examined.
At the level of arrangement, the order from perception to cause and the fourfold division of causality operate.
At the hyper-strategic level, the history of opinions becomes an instrument for confirming the causal schema and producing aporiai.
At the level concerning being and time, what comes to be is understood through causes prior by nature, while the historically later theory returns to what is ontologically first.
The extracted axioms are sufficient for reconstructing the ascent from perception to the wisdom of first causes.
The arrangement is strongest where the distinction between the that and the why is connected with cause, teaching, and universality.
The apparent contradiction whereby the experienced person acts better but the artisan is wiser is resolved through the distinction between practical success and causal knowledge.
It remains more indeterminate how universal science somehow knows all things without particular knowledge and how this is reconciled with the necessity of what is known beforehand.
The completeness of the fourfold division rests upon prior natural theory and upon the induction that none of the earlier thinkers touched upon another cause.
The freedom and divinity of wisdom rest upon the analogy of the free human being and upon common opinions concerning the wise person.
The final cause is necessarily introduced through the good and order, but is confirmed more dimly from examination of earlier thinkers than matter and motion are.
The critique of forms shows that separate substance does not adequately account for sensibles, but it does not here fully explain how substance inheres in things.
Attributions concerning the most ancient thinkers, poets, and the priority of each are retained as plausible or reported claims and not as necessary confirmations.

The reconstruction preserves the true movement of the argument: it proceeds from the desire to know to the definition of wisdom, thence to fourfold causality, the examination of earlier thinkers, and the later aporiai.
Ἡ περὶ ἀληθείας ζήτησις χαλεπὴ φαίνεται, ὅτι τὸ ὅλον οὐχ ὑπὸ ἑνὸς καταλαμβάνεται, ῥᾳδία δέ, ὅτι οὐδεὶς παντελῶς ἀποτυγχάνει τῆς φύσεως.
Ἡ μερικὴ τῶν πολλῶν συμβολὴ ἀθροιζομένη μέγεθός τι ἀληθείας ποιεῖ, ἀλλὰ ἡ ὅλη αἰτιακὴ τάξις ζητεῖται.
Τὸ ἀληθὲς οὐκ ἄνευ αἰτίας γιγνώσκεται, καὶ τὸ μάλιστα ὂν καὶ αἴτιον τῶν ἄλλων μάλιστα ἀληθές ἐστιν.
Ἡ ἀπείρως προϊοῦσα αἰτιότης ἀναιρεῖ καὶ πρῶτον αἴτιον καὶ τέλος καὶ ὁρισμὸν καὶ γνῶσιν.
Δεῖ οὖν πεπερασμένας εἶναι τὰς ἀρχὰς κατὰ ὕλην, κίνησιν, οὗ ἕνεκα καὶ τί ἦν εἶναι.
Ἡ ζήτησις περὶ τῶν ἀρχῶν μεταπίπτει εἰς ζήτησιν τοῦ προσήκοντος τρόπου ἀκροάσεως, ἐπειδὴ τὸ ἔθος τὸν τρόπον τῆς παραδοχῆς προδιατάσσει.
Ἡ ἀκριβολογία οὐ καθόλου ἐφαρμοστέα, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὴν ὕλην καὶ τὴν φύσιν τοῦ ὑποκειμένου μετρητέα.
Ἕκαστος τῶν ζητούντων λέγει τι περὶ τῆς φύσεως, κἂν μικρὸν ᾖ τὸ συμβαλλόμενον.
Ἡ καθόλου ἀλήθεια οὐκ ἐκ μιᾶς ἰδίας ἐπιβολῆς, ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ συναθροίσεως μερικῶν ἐπιβολῶν προσεγγίζεται.
Ἡ δυσχέρεια τῆς ἀληθείας οὐκ ἐν τοῖς πράγμασιν μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν τῇ πρὸς τὰ φανερώτατα ἀσθενείᾳ τοῦ νοῦ κεῖται.
Ἡ θεωρητικὴ ἐπιστήμη τὴν ἀλήθειαν τέλος ἔχει, ἡ δὲ πρακτικὴ τὸ ἔργον.
Τὸ ἀληθὲς οὐ γιγνώσκεται ἄνευ τοῦ αἰτίου.
Τὸ αἴτιον τοῖς ἄλλοις ὑπάρχειν ποιεῖ ὃ αὐτὸ μάλιστα κατέχει.
Αἱ τῶν ἀεὶ ὄντων ἀρχαὶ ἀεὶ καὶ μάλιστα ἀληθεῖς εἰσιν, ἐπειδὴ αὐταὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις τοῦ εἶναι αἴτιαι εἰσίν.
Εἰ μηδὲν πρῶτον ἐστίν, οὐδὲν αἴτιον ἐστίν.
Τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα τέλος ἐστίν, καὶ τὸ τέλος οὐκ ἄλλου ἕνεκα ὑπάρχει.
Ἄνευ πεπερασμένου ὁρισμοῦ οὔτε ἐπίστασθαι οὔτε νοεῖν δυνατὸν ἐστίν.
Τὰ αἴτια, ἐὰν ἀπείρως πλήθει προΐῃ, οὐκ ἐν πεπερασμένῳ χρόνῳ γνωσθῆναι δύναται.
Ὁ προσήκων τρόπος ἀποδείξεως ἐκ τῆς τοῦ ὑποκειμένου φύσεως λαμβάνεται, οὐκ ἐκ τῆς συνήθειας τοῦ ἀκροατοῦ μόνον.
Ἡ ἀλήθεια οὐκ ἀνέφικτος ἐστίν, ἐπειδὴ πάντες ἄνθρωποι παντελῶς ἀποτυγχάνουσιν αὐτῆς.
Ἡ ἀλήθεια οὐκ ἰδίᾳ καὶ τελείᾳ κτῆσις ἑνὸς ζητητοῦ ἐστίν.
Ἡ ἀλήθεια οὐκ ἀναιτίως ἔχει, οὐδὲ ἡ γνῶσις ἀνεξέταστον παράθεσιν δοξῶν ἐστίν.
Ἡ ὑλικὴ, κινητικὴ, τελικὴ καὶ ὁριστικὴ αἰτιότης οὐκ εἰς ἄπειρον ἐκτείνεται.
Τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα οὐκ ἀναιρεῖται ἄνευ τοῦ συναφανίζειν τὴν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ φύσιν.
Ὁ ὁρισμὸς οὐκ ἀναλύεται εἰς ἀεὶ πλεονάζοντα ὁρισμὸν ἄνευ πρώτου λόγου.
Ἡ μαθηματικὴ ἀκρίβεια οὐκ ἀπαιτητέα ἐν παντὶ γένει λόγου.
Τὸ σύνηθες οὐκ αὐτόθεν κριτήριον τοῦ ἀληθοῦς οὐδὲ τοῦ προσήκοντος τρόπου ἐστίν.
Ἡ προγενεστέρα δόξα, κἂν ἐπιπολαία ᾖ, ὄργανον γίνεται τῆς ἑξῆς ζητήσεως, ἐπειδὴ τὴν ἕξιν τοῦ ζητεῖν προασκεῖ.
Ἡ φιλοσοφία δικαίως ἐπιστήμη τῆς ἀληθείας καλεῖται, ἐπειδὴ θεωρητικῶς πρὸς τὸ ἀληθὲς τελευτᾷ.
Τὰ ἀεὶ ὄντα μᾶλλον ἀληθῆ λέγεται, καθόσον μᾶλλον τοῦ εἶναι αἴτια τοῖς ὑστεροῖς ἐστίν.
Ἡ ἀναίρεσις τοῦ πρώτου αἰτίου ἀναιρεῖ τὴν αἰτιακὴν ἐξήγησιν καθόλου, ἐπειδὴ πάντα τὰ ἐν ἀπείρῳ μέσοις ἔσται.
Ἡ ἀπειρία τῶν τελικῶν αἰτίων καθιστᾷ πᾶσαν πρᾶξιν ἄνευ πέρατος καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἀνόητον.
Ἡ ἀπειρία τῶν ὁρισμῶν ἀναιρεῖ τὴν εἴδησιν, ἐπειδὴ ἡ διάνοια οὐκ ἥκει εἰς ἄτομα νοητά.
Ἡ φυσικὴ ζήτησις οὐ μαθηματικῇ ἀκριβείας ὑποτάσσεται, ἐπειδὴ ἡ φύσις ὕλην ἔχει.
Ἡ ἀλήθεια τάξις αἰτιακὴ γίνεται, ἐν ᾗ ὁ βαθμὸς τοῦ εἶναι καὶ ὁ βαθμὸς τοῦ ἀληθεύειν ἀλλήλοις ἀκολουθοῦσιν.
Ἡ μεταφυσικὴ ζήτησις ἀπαιτεῖ πεπερασμένην ἀρχὴν, ἵνα καὶ αἰτία καὶ τέλος καὶ ἐπιστήμη καὶ νοῦς σώζωνται.
Ἡ ὀρθὴ μέθοδος οὐκ ἑνιαία τέχνη τοῦ λέγειν ἐστίν, ἀλλὰ συμμετρία λόγου πρὸς τὸ εἶδος τοῦ πράγματος.
Ἡ παράδοσις τῶν δοξῶν οὐκ αὐτάρκης πηγὴ ἀληθείας, ἀλλὰ γενεαλογικὸς ὅρος δι᾽ οὗ ἡ νῦν ζήτησις δυνατὴ γίνεται.
Οὐδεμία ἀλήθεια καθόλου νοητὴ μένει, εἰ τὸ αἴτιον οὐκ ἔχει πρὸς τὸ αἰτιατὸν τάξιν προτέρου καὶ ὑστέρου.
Οὐδεμία πράξις ἔμφρων μένει, εἰ τὸ πρακτὸν οὐκ ἔχει πέρας πρὸς ὃ κινείται.
Οὐδεμία ἐπιστήμη μένει, εἰ ἡ ἀνάλυσις τῶν αἰτίων καὶ ὁρισμῶν οὐδέποτε παύεται.
Οὐδεμία μέθοδος ὀρθὴ μένει, εἰ ὁ τρόπος τοῦ λέγειν κρίνεται μόνῃ τῇ ἡδονῇ ἢ συνήθειᾳ τοῦ ἀκούοντος.
Ἀποκλείεται κόσμος ἐν ᾧ τὰ ὄντα μόνον ἀλλήλων συνέπειαι εἰσίν, μηδεμιᾶς ἀρχῆς τὴν τάξιν θεμελιούσης.
Ἀποκλείεται νοῦς ὃς ἐνεργεῖ ἄνευ τέλους, ἐπειδὴ τὸ νοεῖν καὶ πράττειν διὰ τι ἀεὶ κινείται.
Ἀποκλείεται γνῶσις ἡ μὴ διακρίνουσα τὸ πεπερασμένον ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀπείρου καὶ τὸ προσήκον μέτρον ἀκριβείας ἀπὸ τῆς ἀμετρίας.
Μερικαὶ δόξαι περὶ φύσεως συναθροιζόμεναι → μερικὴ πρόσβασις πρὸς ἀλήθειαν → ἀνάγκη ζητήσεως τοῦ ὅλου.
Ζήτησις τοῦ ὅλου → ζήτησις αἰτίας → ἀνάβασις πρὸς τὸ μάλιστα αἴτιον καὶ μάλιστα ἀληθές.
Ἀναίρεσις ἀπείρου προόδου → θέσις πρώτης ἀρχῆς → σωτηρία αἰτιότητος, τέλους, ὁρισμοῦ καὶ γνώσεως.
Διάκρισις τῶν γενῶν τοῦ ὄντος → διάκρισις τῶν προσήκοντων τρόπων λόγου → περιορισμὸς τῆς μαθηματικῆς ἀκριβείας.
Ἔθος τῶν ἀκροατῶν → πλάνη περὶ τοῦ δέοντος τρόπου → παιδεία πρὸς κρίσιν τοῦ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον μέτρου.
Μερικὴ ἐπιτυχία τῶν πολλῶν → δυσχέρεια τοῦ ὅλου → ζήτησις τῆς αἰτίας.
Αἰτία τοῦ ἀληθεύειν → βαθμὸς τοῦ εἶναι → πρωτεῖον τῶν ἀϊδίων ἀρχῶν.
Ἀπειρία αἰτίων → ἀναίρεσις πρώτου καὶ τέλους → ἀναίρεσις γνώσεως καὶ πράξεως.
Ἀδυναμία ἀπείρου → περατότης τῶν ἀρχῶν → δυνατότης ἐπιστήμης.
Ἔθος ἀκροάσεως → ποικιλία ψευδῶν ἀπαιτήσεων → μέτρησις τῆς ἀκριβείας κατὰ τὸ ὑποκείμενον.
Ἡ ἀλήθεια ἐκ μεμονωμένου κτήματος μετατίθεται εἰς κοινὴν καὶ διαχρονικὴν συναγωγὴν μερικῶν θεωριῶν.
Ἡ ἀλήθεια οὐκέτι ψιλὴ συμφωνία λόγου γίνεται, ἀλλὰ ἰδιότης ἐξαρτωμένη ἀπὸ τοῦ βαθμοῦ τῆς αἰτιακῆς ἀρχῆς.
Τὸ ἄπειρον μετατίθεται ἐκ ἀορίστου μεγέθους εἰς ἀπειλὴν κατὰ τῆς αἰτιότητος, τῆς τελεολογίας καὶ τῆς γνωσιμότητος.
Ἡ διάκρισις θεωρητικοῦ καὶ πρακτικοῦ μεταβάλλει τὸ τέλος τῆς ζητήσεως, ἀληθείας μὲν τῷ θεωρητικῷ, ἔργου δὲ τῷ πρακτικῷ.
Ἡ ἀκρίβεια μετατίθεται ἐκ καθολικῆς ἀξιώσεως εἰς σχετικὸν μέτρον πρὸς τὴν ὕλην τοῦ ζητουμένου.
Ἐπιφανειακῶς ὁ λόγος περὶ ἀληθείας, αἰτίων, ἀπείρου καὶ τρόπων ἀκροάσεως διαλέγεται.
Κατὰ διάταξιν ὁ λόγος τὴν ἐπιστήμην ἐπὶ τάξει προτέρου καὶ ὑστέρου, ἀρχῆς καὶ ἐπακολουθήματος θεμελιοῖ.
Ὑπερστρατηγικῶς ὁ λόγος τὴν διαφωνίαν τῶν δοξῶν οὐκ ὡς κώλυμα, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς ὕλην καὶ προπαίδευσιν τῆς ζητήσεως τίθησιν.
Περὶ ὄντος ὁ λόγος τὸ εἶναι, τὸ ἀληθεύειν καὶ τὸ αἰτιᾶσθαι κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν βαθμὸν συντάττει.
Περὶ χρόνου ὁ λόγος τὸ ἀΐδιον οὐχ ὡς μακρὸν χρόνον μόνον, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς ἀναίτιον καὶ αἴτιον τῶν ἄλλων νοεῖ.
Τὰ ἀξιώματα ἀρκεῖ πρὸς ἀνασύστασιν τοῦ πυρήνος, ἐπειδὴ ἐξ αὐτῶν ἡ μετάβασις ἀπὸ τῆς ἀληθείας εἰς τὰς πεπερασμένας ἀρχὰς ἀκολουθεῖ.
Ἡ ἰσχυροτάτη σύναψις τοῦ συστήματος κεῖται ἐν τῷ δεσμῷ αἰτίας, ἀληθείας, εἶναι καὶ γνώσεως.
Ἡ ἀναίρεσις τοῦ ἀπείρου ἐνεργεῖ ὡς ἀναγκαῖος ὅρος τοῦ συστήματος, ἀλλὰ ἡ ἀπόδειξις προϋποτίθεται τὴν ἀξίαν τοῦ πρώτου μᾶλλον ἢ ἐκ παντὸς ἀναγκαστικῶς ἐκφέρει αὐτήν.
Ἡ σχέσις μεταξὺ τῆς συλλογικῆς προόδου τῶν δοξῶν καὶ τῆς ἱεραρχίας τῶν ἀληθεστέρων ἀρχῶν μένει οὐ παντελῶς διηρθρωμένη.
Ἡ ἀνασύστασις σῴζει τὴν κίνησιν τοῦ λόγου, ἐὰν τὸ τελευταῖον μέρος περὶ ἀκροάσεως νοηθῇ ὡς μεθοδικὸς περιορισμὸς τῆς προτέρας αἰτιολογικῆς ζητήσεως.
The inquiry concerning truth appears difficult, because the whole is not grasped by one person, but easy, because no one fails utterly to attain nature.
The partial contribution of the many, when accumulated, produces some magnitude of truth, but the whole causal order is sought.
The true is not known without a cause, and that which is most fully is and is the cause of the others is most true.
Causality proceeding to infinity removes both a first cause and an end and a definition and knowledge.
Therefore the principles must be finite with respect to matter, motion, that for the sake of which, and what-it-was-to-be.
The inquiry concerning principles shifts into an inquiry concerning the appropriate manner of hearing, since habit predisposes the manner of reception.
Exactness is not to be applied universally, but is to be measured according to the matter and the nature of the subject.
Each of those who inquire says something concerning nature, even if what is contributed is small.
Universal truth is approached not from one private apprehension but from the gathering together of partial apprehensions.
The difficulty of truth lies not only in things, but also in the weakness of intellect in relation to the things most evident.
Theoretical science has truth as its end, whereas practical science has the work.
The true is not known without the cause.
The cause makes the others possess that which it itself possesses most fully.
